Episteme is knowledge of universal truths through demonstration: knowledge of why things are as they are, not merely that they are. It is the systematic understanding of causal structures. Cultivate the desire to understand, not merely to know.

(NE VI.3, VI.6; Posterior Analytics I.2.)

**Plain words** Knowing that something is true is one thing. Knowing why is another. Aristotle prizes the second: understanding causes, not just collecting facts. Wanting to understand is a habit, and it changes how you read and what you ask.

*For example:* Memorising that interest compounds is knowing. Working out on paper why a small difference in rate gives such a big gap after thirty years is understanding.
e.c: Layer III - Intellectual Virtues
p: **Need for cognition and intellectual engagement** (Cacioppo and Petty, 1982)
**Openness to experience predicts well-being** (Kaufman et al., 2016)
f: **Wonder as the beginning of philosophy** (Aristotle, Metaphysics I.2)
reflections: What is something you know well enough to repeat but not well enough to explain from the ground up? What would it take to truly understand it?
Does understanding why a thing is so change how you feel about it? Recall a case where knowing the cause altered your response, whether grief, anger or fear.
Understanding the causes of suffering is central to several traditions. Is understanding enough to relieve it, or is something else needed?

e.t: Cultivate art and craft (techne)
e.x:
Techne is the capacity to make things well, guided by reason: the knowledge of how to produce. It is not merely skill but understanding of the principles of production. Make things. Craft something with your hands and your mind. The maker's knowledge is irreplaceable.

(NE VI.4; Metaphysics I.1.)

**Plain words** Making things well takes more than a knack. Aristotle's techne means you understand why the method works. So make something with your hands and your head. What a maker knows can't be borrowed from anyone who hasn't made it.

*For example:* Baking the same loaf ten times and changing one thing each time teaches you more about bread than reading ten recipes.
e.c: Layer III - Intellectual Virtues
p: **Deliberate practice and expertise** (Ericsson et al., 1993)
**Everyday creative activities and well-being** (Conner et al., 2018)
f: **Respect the material: work with its grain** (Dewey, Art as Experience)
reflections: What do you make with your hands, however badly, and what does that making teach you that thinking alone cannot?
Techne combines skill with understanding. When has skill without understanding, or understanding without skill, left you stranded?
Can the craft of caring for others, nursing, teaching or listening, be treated as a techne? What would mastery look like?

e.t: Cultivate theoretical wisdom (sophia)
e.x:
Sophia is the combination of nous (grasp of first principles) and episteme (demonstrative knowledge). It is the highest intellectual virtue: the capacity to understand the most fundamental truths about reality. Make space for deep, sustained reflection on the largest questions.

(NE VI.6-7, VI.12.)

**Plain words** Sophia is the top of Aristotle's intellectual ladder: grasping first principles and the reasoning built on them, about the biggest questions. It needs room. So set aside real time, uninterrupted, for the large questions you normally brush off.

*For example:* A long walk with no podcast, thinking about what the point of your work is, counts. So does an afternoon with one hard book.
e.c: Layer III - Intellectual Virtues
p: **Awe and self-transcendent experiences** (Yaden et al., 2017)
**Openness to experience** (Kaufman et al., 2016)
reflections: Which large question do you keep postponing, and what are you protecting yourself from by not facing it?
Sophia sits at the top of Aristotle's ladder, yet many wise people seem to lack theoretical learning. What does the wisdom of ordinary lives add or correct?
How would you spend one unhurried day if its only aim were to understand something deeply? What gets in the way of giving yourself that?

e.t: Distinguish cleverness (deinotes) from practical wisdom
e.x:
Cleverness is the capacity to find means to any end, good or bad. Practical wisdom is cleverness directed toward the good. Be clever, but ensure your cleverness serves worthy ends. Intelligence without virtue is dangerous.

(NE VI.12, VI.13.)

**Plain words** Cleverness finds a way to get whatever you're after, good or bad. Practical wisdom is cleverness aimed at something worth getting. Aristotle doesn't mind being clever. He minds smart people serving poor goals. Check what yours is for.

*For example:* A brilliant marketer who builds a sleek campaign to sell people things they don't need is clever. Using the same skill to get a useful product noticed is wise.
e.c: Layer III - Intellectual Virtues
p: **Moral disengagement research**, intelligent people can rationalise harmful behaviour (Bandura, 1999)
**Dark triad research**, intelligence in service of Machiavellian ends (Paulhus and Williams, 2002)
reflections: When have you used skill in service of something you later felt uneasy about? What would have made you notice at the time?
Intelligence without virtue is dangerous. Name an example from public life or your own field, and trace how cleverness cut loose from purpose did harm.
How would you teach a very capable young person to ask what their abilities are for, without lecturing them?

e.t: Cultivate practical judgment (gnome)
e.x:
Gnome is the capacity to reach correct judgments in particular cases, especially where general rules do not apply. It is related to synesis but concerns not only understanding what follows from what, but what is fitting and equitable. Practise the art of equitable judgment.

(NE VI.11.)

**Plain words** Gnome is judging a particular case fairly, especially when the rules don't quite fit. It goes past "what follows from what" to "what's decent here?" You build it by weighing real situations, one at a time, and asking what fairness asks.

*For example:* A teacher gives an extension to a student whose parent was in hospital, though the policy says no. She can explain why it's fair to the rest of the class.
e.c: Layer III - Intellectual Virtues
p: **Moral situation research**, context dominates in real moral choice (Doris, Lack of Character)
**Contextual intelligence** (Sternberg, 2019)
f: **The moral situation** (Dewey, Human Nature and Conduct)
reflections: Recall a case where a rule fitted badly and you used your own sense of what was fair. How did you justify it, and was it sound?
Equitable judgement requires trust in the judge. How do you protect against bias disguised as fairness, in yourself or in institutions?
Who has been treated unfairly by a rule applied without gnome? What would a more equitable response have required?

e.t: Value experience over theory in practical matters
e.x:
In matters of practice, experience often outranks theory. The experienced person may not be able to articulate principles but can judge correctly in particular cases. Do not dismiss the practical wisdom of those who lack formal knowledge.

(NE VI.8, VI.11; Metaphysics I.1.)

**Plain words** In practice, the person who's done it often beats the person who's read about it. They may not be able to state the rules, but they get the case right. So don't dismiss people just because they lack the vocabulary or the degree.

*For example:* A veteran bus driver knows which stop gets rowdy on Fridays and how to prevent it. No manual says so.
e.c: Layer III - Intellectual Virtues
p: **Intuitive expertise**, pattern recognition in high-feedback domains (Kahneman and Klein, 2009)
**Tacit knowledge research** (Polanyi, The Tacit Dimension)
reflections: Whose practical know-how have you undervalued because of how they speak or what they studied? What did you miss?
Experience can also calcify into habit and prejudice. How do you tell hard-won wisdom from long-held error?
For people in grief or illness, who teaches best, the expert or the person who has been through it? What does each offer that the other cannot?

e.t: Practise the unity of the virtues
e.x:
The virtues are not isolated dispositions. They form a unified character. Courage without temperance is recklessness; generosity without justice is caprice. Work on the whole person, not on isolated virtues.

(NE VI.12-13, X.9; EE VIII.3.)

**Plain words** Virtues aren't separate gadgets. They're one character. Courage without temperance turns reckless. Generosity without justice turns arbitrary. So don't polish one trait and ignore the rest. Work on the whole person.

*For example:* Someone proud of being brave who ignores fairness will cheerfully charge in to rescue one friend while shortchanging everyone else.
e.c: Layer III - Intellectual Virtues
p: **Virtuous spirals of practice and identity** (Kristjánsson, 2018)
**Integrated self and well-being** (Ryan and Deci, 2001)
reflections: Which of your strongest traits works alone, without the balance of another? Describe a time that imbalance caused harm.
If the virtues are united, can someone be truly courageous but unjust? What would that tell us about whether virtue is one thing or many?
How does a fixation on one virtue, such as self-control, become a kind of vice? Think of a person you know or a public figure.

e.t: Know that virtue aims at the beautiful (to kalon)
e.x:
The virtuous person acts not merely for the useful or the pleasant but for the kalon: the noble, the beautiful, the fine. The aesthetic dimension of ethics is not decoration but substance. Let your actions be done for the sake of what is noble, not merely what is useful.

(NE I.7, II.3, III.7, IV.2.)

**Plain words** The good person acts for what's noble, not just what's useful or pleasant. Aristotle calls that kalon: the fine, the beautiful. Taste and ethics overlap. So ask not only "does it work?" but "is it worth being the kind of person who does this?"

*For example:* Staying to help a stranger carry shopping up the stairs, when it earns you nothing, is the thing done for its own fineness.
e.c: Layer III - Intellectual Virtues
p: **Eudaimonic motivation, intrinsic goals** (Deci and Ryan, 2000)
**Self-transcendent values** (Schwartz, 1992)
reflections: Name an action you took only because it was fine, with no benefit to you. What made it feel that way?
Does the beautiful in ethics risk valuing appearance over substance? How could you check that your sense of the noble is not just taste or status?
Think of an act of care that was also beautiful in form, such as a funeral, a meal for a grieving family or a quiet visit. What made it so?

e.t: Recognise that virtue is a hexis, not a feeling
e.x:
Virtue is a settled disposition (hexis), not a temporary state (pathos). You are not generous because you feel generous once; you are generous because generosity has become part of who you are. Invest in building dispositions, not in chasing feelings.

(NE II.5, II.6.)

**Plain words** Virtue is a settled disposition, not a mood. Being generous once, on a good day, doesn't make you generous. Being generous even when it's inconvenient does. So build dispositions through repetition, instead of chasing the feeling.

*For example:* Tipping well only when you're in a good mood isn't generosity. Doing it as a standing habit is.
e.c: Layer III - Intellectual Virtues
p: **Trait theory and personality stability** (Roberts et al., 2006)
**Habit formation and automaticity** (Lally et al., 2010; Wood and Neal, 2007)
f: **Belief as habit of action** (Peirce, "How to Make Our Ideas Clear")
reflections: Which of your good qualities only appears when you're in a good mood? What would make it dependable?
If virtue is a disposition, how do we judge someone by one act? What would you want to see before trusting a person's character?
People in depression or burnout often lose their usual dispositions. Is that a loss of virtue, or an illness of the conditions that carry it?

e.t: Develop phronesis: practical wisdom
e.x:
Phronesis is the capacity to deliberate well about what is good and expedient for a human life, in particular circumstances, with respect to particular facts. It is not theoretical knowledge. It is the trained ability to see what this situation requires and to act accordingly. Cultivate it through experience, reflection, and the study of exemplary lives.

(NE VI.5, VI.7-8.)

**Plain words** Phronesis is knowing what this situation, with these people, actually calls for. It's no textbook, but it can be trained: through experience, reflection, and watching people who do it well. Pay attention to how good judges handle the details.

*For example:* A senior doctor who tells a patient the truth gently, at the right pace, isn't following a script. She's reading the person.
e.c: Layer IV - Practical Wisdom: Phronesis
p: **Phronesis as contextual integrative thinking**, the capacity to integrate conflicting values, perspectives, and emotions in concrete situations ([Schwartz, 2022)
**Wisdom research**, the Berlin Wisdom Model and the More-Wise framework (Baltes and Staudinger, 2000; Grossmann et al., 2020)
f: **The prudent person as norm** (Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II.47)
reflections: Who do you know with excellent practical judgement, and what do they actually pay attention to? Describe one thing they notice that you would have missed.
Phronesis is learned from exemplars. How do you pick whom to learn from, and what could go wrong if you choose badly?
What makes judgement wise rather than merely experienced? Write about the role of reflection in turning events into understanding.

e.t: Learn from experience
e.x:
Phronesis cannot be taught from a textbook. It comes from lived experience, attended to and reflected upon. Young people can be clever but not practically wise, because they lack the years of particular cases that build the capacity for judgment. Value your experience as your primary teacher.

(NE VI.8.)

**Plain words** You can't learn practical judgement from a book. It comes from lived cases, paid attention to and thought about. That's why the young can be clever but not wise. They haven't seen enough. Treat your experience as your best teacher.

*For example:* Someone who has run three failed projects often sees the fourth go wrong at the planning stage. The first-time manager can't.
e.c: Layer IV - Practical Wisdom: Phronesis
p: **Experiential learning cycle**, experience, reflection, conceptualisation, experimentation (Kolb, 1984)
**Deliberate practice and expertise** (Ericsson et al., 1993)
f: **Phenomenological return to the things themselves** (Husserl, Ideas I)
reflections: What did a failure teach you that no book could? Describe how long it took for the lesson to arrive.
Experience isn't automatically educational. Name a mistake you repeated for years, and what finally interrupted it.
What can the old teach the young, and what can the young teach the old about judgement? Where does each fail?

e.t: Deliberate well
e.x:
Deliberation is not endless analysis. It is the process of working out what is in our power, what we can do, and what course of action leads to the good. Good deliberation considers the right things, in the right order, for the right amount of time, and reaches a conclusion. Do not deliberate about what cannot be otherwise.

(NE III.2-3, VI.9.)

**Plain words** Deliberation isn't endless analysis. It's working out what's in your power and which path leads somewhere good, in the right order and in reasonable time, and then concluding. Don't weigh things you can't change.

*For example:* Deciding how to respond to a delayed flight means looking at rebooking options, not rehearsing why the airline failed.
e.c: Layer IV - Practical Wisdom: Phronesis
p: **Decision-making research**, satisficing versus maximizing (Schwartz, 2004)
**Implementation intentions and planning** (Gollwitzer, 1999)
f: **Pragmatic maxim** (Peirce, "How to Make Our Ideas Clear")
reflections: What are you turning over in your mind that is outside your power to change? What would it take to let that go and turn to what you can do?
Deliberation can become avoidance. How do you tell careful thinking from procrastination dressed up as it?
In crisis, people cannot deliberate at length. How do trained habits make good action possible when there is no time to think?

e.t: See the particular
e.x:
Phronesis concerns particulars, and perception of particulars is the work of a trained eye. Universal rules are necessary but insufficient. The practically wise person sees what is called for here, now, with these people, in this situation. Train your perception of the concrete.

(NE VI.8, VI.11.)

**Plain words** Rules help, but they stop short of the real case. The wise person sees what's called for here, now, with these people. That perception is trained. So practise noticing the concrete details, not just applying the general principle.

*For example:* Telling a nervous new hire "great work" might be right. Noticing she needs a specific, honest correction instead is the trained eye at work.
e.c: Layer IV - Practical Wisdom: Phronesis
p: **Moral situation research**, context dominates in real moral choice (Doris, Lack of Character)
**Situation awareness in expert performance** (Klein, 2009)
f: **The moral situation** (Dewey, Human Nature and Conduct)
reflections: Describe a time when you applied a sound general rule to a particular case and got it wrong. What did you fail to see?
What practices train perception of particulars, such as reading novels, listening to patients, or spending time with different people? Which have trained you?
How does attention to the particular change the way we respond to someone suffering, compared with applying a general theory about suffering?

e.t: Let practical wisdom unify the virtues
e.x:
The moral virtues are not a checklist. They are integrated by phronesis into a coherent character. Courage without temperance is not courage; generosity without justice is not generosity. Work on the whole person, not on isolated virtues.

(NE VI.12-13.)

**Plain words** The moral virtues aren't a checklist. Practical wisdom ties them into a single character. Courage without temperance isn't really courage, and generosity without justice isn't really generosity. Work on how they fit together.

*For example:* Giving a big gift while underpaying your staff doesn't add up to generosity. Wisdom spots the contradiction.
e.c: Layer IV - Practical Wisdom: Phronesis
p: **Virtuous spirals of practice and identity** (Kristjánsson, 2018)
**Integrated self and well-being** (Ryan and Deci, 2001)
reflections: Which of your virtues is quietly undermined by another habit? Describe how they pull against each other.
Practical wisdom is said to unify the virtues. Can you think of an example where two virtues conflict, such as honesty and kindness, and how judgement resolves it?
Who in your life shows a unified character, and what is it like to be around them?

e.t: Act in the right way, at the right time, toward the right objects, in the right manner
e.x:
This is Aristotle's formula for virtuous action, and it is deceptively simple. The whole difficulty is knowing what "right" means in each case. That is what phronesis provides. Do not simplify the formula; let it train your attention to context.

(NE II.6, VI.1.)

**Plain words** Aristotle's formula sounds simple: right way, right time, right objects, right manner. The difficulty is knowing what "right" means each time. Don't flatten it into a slogan. Let it make you look harder at the context.

*For example:* Saying "I'm sorry" sincerely and promptly after hurting someone is right. Saying it weeks later by text may not be.
e.c: Layer IV - Practical Wisdom: Phronesis
p: **Contextual intelligence and situational judgment** (Sternberg, 2019)
**Functional analysis**, the ABC (antecedent-behavior-consequence) of behavior (Hayes et al., 2020)
f: **Acting in the situation, not from the rulebook** (Dewey, Human Nature and Conduct)
reflections: Think of a good thing you did at the wrong time or in the wrong way. What would the right version have required you to notice?
Which of the four conditions, right time, objects, manner or measure, do you most often miss? What would help?
Telling someone a hard truth at the right time can heal, and at the wrong time can wound. What cues help you know when to speak?

e.t: Seek the counsel of the practically wise
e.x:
When uncertain, ask someone whose judgment you trust. Phronesis is partly social: the wise person recognises other wise persons and learns from them. Do not rely solely on your own deliberation; test it against the deliberation of those whose lives you admire.

(NE VI.5, VI.11; NE IX.1-3.)

**Plain words** When you're stuck, ask someone whose judgement you trust. Practical wisdom is partly social: wise people recognise each other and learn from each other. Test your own reasoning against the reasoning of people whose lives you admire.

*For example:* Before taking a risky job, you talk it through with a friend who has changed careers twice and is honest with you about it.
e.c: Layer IV - Practical Wisdom: Phronesis
p: **Wisdom of crowds and collective intelligence** (Woolley et al., 2010)
**Mentorship and developmental relationships** (Ragins and Kram, 2007)
reflections: Whose judgement do you seek when you are uncertain, and why them? What happens when you avoid asking?
Wise advisers can also reinforce your biases. How do you choose counsel that challenges you?
In suffering, people often isolate. What does seeking counsel from someone wise offer that private reflection cannot?

e.t: Practise perceptiveness (aisthesis)
e.x:
Phronesis depends on the capacity to perceive the salient features of a situation: what matters, what is at stake, what is called for. This perceptiveness is trainable. Practise noticing what others miss. The practically wise person sees what the situation requires before they can articulate why.

(NE VI.8, VI.11, II.9.)

**Plain words** Wise action starts with seeing what matters in a situation. Aristotle says that perceptiveness can be trained. So practise noticing what others miss. The wise person often sees what's needed before they can say why.

*For example:* A host who notices the quiet guest hasn't been included, and gently draws her in, is seeing what's called for.
e.c: Layer IV - Practical Wisdom: Phronesis
p: **Situation awareness in expert performance** (Klein, 2009)
**Mindfulness as attentional control** (Kabat-Zinn, 1990; Lutz et al., 2008)
f: **Return to the things themselves** (Husserl, Ideas I)
**Perception as action** (Varela, Thompson and Rosch, The Embodied Mind)
reflections: What did you notice recently that others in the room missed? How did you come to see it?
Perception can be sharpened or dulled by habit, fatigue and fear. What dulls yours?
What would it mean to be perceptive about someone else's unspoken pain? What do you do when you see it?

e.t: Practise equity (epieikeia)
e.x:
Equity is the correction of legal justice: the recognition that strict application of a rule can produce injustice in a particular case. The equitable person knows when to bend the rule for the sake of justice itself. Do not let consistency become cruelty.

(NE V.10.)

**Plain words** Applying a rule strictly can sometimes create injustice. Aristotle's equity means knowing when to bend it, for the sake of justice itself. Don't let being consistent turn into being cruel.

*For example:* A landlord who waives a late fee for a tenant who just lost a family member isn't being inconsistent. He's serving what the rule was for.
e.c: Layer IV - Practical Wisdom: Phronesis
p: **Moral situation research**, context dominates in real moral choice (Doris, Lack of Character)
**Procedural justice** (Tyler, 2006)
f: **Equity as correction of law** (Aristotle, NE V.10)
**The moral situation** (Dewey, Human Nature and Conduct)
reflections: Recall a case where applying a rule exactly produced an injustice. What did you do, and what would you do now?
Equity gives discretion to those with authority. How do you prevent it from becoming favouritism or arbitrary power?
Whose suffering is created by systems that cannot bend? What would equity require of those who run them?

e.t: Know when to depart from rules
e.x:
Rules are necessary but not sufficient. The practically wise person knows when a rule should be followed strictly and when it should be adapted. The test is whether following the rule serves the purpose for which it was made.

(NE V.10, VI.8; EE II.3.)

**Plain words** Rules are useful but not enough. The wise person knows when to follow one strictly and when to adapt it. The test is whether following it still serves the purpose it was made for.

*For example:* A "no phones at dinner" rule is great, until your daughter is waiting for news from a hospital. You make an exception, and everyone understands why.
e.c: Layer IV - Practical Wisdom: Phronesis
p: **Moral dilemma research** (Kohlberg, 1981; Haidt, 2001)
**Dual-process models of moral judgment** (Greene et al., 2001)
reflections: Which rule do you follow without recalling its purpose? What would change if you checked?
How do you distinguish a genuine exception from a convenient excuse? Share a case where you were uncertain.
Some rules protect the vulnerable precisely by not bending. When is rigidity a form of care?

e.t: Act voluntarily
e.x:
A voluntary action is one where the agent knows what they are doing, chooses it, and does it from an internal origin. Virtue and vice are voluntary. You are the origin of your character, shaped through your choices. Own your actions as your own.

(NE III.1.)

**Plain words** An action is voluntary when you know what you're doing, choose it, and it starts in you. Aristotle says virtue and vice are voluntary in this sense. You're the origin of your character. So own what you do as yours.

*For example:* Telling yourself "I had no choice" about a snappy reply you sent knowingly, at your desk, with time to think, isn't quite true.
e.c: Layer V - Voluntary Action, Choice, and Akrasia
p: **Locus of control**, internal locus predicts well-being and health (Rotter, 1966)
**Self-efficacy**, belief in one's capacity to act predicts outcomes (Bandura, 1977)
f: **Freedom as power** (Dewey, Human Nature and Conduct)
**Condemned to be free** (Sartre, Being and Nothingness)
reflections: What have you described as forced that was really chosen? What did calling it forced protect you from?
Owning your actions has limits when circumstances, upbringing or illness restrict choice. Where does responsibility begin and end?
How would taking ownership of a past wrong be different from punishing yourself for it? What does each do to your future?

e.t: Choose deliberately (prohairesis)
e.x:
Choice is not desire, not impulse, not opinion. It is deliberate desire for something within our power. It is the point where reason and desire meet and produce action. Your choices are what make you who you are. Take them seriously.

(NE III.2-4, VI.2-4.)

**Plain words** Choice isn't impulse or opinion. It's reasoned desire for something you can actually do, the point where thinking and wanting produce action. Your choices make you who you are, so don't treat them lightly.

*For example:* Choosing to apologise first, after thinking it through, is different from blurting it out or wishing you could. It shapes you.
e.c: Layer V - Voluntary Action, Choice, and Akrasia
p: **Self-determination theory**, autonomous choice predicts well-being (Deci and Ryan, 2000)
**Choice architecture and agency** (Thaler and Sunstein, 2008)
f: **Will as conscious choosing** (James, The Principles of Psychology)
reflections: Which recent choice felt like a decision and which just happened? What differentiated them?
Prohairesis joins reason and desire. When have your reasons and desires pulled in different directions, and how did you choose?
If your choices make you who you are, what do your choices under stress reveal about your deepest priorities?

e.t: Understand that you are responsible for your character
e.x:
You did not choose your starting conditions, but you chose the acts that built your character. The person who is unjust became so by doing unjust acts; the person who is just became so by doing just acts. This is both a burden and a freedom: you are the author of who you are becoming.

(NE III.5.)

**Plain words** You didn't choose where you started. You did choose the acts that shaped you. Someone became unjust by doing unjust things. That's a burden and also a freedom: you're writing who you're becoming.

*For example:* A person raised in a cynical household who starts keeping small promises as an adult is rewriting their own character, one act at a time.
e.c: Layer V - Voluntary Action, Choice, and Akrasia
p: **Growth mindset**, the belief that abilities are developable predicts persistence and achievement (Dweck, 2006)
**Narrative identity**, authorship of one's life story predicts well-being (McAdams, 2013)
f: **Existence precedes essence** (Sartre, Existentialism Is a Humanism)
reflections: Which traits did you inherit or absorb, and which did you build through what you did? Is the line clearer or blurrier than you expected?
Aristotle says you are responsible for your character even if upbringing shaped you. Is that fair to someone raised in cruelty? How would you refine it?
What is the first act that could start changing a trait you dislike? Why have you not done it?

e.t: Recognise akrasia: weakness of will
e.x:
Akrasia is knowing what is good but doing otherwise. It is not ignorance of the principle but a failure to apply it in the moment, when desire overcomes reason. Name it when it happens. Do not pretend it is rationalisation; it is a real and familiar human experience.

(NE VII.1-10.)

**Plain words** Akrasia is knowing what's good and doing the other thing anyway. It's not ignorance, it's desire beating reason in the moment. Name it when it happens. Don't wave it away. It's real and almost everyone has been there.

*For example:* You know you should leave the party at midnight for tomorrow's early start. You stay until two, knowing it, and feel worse for it.
e.c: Layer V - Voluntary Action, Choice, and Akrasia
p: **Dual-process models and self-control failure**, the conflict between deliberative and automatic systems (Kahneman, 2011)
**Ego depletion and self-regulation failure** (Baumeister et al., 1998; Hagger et al., 2010)
f: **The will as endless lack** (Schopenhauer, The World as Will and Representation)
reflections: Where do you routinely know better than you do? Describe the moment when desire wins and what you tell yourself afterwards.
Socrates denied akrasia, saying people only do wrong from ignorance. Does your experience support him, or Aristotle?
How does shame about weakness of will make it worse? What might it look like to name akrasia with curiosity?

e.t: Know that akrasia is not invincible
e.x:
The person who knows the good but fails to do it is in a state that can be changed. Habituation, practice, and the cultivation of phronesis gradually close the gap between knowing and doing. The gap is not a metaphysical fact; it is a developmental stage.

(NE VII.3, VII.8-10.)

**Plain words** The gap between knowing and doing isn't permanent. Habit, practice, and growing wisdom gradually narrow it. Aristotle sees it as a stage of development, not a built-in flaw. So don't read your slips as final.

*For example:* A new runner who skips training days gets more reliable after a season of showing up, even without any new motivation.
e.c: Layer V - Voluntary Action, Choice, and Akrasia
p: **Implementation intentions**, specific if-then plans bridge the intention-behaviour gap (Gollwitzer, 1999)
**Behavioral activation and habit formation** (Lally et al., 2010)
reflections: What gap between knowing and doing has narrowed over time? Trace the steps that closed it.
If akrasia is a developmental stage, what supports help people move through it, and what do we owe those still struggling?
Does treating failure as a stage rather than a verdict change how you treat others? Where do you need that patience most?

e.t: Distinguish continence from virtue
e.x:
The continent person (enkrates) feels desire that pulls against reason but masters it. The virtuous person (sophron) feels no such conflict because desire is trained to follow reason. Continence is a real achievement, but it is not the endpoint. Aim beyond self-control toward integrated character.

(NE I.13, VII.1-2.)

**Plain words** The continent person feels the pull and masters it. The virtuous person doesn't feel the same pull, because desire has been trained. Self-control is a real achievement. But Aristotle says aim past it, toward a character where doing well feels natural.

*For example:* Resisting the biscuit tin through willpower is continence. Not wanting it by mid-afternoon, because your meals now keep you full, is something more.
e.c: Layer V - Voluntary Action, Choice, and Akrasia
p: **Autonomous versus controlled motivation**, integrated regulation versus introjected regulation (Deci and Ryan, 2000)
**Self-determination continuum** (Ryan and Deci, 2001)
reflections: Where do you rely on willpower where a change of environment or habit might serve better? What stops you from changing it?
Is there something admirable in the struggle of the continent person that the settled virtuous person has lost? What might it be?
In recovery from addiction, sustained self-control matters enormously. How does Aristotle's ideal of integrated character fit with that reality?

e.t: Distinguish incontinence from vice
e.x:
The incontinent person knows the good but fails to do it; the vicious person does not know the good or does not care. Incontinence is curable; vice is harder. Do not confuse weakness with corruption.

(NE VII.1-10, VII.8.)

**Plain words** A person with weak will knows the good and fails at it. A vicious person doesn't know the good or doesn't care. Weak will can be cured. Vice is far harder. So don't confuse a lapse with a rotten character.

*For example:* A person who lies once under pressure and feels awful is in a different place than someone who lies routinely and feels nothing.
e.c: Layer V - Voluntary Action, Choice, and Akrasia
p: **Dual-process models** (Kahneman, 2011)
**Moral disengagement research** (Bandura, 1999)
reflections: When have you judged a lapse as a deeper flaw than it was? What would a fair judgement have said?
How do you distinguish weakness from not caring, in yourself? What evidence would you accept?
Society often treats weakness of will as vice. What happens when it is treated as something that can be helped?

e.t: Forgive but do not excuse
e.x:
Aristotle holds us responsible for our character, but he also recognises that some acts are done in ignorance or under compulsion. The distinction matters: voluntary wrongs require correction; involuntary wrongs require understanding. Hold yourself accountable without self-flagellation.

(NE III.1, V.8-9.)

**Plain words** Aristotle holds you responsible for your character, but he also sees acts done in ignorance or under compulsion. Voluntary wrongs call for correction. Involuntary ones call for understanding. Be accountable without beating yourself up.

*For example:* Forgetting a friend's birthday because of a hospital stay is different from deliberately ignoring it. One needs an apology and understanding, the other needs a change.
e.c: Layer V - Voluntary Action, Choice, and Akrasia
p: **Self-compassion research**, accepting imperfection without self-attack predicts well-being (Neff, 2003; MacBeth and Gumley, 2012)
**Self-forgiveness research** (Hall and Fincham, 2005)
reflections: What are you punishing yourself for that was largely outside your control? And what are you excusing that you chose?
Accountability without self-flagellation sounds simple. What practices make it possible when you feel guilt?
How does the legal and moral difference between involuntary and voluntary wrongs show up in the way we forgive?

e.t: Distinguish the involuntary from the non-voluntary
e.x:
An involuntary act is done through ignorance, and the agent feels regret afterward. A non-voluntary act is also done through ignorance, but the agent feels no regret. The distinction matters: regret is a sign that the person understood the wrong.

(NE III.1.)

**Plain words** Both kinds of act are done through ignorance. But in the involuntary case you feel regret when you find out. In the non-voluntary case you don't. Aristotle's point is that regret shows you understood the wrong.

*For example:* Someone who accidentally shares a private message and feels sick about it differs from someone who shrugs. The sick feeling is evidence of care.
e.c: Layer V - Voluntary Action, Choice, and Akrasia
p: **Guilt versus shame research**, guilt (behavioural) predicts adaptive response; shame (global self) predicts maladaptive response (Tangney and Dearing, 2002)
**Remorse and moral emotion research** (Haidt, 2003)
reflections: What does your regret about a past wrong tell you about what you value? Is it a reliable guide?
Someone who feels no regret about a harm may not have understood it. How do you help someone reach understanding without shaming them?
How might regret turn into repair, and how into rumination? What separates them?

e.t: Recognise that choice reveals character
e.x:
Your choices are not isolated events; they are expressions of who you are. Each choice strengthens or weakens a disposition. Over time, the pattern of choices becomes character, and character becomes destiny. Take each choice seriously as a building block of selfhood.

(NE III.5, VI.2-4.)

**Plain words** Choices aren't isolated. Each one strengthens or weakens a disposition, and over time the pattern becomes character. So treat each choice as a building block, not a one-off.

*For example:* Skipping your usual walk "just once" a few times in a row quietly changes you into someone who doesn't walk.
e.c: Layer V - Voluntary Action, Choice, and Akrasia
p: **Self-determination and identity formation** (Deci and Ryan, 2000)
**Narrative identity and life story** (McAdams, 2013)
f: **Existence precedes essence** (Sartre, Existentialism Is a Humanism)
reflections: Which repeated small choice is shaping you most right now, and where does it lead if it continues for ten years?
If every choice is a building block, how do you forgive yourself a bad one without treating it as a crack in the foundation?
Consider someone you know whose life changed direction late. Which choice, in retrospect, started it?

e.t: Recognise that friendship is necessary for flourishing
e.x:
No one would choose to live without friends, even if they had all other goods. Friendship is the context for virtue, the test of character, the solace in misfortune, and the joy in prosperity. Invest in friendships as a condition of your own flourishing.

(NE VIII.1.)

**Plain words** Nobody would choose to live without friends, even with every other good thing. Aristotle says friendship is where virtue gets practised and tested. Invest in friends as part of your own flourishing, not as an extra.

*For example:* A person with a good job and a nice flat who hasn't had a real conversation in weeks is missing something no promotion supplies.
e.c: Layer VI - Friendship
p: **Social relationships and mortality risk**, meta-analyses show social connection predicts survival as strongly as smoking cessation (Holt-Lunstad, Smith and Layton, 2010)
**The longest study on adult development**, the Harvard Study of Adult Development finds quality of relationships as the strongest predictor of life satisfaction (Waldinger and Schulz, 2023)
f: **I-Thou as the primary relation** (Buber, I and Thou)
**Ubuntu: I am because we are** (African relational philosophy)
reflections: Who would you call if you had terrible news at two in the morning? What does that list say about the state of your friendships?
Aristotle says no one would choose life without friends. What do you make of people who live well in solitude, like hermits and monks? Is their friendship found elsewhere?
Loneliness is now widely discussed as a health risk. What would Aristotle say a society should do about it?

e.t: Know the three kinds of friendship
e.x:
Friendships of utility serve mutual benefit. Friendships of pleasure arise from shared enjoyment. Friendships of virtue are based on mutual admiration of character and wishing the good of the other for their own sake. The first two are fragile; the third is durable. Know which kind you are in, and aim for the third.

(NE VIII.3.)

**Plain words** Some friendships run on usefulness, some on fun, and some on admiring each other's character and wanting the other's good. The first two are fragile. The third lasts. Know which kind you're in, and where you can, aim for the third.

*For example:* A colleague you only talk to about work and a friend you'd drive across the country for are not the same type of friend.
e.c: Layer VI - Friendship
p: **Relationship categorisation research**, distinguishing instrumental, consummatory, and identity-relevant relationships (Fehr, 1996)
**Companionate versus passionate love** (Berscheid and Hatfield, 1969)
reflections: Sort your friendships into utility, pleasure and virtue. What surprised you about where people landed?
Friendships of virtue are rare. Is it realistic to aim for them, or does that standard make ordinary friendships feel second-rate?
What does it take to move a friendship from pleasure to something deeper, and what do you risk by trying?

e.t: Wish good for your friend for their own sake
e.x:
The defining mark of true friendship is that you wish the good of your friend for the friend's sake, not for what you get from it. This is what makes the friendship virtuous and lasting. Test your friendships by this criterion: do I want their good, or do I want what they give me?

(NE VIII.2, IX.4.)

**Plain words** A true friend wants your good for your sake, not for what they get from you. Aristotle makes that the test. Ask yourself in a friendship: do I want their good, or what they give me?

*For example:* Being genuinely glad when a friend gets a job in another city, even though you'll see less of them, is the test passed.
e.c: Layer VI - Friendship
p: **Compassionate love research**, love that centres on the other's welfare (Underwood, 2009; Berscheid, 2010)
**Unconditional positive regard outcomes** (Rogers, 1957)
f: **The face as ethical summons** (Levinas, Totality and Infinity)
**Care as ontological structure** (Heidegger, Being and Time)
reflections: In which friendship do you most clearly want the other person's good, even at some cost to you? What does that feel like?
Can you wish someone well for their own sake and still need them? Is pure unselfishness even possible, or desirable?
When a friend makes choices you think will harm them, how do you balance wishing their good with respecting their freedom?

e.t: Be a friend to yourself first
e.x:
The foundation of friendship is the relationship one has with oneself. The good person is their own best friend: they are at one with themselves, approve of themselves, and take pleasure in their own company. A bad person is at war with themselves. Work on self-friendship as the condition of all other friendship.

(NE IX.4, IX.8.)

**Plain words** Friendship starts with how you treat yourself. Aristotle says the good person is at peace with themselves and enjoys their own company. A person at war with themselves finds it hard to befriend anyone. Work on that first.

*For example:* Someone who can spend an evening alone without restlessness or self-criticism is usually easier company for others.
e.c: Layer VI - Friendship
p: **Self-compassion as foundation of relational health** (Neff and Beretvas, 2013)
**Authenticity and the true self** (Schlegel and Hicks, 2011)
f: **Amour de soi versus amour-propre** (Rousseau, Discourse on the Origin of Inequality)
reflections: How do you speak to yourself after a failure? Imagine saying the same words to your closest friend and notice the difference.
Aristotle says the bad person is at war with themselves. What does inner conflict feel like in your experience, and what has brought a truce?
Self-compassion practices in psychology echo this idea. Does being a friend to yourself risk indulgence, or is it a precondition for honesty?

e.t: Practise equality in friendship
e.x:
True friendship requires a kind of equality: not necessarily in status or resources, but in goodwill, in mutual regard, in the willingness to give and receive. Friendships between unequals (parent and child, ruler and subject) can exist but must adjust the degree of affection to the distance. Seek mutuality in your closest friendships.

(NE VIII.7, VIII.13.)

**Plain words** Real friendship needs a kind of equality, not in status or money but in goodwill and in giving and receiving. Unequal friendships, like parent and child, can work if the affection fits the distance. Look for mutuality in your closest ones.

*For example:* A friendship where one person always listens and the other always talks has drifted from the real thing, whatever the title says.
e.c: Layer VI - Friendship
p: **Equity theory in relationships**, perceived fairness predicts satisfaction (Hatfield et al., 1985)
**Mutual responsiveness and relationship quality** (Reis and Shaver, 1988)
f: **Reciprocity as foundation of ethics** (Gilligan, In a Different Voice)
reflections: Which close relationship feels most unequal, and in which direction? What would it take to rebalance, or to accept it?
Aristotle allows friendship across unequal roles, adjusting affection to the distance. When does that become an excuse for exploitation?
How do power imbalances, wealth, age or health, change what friendship can be? Describe one that worked well.

e.t: Maintain friendships through presence in misfortune
e.x:
The true test of friendship is not shared prosperity but shared adversity. The friend who stays when things go wrong is the friend who matters. Be that friend. Do not abandon people when they become inconvenient or costly.

(NE VIII.4, IX.11.)

**Plain words** Good times show who's around. Bad times show who's a friend. Aristotle says the one who stays when things go wrong matters most. Be that person. Don't drop people when they become costly or awkward.

*For example:* Visiting a friend who has had a divorce and doesn't want to talk, and just sitting with her, is the test.
e.c: Layer VI - Friendship
p: **Social support and resilience**, perceived support buffers stress (Cohen and Wills, 1985)
**Companionate love in adversity** (Berscheid, 2010)
f: **Compassion as co-suffering** (Scheler, The Nature of Sympathy)
reflections: Who stayed when things were bad for you, and who vanished? What did you learn about each, and about yourself?
Is it fair to judge a friendship by how people behave in a crisis, given that people have limits? When is withdrawal self-preservation, not betrayal?
What does staying with someone in suffering actually involve, if you cannot fix anything?

e.t: Seek concord (homonoia)
e.x:
Concord is political friendship: shared vision about what matters and how to live. It is not agreement on everything but agreement on the great ends. In families, teams, and communities, cultivate concord by making shared values explicit and working toward them together.

(NE IX.6.)

**Plain words** Concord is shared vision about what matters and how to live, not agreement on everything. In families, teams and communities, make the shared values explicit and work toward them together.

*For example:* A team that disagrees about tactics but all want customers to be well served has concord. One with no shared aim just has meetings.
e.c: Layer VI - Friendship
p: **Shared vision and collective efficacy** (Bandura, 2000)
**Superordinate goals reduce conflict** (Sherif, Robbers Cave; Gaertner and Dovidio, 2000)
f: **Solidarity without demanding consensus** (Rorty, Contingency, Irony, and Solidarity)
reflections: What do you and your family, team or community actually share at the level of ends? Has it ever been said aloud?
Concord allows disagreement about means. How do you tell a healthy disagreement from the sign of a deeper split in values?
What shared aims could help a divided community move toward concord? What stops them now?

e.t: Understand the asymmetry of benefaction
e.x:
Aristotle notes that the benefactor seems to love the beneficiary more than the beneficiary loves the benefactor. This is because the benefactor has invested something of themselves in the relationship. Do not keep a ledger of what you have given; give freely and let go.

(NE IX.7.)

**Plain words** The giver tends to care more about the receiver than the reverse, because they've put something of themselves in. Aristotle notes it. So don't keep a ledger of what you've given. Give freely and let it go.

*For example:* A parent who drove their kid to training for years doesn't hold it as a debt. If they start listing it, the giving has gone sour.
e.c: Layer VI - Friendship
p: **Prosocial behaviour and well-being** (Dunn, Aknin and Norton, 2008)
**Self-determination and relatedness** (Deci and Ryan, 2000)
reflections: Where are you keeping a mental ledger of what you've given? How does it change your giving and your feelings toward the person?
Why might the benefactor love the beneficiary more than the reverse? What does this suggest about how love and effort are connected?
How can receiving be as generous as giving? Describe a time you received gracefully, or failed to.

e.t: Recognise that self-love is the foundation
e.x:
Aristotle distinguishes two forms of self-love: the lower form (seeking external goods, honours, pleasures for oneself) and the higher form (seeking nobility, virtue, and the good for oneself). The higher self-love is the foundation of all friendship and virtue.

(NE IX.8.)

**Plain words** There are two kinds of self-love. The low kind chases honours and pleasures for yourself. The higher kind wants nobility and virtue for yourself. Aristotle says the higher one is the root of friendship and virtue.

*For example:* Wanting to be someone people can trust, even when it costs you a deal, is the higher kind. Wanting the deal at any price is the lower.
e.c: Layer VI - Friendship
p: **Self-compassion research** (Neff, 2003)
**Healthy self-esteem versus narcissism** (Kernis, 2003; Paulhus and Williams, 2002)
f: **Amour de soi** (Rousseau, Discourse on the Origin of Inequality)
reflections: When have self-interest and character pulled you apart? Which won, and how did you feel afterwards?
Aristotle's higher self-love wants virtue for oneself. How is that different from vanity about being virtuous?
What does it mean to love yourself in a way that makes you better at loving others, rather than worse?

e.t: Practise living together (suzēn)
e.x:
Friendship is not merely affection but shared life. Friends live together, share activities, eat together, talk together, work together. The deepest friendship is the one that becomes a shared form of life. Invest in shared activity, not merely shared feeling.

(NE VIII.5, IX.12.)

**Plain words** Friendship isn't only affection. It's a shared life: eating, talking, working together. The deepest kind becomes a way of living. So put time into doing things together, not just feeling warmly about each other.

*For example:* Friends who cook together every Sunday, even badly, build more than friends who text "we should catch up" for years.
e.c: Layer VI - Friendship
p: **Shared activities and relationship quality** (Reis and Shaver, 1988)
**Cooperative learning and interdependence** (Johnson and Johnson, 1989)
f: **I-Thou as shared presence** (Buber, I and Thou)
reflections: What do you regularly do with a friend, as distinct from talking about doing? What would you lose if it stopped?
Shared life is hard when friends live far apart. What substitutes for suzēn, and what cannot be replaced?
How do shared routines, meals, walks and work, carry care when words fail, particularly in times of grief?

e.t: Distinguish friendship from partnership
e.x:
Not every partnership is a friendship. You can work with someone, trade with someone, or cooperate with someone without being their friend. Friendship requires a deeper bond: mutual goodwill, shared values, and the wish for the other's good. Do not confuse useful cooperation with friendship.

(NE VIII.3, VIII.6.)

**Plain words** Working, trading and cooperating with someone doesn't make them your friend. Friendship needs goodwill, shared values, and wishing the other well. Don't mistake useful cooperation for it, and don't ask it to carry what it can't.

*For example:* A great colleague who disappears once the project ends was a partner, not a friend. That's fine, as long as you didn't expect more.
e.c: Layer VI - Friendship
p: **Relationship categorisation** (Fehr, 1996)
**Social exchange theory** (Homans, 1958)
reflections: Which of your relationships do you call friendship that may really be partnership? What do you expect from it that it cannot give?
Is there anything wrong with useful relationships? What does a life look like that insists every relationship be a deep friendship?
How do you honour a working relationship without pretending it is more or treating it as less?

e.t: Be generous in interpreting friends' actions
e.x:
The good friend assumes the best about the other's motives. Do not be quick to take offense. Do not attribute malice where ignorance or fatigue may be the cause. Generosity of interpretation is itself a virtue of friendship.

(NE VIII.5, IX.3, IX.4; EE VII.2.)

**Plain words** A good friend assumes the best about your motives. Don't take offence quickly, and don't see malice where ignorance or tiredness would explain it. Reading a friend generously is itself part of friendship.

*For example:* A friend who cancels twice might be exhausted, not careless. A message asking "you okay?" does more than a cold reply.
e.c: Layer VI - Friendship
p: **Attribution research**, fundamental attribution error (Ross, 1977)
**Charitable interpretation and relationship quality** (Gottman, 1999)
reflections: Recall a time you read a friend's action uncharitably and were wrong. What did it cost, and what changed your mind?
Generosity of interpretation can enable ongoing harm. At what point does charity become denial?
How might assuming good motives change the way people with conflicting views talk to each other?

e.t: Recognise that friendships change over time
e.x:
Friendships of utility end when the utility ends. Friendships of pleasure end when the pleasure changes. Friendships of virtue are more durable but even they can end if one party changes. Accept that some friendships are seasonal; hold the durable ones more dearly.

(NE VIII.3, VIII.13.)

**Plain words** Friendships of use end when the use ends. Friendships of pleasure end when the fun changes. Even deep ones can end if one person changes. Accept that some are seasonal, and hold the durable ones more dearly.

*For example:* Two parents who became close while their kids were in the same class often drift apart after the school years. That's a season ending, not a failure.
e.c: Layer VI - Friendship
p: **Relationship dissolution research** (Duck, 1982)
**Lifespan development and friendship** (Roberts et al., 2006)
reflections: Which friendship are you mourning that may have run its season? What did it give you, and what would honouring its end look like?
Is it a failure of loyalty to let a friendship fade? What do we owe people from earlier chapters?
Aristotle says virtue friendships are durable but can end if one person changes. How would you handle a good friend becoming someone you can no longer respect?

e.t: Practise friendship across difference
e.x:
Aristotle notes that friendships can form between people of different ranks and capacities, but they require adaptation. The friendship of a parent and child, a teacher and student, an elder and younger person has its own form. Do not demand sameness; adapt to the difference.

(NE VIII.7, VIII.8, VIII.11.)

**Plain words** Friendships can span rank and ability, but they need adaptation. A parent and child, a teacher and student, an elder and a younger person, each have their own form. Don't demand sameness. Adjust to the gap.

*For example:* A grandmother and teenager who bond over cooking get along because each lets the other be what they are.
e.c: Layer VI - Friendship
p: **Intergroup contact hypothesis** (Allport, 1954; Pettigrew and Tropp, 2006)
**Perspective-getting** (Epley et al., 2007)
f: **Let the other remain other** (Levinas, Totality and Infinity)
reflections: Which of your friendships crosses a big gap of age, class or background? What adjustments does it ask of you?
Do cross-difference friendships teach something that similar friendships cannot? Recall one lesson.
What are the limits of friendship across power differences, such as between a teacher and a student, or a carer and someone they care for?

e.t: Honour friendship in prosperity as well as adversity
e.x:
It is easy to be a friend in adversity. It is harder to be a friend in prosperity: not to be envious of another's success, not to be too busy, not to take the friend for granted. Celebrate your friends' good fortune as if it were your own.

(NE VIII.5, VIII.9, IX.11; EE VII.3.)

**Plain words** Being a friend in hard times is easy to admire. Being one in good times is harder: not envying their success, not being too busy, not taking them for granted. Celebrate your friends' luck as if it were your own.

*For example:* Showing up to a friend's launch party, and meaning your congratulations, is harder than showing up to their bad day.
e.c: Layer VI - Friendship
p: **Sympathetic joy (mudita) research** (Condon and Makransky, 2020)
**Active constructive responding** (Gable, Reis, Impett and Asher, 2004)
f: **Wish good for your friend for their own sake** (Aristotle, NE VIII.2)
reflections: Whose good news have you found hard to celebrate? Be honest about what was underneath it.
Is it harder to be glad for people near your own life than for those far from it? What does that reveal about envy?
How does celebrating others change your own happiness over time? Give an example from your life.

e.t: Recognise that the best friendship is between the good
e.x:
True friendship requires both parties to be good. Only the good can wish the other's good for its own sake. Only the good are stable enough to sustain a friendship through fortune and time. If you want good friends, become a good person.

(NE VIII.3, VIII.4, IX.5; EE VII.2.)

**Plain words** A friendship that lasts needs two good people. Only someone with decent character can wish you well for your own sake and stay steady through changing fortune. So if you want good friends, start by becoming someone worth being friends with.

*For example:* You notice the friends who stayed through your messy year were the ones who were also straight with others. Like attracts like.
e.c: Layer VI - Friendship
p: **Similarity and attraction research** (Byrne, 1971)
**Virtuous spirals of practice and identity** (Kristjánsson, 2018)
reflections: Look at your closest friends. What qualities do they share, and what do those say about you?
Aristotle claims only the good can be true friends. Is that too demanding or too optimistic? Describe a friendship with someone flawed that you consider true.
How does one become good enough to deserve good friends without becoming self-righteous?

e.t: Do not demonise pleasure
e.x:
Pleasure is not the same as the good, but it is not an enemy of the good. Pleasure completes activity as a kind of bloom. The question is not whether to enjoy but what activities are worth enjoying. Seek pleasures that complete worthy activities, not pleasures that distract from them.

(NE VII.11-15, X.1-5.)

**Plain words** Pleasure isn't the good, but it isn't the enemy either. Aristotle says it's like a bloom on an activity done well. So the question isn't whether to enjoy things, it's which activities are worth enjoying.

*For example:* Enjoying a long meal with people you like, after a day of work you're proud of, belongs to a good life. Pleasure doesn't need an apology.
e.c: Layer VII - Pleasure
p: **Dual-process models of pleasure**, "wanting" versus "liking" systems (Berridge and Kringelbach, 2015)
**Savoring research**, the capacity to prolong and deepen enjoyment predicts well-being (Bryant and Veroff, 2007)
f: **The having versus being mode** (Fromm, To Have or To Be?)
reflections: Which pleasure do you feel guilty about, and where did that guilt come from? Is it deserved?
Many ascetic traditions treat pleasure as a hazard, while Aristotle treats it as a bloom on good activity. Where do you stand, and what experience has shaped that?
How can pleasure in a suffering world be justified without callousness? What does enjoying life well owe to those who cannot?

e.t: Choose activities for their completeness
e.x:
The best activities are those that are chosen for their own sake, not for what they produce. Pleasure in such activities is not a separate goal but the completion of the activity itself. Prefer activities that are worth doing for their own sake.

(NE X.3-4.)

**Plain words** The best activities are chosen for their own sake, not for what they produce. The pleasure in them isn't a separate prize. It's the activity finished well. So lean toward things worth doing for themselves.

*For example:* Playing the piano badly on Sunday evening, just because you like it, counts. So does a walk with no step-tracker.
e.c: Layer VII - Pleasure
p: **Intrinsic motivation and autotelic activity** (Deci and Ryan, 2000; Csikszentmihalyi, 1990)
**Process goals versus outcome goals** (Vallerand, 2010)
reflections: Which activities in your week are chosen for their own sake? Which exist only to produce something else?
What happens to an activity loved for its own sake when it becomes a job or a metric? Describe an example.
What activity would you keep doing if no one ever knew or paid? What does that say about what you value?

e.t: Recognise that pleasure completes activity
e.x:
Pleasure is not an added ingredient; it is the natural completion of an activity performed well. When you do something well, pleasure follows. Do not seek pleasure directly; seek the activity, and let pleasure complete it.

(NE X.4, X.5.)

**Plain words** Pleasure isn't an extra ingredient you add. It's what naturally comes when you do something well. So don't hunt for pleasure directly. Do the thing, and let it arrive.

*For example:* Fixing a bike properly gives a quiet satisfaction that scrolling for it never does.
e.c: Layer VII - Pleasure
p: **Flow research**, absorption in activity produces positive affect (Csikszentmihalyi, 1990)
**Savoring with awareness** (Bryant and Veroff, 2007)
f: **The beautiful (kalon) as aim of action** (Aristotle, NE II.3)
reflections: Recall a time pleasure arrived uninvited because you were absorbed in doing something well. What was it like?
Chasing pleasure directly often fails, while pursuing activities brings it as a by-product. Does this explain the paradox of happiness research?
What does this suggest for someone in depression who cannot feel pleasure? Could activity come first?

e.t: Distinguish good pleasures from bad pleasures
e.x:
The same activity can produce pleasure in a good person and a bad person, but the pleasure is different. The pleasure of the virtuous person completes a worthy activity; the pleasure of the vicious person completes a base one. Be mindful of what your pleasures are completing.

(NE X.5.)

**Plain words** Two people can enjoy the same thing, but the pleasure differs. The good person's pleasure completes something worthwhile. The bad person's completes something low. So notice what your pleasures are finishing.

*For example:* Enjoying a competition with a rival you respect is not the same as enjoying their failure, though both feel like "winning."
e.c: Layer VII - Pleasure
p: **Values-affirmation and pleasure congruence** (Cohen and Sherman, 2014)
**Intrinsic versus extrinsic goal content** (Kasser and Ryan, 1996)
f: **The having versus being mode** (Fromm, To Have or To Be?)
reflections: What is one of your regular pleasures completing, and are you proud of it?
Schadenfreude and cruelty feel pleasant to some. How would Aristotle explain why those pleasures differ from the pleasure of excellence?
Could a pleasure change its quality by changing what it accompanies? Think of an example from your own life.

e.t: Recognise that bodily pleasures are not the highest
e.x:
Bodily pleasures (food, drink, sex) are necessary but not the highest. The highest pleasures are those of the intellect: the pleasure of understanding, of contemplation, of friendship. Do not arrange your life around bodily pleasure; include it but do not make it the centre.

(NE X.3, X.5, VII.14.)

**Plain words** Eating, drinking and sex are necessary, not the top of the ladder. Aristotle ranks the pleasures of understanding, contemplation and friendship higher. Include the bodily ones, just don't build your life around them.

*For example:* A holiday planned entirely around meals can be lovely. A life planned that way gets thin.
e.c: Layer VII - Pleasure
p: **Eudaimonic versus hedonic well-being** (Ryff, 1989; Huta and Ryan, 2010)
**Self-actualisation and being-values** (Maslow, Toward a Psychology of Being)
reflections: What occupies the centre of your free time, and is it a bodily pleasure or something deeper?
Is the hierarchy of pleasures elitist? Does anything justify calling understanding a higher pleasure than food?
For people who are hungry, tired or in pain, bodily goods are no small matter. How should a philosophy of flourishing treat them?

e.t: Understand that pleasure is not the good but accompanies it
e.x:
Pleasure is not the highest good, but it is not irrelevant. It accompanies the good life as a companion, not as a master. Let pleasure follow virtue, not lead it.

(NE I.8, X.2, X.5; EE II.8.)

**Plain words** Pleasure walks beside the good life as a companion, not the boss. Aristotle says to let it follow virtue, not lead it. When pleasure leads, you get dragged. When it follows, you enjoy the good life you're building.

*For example:* Enjoying the evening after finishing something hard feels different from enjoying an evening to avoid it.
e.c: Layer VII - Pleasure
p: **Hedonic adaptation** (Lyubomirsky, 2011)
**Eudaimonic well-being beyond pleasure** (Ryff, 1989)
f: **Eudaimonia as activity, not pleasure** (Aristotle, NE I.7)
reflections: Where does pleasure lead your choices instead of following them? How do you notice?
Can a good life be planned around virtue and still be enjoyable? What would Aristotle say to someone who finds virtue joyless?
How does the experience of pleasure differ when it arrives after doing good compared to when it is the goal?

e.t: Practise moderation in pleasure
e.x:
Excessive pursuit of pleasure destroys the capacity for it. The person who constantly seeks novelty becomes insensitive to it. The person who indulges every appetite loses the ability to enjoy simple things. Practise restraint to preserve the capacity for enjoyment.

(NE III.11, III.12, VII.14.)

**Plain words** Chasing pleasure too hard wears out the capacity to feel it. Novelty-seekers get numb. People who indulge every appetite lose the taste for simple things. Some restraint keeps your enjoyment alive.

*For example:* Someone who eats rich food every night finds ordinary soup bland. After a week of simple meals, it tastes good again.
e.c: Layer VII - Pleasure
p: **Hedonic adaptation and novelty seeking** (Lyubomirsky, 2011)
**Self-regulation and delay of gratification** (Mischel et al., 1989)
reflections: Where have you gone numb from too much of something? What did you try to restore sensitivity?
Hedonic adaptation is well documented in psychology. How does Aristotle's moderation anticipate it, and what might it add?
Is there a form of moderation that is really fear of enjoyment? How do you tell them apart?

e.t: Recognise that pain is not always bad
e.x:
Some pain is necessary for growth. The person who avoids all pain becomes incapable of courage, endurance, or achievement. Do not flee all discomfort. Distinguish necessary pain from unnecessary suffering, and accept the former.

(NE VII.13, VII.14, II.3, II.9; EE II.8.)

**Plain words** Some pain is the price of growing. If you dodge all of it, you can't be brave, patient, or achieve much. Aristotle's advice: tell necessary pain from pointless suffering, and accept the necessary kind.

*For example:* Sore muscles after a first week of training are the price of getting fitter. A badly fitting shoe that rubs a blister isn't.
e.c: Layer VII - Pleasure
p: **Stress-as-challenge mindset** (Crum et al., 2013)
**Acceptance-based coping** (Hayes et al., 2011)
f: **The obstacle is the way** (Marcus Aurelius, Meditations V.20)
**Let obstruction do its work** (Dewey, Experience and Nature)
reflections: What discomfort are you avoiding that would help you grow? And what pain are you putting up with that serves nothing?
How do you tell necessary pain from unnecessary suffering? What would you say to someone whose suffering is the second kind but who has been told it builds character?
Some people suffer so much that growth is impossible. What does Aristotle's view of pain owe them?

e.t: Seek the pleasure of contemplation
e.x:
The pleasure of the intellect is superior to bodily pleasure because it is more continuous, more self-sufficient, and less subject to satiety. Cultivate the capacity for intellectual pleasure: reading, thinking, wondering, discussing.

(NE X.7, X.8; EE VIII.3.)

**Plain words** The pleasure of thinking lasts longer and stays satisfying longer than bodily pleasures. It's more self-sufficient and doesn't cloy. So build the capacity for it: read, think, wonder, discuss.

*For example:* Spending a Sunday on a hard book and a long chat about it can leave you more content than a day out spent buying things.
e.c: Layer VII - Pleasure
p: **Need for cognition** (Cacioppo and Petty, 1982)
**Openness to experience and well-being** (Kaufman et al., 2016)
f: **Wonder as the beginning of philosophy** (Aristotle, Metaphysics I.2)
reflections: When did you last enjoy a thought for its own sake? What made it satisfying?
Intellectual pleasure is said to be more continuous and less subject to satiety. Does your experience agree?
What might a person who cannot read or study find in place of this pleasure? Is contemplation open to everyone?

e.t: Recognise that pleasure varies with the activity
e.x:
Each activity has its own proper pleasure. The pleasure of eating is different from the pleasure of thinking, which is different from the pleasure of friendship. Do not judge all pleasures by the same standard. Honour the distinctive pleasure of each worthy activity.

(NE X.5, X.6.)

**Plain words** Each activity has its own pleasure. Eating, thinking and friendship feel different, and each is a different quality. Don't measure them all on one scale. Respect what is distinctive about each good activity.

*For example:* The satisfaction of solving a puzzle isn't comparable to the warmth of a long dinner, and neither needs to be ranked against the other.
e.c: Layer VII - Pleasure
p: **Savoring and distinct positive emotions** (Fredrickson, 2001)
**Psychological richness as distinct from pleasure and meaning** (Oishi and Westgate, 2022)
reflections: Which pleasure do you undervalue because it doesn't resemble your favourite? Describe one.
Does it make sense to compare pleasures at all? What does the claim that each has its own quality imply about ranking?
Can you describe what distinguishes the pleasure of friendship from the pleasure of thinking, in your own words?

e.t: Practise contemplation (theoria)
e.x:
Contemplation is the highest human activity: the exercise of the highest part of us (intellect) on the highest objects (truth). It is sought for its own sake, produces nothing, and is the closest a human comes to the divine. Make space for contemplative activity: reflection, study, wonder, attention to what is.

(NE X.7-8.)

**Plain words** Contemplation is the highest human activity for Aristotle: using the best part of you on the highest things, for its own sake. It makes nothing. So make room for it: reflection, study, wonder, simply paying attention to what is.

*For example:* Sitting with a hard question on a bench for an hour, with no phone and no goal, is contemplation in his sense.
e.c: Layer VIII - Contemplation and the Theoretical Life
p: **Awe and self-transcendent experiences**, contemplative states reliably produce the small-self effect and predict well-being (Yaden et al., 2017)
**Open-monitoring meditation research** (Lutz et al., 2008)
f: **The specious present and pure experience** (James, Essays in Radical Empiricism)
reflections: When do you allow yourself to think without trying to produce anything? What gets in the way?
Contemplation is said to be the closest humans come to the divine. What do you make of that without religion?
Is contemplation a privilege of the leisured? How might people who work long hours find their own version of it?

e.t: Recognise that the theoretical life is not for everyone
e.x:
Aristotle acknowledges that the contemplative life is the highest, but it is not the only life worth living. The political life, the life of practical action, is also a life of virtue. Do not feel inadequate if you are not a contemplative. Find your mode of flourishing and live it well.

(NE X.8.)

**Plain words** Aristotle puts contemplation highest but doesn't say it's the only good life. The life of action, in public affairs and practical work, is also virtuous. So don't feel inadequate if you're not a thinker. Find your way and live it well.

*For example:* A person who runs a local clinic may never read philosophy and still lives a full life of virtue.
e.c: Layer VIII - Contemplation and the Theoretical Life
p: **Multiple independent pathways to flourishing**, hedonic and eudaimonic strands contribute separately (Huta and Ryan, 2010)
**Calling orientation diversity** (Wrzesniewski et al., 1997)
f: **Both-and where you can** (James, A Pluralistic Universe)
reflections: Which way of life suits you better, reflection or action? Have you felt pressure to be the other kind?
If the political and practical life is also virtuous, what are people who feel inadequate beside philosophers missing?
Whose way of flourishing have you underrated because it didn't look like yours?

e.t: Integrate contemplation and action
e.x:
The best life is not purely theoretical or purely practical but combines both. Contemplation without action is sterile; action without contemplation is blind. Alternate between them: study the world, then act in it; act, then reflect on what you learned.

(NE X.8; Politics VII.1-3.)

**Plain words** The best life mixes both. Contemplation without action goes nowhere, and action without contemplation is blind. So alternate: study the world, then act in it, then reflect on what happened.

*For example:* A teacher who tries a new method, then sits with the results over the weekend, and tweaks it, is combining the two.
e.c: Layer VIII - Contemplation and the Theoretical Life
p: **Experiential learning cycle**, action and reflection in alternation (Kolb, 1984)
**Reflective practice** (Schön, 1983)
reflections: Which do you tend to skip, reflection or action? What does the skipped half cost?
Describe a recent action you haven't properly reflected on. What would honest reflection reveal?
How would a rhythm of contemplation and action help someone who is in prolonged suffering, either their own or another's?

e.t: Find joy in learning
e.x:
The exercise of the intellect is naturally pleasant. Learning is not a chore but a form of flourishing. Curiosity, the desire to know, is a basic human drive. Follow it. Do not let it die under the weight of obligation.

(NE IV.7, X.7; Metaphysics I.1.)

**Plain words** Using your mind is naturally pleasant. Aristotle treats learning as part of flourishing, not a chore. Curiosity is a basic drive. Follow it, and don't let it be buried under obligations.

*For example:* A person who spends an evening reading about birdsong, for no reason, is doing something very human.
e.c: Layer VIII - Contemplation and the Theoretical Life
p: **Need for cognition and intellectual engagement** (Cacioppo and Petty, 1982)
**Openness to experience predicts well-being and creative achievement** (Kaufman et al., 2016)
f: **Wonder as the beginning of philosophy** (Aristotle, Metaphysics I.2)
reflections: What are you curious about that you have set aside? Why?
How do school and work sometimes kill the very curiosity they set out to cultivate?
Is curiosity a basic human good, or only a pleasure of those with time? Argue both sides.

e.t: Take proper pleasure in the right things
e.x:
Pleasure is good when it completes a worthy activity and bad when it completes a base one. The same pleasure can be good for one person and bad for another, depending on the activity it completes. Be mindful of what your pleasures are completing.

(NE X.5.)

**Plain words** A pleasure is good when it completes something worth doing, and bad when it completes something base. The same pleasure can be fine for one person and not for another, depending on what it's attached to. Check what yours is finishing.

*For example:* Laughing with friends after a hard rehearsal is fine. Laughing at someone's expense to feel big isn't.
e.c: Layer VIII - Contemplation and the Theoretical Life
p: **Values-affirmation and pleasure congruence** (Cohen and Sherman, 2014)
**Intrinsic versus extrinsic goal content** (Kasser and Ryan, 1996)
f: **The having versus being mode** (Fromm, To Have or To Be?)
reflections: What are your regular pleasures attached to? Which would you drop if you saw clearly what they completed?
Can the same pleasure be good for one person and bad for another? Give an example.
How would you introduce a new pleasure that completes something you value, such as music, craft or service?

e.t: Recognise the divine in the human
e.x:
Aristotle says that the intellect is divine, or the most divine part of us. Contemplation is the activity through which we participate in the divine. This does not require religious belief; it is the recognition that the capacity for truth and understanding is the highest thing in us. Honour that capacity.

(NE X.7, X.8.)

**Plain words** Aristotle calls intellect the divine part of us. Using it is how we share in the divine. You don't need religion for that. It's recognising that our capacity for truth and understanding is the best thing in us.

*For example:* The moment you finally understand a hard proof, or why a piece of music works, you feel something larger than yourself.
e.c: Layer VIII - Contemplation and the Theoretical Life
p: **Self-transcendent experiences** (Yaden et al., 2017)
**Awe research** (Keltner and Haidt, 2003)
reflections: When did understanding something give you a sense of awe or reverence? What did it feel like?
Aristotle says intellect is divine. How do you reconcile this with the ways intelligence has been used for harm?
What would it mean to honour another person's capacity to understand, even when they are suffering or confused?

e.t: Practise self-sufficiency (autarkeia)
e.x:
The contemplative life is the most self-sufficient: it requires fewer external goods than any other activity.
