The person who can find satisfaction in thought, in wonder, in attention, needs less from the world. Cultivate this self-sufficiency, not as withdrawal but as freedom from dependency on externals.

(NE X.7, X.8; EE VIII.3.)

**Plain words** A life of thought needs fewer outside goods than any other. If you can find satisfaction in thinking, wonder and attention, you're less at the mercy of circumstances. Aristotle means freedom, not withdrawal.

*For example:* Someone who can be content with a book and a walk is less rattled by a missed holiday or a smaller pay rise.
e.c: Layer VIII - Contemplation and the Theoretical Life
p: **Nonattachment research**, nonattachment predicts well-being beyond mindfulness (Sahdra et al., 2010)
**Psychological flexibility** (Kashdan and Rottenberg, 2010)
reflections: What can make you content without anyone else's help? How reliable is that source?
Self-sufficiency can drift into isolation. How do you cultivate independence while staying open to others?
How does reducing dependence on externals help in loss, and what does it cost in intimacy?

e.t: Practise distributive justice
e.x:
Distributive justice concerns the proportional allocation of honour, money, and goods according to merit. In any group you lead or belong to, ask: is the distribution proportionate to contribution and need? Inequality is not inherently unjust, but disproportion is.

(NE V.3; Politics III.9-13.)

**Plain words** Distributive justice means sharing honour, money and goods in proportion to merit. In any group you lead or belong to, ask whether rewards match contribution and need. Inequality isn't automatically unjust. Disproportion is.

*For example:* A manager who gives the biggest bonus to the person who carried the project, and explains why, is distributing fairly.
e.c: Layer IX - Justice, Equity, and Law
p: **Equity theory**, perceived fairness of distribution predicts satisfaction (Adams, 1965)
**Social comparison and relative deprivation** (Festinger, 1954; Runciman, 1966)
f: **Justice as fairness** (Rawls, A Theory of Justice)
reflections: Where in a group you belong to are rewards out of proportion to contribution? Who is under-credited?
Merit is not the only claim on a share. How should need, effort and luck weigh against desert?
What would a fairer distribution cost you personally, and what would you gain?

e.t: Practise corrective justice
e.x:
When a wrong is done, corrective justice restores balance: the wrongdoer returns what was taken or suffers a penalty proportionate to the harm. In your own life, when you wrong someone, make it right. When someone wrongs you, seek proportionate restoration, not vengeance.

(NE V.4.)

**Plain words** When you do wrong, put it right. When you're wronged, look for proportionate repair, not vengeance. Aristotle's corrective justice restores balance instead of adding more harm.

*For example:* Paying for the window your ball broke and offering to help fix it is corrective justice. So is a firm but fair boundary after someone wrongs you.
e.c: Layer IX - Justice, Equity, and Law
p: **Restorative justice research**, processes that centre repair rather than punishment predict satisfaction and recidivism reduction (Sherman and Strang, 2007)
**Forgiveness research** (Worthington et al., 2007)
f: **The face as ethical summons** (Levinas, Totality and Infinity)
**Restorative rather than retributive** (Gilligan, In a Different Voice)
reflections: What wrong do you still owe someone a repair for? What has stopped you?
What is proportionate when the harm cannot be undone, such as a death or a betrayal? Is repair possible then?
How do apologies and restitution differ, and why does each matter to the person who was wronged?

e.t: Recognise natural justice (physikon dikaion)
e.x:
Aristotle distinguishes natural justice (what is just by nature, the same everywhere) from legal justice (what is just by convention, varying from place to place). Some things are unjust regardless of what any law says. Learn to distinguish what is merely legal from what is genuinely just.

(NE V.7, V.10; Politics I.5.)

**Plain words** Some things are just by nature, the same everywhere. Others only by convention, and vary. Some acts are wrong whatever a law says. Learn to tell what's merely legal from what's actually just.

*For example:* A company may legally pay a worker nothing for an hour of required setup. Many would still call that unjust.
e.c: Layer IX - Justice, Equity, and Law
p: **Moral foundations theory**, some moral intuitions appear cross-culturally (Haidt, 2012)
**Moral universals research** (Curry, Mullins and Whitehouse, 2019)
reflections: What is legal but unjust, in your experience? How did you respond?
What makes you confident some acts are wrong whatever any law says? Is that confidence cultural or universal?
How should people act when law and justice conflict, as in civil disobedience? What would you need to be willing to risk?

e.t: Recognise political justice (politikon dikaion)
e.x:
Political justice is justice within a polis: the framework of laws, institutions, and customs that govern the community. It includes both natural and conventional elements. Do not treat politics as separate from ethics; the conditions of flourishing are partly political.

(NE V.6, V.7; Politics III.1.)

**Plain words** Political justice is the framework of laws and customs that shape a community. Part natural, part conventional. Aristotle says politics isn't separate from ethics. Some of the conditions for flourishing are political.

*For example:* A neighbourhood with good public transport makes it easier for everyone to live well, whatever their personal virtue.
e.c: Layer IX - Justice, Equity, and Law
p: **Social determinants of well-being** (Marmot, 2004)
**Procedural justice** (Tyler, 2006)
f: **Justice as fairness** (Rawls, A Theory of Justice)
**Democracy as associated living** (Dewey, Democracy and Education)
reflections: Which political conditions most shape your own chances of flourishing, and which did you not choose?
If flourishing depends partly on politics, is withdrawal from public life a failure of virtue?
What small civic action is within reach and would make flourishing easier for someone else?

e.t: Practise reciprocity (antapodosis)
e.x:
Reciprocity is the principle that governs exchanges between people: give what is due, return what is received, maintain proportion. Reciprocity is not mere tit-for-tat but proportionate exchange guided by a sense of fairness.

(NE V.5, V.6; EE IV.4; MM I.33.)

**Plain words** Reciprocity governs exchange: give what's due, return what's received, keep it proportionate. It's not just tit-for-tat. It's fairness in giving back.

*For example:* Bringing a meal to the neighbour who helped you move isn't a tit-for-tat. It's matching their care in a fitting way.
e.c: Layer IX - Justice, Equity, and Law
p: **Reciprocal altruism research** (Trivers, 1971)
**Social exchange theory** (Homans, 1958)
f: **Reciprocity as foundation of ethics** (Gilligan, In a Different Voice)
reflections: Who gave you something you haven't returned? What would a fitting return look like?
Where do you give much more than you receive, and why do you keep doing it?
Can reciprocity be too strict, as when it turns care into a ledger? What does a relationship that exceeds reciprocity look like?

e.t: Recognise that law is a teacher
e.x:
Law habituates citizens to virtue by requiring just action before they understand why. Good laws make good people. Respect the law not as a constraint but as an educator of character. Where laws are unjust, work to change them; do not simply break them.

(NE V.1, V.3, X.9; Politics III.1.)

**Plain words** Laws teach virtue by making you act justly before you fully understand why. Good laws help make good people. Respect them as teachers of character. Where they're unjust, work to change them instead of simply breaking them.

*For example:* Following a seat-belt law until it becomes a habit turns a rule into your own care.
e.c: Layer IX - Justice, Equity, and Law
p: **Procedural justice**, perceived fairness of law predicts compliance and well-being (Tyler, 2006)
**Moral foundations and authority** (Haidt, 2012)
f: **Justice as fairness** (Rawls, A Theory of Justice)
**Law as moral educator** (Dewey, The Public and Its Problems)
reflections: Recall a rule that you resented and later came to value. What changed?
Where should the line fall between working to change an unjust law and refusing to obey it?
What do laws teach a community about itself, beyond what they forbid?

e.t: Distinguish justice from revenge
e.x:
Justice is proportionate; revenge is excessive. Justice is public; revenge is private. Justice aims at restoration; revenge aims at suffering. When wronged, seek justice, not revenge. The difference is in the motive, the measure, and the method.

(NE V.4, V.11; Rhetoric I.10, II.2.)

**Plain words** Justice is proportionate, public and aims to restore. Revenge is excessive, private and aims to make someone suffer. When wronged, look for justice. The difference lies in motive, measure and method.

*For example:* Reporting a theft to the police and asking for the item back is justice. Slashing the thief's tyres isn't.
e.c: Layer IX - Justice, Equity, and Law
p: **Forgiveness research** (Worthington et al., 2007)
**Restorative justice** (Sherman and Strang, 2007)
f: **The face as ethical summons** (Levinas, Totality and Infinity)
reflections: When wronged, what in your reaction tells you whether you want repair or the other person's pain?
Justice and revenge can look alike from outside. What would an honest observer need to see to tell them apart?
How do societies' punishments serve restoration or revenge, and what would it take to shift the balance?

e.t: Recognise that some actions are always wrong
e.x:
Aristotle holds that some acts are always wrong regardless of circumstances: murder, theft, adultery. These are wrong in themselves, not because of excess or deficiency. Know your unconditional commitments.

(NE II.6.)

**Plain words** Aristotle says some acts are wrong whatever the circumstances, like murder and theft. They aren't wrong by being too much or too little. Know your own non-negotiables, and decide them before you're under pressure.

*For example:* A person who decides in advance "I'll never falsify a record" doesn't weigh it up when a boss leans on them.
e.c: Layer IX - Justice, Equity, and Law
p: **Moral foundations theory**, sanctity/degradation and harm/care as moral universals (Haidt, 2012)
**Moral universals research** (Curry, Mullins and Whitehouse, 2019)
reflections: What are your non-negotiables, the things you would never do? Where did they come from?
Does having absolute rules make a person more or less wise? When have you been tempted to weigh up something you should have refused outright?
How do absolute commitments protect people in suffering from being treated as a means to an end?

e.t: Practise equity over strict legality
e.x:
Equity (epieikeia) is the virtue that corrects the rigidity of law. Sometimes strict application of a rule produces injustice because the particular case was not foreseen by the legislator. The equitable person knows when to bend the rule for the sake of justice itself.

(NE V.10.)

**Plain words** Equity corrects the stiffness of law. Sometimes applying a rule rigidly causes injustice because nobody foresaw this case. The equitable person knows when to bend it for justice's sake.

*For example:* A school dropping a penalty for a student who missed an exam during a family emergency is being equitable.
e.c: Layer IX - Justice, Equity, and Law
p: **Moral situation research**, context dominates in real moral choice (Doris, Lack of Character)
**Contextual intelligence** (Sternberg, 2019)
f: **Equity as correction of law** (Aristotle, NE V.10)
reflections: When did strict rule-following hurt someone you know? What was the rule's real purpose?
How do you ensure equity does not become a cover for favouring your friends?
What does it feel like to be on the receiving end of a rule's rigidity? Describe a time you were.

e.t: Recognise the limits of law
e.x:
Law is general; particular cases are specific. No law can anticipate every situation. The gap between law and justice is filled by phronesis: the practical wisdom that knows when to follow the law and when to depart from it.

(NE V.10, VI.8; Politics III.11.)

**Plain words** Law is general and cases are specific, so no law covers everything. The gap between law and justice is filled by practical wisdom, which knows when to follow the law and when to depart from it.

*For example:* A speed limit is sensible, but a driver rushing a bleeding passenger to hospital is a case the rule didn't have in mind.
e.c: Layer IX - Justice, Equity, and Law
p: **Moral dilemma research** (Kohlberg, 1981)
**Dual-process models of moral judgment** (Greene et al., 2001)
f: **The moral situation** (Dewey, Human Nature and Conduct)
reflections: What rule do you think fails to fit your situation? How do you decide whether to depart from it?
If the gap between law and justice is filled by practical wisdom, who should we trust to have it?
Describe a case where following the law cost someone dearly and a wise person acted differently.

e.t: Recognise that virtue is taught through habituation
e.x:
Virtue is not innate; it is cultivated through education and habituation. Law and education shape character from the outside in. Support educational practices that cultivate virtue, not merely skills. In your own life, treat education as character formation, not information transfer.

(NE I.9, II.1, X.9; Politics VIII.1.)

**Plain words** Virtue isn't inborn. It's grown through education and habit. So treat education as shaping character, not just handing over information. Support teaching that builds good people, not only skilled ones.

*For example:* A teacher who makes students practise fair debate, taking turns and admitting errors, is teaching more than the topic.
e.c: Layer X - Education and Habituation
p: **Learning orientation versus performance orientation** (Dweck and Leggett, 1988)
**Character education programmes** (Berkowitz and Bier, 2007)
f: **The child and the curriculum** (Dewey, The Child and the Curriculum)
reflections: What did your own schooling teach you about character beyond subjects? What was missing?
Can virtue be taught, or only practised? What would a school that aimed at it look like?
How do the habits of a household or classroom shape how people later treat the suffering?

e.t: Support education as the foundation of virtue
e.x:
The polis exists for the sake of the good life, and the good life requires good citizens. Education is the process by which the polis creates good citizens. Support educational practices that cultivate virtue, not merely skills.

(NE X.9; Politics VIII.1, VIII.3.)

**Plain words** The city exists for the good life, and that needs good citizens. Education is how it makes them. Aristotle asks us to support schooling that builds virtue, not merely skills.

*For example:* A parent-teacher group that argues for time on cooperation and honesty, not just exam results, is acting on this.
e.c: Layer X - Education and Habituation
p: **Character education programmes** (Berkowitz and Bier, 2007)
**Moral development research** (Kohlberg, 1981)
f: **Social democracy as ethical ideal** (Dewey, The Public and Its Problems)
reflections: What do you want education to do beyond skills? Who would object to your answer?
Whose responsibility is moral education: schools, families or the state? What are the risks of each?
How might education help a society respond to suffering rather than look away?

e.t: Practise habituation through repeated action
e.x:
Character is built through repetition. You become just by doing just acts, brave by doing brave acts. The first acts are awkward and conscious; later they become natural and effortless. Do not wait for the right feeling; act first, and the disposition follows.

(NE II.1, II.4, II.5.)

**Plain words** Character comes through repetition. You become just by doing just things, brave by doing brave things. Early attempts are awkward and deliberate, later ones become natural. Don't wait for the mood.

*For example:* A person trying to be more patient starts by pausing before every reply for a week. By week four it happens without effort.
e.c: Layer X - Education and Habituation
p: **Habit formation research**, automaticity builds through repetition (Lally et al., 2010; Wood and Neal, 2007)
**Behavioral activation** (Dimidjian et al., 2011)
f: **Belief as habit of action** (Peirce, "How to Make Our Ideas Clear")
**Habit as will** (Dewey, Human Nature and Conduct)
reflections: What act could you repeat daily to build a trait you want? What stopped you last time you tried?
Is there a risk that habit becomes mere routine without understanding? How do you keep it alive?
How have repeated small acts of kindness changed someone you know, or you?

e.t: Start moral education early
e.x:
Aristotle insists that moral education must begin in childhood, when the soul is most plastic. The habits formed in youth shape the character of the adult. If you have children, take their moral education seriously. If you are educating yourself, start where you are.

(NE II.1, II.3, X.9; Politics VII.15-17, VIII.1.)

**Plain words** Aristotle says moral education has to begin young, when the soul is most formable. Childhood habits shape the adult. If you have children, take it seriously. If you're educating yourself, start from where you are.

*For example:* Teaching a five-year-old to say thank you and mean it is an early lesson. You can start at forty with one small habit.
e.c: Layer X - Education and Habituation
p: **Developmental psychology and character formation** (Thompson and Gullone, 2008)
**Early childhood education research** (Heckman, 2006)
f: **The child and the curriculum** (Dewey, The Child and the Curriculum)
reflections: Which habit from your early years still shapes you, for good or ill? Where did it come from?
If early habits matter so much, what is the situation of those who got a poor start? Is it ever too late?
What would you begin today, at your age, that you wish someone had taught you earlier?

e.t: Use music and the arts for moral education
e.x:
Aristotle argues that music and the arts are not merely entertainment but tools of moral education. They shape character by cultivating the right pleasures and aversions. Engage with art that elevates: music, poetry, drama that teaches you to feel the right things.

(Politics VIII.5-7; NE II.2, X.9; Poetics 4-6.)

**Plain words** Music and the arts aren't just entertainment. They shape what you enjoy and dislike. Aristotle recommends art that lifts: music, poetry and drama that teach you to feel the right things.

*For example:* A play that makes you feel real sympathy for someone you'd normally dismiss trains something in you.
e.c: Layer X - Education and Habituation
p: **Music and emotion research** (Juslin and Sloboda, 2010)
**Narrative empathy and moral education** (Mar and Oatley, 2008)
reflections: What piece of art changed how you feel about other people? Describe the change.
Does art teach moral feeling, or merely show it? How would you know?
What does it mean that tragedy gathers people to feel pity and fear together? What might that do for a community in grief?

e.t: Practise leisure (scholē) as the end of work
e.x:
Aristotle argues that leisure is the end of work, not the reverse. We work in order to have leisure; we do not have leisure in order to work. Leisure is not idleness but the free activity of the soul for its own sake: contemplation, friendship, play. Do not confuse leisure with consumption.

(Politics VII.14-15; NE X.7; MM I.34.)

**Plain words** We work in order to have leisure, not the other way round. Leisure isn't idleness. It's free activity for its own sake: thinking, friendship, play. Don't mistake it for consumption.

*For example:* Spending Saturday cooking with friends and talking is leisure. Spending it clicking through shopping apps is something else.
e.c: Layer X - Education and Habituation
p: **Time affluence** (Kasser and Sheldon, 2009)
**Autotelic activity** (Csikszentmihalyi, 1990)
f: **The specious present** (James, The Principles of Psychology)
reflections: What does leisure mean in your week, as distinct from rest or entertainment? What did you do the last time you had it?
If work is for the sake of leisure, how do societies that overwork their people fail them?
Who has leisure in your community, and who doesn't? What does that say about who gets to flourish?

e.t: Distinguish leisure from amusement
e.x:
Amusement is a form of rest, not an end in itself. Leisure (scholē) is higher than amusement: it is activity for its own sake, not for recovery from work. Do not arrange your life around amusement. Arrange it around leisure in the Aristotelian sense.

(Politics VII.14-15; NE X.6.)

**Plain words** Amusement is a rest from work, not a goal. Leisure is higher: activity for its own sake. Aristotle says to arrange life around leisure, not just amusement.

*For example:* Binge-watching to recover from work is amusement. Spending the same hours learning the guitar is closer to leisure.
e.c: Layer X - Education and Habituation
p: **Intrinsic motivation** (Deci and Ryan, 2000)
**Process goals versus outcome goals** (Vallerand, 2010)
reflections: How much of your free time is recovery, and how much is real leisure? What would you change?
Is there anything wrong with amusement? When does it become a way of avoiding something?
What activity would be leisure for you, something done only for its own sake and worth the whole afternoon?

e.t: Make your household a school of virtue
e.x:
Aristotle's ethics extends into the household: the relationships of parent and child, husband and wife, master and servant are contexts for virtue. Your family life is not separate from your moral life; it is where most of your virtue is practised. Treat your household as the primary site of character formation.

(NE VIII.10-12; Politics I.3-13.)

**Plain words** Ethics begins at home. Relationships between parents and children, partners, and others in the household are where most virtue is practised. Treat your household as your main school of character.

*For example:* How you handle a spilled drink at dinner teaches more about patience than any lecture.
e.c: Layer X - Education and Habituation
p: **Family systems theory** (Bowen, 1978)
**Authoritative parenting and child outcomes** (Baumrind, 1991)
f: **The household as moral community** (Confucian tradition, Analects)
reflections: What does your household teach about character, by what it praises and what it permits?
Which virtue is hardest to practise at home? Why does that setting test it so?
Households can also be where harm happens. How does a philosophy of the household speak to those for whom home is not safe?

e.t: Understand that emotions are cognitive
e.x:
Aristotle's theory of emotions is not that they are mere feelings but that they involve judgments about situations. Anger is a judgment of injustice; fear is a judgment of danger; pity is a judgment of undeserved suffering. Understand your emotions as judgments, not as raw sensations.

(Rhetoric II.1-11; NE II.5.)

**Plain words** Emotions aren't just raw feelings. They carry judgements. Anger judges injustice, fear judges danger, pity judges undeserved suffering. So read your emotions as judgements you can examine.

*For example:* Feeling furious at a colleague contains a judgement that you were treated unfairly. You can ask whether that's true.
e.c: Layer XI - Emotions and Practical Reasoning
p: **Cognitive appraisal theory of emotion** (Lazarus, 1991)
**Appraisal theory research** (Scherer, Schorr and Johnstone, 2001)
f: **Emotions as judgments** (Stoic tradition; Nussbaum, Upheavals of Thought)
**Where phronesis and emotions connect** (Aristotle, NE VI)
reflections: What judgement sits inside your strongest recent emotion? Is it accurate?
If emotions are judgements, can they be corrected by argument alone? What else changes them?
How does treating emotions as judgements change how you listen to someone who is distressed?

e.t: Understand anger (orge)
e.x:
Aristotle defines anger as a distressed desire for conspicuous revenge caused by a conspicuous slight. Anger involves a judgment: that you have been wronged and that revenge is appropriate. Examine the judgment behind your anger. Is the slight real? Is revenge appropriate?

(Rhetoric II.2; NE IV.5.)

**Plain words** Aristotle defines anger as distress wanting visible revenge after a visible slight. It contains a judgement: that you've been wronged and revenge fits. So check both. Was the slight real, and is revenge appropriate?

*For example:* Someone didn't thank you in a meeting. You feel angry. Asking "was that a slight, or just forgetfulness?" changes what you do next.
e.c: Layer XI - Emotions and Practical Reasoning
p: **Anger regulation research** (Gross, 2015)
**Cognitive-behavioural approaches to anger** (Beck, 1976)
reflections: When did anger last make a claim about being wronged? Was the claim true?
Aristotle links anger to a wish for conspicuous revenge. Have you felt that, and what did you do with it?
How might examining the judgement behind anger, rather than suppressing it, change a conflict you are in?

e.t: Understand fear (phobos)
e.x:
Fear is a pain or disturbance caused by the imagination of future evil. Fear involves a judgment about danger: that something bad is coming and that you are vulnerable. Examine your fears. Are the imagined evils real? Is your vulnerability as great as you think?

(Rhetoric II.5; NE III.6.)

**Plain words** Fear is distress about imagined future harm. It judges that something bad is coming and that you're vulnerable. So check the picture. Is the harm real? Are you as exposed as it feels?

*For example:* Dreading a talk, you picture the room laughing. Asking what's most likely to happen puts the fear in proportion.
e.c: Layer XI - Emotions and Practical Reasoning
p: **Fear conditioning and anxiety research** (LeDoux, 1996)
**Cognitive-behavioural therapy for anxiety** (Beck, 1976)
f: **Courage as the mean in fear** (Aristotle, NE III.6-9)
**Do not fear what you cannot control** (Epictetus, Enchiridion 1)
reflections: What are you afraid of that hasn't happened? How likely is it, if you're honest?
Some fears are justified. How do you separate wise caution from imagined evils?
How does chronic fear shape a person's judgement, and what helps?

e.t: Understand pity (eleos)
e.x:
Pity is a pain caused by the sight of an evil that appears undeserved and likely to happen to oneself or one's own. Pity involves a judgment: that the suffering is undeserved and that one is vulnerable to similar fate. Practise pity where it is warranted, but examine whether the suffering is truly undeserved.

(Rhetoric II.8; NE II.7.)

**Plain words** Pity is pain at suffering that looks undeserved and could happen to you or yours. It judges the suffering as undeserved and yourself as vulnerable. Use it where it's warranted, but check whether the suffering really is undeserved.

*For example:* Feeling for a laid-off colleague is warranted. Asking whether it was truly out of their control keeps your pity honest.
e.c: Layer XI - Emotions and Practical Reasoning
p: **Empathy and compassion research** (Goetz et al., 2010; Zaki, 2014)
**Just-world belief and empathy** (Lerner, 1980)
f: **Compassion as co-suffering** (Scheler, The Nature of Sympathy)
**The face as ethical summons** (Levinas, Totality and Infinity)
reflections: Whom do you pity, and whom do you refuse to? What judgement about desert sits underneath?
Pity can be condescending. How might compassion differ from it?
How does the thought "this could happen to me" change how a society treats suffering?

e.t: Understand shame (aischynē)
e.x:
Shame is a pain or disturbance concerning evils that seem to bring us into disrepute. Shame involves a judgment about reputation: that what we have done would diminish us in the eyes of others. Distinguish healthy shame (which guides behaviour) from toxic shame (which attacks the self).

(Rhetoric II.6; NE IV.9.)

**Plain words** Shame is distress about things that would bring disrepute. It judges that what you did would diminish you in others' eyes. Healthy shame guides behaviour. Toxic shame attacks the person. Learn to tell them apart.

*For example:* Feeling uneasy about padding an expense claim is healthy. Replaying an awkward comment from years ago and feeling worthless isn't.
e.c: Layer XI - Emotions and Practical Reasoning
p: **Shame and guilt research** (Tangney and Dearing, 2002)
**Self-conscious emotions research** (Tracy and Robins, 2004)
reflections: Which shame guides you well, and which just hurts? How do you tell them apart?
Many people are shamed for things that are not their fault. What does this say about shame as a social tool?
How might you respond to a person caught in toxic shame, without excusing real wrongdoing?

e.t: Understand envy (phthonos)
e.x:
Envy is a pain caused by the good fortune of others. It involves a judgment that another's success diminishes you. Examine your envy. Does another's good truly threaten you? Can you convert envy into emulation (zeal to equal or surpass)?

(Rhetoric II.10; NE II.7, IV.9.)

**Plain words** Envy is pain at someone else's good fortune, and it judges that their success shrinks you. Ask whether it truly does. Then see if you can turn it into emulation: wanting to rise to their level, not pull them down.

*For example:* Seeing a friend's book deal sting, then asking "what could I learn from how she worked?" turns the sting into a plan.
e.c: Layer XI - Emotions and Practical Reasoning
p: **Social comparison research** (Festinger, 1954)
**Benign versus malicious envy** (van de Ven, Zeelenberg and Pieters, 2009)
reflections: Whose success stings you, and what is the story behind that sting?
Does another's success diminish you? How does the belief that it does come about?
What would it take to turn envy into learning, and what would it mean for friendships?

e.t: Understand emulation (zelos)
e.x:
Emulation is a distress caused by the presence of good things that are highly valued and not possessed by oneself, combined with a desire to obtain them. Unlike envy, emulation does not wish to deprive the other but to rise to their level. Convert envy into emulation.

(Rhetoric II.11; NE II.7.)

**Plain words** Emulation is distress at lacking something valued that others have, with a drive to get it. Unlike envy, it doesn't want to take it from them. It wants to rise. Turn envy into emulation.

*For example:* A junior designer who sees a colleague's polished portfolio and starts studying how it's built is emulating.
e.c: Layer XI - Emotions and Practical Reasoning
p: **Mastery goals versus performance goals** (Dweck and Leggett, 1988)
**Role model research** (Lockwood and Kunda, 1997)
f: **Pursue becoming, not arrival** (Maslow, Toward a Psychology of Being)
reflections: Who do you most want to equal? What is the first concrete step toward their level?
How do you keep emulation from sliding into envy or despair? What would prevent that?
Do societies encourage emulation or only comparison? What changes between the two?

e.t: Practise persuasion through ethos
e.x:
Aristotle argues that persuasion depends on three things: the character of the speaker (ethos), the emotional state of the audience (pathos), and the logical force of the argument (logos). Of these, ethos is the most powerful. Build credibility through character, not through rhetoric.

(Rhetoric I.2, II.1; NE I.6.)

**Plain words** Persuasion rests on character, audience feeling, and the argument. Aristotle says character matters most. So build credibility through who you are, not through clever talk.

*For example:* A colleague with a record of being straight gets listened to even when her slides are plain.
e.c: Layer XI - Emotions and Practical Reasoning
p: **Source credibility research** (Hovland and Weiss, 1951)
**Trust and persuasion** (Cialdini, 2007)
reflections: What are you trusted for, and how did you earn it? What could erode it quickly?
If character persuades more than argument, how does this affect public life where image often substitutes for character?
Whom have you been persuaded by because of who they are, not what they said? Was it justified?

e.t: Recognise that emotions shape judgment
e.x:
Emotions are not separate from reasoning; they shape how we perceive, what we attend to, and what conclusions we reach. The practically wise person does not suppress emotion but understands its role in judgment and uses it as information.

(Rhetoric I.1, II.1-11; NE II.5, VI.2; De Anima I.1.)

**Plain words** Emotions shape what you see, what you notice, and what you conclude. The wise person doesn't suppress them. They understand what they're doing and use them as information.

*For example:* Feeling uneasy before signing a contract, and asking what that unease points to, is using the emotion as data.
e.c: Layer XI - Emotions and Practical Reasoning
p: **Affect as information** (Schwarz and Clore, 1983)
**Moral intuition research**, moral judgments often precede reasoning (Haidt, 2001)
f: **Where phronesis and emotions connect** (Aristotle, NE VI)
reflections: What emotion shaped your last important decision? What was it telling you that your reasoning missed?
Emotions can mislead. How do you tell useful information from distortion?
How does attention to feeling change how you decide in situations where others' pain is involved?

e.t: Distinguish what is up to you from what is not
e.x:
Some things are within your control (prohairesis): your judgements, intentions, desires, and aversions. Other things are not: your body, reputation, possessions, other people's opinions, and external events. Focus your energy exclusively on what is within your control. What is not up to you is none of your concern.

(Ench. 1; Disc. I.1, I.22.)

**Plain words** Some things are yours to decide: what you judge, intend, want, and avoid. Everything else, your body, your name, your money, other people's opinions, isn't. Spend your effort on the first list. Anxiety is mostly energy aimed at the second.

*For example:* Before an exam you can't control the questions, only how you prepare and how you take a bad start. Epictetus says put all your attention on those two.
e.c: Layer I - First Principles: The Dichotomy of Control and Virtue
p: **Locus of control**, internal locus predicts well-being and health (Rotter, 1966)
**Acceptance and Commitment Therapy**, the distinction between what can be changed and what must be accepted is the foundation of psychological flexibility (Hayes, Strosahl and Wilson, 2011)
f: **Serene acceptance of necessity** (Epictetus, Enchiridion; echoed in Spinoza, Ethics V)
reflections: List what you worried about this week. Sort each item honestly into "mine" and "not mine", and notice what the worry was actually trying to do.

The dichotomy can sound like permission to ignore politics, illness or injustice because they are "outside our control." Where does it help you act, and where could it become an excuse? Test it on a cause you care about.
Some people have very little control over their circumstances: a prisoner, a refugee, a patient. What does this principle offer them that isn't an insult, and what would they be right to reject?

e.t: Make virtue the only genuine good
e.x:
Wealth, health, reputation, and pleasure are "preferred indifferents": they have value but are not good in the strict sense. Only virtue, the excellent condition of the rational soul, is genuinely good. Only vice is genuinely bad. Everything else is indifferent. Orient your life around this hierarchy: virtue above all, then preferred indifferents, never confusing the two.

(Ench. 1; Disc. II.19; Med. III.6, VI.13.)

**Plain words** Money, health, reputation and pleasure are worth having, but they aren't good in the strict sense. Only the state of your own reasoning soul is. So organise life with virtue first, the preferred things second, and don't confuse the two when the second starts shouting.

*For example:* You can prefer the bigger flat. But if getting it means shading the truth with your landlord, the Stoic says you've swapped a good for an indifferent.
e.c: Layer I - First Principles: The Dichotomy of Control and Virtue
p: **Intrinsic versus extrinsic goal content**, intrinsic goals (growth, connection, contribution) predict well-bei...)
**Values clarification in ACT**, values as chosen qualities of action that organise behaviour (Hayes et al., 2011)
f: **Eudaimonia as activity of the soul in accord with virtue** (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.7)
reflections: Recall a time you traded something virtuous for something preferred. What did the trade feel like at the time, and what did it feel like a year later?
Calling health and wealth "indifferent" can sound absurd to someone who is ill or poor. What is the strongest version of the Stoic claim, and what is the strongest objection?
If only virtue is good, what is the status of suffering in other people's lives? Does it matter less, and how would you want a Stoic to treat it?

e.t: Recognise that you are disturbed not by things but by your judgements about them
e.x:
It is not events that upset you but your interpretation of them. The same event can be seen as catastrophe or as indifference, depending on the story you tell. The work is not to change the event but to examine the judgement.

(Ench. 5; Disc. I.1; Med. IV.7, VIII.47.)

**Plain words** Events don't upset you. Your judgement about them does. The same news can feel like disaster or like a nuisance depending on the story you attach. The work isn't to change the event but to look at the judgement behind your reaction.

*For example:* Two cyclists get a flat tyre on the same road. One reads it as ruin of the day, one as a chance to stretch her legs.
e.c: Layer I - First Principles: The Dichotomy of Control and Virtue
p: **Cognitive-behavioural therapy**, the core CBT model: thoughts mediate between events and emotions, and changing the thought changes the emotion (Beck, 1976; [Stoic origins of CBT](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go...)
**Cognitive reappraisal**, changing the interpretation of a situation to change its emotional impact (Gross, 2015)
reflections: Pick an event that is currently upsetting you. Write down the event in neutral terms, then the judgement you've added. How much of the distress lives in the second sentence?
Some events are terrible by any standard, such as the death of a child. What does the claim "it's your judgement" do or fail to do there?
Who benefits when people are told their suffering is a matter of interpretation? Where might this idea be misused?

e.t: Train your capacity to give or withhold assent to impressions
e.x:
Every experience presents itself as an impression (phantasia): an appearance of how things are. You have a moment of choice: to accept the impression as true or to withhold assent. The trained person pauses, examines, and then decides. The untrained person assents automatically. Practise the pause.

(Disc. I.20, II.18, III.2-3, III.12; Ench. 1.)

**Plain words** Every experience arrives as an impression, an appearance of how things are. There's a gap between the appearance and your agreement to it. The trained person uses the gap: "You seem like an insult. Let me check." The untrained person agrees at once.

*For example:* A friend doesn't reply for two days and your mind says "they're angry with me." The practice is to say "that's what it looks like" before believing it.
e.c: Layer I - First Principles: The Dichotomy of Control and Virtue
p: **Mindfulness as present-moment awareness with non-judgmental observation**, creating a gap between stimulus and response (Kabat-Zinn, 1990; Baer et al., 2006)
**Response inhibition and cognitive control** (Aron, 2007)
f: **Suspension of judgement (epochē)** (Pyrrho/Sextus Empiricus, Outlines of Pyrrhonism)
reflections: Think of a belief you formed in seconds that shaped a whole afternoon. What would the pause have looked like?
Social media and news are built to provoke instant assent. What does protecting the gap require in practice, and what would it cost you?
How does the capacity to withhold assent relate to freedom, in your experience? Is it possible to be free without it?

e.t: Live according to nature
e.x:
Nature (physis) has a rational order. To live well is to live in accordance with that order: to accept what happens as part of the whole, to fulfil your role in the larger system, and to use reason as the faculty that distinguishes humans from other animals. Study what nature requires of you and align your life with it.

(Med. II.9, IV.10, VII.53; Seneca, Letters 41, 76; Disc. I.6.)

**Plain words** Nature has a rational order, and to live well is to live in line with it: take what happens as part of the whole, fill your role, and use reason, the thing that's distinctive in humans. Study what nature asks of you and fit your life to that.

*For example:* A doctor who accepts that bodies age and die can spend her energy on comfort, not on fighting what can't be fought.
e.c: Layer I - First Principles: The Dichotomy of Control and Virtue
p: **Self-concordance theory**, goals aligned with one's authentic nature predict well-being (Sheldon and Elliot, 1999)
**Values clarification and committed action** (Hayes et al., 2011)
f: **Living according to nature** (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics; Laozi, Daodejing 25)
reflections: What in your life are you resisting that you could, if you looked hard, recognise as simply how things are?
The idea of a rational cosmos is a metaphysical claim many of us don't hold. Can the practical content of "living according to nature" survive without it?
Appeals to "nature" have been used to justify injustice. How would you distinguish a Stoic appeal to nature from those?

e.t: Remember that you are a citizen of the cosmos
e.x:
You belong to a larger community: the city of gods and humans. Act as a citizen of that city, not merely of your household or nation. The Stoic is a cosmopolitan: at home everywhere, obligated to all. Broaden your circle of concern beyond your immediate group.

(Med. IV.4; Disc. I.9, II.10; Seneca, Letters 28, 44.)

**Plain words** You belong to a bigger community, the city of gods and humans. Act as its citizen, not only your household's or your nation's. At home everywhere, owing something to everyone. Widen the circle of concern past the people close to you.

*For example:* Giving a seat to a stranger and also taking an interest in what a distant war does to ordinary people are the same habit at two sizes.
e.c: Layer I - First Principles: The Dichotomy of Control and Virtue
p: **Moral circle expansion research**, the tendency for moral concern to expand over historical time (Crimston et al., 2016)
**Intergroup contact hypothesis** (Allport, 1954; Pettigrew and Tropp, 2006)
f: **Ubuntu: I am because we are** (African relational philosophy)
reflections: Draw your circle of concern as it actually works on an ordinary day, not as you'd like it. Who is at the edge, and who is outside?
Is concern for all of humanity psychologically realistic, or does it dilute care for those near us? How do you hold both?
What would change in your daily choices, what you buy, read, support, if you thought of yourself as a citizen of the world?

e.t: Accept what happens as the will of providence
e.x:
The Stoic accepts what occurs, not passively but as the unfolding of a rational order. What seems like misfortune may be a necessary part of the whole. This is not fatalism; it is the refusal to demand that the universe conform to your preferences. Practise saying "this too is nature."

(Med. IV.10, V.8, VIII.50; Disc. I.12, I.17; Seneca, Letters 107, On Providence.)

**Plain words** The Stoic accepts what happens, not passively but as part of an unfolding order. What looks like misfortune may be a needed piece of the whole. It isn't fatalism. It's refusing to insist the universe match your preferences. Practise saying "this too is nature."

*For example:* A promotion falls through. After the sting, you ask what the world is now offering instead of arguing with the verdict.
e.c: Layer I - First Principles: The Dichotomy of Control and Virtue
p: **Radical acceptance**, accepting reality as it is, not as you wish it to be (Linehan, 1993)
**Amor fati and acceptance-based coping** (Hayes, Strosahl and Wilson, 2011)
reflections: What have you accepted that you once fought? What shifted, the situation or you?
Is acceptance the right response to injustice? Where does "this too is nature" become complicity?
How could this principle be said honestly to someone in the middle of a loss, without sounding like a sermon?

e.t: Remember that virtue is sufficient for flourishing
e.x:
The Stoic holds that virtue alone is necessary and sufficient for eudaimonia. External goods, health, and success are not required. This is a radical claim and a difficult practice. It does not mean ignoring the body or the community; it means not making flourishing dependent on what you cannot control.

(Disc. I.25, II.19, IV.1; Med. VII.44, IX.6.)

**Plain words** For the Stoics, virtue is necessary and sufficient for flourishing. That's a radical claim. It doesn't mean ignoring your body or your community. It means not making your well-being depend on what you can't control.

*For example:* A person who loses her savings and her health but stays honest and kind can, on this view, still be doing life well.
e.c: Layer I - First Principles: The Dichotomy of Control and Virtue
p: **Psychological flexibility as the master skill**, the capacity to be open, aware, and engaged predicts well-being across hundreds of studies (Kashdan and Rottenberg, 2010; Hayes et al., 2011)
**Eudaimonic well-being beyond circumstances** (Ryff, 1989)
f: **The good life as process** (Rogers, On Becoming a Person)
**Self-sufficiency of virtue** (Aristotle, NE I.8, with qualification)
reflections: Do you believe virtue is enough? Test the claim against the hardest case you know.
Compare the Stoic view with Aristotle's, which allows that misfortune can damage flourishing. Which is more livable, and which is more honest?
What would it take for a society to take the Stoic claim seriously and still care about people's material conditions?

e.t: Make philosophy a way of life, not a set of doctrines
e.x:
Stoicism is not a body of knowledge to master but a set of practices to embody. The point is not to be able to recite Stoic doctrine but to live differently. Philosophy is training (askesis) for the soul. Treat it as you would physical training: daily, progressive, applied.

(Disc. III.21; Seneca, Letters 16, 71; Med. I.1, II.1; Musonius Rufus, Lectures.)

**Plain words** Stoicism isn't a body of knowledge to master. It's a set of practices to live. The point isn't reciting doctrine but living differently, and that takes training like physical training: daily, gradual, applied.

*For example:* A person who can quote Marcus Aurelius but still snaps at the waiter hasn't done the work. One who pauses before snapping has.
e.c: Layer I - First Principles: The Dichotomy of Control and Virtue
p: **Behavioural activation**, action precedes and produces motivation (Dimidjian et al., 2011)
**Habit formation research**, automaticity builds through repetition (Lally et al., 2010)
f: **Treat these as practices, not beliefs** (Aristotle, NE II.1)
**Belief as habit of action** (Peirce, "How to Make Our Ideas Clear")
reflections: What philosophy do you know well in words and poorly in practice? Where does the gap hurt most?
What would a daily training plan for one Stoic idea look like for you, and how would you tell whether it was working?
Is there a risk of turning philosophy into self-improvement, a productivity tool, instead of a way of questioning how to live?

e.t: Practise oikeiosis: appropriate self-love
e.x:
The Stoic doctrine of oikeiosis holds that every animal has a natural affinity for its own preservation and well-being. In humans, this extends from self-preservation to self-knowledge to concern for others. You do not need to suppress self-interest; you need to extend it. Begin with care for your own reason and virtue, then extend it to family, community, and all humanity.

(Disc. I.19; Cicero, De Finibus III.16-18; Hierocles, fragments.)

**Plain words** Every animal has an instinct for self-preservation. In humans it grows into self-knowledge and then concern for others. You don't have to kill self-interest. You extend it: start with caring for your own reason and virtue, then widen to family, community and all people.

*For example:* Looking after your own sleep and sanity so you can show up for your children isn't selfish. It's the first ring of the widening circle.
e.c: Layer I - First Principles: The Dichotomy of Control and Virtue
p: **Self-compassion research** (Neff, 2003)
**Social identity and prosocial behaviour** (Cialdini, Brown, Lewis, Luce and Neuberg, 1997)
f: **Ubuntu: I am because we are** (African relational philosophy)
reflections: Where in your life is self-care really care for others in disguise, and where is it only self-indulgence?
How do you move from self-interest to concern for strangers? What experiences expanded your circle?
Some traditions say self-love is the root of suffering. How does oikeiosis answer them, and are you convinced?

e.t: Recognise the three topoi: the three disciplines
e.x:
Epictetus organises Stoic practice into three disciplines: the discipline of desire (what to want and avoid), the discipline of action (how to behave), and the discipline of assent (how to judge). These three correspond to the three parts of philosophy: physics, ethics, and logic. Know which discipline you are practising at any given moment.

(Disc. III.2; Ench. 1-3.)

**Plain words** Epictetus sorts practice into three: desire, action, judgement. What to want and avoid, how to behave, how to assess impressions. Know which one you're working on at any moment. They correspond to the three parts of Stoic philosophy.

*For example:* Feeling jealous? That's desire. Unsure what to do about a late colleague? Action. Convinced they did it out of spite? Judgement.
e.c: Layer I - First Principles: The Dichotomy of Control and Virtue
p: **Self-regulation research**, the integration of motivation, behaviour, and cognition (Carver and Scheier, 1998)
**Psychological flexibility model** (Hayes et al., 2011)
f: **The three trainings** (Buddhist tradition: sila, samadhi, prajna)
reflections: Which of the three disciplines is your weakest at the moment? Give a recent example of where it failed you.
Why might it help to name which discipline a problem belongs to? Does it ever hide the connection between them?
Design a one-week experiment on one discipline, with a clear way to check results.

e.t: Remember that you are a rational being
e.x:
The Stoic holds that what distinguishes humans is reason (logos). Your highest function is to use reason well. When you act irrationally, you act against your own nature. Cultivate your rational capacity as the core of your humanity.

(Disc. I.1, I.6; Med. II.9, IV.16, VII.11; Seneca, Letters 41, 76.)

**Plain words** What marks humans out is reason, and using it well is your highest function. When you act irrationally you act against your nature. So cultivate reasoning as the core of what you are.

*For example:* Choosing to count to ten and think before sending the angry email is reason doing its job.
e.c: Layer I - First Principles: The Dichotomy of Control and Virtue
p: **Dual-process models**, Type 2 (deliberative) reasoning as a distinct human capacity (Kahneman, 2011)
**Rationality research** (Stanovich, 2011)
reflections: When do you reason best, and when do you not at all? What conditions help or hinder?
Emotion and intuition seem equally human. How should a Stoic account of reason make room for them, and does it?
What happens to the dignity of people whose reasoning is impaired by illness, age or disability, if reason is our highest function?

e.t: Discipline your desires
e.x:
Most suffering comes from wanting what you cannot have or avoiding what you cannot escape. Train yourself to want only what is within your control: virtuous action. Everything else, accept when it comes and let it go when it leaves.

(Disc. I.4, III.2; Ench. 2; Med. VI.41, VII.33.)

**Plain words** Most suffering comes from wanting what you can't have or dodging what you can't escape. Train yourself to want only what lies in your control: acting well. Accept the rest when it comes and let it go when it leaves.

*For example:* Hoping for a particular reply from a friend makes the wait unbearable. Wanting to write a kind message makes it done once you've sent it.
e.c: Layer II - The Discipline of Desire
p: **Desire experience-sampling**, desires occupy roughly half of waking hours and resisting them is effortful (Hofmann et al., 2012)
**Craving and self-control research** (Berridge and Kringelbach, 2015)
f: **Craving (tanha) as the root of suffering** (Buddha, Samyutta Nikaya)
**The will as endless lack** (Schopenhauer, The World as Will and Representation)
reflections: What are you wanting right now that is outside your control? What would wanting only the action change?
Is it possible, or desirable, to stop wanting things like love, health or justice for others? Where do you draw the line?
How does this advice relate to ambition? Can a person be driven and still discipline desire this way?

e.t: Want what actually happens
e.x:
Do not wish for things to be other than they are. The person who wants reality to conform to their desires is perpetually frustrated. The person who wants reality as it is has no frustration. Practise the reframing: "this is what I wanted," meaning, "this is what nature has produced, and I accept it."

(Disc. I.12, I.17; Med. IV.10, VIII.50; Seneca, On Providence.)

**Plain words** Don't wish things were otherwise. The person who wants reality to match their desires is permanently frustrated, and the one who wants reality as it is has no frustration. The practice is to reframe: "this is what nature has produced, and I'm taking it."

*For example:* Rain on your wedding day. Wanting dry weather ruins it. Wanting this day, rained on, saves it.
e.c: Layer II - The Discipline of Desire
p: **Acceptance-based behaviour therapy**, acceptance reduces suffering at constant pain (McCracken, 1998; Vowles et al., 2014)
**Cognitive reappraisal as meaning-making** (Gross, 2015)
reflections: What fact about your life do you spend the most energy wishing were different? What would it mean to want it as it is, even for one day?
Is wanting what happens just resignation dressed up? Describe a difference you've lived.
Can this stance sit alongside the energy needed to change an unjust situation? How?

e.t: Distinguish preferred from dispreferred indifferents
e.x:
Health, wealth, and reputation are not goods but preferred indifferents: you may reasonably pursue them, but your flourishing does not depend on them. Sickness, poverty, and disrepute are dispreferred but not bad. Hold preferred indifferents loosely: pursue them without attachment, lose them without grief.

(Disc. II.19, IV.1; Med. III.6; Seneca, Letters 71, 82, 92.)

**Plain words** Health, wealth and reputation aren't goods but preferred indifferents: you can sensibly pursue them without your flourishing depending on them. Sickness, poverty and disrepute are dispreferred but not bad. Hold the preferred things loosely.

*For example:* You can work for a raise and treat it as a nice extra rather than the measure of your worth.
e.c: Layer II - The Discipline of Desire
p: **Nonattachment research**, nonattachment predicts well-being beyond mindfulness (Sahdra et al., 2010)
**Intrinsic versus extrinsic goal content** (Kasser and Ryan, 1996)
f: **The having versus being mode** (Fromm, To Have or To Be?)
reflections: Which preferred thing do you hold too tightly? What would loosening look like?
What is the difference between pursuing something with attachment and without? Describe it in a situation you know.
How does the idea of dispreferred indifferents change how we should treat the poor, sick and disgraced? Does it make us kinder or colder?

e.t: Do not desire what belongs to others
e.x:
Envy is the desire for what you do not have, directed at someone who has it. It poisons relationships and distorts judgment. The Stoic trains to be content with what they have and to rejoice in others' good fortune. Practise sympathetic joy: when others succeed, feel glad, not diminished.

(Med. VI.13, VI.16, IX.34; Seneca, Letters 109.)

**Plain words** Envy is wanting what someone else has. It poisons relationships and warps judgement. The Stoic trains to be content with their own and glad of others' good luck. When someone succeeds, practise being glad instead of smaller.

*For example:* A friend gets the job you wanted. You send a real congratulation, and then find your own work a little lighter.
e.c: Layer II - The Discipline of Desire
p: **Social comparison processes** (Festinger, 1954)
**Sympathetic joy (mudita) research** (Condon and Makransky, 2020)
f: **Amour-propre as comparative vanity** (Rousseau, Discourse on the Origin of Inequality)
reflections: Whose good fortune do you find hardest to celebrate? What is the envy telling you that you want?
Can envy ever be useful as information about your own values? How is that different from letting it rule you?
How do comparison-driven environments like social media shape envy, and how might you protect yourself?

e.t: Refuse to see externals as good or bad
e.x:
The judgement that wealth is good or poverty is bad is the source of endless disturbance. Externals are indifferent. The only good is virtue; the only bad is vice. Practise this distinction until it becomes habitual.

(Disc. I.30, II.19, III.3; Med. III.6, VI.13; Ench. 1.)

**Plain words** Calling wealth good or poverty bad is the source of endless disturbance. Externals are indifferent. Only virtue is good and only vice is bad. Keep practising that distinction until it's automatic.

*For example:* Losing a client feels like a disaster until you ask whether you acted honestly. If you did, the loss is only a loss of income.
e.c: Layer II - The Discipline of Desire
p: **Cognitive defusion**, seeing thoughts and labels as mental events rather than literal truths (Hayes et al., 2011)
**Nonattachment** (Sahdra et al., 2010)
f: **The map is not the territory** (Korzybski, Science and Sanity)
reflections: What outcome do you currently treat as a disaster? Re-describe it using only "virtue" and "vice" and see what changes.
Is this stance realistic for people for whom money or illness decides whether their children eat? How should it be said to them?
What would you lose, and gain, if you really believed only virtue mattered?

e.t: Accept loss without devastation
e.x:
What you have was given; what is given can be taken. When you lose something, do not say "I have lost what is mine." Say: "it has returned to where it came from." Nothing is truly yours except your character.

(Ench. 11, 15; Med. II.11, IV.1, VI.14; Seneca, Letters 24, 91, 99.)

**Plain words** What you have was given, and what's given can be taken. When you lose something, don't say "I lost what was mine." Say "it went back to where it came from." Nothing is truly yours except your character.

*For example:* When a friend moves abroad, you can resent the loss, or you can be grateful she was in your life at all.
e.c: Layer II - The Discipline of Desire
p: **Grief and meaning-making research**, the dual-process model of grief (Stroebe and Schut, 1999)
**Acceptance and commitment therapy for loss** (Hayes et al., 2011)
reflections: What have you lost that you still speak of as taken rather than returned? What would it be like to change the verb?
Is the idea that nothing but character is yours comforting or cold? Discuss with a specific loss in mind.
How might this principle fail people who have been robbed, abused or wronged? What should be said to them instead?

e.t: Prepare for adversity before it arrives
e.x:
Premeditation of evils (praemeditatio malorum) is the practice of rehearsing misfortune in advance: poverty, illness, loss, death. Not to induce anxiety but to reduce shock. The mind that has rehearsed is not overwhelmed when reality arrives. Practise this daily, briefly, calmly.

(Seneca, Letters 18, 24, 107; Med. III.1, VI.34; Disc. I.14, III.26.)

**Plain words** Premeditation of evils means rehearsing misfortune ahead of time: poverty, illness, loss, death. Not to create anxiety but to reduce shock. A mind that has rehearsed isn't flattened when reality arrives. Do it daily, briefly, calmly.

*For example:* Before a long flight with your elderly parent, you quietly think through what you'd do if she fell ill, then board feeling steadier.
e.c: Layer II - The Discipline of Desire
p: **Mental contrasting (WOOP)**, anticipating obstacles improves goal purs...)
**Stress inoculation training** (Meichenbaum, 1985)
f: **The obstacle is the way** (Marcus Aurelius, Meditations V.20)
reflections: What misfortune do you avoid rehearsing, and what does the avoidance protect you from?
When does rehearsal become rumination? What distinguishes a calm visualisation from anxiety?
Have you been prepared for a loss and still devastated? What does that tell you about the limits of premeditation?

e.t: Remember that nothing can harm you except your own judgement
e.x:
No external event can touch your character. Only your response can. The person who insults you cannot harm you; only your anger at the insult can. The person who takes your property cannot harm you; only your desire for the property can. Practise the distinction between event and response.

(Disc. I.1, I.18, I.28; Ench. 5; Med. IV.7, VIII.47.)

**Plain words** No outside event can touch your character, only your response can. The person who insults you can't harm you. Your anger at the insult can. The person who takes your property can't harm you. Your craving for it can. Practise separating event from response.

*For example:* A rude email lands. The email is a fact. The three hours of seething afterwards are yours.
e.c: Layer II - The Discipline of Desire
p: **Cognitive-behavioural model**, interpretations mediate between events and emotions (Beck, 1976)
**Psychological flexibility** (Kashdan and Rottenberg, 2010)
reflections: What harm have you attributed to others that you actually did to yourself afterwards? Be specific.
Is there harm that no response can cancel, such as being physically hurt or exploited? How does the Stoic claim handle it?
What is the relationship between "nothing can harm you" and the need for protection and justice for the vulnerable?

e.t: Do not desire externals as if they were permanent
e.x:
Everything external is subject to change: wealth, status, health, relationships. The person who depends on externals for happiness builds on sand. Anchor your well-being in what cannot be taken: your own character.

(Disc. I.25, II.5; Med. II.11, IV.1, VI.14; Seneca, Letters 8, 71, 87.)

**Plain words** Everything external changes: wealth, status, health, relationships. Anyone who depends on them for happiness builds on sand. Anchor your well-being in what can't be taken: your own character.

*For example:* A person whose confidence rests on her job title is shaken at redundancy. One whose confidence rests on how she treats people carries it to the next job.
e.c: Layer II - The Discipline of Desire
p: **Hedonic adaptation**, gains and losses both fade toward baseline (Lyubomirsky, 2011)
**Nonattachment** (Sahdra et al., 2010)
f: **The having versus being mode** (Fromm, To Have or To Be?)
reflections: What is the sand under your sense of well-being, the thing you would panic to lose? What would anchoring elsewhere mean?
Is anchoring in character itself fragile? Illness or trauma can change character. What then?
How do you hold deep attachments, such as love for a child, alongside a view that externals are unstable?

e.t: Do not fear poverty
e.x:
Poverty is a dispreferred indifferent, not an evil. The Stoic can live well in poverty. Seneca practised voluntary poverty to demonstrate that wealth is not necessary for flourishing. Do not make your well-being dependent on your bank balance.

(Seneca, Letters 17, 18, 87; Epictetus, Disc. I.9, III.7; Med. III.6, VI.13.)

**Plain words** Poverty is a dispreferred indifferent, not an evil. A Stoic can live well in it. Seneca practised voluntary poverty to show wealth wasn't necessary. Don't make your well-being depend on your bank balance.

*For example:* Spending a week on the bare minimum and finding you were fine, apart from small pains, loosens the fear a little.
e.c: Layer II - The Discipline of Desire
p: **Income and well-being**, diminishing but context-dependent returns (Kahneman and Deaton, 2010; Killingsworth, Kahneman and Mellers, 2023)
**Simple living and well-being** (Brown and Kasser, 2005)
reflections: What would you actually miss if you lost half your income? What would you discover you didn't need?
There is a difference between voluntary and involuntary poverty. What can a wealthy person like Seneca not know about it?
How should this principle be held in a society where poverty also means insecurity, lack of care and shame?

e.t: Do not fear pain
e.x:
Pain is a dispreferred indifferent. It is unpleasant but not evil. The Stoic faces pain with dignity, knowing that it cannot harm the character. Seneca argues that suffering can even strengthen virtue. Do not flee pain at the cost of integrity.

(Seneca, Letters 24, 67, 78, 107; Med. VII.33, IX.41, X.33; Disc. I.1, I.6, I.14.)

**Plain words** Pain is unpleasant but not evil, and it can't harm your character. The Stoic faces it with dignity, and Seneca argues it can even strengthen virtue. Don't run from pain at the cost of your integrity.

*For example:* Getting through a hard physical therapy session without complaint, because the recovery matters more than the comfort.
e.c: Layer II - The Discipline of Desire
p: **Acceptance-based behaviour therapy for chronic pain** (McCracken, 1998; Vowles et al., 2014)
**Radical acceptance** (Linehan, 1993)
f: **The mean in pleasure and pain** (Aristotle, NE II.6)
reflections: What pain have you faced that changed you? What did it teach, and what did it only damage?
Is stoic endurance always healthy? When does it become denial or an obstacle to seeking help?
How do we honour chronic pain that cannot be endured nobly, and that has no lesson in it?

e.t: Do not fear death
e.x:
Death is a natural event, not an evil. The Stoic holds that death is either the end of consciousness (in which case there is nothing to fear) or a transition (in which case there is nothing to fear). More practically: the fear of death is a judgement that death is bad, and that judgement can be examined and revised.

(Med. II.11, II.14, III.1, IV.19, VII.2, VII.29; Seneca, Letters 24, 82, 99, 104, 122; Disc. I.14.)

**Plain words** Death is natural, not an evil. Either consciousness ends, so nothing is felt, or it continues somehow, so nothing is lost. More practically, fear of death is a judgement that death is bad, and judgements can be examined and revised.

*For example:* A person who spends time thinking calmly about her own death finds she's less frantic about small things.
e.c: Layer II - The Discipline of Desire
p: **Terror management theory** (Greenberg et al., 1986)
**Death reflection** (Cozzolino, 2006)
f: **Memento mori** (Seneca, On the Shortness of Life)
reflections: What exactly do you fear about death? Separate the fear of dying, of the end, of leaving others, and of unfinished life.
Does the Stoic argument actually remove fear, or only reframe it? Where does it stop working for you?
What does it mean to live well knowing you will die? Write about one thing you'd change if you took it seriously.

e.t: Do not seek pleasure as the highest good
e.x:
The Stoic is not an ascetic, but neither is pleasure the goal. Pleasure is a preferred indifferent, not a good. The person who arranges their life around pleasure is enslaved to the things that produce it. Arrange your life around virtue, and let pleasure follow.

(Disc. II.9, II.18, II.19; Med. VI.16, VII.33; Seneca, Letters 59, 71.)

**Plain words** The Stoic isn't an ascetic, but pleasure isn't the goal either. It's a preferred indifferent. Arrange your life around pleasure and you're enslaved by what produces it. Organise around virtue and let pleasure follow.

*For example:* Someone who wants only good dinners becomes a hostage of restaurants. Someone who values good company enjoys the dinner without needing it.
e.c: Layer II - The Discipline of Desire
p: **Eudaimonic versus hedonic well-being** (Ryff, 1989; Huta and Ryan, 2010)
**Intrinsic versus extrinsic goals** (Kasser and Ryan, 1996)
f: **Eudaimonia as activity, not pleasure** (Aristotle, NE I.7)
reflections: Which pleasure is most able to steer your decisions? What would happen if you lost it?
Is there something self-defeating in making pleasure the goal? Does your experience support this?
How would you distinguish enjoying pleasure from being ruled by it?

e.t: Practise contentment with what you have
e.x:
Contentment (autarkeia) is the Stoic ideal of self-sufficiency. Not isolation, but the capacity to be well regardless of external circumstances. Practise contentment: appreciate what you have, do not fixate on what you lack, and recognise that what you need is less than what you want.

(Disc. I.1, I.25; Ench. 15, 16; Med. IV.3, VII.44, IX.6; Seneca, Letters 9, 110.)

**Plain words** Autarkeia is self-sufficiency: not isolation, but the ability to be well regardless of circumstances. Appreciate what you have, don't fixate on what's missing, and notice that you need less than you want.

*For example:* Making a good dinner from what's in the cupboard, rather than going out to buy the missing ingredient.
e.c: Layer II - The Discipline of Desire
p: **Gratitude research**, gratitude for what one has predicts well-being (Emmons and McCullough, 2003)
**Sufficiency and simple living** (Brown and Kasser, 2005)
reflections: What do you have now that you once wanted badly and now barely notice? What does that suggest about wanting?
Is contentment the same as complacency? How do you tell, in practice?
What would genuine self-sufficiency feel like, and what would it mean for your relationships?

e.t: Do not crave fame
e.x:
Fame is a preferred indifferent at best, a distraction at worst. The person who seeks fame is seeking the approval of people whose judgment may be worthless. The Stoic seeks the approval of their own reason, not the applause of the crowd.

(Med. I.6, III.4, IV.3, VI.16, VIII.45; Seneca, Letters 20, 29, 73, 79, 94, 103.)

**Plain words** Fame is at best a preferred indifferent and at worst a distraction. Seeking it means seeking the approval of people whose judgement may be worthless. The Stoic looks to their own reason, not the crowd's applause.

*For example:* Declining to post the clever thing you made because you already know it's good, and being fine with that.
e.c: Layer II - The Discipline of Desire
p: **Extrinsic motivation and well-being**, fame-seeking predicts lower well-being (Kasser and Ryan, 1993)
**Social comparison and self-esteem** (Crocker and Wolfe, 2001)
f: **Contempt for fame** (Seneca, Letters from a Stoic)
**The having versus being mode** (Fromm, To Have or To Be?)
reflections: Whose approval do you seek, and would you trust that person's judgement on other matters?
What is the difference between wanting recognition and wanting to be good? Can you separate them?
How does a culture of metrics, likes and followers change how people measure themselves?

e.t: Distinguish between needing and wanting
e.x:
You need less than you think. Most of what you want is not needed for flourishing. The Stoic practises the distinction: identify what you need (virtue, reason, the basic necessities) and treat the rest as optional. This does not mean living in poverty; it means living without attachment.

(Disc. I.1, I.25; Ench. 15; Med. III.6, VI.13; Seneca, Letters 2, 110.)

**Plain words** You need less than you think. Identify what you truly need, virtue, reason, the basics, and treat the rest as optional. That doesn't mean poverty. It means living without clinging.

*For example:* Looking at a full wardrobe and realising you wear a fifth of it.
e.c: Layer II - The Discipline of Desire
p: **Materialistic aspirations predict lower well-being** (Kasser and Ryan, 1993)
**Sufficiency research** (Brown and Kasser, 2005)
f: **The natural and necessary desires** (Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus)
reflections: What do you spend effort and money on that you don't need? What does it do for you instead?
How do you tell a need from a want when emotions are involved, as with companionship or comfort?
What would a life of enough look like for you, in specifics?

e.t: Fulfil your roles well
e.x:
You are a son or daughter, a parent, a citizen, a friend, a worker. Each role carries duties. The Stoic does not reject roles but fulfils them excellently. Ask: what does this role require of me, right now? Then do it.

(Disc. II.10, III.7, III.23; Med. VI.30; Seneca, Letters 44, 71, 95.)

**Plain words** You're a child, parent, citizen, friend, worker. Each role has duties. The Stoic doesn't reject roles but does them well. Ask what this role requires of you right now, then do it.

*For example:* Dragging yourself to your daughter's recital after a long day, because being her father right now means being there.
e.c: Layer III - The Discipline of Action
p: **Role identity and goal pursuit**, role-based goals predict engagement (Houser-Marko and Sheldon, 2006)
**Self-determination theory**, autonomy within roles (Deci and Ryan, 2000)
reflections: Which of your roles do you currently perform worst? What does it ask of you that you aren't giving?
What happens when roles conflict, as when work and family compete? How would you choose?
Can roles become a prison? When is it right to step out of one?

e.t: Act for the common good
e.x:
The Stoic is not a solitary sage. Every action should serve the community. You are a part of a larger whole, and your actions affect it. Ask of any action: does this serve the common good? If not, revise it.

(Med. II.1, VII.5, VII.55, IX.6; Disc. II.10, III.7, III.24; Seneca, Letters 48, 95.)

**Plain words** The Stoic isn't a solitary sage. Every action should serve the community, because you're part of a larger whole and your actions affect it. Ask of any plan: does this serve the common good? If not, revise it.

*For example:* Before taking a shortcut at work that benefits you, you consider who has to clean up after it.
e.c: Layer III - The Discipline of Action
p: **Prosocial behaviour research**, acting for others increases well-being (Dunn, Aknin and Norton, 2008)
**Social value orientation** (Van Lange et al., 2007)
f: **Ubuntu: I am because we are** (African relational philosophy)
**Democracy as associated living** (Dewey, Democracy and Education)
reflections: What recent decision of yours served only you? What would a version that served others have looked like?
How do you identify the common good when people disagree about it?
Is there a danger in making the community the measure of everything? Where might it override individual lives?

e.t: Do what is fitting, not what is easy
e.x:
The Stoic does not shrink from difficulty when duty calls. The right action is often the hard one: the honest conversation, the refusal to participate in injustice, the work that no one will notice. Do what is fitting because it is fitting, not because it is rewarded.

(Med. II.5, VI.12, VII.15, IX.6; Disc. III.24; Seneca, Letters 20, 71, 104.)

**Plain words** The Stoic doesn't shrink from difficulty when duty calls. The right action is often the hard one: the honest conversation, the refusal to join an injustice, the work no one will notice. Do it because it's fitting, not because it's rewarded.

*For example:* Telling your team the project is behind schedule, rather than letting it slide until someone else finds out.
e.c: Layer III - The Discipline of Action
p: **Moral courage research** (Hannah, Avolio and Walumbwa, 2011)
**Self-determination and autonomous morality** (Deci and Ryan, 2000)
reflections: What right action are you currently avoiding because it's difficult? What are you telling yourself?
How do you decide what is fitting when duties conflict or when no one can see?
Why might doing right without reward be good for us, not only for others?

e.t: Work with others, not against them
e.x:
Marcus reminds himself that no one acts wrongly on purpose. People err because they do not know what is good. Approach wrongdoers with patience and instruction, not anger. The Stoic cooperates even with the difficult.

(Med. II.1, II.13, IV.3, VII.22, IX.4, IX.11.)

**Plain words** Marcus reminds himself that no one does wrong on purpose. People err because they don't know what's good. Meet wrongdoers with patience and teaching, not anger. The Stoic works with the difficult.

*For example:* A coworker steals credit, and you ask yourself what he's afraid of, then talk to him directly.
e.c: Layer III - The Discipline of Action
p: **Perspective-getting**, asking rather than guessing outperforms for accuracy (Epley et al., 2007)
**Compassion research** (Goetz et al., 2010)
f: **The face as ethical summons** (Levinas, Totality and Infinity)
reflections: Think of someone who wronged you. What did they not understand, and what would it take to help them see it?
Is it true that no one does wrong on purpose? Test it against a case of deliberate cruelty.
When does patience with wrongdoers become an excuse for letting harm continue?

e.t: Do not retreat from the world
e.x:
The Stoic is not a recluse. Marcus was an emperor; Seneca was a politician and investor; Epictetus was a teacher. The philosophy is lived in the marketplace, the senate, and the household. Do not use philosophy as an excuse to withdraw from your obligations.

(Med. IV.3, V.1, VI.7, IX.6; Seneca, Letters 5, 20; Disc. III.7, III.21; Musonius Rufus, Lectures.)

**Plain words** The Stoic isn't a recluse. Marcus was an emperor, Seneca a politician and investor, Epictetus a teacher. The philosophy gets lived in the marketplace, the senate and the household. Don't use it as an excuse to withdraw.

*For example:* Taking on a difficult committee role rather than retreating to quiet reading, because that's where the practice is tested.
e.c: Layer III - The Discipline of Action
p: **Behavioural activation**, engagement with life predicts well-being (Dimidjian et al., 2011)
**Social connectedness and flourishing** (Holt-Lunstad, Smith and Layton, 2010)
f: **Participate: do with, not to** (Dewey, Democracy and Education)
reflections: Where have you used a calming practice or philosophy to avoid an obligation?
When is withdrawal wise? What would you say to someone who needs rest from the world?
How would your practice look different if you tested it in the places you find hardest?

e.t: Let your actions be consistent with your words
e.x:
Integrity is the alignment of speech and action. The Stoic does not say one thing and do another. This is not moralism but practical wisdom: inconsistency breeds inner conflict, and inner conflict breeds suffering. Practise saying less and doing more.
