(Med. IV.16, V.9; Seneca, Letters 20, 75, 108; Disc. III.21.)

**Plain words** Integrity is when what you say matches what you do. The Stoic doesn't preach one thing and live another. It isn't moralism but practical sense: inconsistency breeds inner conflict and inner conflict breeds suffering. Say less, do more.

*For example:* Not telling your children to be honest, then being honest where they can see you.
e.c: Layer III - The Discipline of Action
p: **Authenticity research**, authentic self-expression predicts well-being (Kernis and Goldman, 2006)
**Congruence in therapy and life** (Rogers, On Becoming a Person)
reflections: Where do your words and deeds diverge? How does the gap feel physically?
Is it better to say nothing than to state an ideal you fail to meet? Argue both ways.
What would you do differently if your actions had to be consistent with every value you profess?

e.t: Be useful
e.x:
The Stoic contributes. Marcus tells himself to be a good human, to do what human nature demands: help others, contribute to the community, leave things better than he found them. Do not merely exist. Be of use.

(Med. VI.16, VII.5, VII.54; Seneca, Letters 9, 48; Disc. III.3, III.24.)

**Plain words** The Stoic contributes. Marcus tells himself to be a good human and do what human nature demands: help others, contribute, leave things better than he found them. Don't merely exist. Be of use.

*For example:* Staying ten minutes to tidy the shared kitchen when no one will notice.
e.c: Layer III - The Discipline of Action
p: **Mattering research**, the sense that one's actions matter predicts well-being (George and Park, 2016)
**Generativity and well-being** (McAdams and de St. Aubin, 1992)
f: **Service as self-transcendence** (Frankl, Man's Search for Meaning)
**Participate in the world's becoming** (Whitehead, Process and Reality)
reflections: What are you of use to, and to whom? Is that enough for you?
How do you stay useful without becoming exhausted or taken advantage of?
What does usefulness mean for people who are ill, old or unable to work? Does the principle exclude them?

e.t: Do not postpone living well
e.x:
Seneca warns that life is not short; we waste most of it. The time to live well is now, not tomorrow. Do not wait for retirement, for the project to finish, for the children to grow. Practise the philosophy today, in this hour, with the materials at hand.

(Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 1, 7, 10; Med. II.4, IV.17, VII.29; Disc. I.1, I.4.)

**Plain words** Seneca says life isn't short, we waste most of it. The time to live well is now, not after retirement, the project, or when the children are grown. Practise philosophy today, in this hour, with what's at hand.

*For example:* Calling a friend you've been meaning to call, now, rather than "when things calm down."
e.c: Layer III - The Discipline of Action
p: **Time affluence**, the subjective sense of having enough time predicts well-being more than material wealth (Kasser and Sheldon, 2009)
**Present-moment focus and well-being** (Killingsworth and Gilbert, 2010)
f: **The specious present** (James, The Principles of Psychology)
**Memento mori** (Seneca, On the Shortness of Life)
reflections: What are you postponing until conditions improve? What would it mean to begin in a small way today?
Is "now" always right? When is waiting the wise choice?
Write about the hour you are in. What would living well in it look like?

e.t: Practise beneficence
e.x:
Seneca's On Benefits argues that giving and receiving well is a core Stoic practice. Give without expectation of return. Receive with gratitude. Do not let gratitude become a debt. The benefit is not the gift but the goodwill behind it.

(Seneca, On Benefits I-VII; Med. I.1, I.3, I.11, I.15; Disc. I.9, III.24.)

**Plain words** Seneca says giving and receiving well is a core practice. Give without expecting anything back. Receive with thanks. Don't let gratitude harden into debt. What matters isn't the gift but the goodwill behind it.

*For example:* A neighbour brings soup when you're ill. You thank her warmly, and later you bring her something, not to settle a bill but because you're glad of her.
e.c: Layer III - The Discipline of Action
p: **Prosocial spending and well-being** (Dunn, Aknin and Norton, 2008)
**Gratitude expression research** (Emmons and McCullough, 2003)
reflections: Think of a gift you gave with an invisible string attached. What did the string do to the gift, and to the relationship?
Receiving can be harder than giving, since it admits need. What makes it hard for you, and what would receiving gracefully look like?
Seneca separates the benefit from the object. Describe a time when the goodwill meant more than the thing given, and a time when it was missing.

e.t: Be a good citizen
e.x:
The Stoic does not withdraw from political life. Marcus was emperor; Seneca was advisor to Nero; Musonius Rufus was exiled for his political stance. The Stoic participates in the political community, not for personal gain but for the common good. Engage with your community politically.

(Med. I.1, I.6, IV.3, V.1, VI.7, IX.6; Seneca, Letters 14, 73, 73, 91; Disc. III.7, III.24.)

**Plain words** The Stoic doesn't withdraw from public life. Marcus ruled, Seneca advised an emperor, Musonius was exiled for his stance. Take part in your community's politics for the common good, not for gain.

*For example:* Showing up to a local planning meeting about the clinic's funding, when you'd rather stay home with a book.
e.c: Layer III - The Discipline of Action
p: **Civic engagement and well-being** (Putterman, 2018)
**Collective efficacy** (Bandura, 2000)
f: **Democracy as associated living** (Dewey, Democracy and Education)
reflections: What public matter affects your life or others' that you've avoided? What is the avoidance protecting?
Seneca's involvement with Nero is often cited as compromise. When does working within a flawed system help, and when does it corrupt?
How would a Stoic approach to politics differ from the anger and tribalism that often drive it?

e.t: Be a good family member
e.x:
The Stoic does not neglect family for philosophy. Epictetus discusses the duties of a parent, a child, a spouse. Marcus writes about his gratitude to his family. Seneca writes letters of consolation to his mother. Treat your family life as a primary site of Stoic practice.

(Med. I.1, I.5, I.17; Disc. II.10, III.7; Seneca, Letters 4, 63, 99, 104, 107; Musonius Rufus, Lectures on marriage and family.)

**Plain words** The Stoic doesn't sacrifice family to philosophy. Epictetus discusses the duties of a parent, child and spouse, Marcus thanks his family, Seneca consoles his mother. Treat family life as a main training ground.

*For example:* Staying calm at the dinner table when your teenager is rude, because this is the practice.
e.c: Layer III - The Discipline of Action
p: **Family systems theory** (Bowen, 1978)
**Attachment theory** (Mikulincer and Shaver, 2007)
f: **The household as moral community** (Confucian tradition, Analects)
**Friendship as necessary for flourishing** (Aristotle, NE VIII.1)
reflections: Which family relationship tests your philosophy most? What does it reveal that solitude doesn't?
What do you owe family members who have hurt you? Where does duty end?
How do the habits you practise alone show up, or fail to, at home?

e.t: Be a good friend
e.x:
Friendship is a Stoic practice. The Stoic friend is reliable, honest, present in adversity, and not dependent on the friend for happiness. Be the friend you would want to have. Do not use friendship as a means to an end.

(Med. I.1, I.5, I.11, I.15; Seneca, Letters 3, 6, 9, 35, 63, 109; Disc. II.10, III.7, III.24; Musonius Rufus, Lectures.)

**Plain words** Friendship is a Stoic practice. The Stoic friend is reliable, honest, present when things go wrong, and doesn't depend on the friend for happiness. Be the friend you'd want, and don't use people.

*For example:* Calling a friend who has just lost a job, not to cheer him up but to listen.
e.c: Layer III - The Discipline of Action
p: **Social support and resilience** (Cohen and Wills, 1985)
**Friendship quality and well-being** (Demir et al., 2015)
f: **Friendship as necessary for flourishing** (Aristotle, NE VIII.1)
**I-Thou as primary relation** (Buber, I and Thou)
reflections: What kind of friend are you in a crisis? Ask someone you trust to tell you honestly.
Can you be a good friend without depending on the friendship for happiness? What would that look like in real life?
What do you do when a friendship has become a means to an end for one of you?

e.t: Do your duty even when it is unpleasant
e.x:
The Stoic does not avoid duty because it is uncomfortable. Marcus writes about getting out of bed in the morning to do the work of a human being. The unpleasant duty is often the most important one. Do not let discomfort determine your actions.

(Med. II.1, V.1, VII.5, VII.45; Disc. III.12, III.24; Seneca, Letters 20, 71, 104.)

**Plain words** The Stoic doesn't dodge duty because it's uncomfortable. Marcus talks himself out of bed to do a human's work. The unpleasant duty is often the most important one. Don't let discomfort pick your actions.

*For example:* Getting up at six to take your father to dialysis, again.
e.c: Layer III - The Discipline of Action
p: **Behavioural activation**, action can precede motivation (Dimidjian et al., 2011)
**Implementation intentions** (Gollwitzer, 1999)
f: **Do what is fitting, not what is easy** (Marcus Aurelius, Meditations II.5)
reflections: Which duty do you most resent? What is its real value, and what happens if you drop it?
Is there a limit to duty? When is refusing the right thing?
What makes duty bearable, a reason, a person, a habit? Describe what works for you.

e.t: Practise non-retaliation
e.x:
When wronged, the Stoic does not retaliate. Retaliation is a passion, not a virtue. The Stoic may seek justice, but not revenge. The distinction is in the motive: justice seeks restoration; revenge seeks suffering.

(Med. II.1, II.13, IV.3, VI.6, VI.16, VII.22, IX.4; Seneca, De Ira I.5, II.1-4; Disc. I.18, III.12, III.22.)

**Plain words** When wronged, the Stoic doesn't retaliate. Retaliation is a passion, not a virtue. You can seek justice but not revenge. The difference is in motive: justice wants repair, revenge wants the other person to suffer.

*For example:* Reporting a fraud to the authorities is justice. Posting the fraudster's address online is something else.
e.c: Layer III - The Discipline of Action
p: **Forgiveness research** (Worthington et al., 2007)
**Anger management** (DiGiuseppe and Tafrate, 2007)
reflections: When did you last want revenge? Describe what you would have done and what you did.
How can you tell your own motives are justice and not revenge? Offer a test.
Does a society need some element of retribution to feel just? Argue against the Stoic view.

e.t: Be patient with difficult people
e.x:
Marcus reminds himself daily that he will meet difficult people and that they are part of nature. The difficult person is not an obstacle to flourishing but material for the practice of patience, justice, and compassion.

(Med. II.1, II.13, IV.3, VII.13, VII.22, IX.4, IX.11, XI.18.)

**Plain words** Marcus reminds himself each morning that he'll meet difficult people and that they're part of nature. They aren't an obstacle to the good life. They're material for practising patience, justice and compassion.

*For example:* A manager known for being abrasive is the person you practise listening on.
e.c: Layer III - The Discipline of Action
p: **Compassion research** (Goetz et al., 2010)
**Emotion regulation** (Gross, 2015)
reflections: Who is today's difficult person? What exact virtue do they give you a chance to practise?
Does expecting difficult people each day make you calmer or more cynical? Why?
When does patience with a difficult person turn into tolerating harm?

e.t: Act as a member of the whole
e.x:
The Stoic sees themselves as a part of a larger whole: the cosmos, the human community, the natural order. No action is purely private. Act with awareness of your place in the whole.

(Med. II.3, IV.10, V.8, V.30, VI.42, VII.9, VII.19, VII.47, VIII.7, VIII.34, VIII.50, VIII.52, X.1, X.6, X.33, XI.1, XI.18, XII.36; Disc. I.12, I.14, I.25, III.10, III.24; Seneca, Letters 71, 95, 107; Ench. 31, 53.)

**Plain words** You're a part of larger wholes: the cosmos, the human community, the natural order. No action is purely private. Act aware of your place in the whole.

*For example:* Throwing away a plastic bottle becomes a slightly different act when you remember where it ends up.
e.c: Layer III - The Discipline of Action
p: **Self-transcendent experiences** (Yaden et al., 2017)
**Mattering and purpose** (George and Park, 2016)
f: **Participate in the world's becoming** (Whitehead, Process and Reality)
reflections: Choose a private habit. Trace its effects on someone outside your life.
Does the thought of belonging to a whole comfort or burden you? Why?
How might awareness of the whole change a decision you are facing?

e.t: Examine every impression
e.x:
When something presents itself to your mind, do not immediately accept it. Ask: is this true? Is it complete? Is it within my control? The unexamined impression drives behaviour. The examined impression is a choice.

(Disc. I.20, II.18, III.2-3, III.12; Ench. 1, 45.)

**Plain words** When something presents itself to your mind, don't swallow it whole. Ask: is this true, is it complete, is it in my control? The unexamined impression drives behaviour. The examined one is a choice.

*For example:* You read an alarming headline. Before sharing it, you ask what's missing.
e.c: Layer IV - The Discipline of Assent
p: **Cognitive defusion**, seeing thoughts as mental events rather than literal truths (Hayes et al., 2011)
**Decentering** (Bernstein et al., 2015)
f: **Suspension of judgement (epochē)** (Sextus Empiricus, Outlines of Pyrrhonism)
**Docta ignorantia** (Nicholas of Cusa, De Docta Ignorantia)
reflections: What impression drove your last bad decision? Which of the three questions would have caught it?
Which questions would you add to the list for your own habits of mind?
Why does the speed of modern information make examination harder, and what would you do about it?

e.t: Do not add to the impression
e.x:
When something happens, the impression is: "this happened." The mind immediately adds: "and this is terrible." The addition is yours, not the event's. Practise catching the addition and withholding it.

(Disc. I.11, I.28; Ench. 5; Med. IV.7, VIII.47.)

**Plain words** Something happens, and the mind says "this happened," then adds "and it's terrible." The addition is yours. Practise catching it and not passing it on.

*For example:* Your flight is delayed. "The flight is delayed" is the fact. "This ruins everything" is the add-on.
e.c: Layer IV - The Discipline of Assent
p: **Cognitive distortions research**, catastrophising, overgeneralisation, and personalisation as patterns to be identified and modified (Beck, 1976)
**Affect labelling**, naming emotion precisely reduces amygdala reactivity (Lieberman et al., 2007)
f: **The map is not the territory** (Korzybski, Science and Sanity)
reflections: Take one recent upset. Strip it to the bare event. What's left?
Which additions do you habitually make: catastrophe, personalisation, blame? What triggers them?
When is the addition justified, and when is it true that something really is terrible?

e.t: See impressions as what they are: appearances, not realities
e.x:
An impression of danger is not danger. An impression of insult is not insult. The impression is a mental event; the reality is something else. Train yourself to see the appearance as an appearance.

(Disc. I.20, II.18, III.6, III.12; Med. VI.13, VII.35.)

**Plain words** An impression of danger isn't danger. An impression of insult isn't an insult. The impression is a mental event, and reality is something else. Learn to see an appearance as an appearance.

*For example:* Hearing a noise at night and thinking "intruder," then recognising it as the radiator.
e.c: Layer IV - The Discipline of Assent
p: **Cognitive defusion in ACT**, "I notice I'm having the thought that..." (Hayes et al., 2011)
**Meta-awareness research** (Schooler et al., 2011)
f: **Language games and meaning as use** (Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations)
reflections: What appearance have you treated as a fact lately? What would checking have cost?
Is it always possible to separate appearance from reality? Where does it break down, as in trauma or paranoia?
How does this principle relate to modern ideas about cognitive distortions?

e.t: Withhold assent when the impression is uncertain
e.x:
If you are not sure whether something is true, do not act as if it were. The discipline of withholding assent is the capacity to live with uncertainty without rushing to judgement. This is not scepticism for its own sake; it is the protection of your peace of mind.

(Disc. I.28, II.18, III.2-3; Ench. 45.)

**Plain words** If you aren't sure something is true, don't act as if it were. Withholding assent is the ability to live with uncertainty without rushing to judgement. It isn't scepticism for its own sake, it protects your peace.

*For example:* You don't reply to a worrying message until you've heard the full story.
e.c: Layer IV - The Discipline of Assent
p: **Tolerance of uncertainty research** (Dugas et al., 1998; Carleton, 2012)
**Mindful uncertainty** (Hayes et al., 2011)
reflections: Where do you rush to judgement because uncertainty feels unbearable?
What is the cost of withholding assent, such as missed chances or indecision? How would you weigh them?
How do you tell healthy openness from avoidance of commitment?

e.t: Replace first movements with considered responses
e.x:
The Stoics recognised "first movements": automatic emotional reactions that arise before reason can intervene. You cannot prevent the first movement, but you can prevent the second. Do not let the first reaction become the final response.

(Seneca, De Ira II.1-4; Med. V.26, VI.6; Disc. I.18, III.2.)

**Plain words** The Stoics noticed first movements: reactions that fire before reason can step in. You can't stop the first, but you can stop the second. Don't let the first reaction be the final response.

*For example:* You flinch at an angry email, which is fine. You don't reply for an hour, which is the practice.
e.c: Layer IV - The Discipline of Assent
p: **Emotion regulation research**, the gap between stimulus and response as the site of regulation (Gross, 2015)
**Urge surfing and the 90-second wave** (Bowen et al., 2011; Taylor, 2006)
f: **The pause between impression and assent** (Epictetus, Discourses)
reflections: Which first movements do you know best in yourself? What triggers them?
How much of your self-blame is about the first movement, which you couldn't help, rather than the second?
What would a gap of one minute, one hour or one day do in a conflict you're in?

e.t: Test your impressions against reality
e.x:
When you have an impression, check it. Is the person really insulting you, or are they having a bad day? Is the situation really hopeless, or are you catastrophising? The test is not introspection but observation.

(Disc. I.20, I.28; Med. IV.7, VI.13, XI.18; Seneca, De Ira III.36.)

**Plain words** When you have an impression, check it against the world. Is the person really insulting you, or having a bad day? Is the situation hopeless, or are you catastrophising? The test is observation, not more introspection.

*For example:* Thinking your boss is angry, you notice she was like that with everyone this morning.
e.c: Layer IV - The Discipline of Assent
p: **Behavioural experiments in CBT**, testing beliefs through action (Bennett-Levy et al., 2004)
**Prediction logging and calibration** (Kahneman and Klein, 2009)
f: **The pragmatic maxim** (Peirce, "How to Make Our Ideas Clear")
reflections: What do you believe about someone that you haven't checked? What would checking involve?
Why is observation sometimes better than introspection for testing a belief?
What are the risks of testing impressions, for instance finding out you were right to be afraid?

e.t: Recognise that your judgements are the source of your distress
e.x:
If you are distressed, trace the distress to the judgement that produced it. The event did not produce it; your interpretation did. Change the interpretation, and the distress changes. This is the core of the Stoic practice and the core of cognitive therapy.

(Disc. I.1, I.11, I.18; Ench. 5; Med. IV.7, VIII.47, XII.8.)

**Plain words** If you're distressed, trace it back to the judgement that produced it. The event didn't, your interpretation did. Change the interpretation and the distress changes. That's the heart of Stoic practice and of cognitive therapy.

*For example:* Feeling worthless after a critical review, you find the judgement "one criticism means I'm incompetent," and see it's not true.
e.c: Layer IV - The Discipline of Assent
p: **Cognitive-behavioural therapy**, the core model: thoughts mediate between events and emotions (Beck, 1976; [Stoic-CBT parallels](https://www.cambridge.org/co...)
**Cognitive reappraisal** (Gross, 2015)
f: **Workability check** (Peirce, "How to Make Our Ideas Clear")
reflections: Trace one current distress back to a judgement. Write it as a sentence and examine it.
What are the limits of cognitive approaches? What kinds of suffering do they not reach?
Why might it take years to change a judgement you can see is false?

e.t: Practise the view from above
e.x:
When distressed by a particular event, shift perspective: imagine looking down on the earth from above. See your city, your country, the planet. Your problem shrinks to its true size. The view from above restores proportion.

(Med. IV.1, VII.48, IX.30, XII.24; Seneca, Letters 91; Disc. I.14, III.24.)

**Plain words** When an event distresses you, look down on it from above: your city, your country, the planet. Your problem shrinks to its true size. The view from above restores proportion.

*For example:* Stuck in a petty dispute, you picture the whole street from a hundred metres up, and it eases.
e.c: Layer IV - The Discipline of Assent
p: **Self-distancing research**, viewing events from a third-person perspective reduces distress and improves reasoning (Kross and Ayduk, 2017)
**Awe and the small-self effect** (Yaden et al., 2017; Piff et al., 2015)
f: **The specious present** (James, The Principles of Psychology)
reflections: What problem would shrink under the view from above, and which wouldn't? What's the difference?
Can proportion become a way of minimising real pain? How do you avoid it?
Write one paragraph describing your current worry as an astronomer or historian would.

e.t: Distinguish between what you control and what you influence
e.x:
Some things are fully within your control (your judgements, choices, efforts). Some things you can influence but not control (other people's behaviour, outcomes of projects). Some things you cannot control at all (the weather, the past, other people's opinions). Focus your energy on what you control, invest in what you can influence, and accept what you cannot control.

(Disc. I.1, I.12, I.22, I.25; Ench. 1.)

**Plain words** Some things you control completely (judgements, choices, effort). Some you influence but don't control (other people, outcomes). Some you can't touch (weather, the past, opinions). Spend energy accordingly: control what you control, invest in what you can influence, release the rest.

*For example:* You can't make an editor accept your piece. You can control the draft, the pitch and the follow-up.
e.c: Layer IV - The Discipline of Assent
p: **Locus of control and well-being** (Rotter, 1966)
**Self-efficacy** (Bandura, 1977)
f: **Freedom as effective power** (Dewey, Human Nature and Conduct)
reflections: Sort a big goal of yours into the three categories. Which category are you putting most effort into?
The middle category is where most of life happens. How does one invest without becoming attached to the outcome?
Is the three-part scheme more useful than the simple two-part one? Why?

e.t: Distinguish between facts and interpretations
e.x:
A fact is what happened. An interpretation is what you think it means. "It rained" is a fact. "It rained and ruined my day" is an interpretation. The Stoic practises separating facts from interpretations and holding interpretations lightly.

(Disc. I.1, I.11, I.28; Ench. 5; Med. IV.7, VI.13, VIII.47.)

**Plain words** A fact is what happened. An interpretation is what you think it means. "It rained" is a fact. "It rained and ruined my day" is an interpretation. Practise separating them and hold interpretations lightly.

*For example:* "She didn't call" is fact. "She doesn't care" is interpretation.
e.c: Layer IV - The Discipline of Assent
p: **Cognitive defusion** (Hayes et al., 2011)
**Mindfulness research** (Kabat-Zinn, 1990)
f: **The map is not the territory** (Korzybski, Science and Sanity)
reflections: Take the last argument you had. Write it twice, once only as facts and once with interpretations. How do they differ?
Can facts be completely separated from interpretation? Where does the distinction blur?
What interpretations do you hold most tightly, and what would happen if you loosened them?

e.t: Do not argue with impressions
e.x:
When an impression arises, do not fight it. Fighting it gives it energy. Simply note it: "this is an impression." Let it pass. The impression is not you; it is a visitor.

(Disc. I.1, I.20, III.3; Ench. 1; Med. VII.35.)

**Plain words** When an impression arises, don't wrestle it. Fighting gives it energy. Just note "this is an impression" and let it pass. It isn't you, it's a visitor.

*For example:* An anxious thought comes during a meeting. You label it and carry on with the agenda.
e.c: Layer IV - The Discipline of Assent
p: **Acceptance-based approaches**, accepting inner experience rather than suppressing it (Hayes et al., 2011)
**Urge surfing** (Bowen et al., 2011)
reflections: What thoughts do you fight hardest? What happens when you fight them?
How is noting different from suppressing? Describe the felt difference.
Is there ever a reason to engage an impression instead of letting it pass?

e.t: Recognise that you can choose your response
e.x:
Between stimulus and response, there is a space. In that space lies your freedom. The Stoic trains to widen that space, to use it, to choose the response that aligns with virtue. This is the core of Stoic practice.

(Disc. I.1, I.4, I.6, I.18, III.2; Ench. 1; Med. VI.6, VII.16, VIII.47.)

**Plain words** Between stimulus and response there's a space, and that's where your freedom is. Stoic training widens it, uses it, and picks the response that fits virtue.

*For example:* Someone cuts in front of you. You feel the rise and in the gap choose a deep breath instead of a horn.
e.c: Layer IV - The Discipline of Assent
p: **Psychological flexibility** (Kashdan and Rottenberg, 2010)
**Response inhibition and cognitive control** (Aron, 2007)
f: **Freedom as power** (Dewey, Human Nature and Conduct)
reflections: Where is your gap narrowest? What would help widen it?
Is the space real, or an illusion produced by a longer chain of causes? Does it matter practically?
How might trauma shrink the gap, and what kind of help widens it?

e.t: Recognise that your thoughts are not you
e.x:
You are not your thoughts. You are the one who observes them. The thought "I am a failure" is a mental event, not a fact about you. The Stoic practises identifying with the observer, not the observed.

(Disc. I.1, I.14, III.3; Ench. 1; Med. VII.35, XII.8.)

**Plain words** You aren't your thoughts. You're the one who observes them. "I'm a failure" is a mental event, not a fact about you. Practise identifying with the observer rather than the observed.

*For example:* Noticing "there's the 'I'm a failure' thought again" and seeing it as weather.
e.c: Layer IV - The Discipline of Assent
p: **Self-as-context in ACT** (Hayes et al., 2011)
**Mindfulness research** (Kabat-Zinn, 1990)
f: **The observing self** (James, The Principles of Psychology)
reflections: What recurring thought do you most take as fact about yourself? What evidence would count against it?
Is there a risk that identifying with the observer becomes detachment from feeling? How do you stay in touch with emotion?
Who is the observer, in your experience? Try to describe it.

e.t: Practise reframing
e.x:
When a situation seems bad, look for another perspective. "This is not happening to me; it is happening, and I can use it." "This is not a setback; it is material for the practice of virtue." The reframe is not denial; it is a change of perspective.

(Disc. I.1, I.14, I.24; Ench. 1; Med. V.8, V.10, V.20, VII.8, VII.19, VII.20, VII.43, VIII.35, VIII.41, X.33.)

**Plain words** When a situation looks bad, find another angle. "This isn't happening to me; it's happening, and I can use it." "This isn't a setback, it's material for practising virtue." Reframing isn't denial, it's a change of view.

*For example:* A cancelled project becomes time to finish the essay you'd put off.
e.c: Layer IV - The Discipline of Assent
p: **Cognitive reappraisal** (Gross, 2015)
**Narrative redemption sequences** (McAdams, 2013)
f: **The obstacle is the way** (Marcus Aurelius, Meditations V.20)
**Let obstruction do its work** (Dewey, Experience and Nature)
reflections: Reframe a current problem in two honest ways. Which one actually helps?
How do you tell a useful reframe from denial or toxic positivity?
Is there a situation where reframing feels wrong or even disrespectful? Why?

e.t: Do not be carried away by passion
e.x:
The Stoics distinguish between passions (pathē), which are excessive and irrational, and eupatheiai, which are healthy emotional responses. The goal is not to feel nothing but to feel appropriately. Anger, fear, grief, and desire, when they exceed what reason approves, are passions. Train yourself to feel within the bounds of reason.

(Seneca, De Ira I.7-9; Med. VI.6, VII.17; Disc. III.2, III.8, III.10.)

**Plain words** The Stoics separate passions, which are excessive and irrational, from healthy feelings. The goal isn't feeling nothing but feeling fittingly. Anger, fear, grief and desire become passions when they exceed what reason endorses.

*For example:* Being sad at a friend's departure is fitting. Spiralling for a week over it is the passion.
e.c: Layer V - Emotions, Passions, and the Inner Citadel
p: **Emotion regulation research**, strategies for modulating emotional response (Gross, 2015)
**Dialectical behaviour therapy, emotion modulation** (Linehan, 1993)
reflections: Which of your emotions most often exceeds the occasion? What marks the point it tips?
Critics say Stoicism asks for emotional restraint that harms people. What is the best reply?
Describe a time when a strong emotion was exactly right.

e.t: Cure anger by understanding its source
e.x:
Seneca's De Ira is a therapeutic manual. Anger arises from the judgement that you have been wronged and that revenge is appropriate. Both judgements can be examined and revised. The cure for anger is not suppression but understanding: see the event clearly, see your judgement of it, and let the judgement go.

(Seneca, De Ira I.1, II.1-4, III.1; Med. I.9, II.1, IV.3, IX.4.)

**Plain words** Seneca's On Anger is a therapy manual. Anger comes from judging that you've been wronged and revenge is fitting. Both judgements can be examined. The cure isn't suppression but understanding: see the event, see your judgement, and let it go.

*For example:* Furious at a colleague's remark, you ask "was it meant that way?" and the heat drops.
e.c: Layer V - Emotions, Passions, and the Inner Citadel
p: **Anger management interventions** (DiGiuseppe and Tafrate, 2007)
**Cognitive-behavioural therapy for anger** (Beck, 1976)
reflections: What judgement lay behind your last anger? Write it down and check it.
Is anger sometimes accurate? How should you act when your judgement of wrong is correct?
Seneca says anger is temporary madness. Do you agree? What have you seen it do?

e.t: Recognise the three stages of anger
e.x:
Seneca identifies three stages: (1) the first movement, the automatic physical reaction; (2) the judgement that revenge is appropriate; (3) the action of revenge. You cannot prevent the first stage. You can prevent the second and third. The work begins at the pause between stage one and stage two.

(Seneca, De Ira II.1-4; Med. V.26, VI.6; Disc. I.18, III.2.)

**Plain words** Seneca names three stages: the automatic reaction, the judgement that revenge is warranted, and the act. You can't stop the first. You can stop the second and third. The work starts at the pause between one and two.

*For example:* Your pulse jumps at an insult, you don't decide yet, and the moment passes.
e.c: Layer V - Emotions, Passions, and the Inner Citadel
p: **Emotion regulation, the gap between stimulus and response** (Gross, 2015)
**Urge surfing and the 90-second wave** (Bowen et al., 2011)
f: **The pause between impression and assent** (Epictetus, Discourses)
reflections: In your last conflict, where was the pause available? What would you have done with it?
What trains the pause: practice, rest, environment? Which helps you?
How do power and fear shorten the gap between stage one and three?

e.t: Do not grieve excessively
e.x:
Grief is natural, but excessive grief is a judgement that loss is unbearable. The Stoic feels the loss, acknowledges it, and then returns to what can be done. Seneca's consolation letters model this: face the loss, see it in proportion, and continue.

(Seneca, Letters 63, 99; Med. IV.1, IV.41; Disc. I.11, III.24.)

**Plain words** Grief is natural, but excessive grief is a judgement that the loss is unbearable. The Stoic feels it, acknowledges it, and returns to what can be done. Seneca's consolations show the way: face it, see its proportion, carry on.

*For example:* After a parent's death, you mourn fully and also call the funeral home the next morning.
e.c: Layer V - Emotions, Passions, and the Inner Citadel
p: **Dual-process model of grief**, oscillation between loss and restoration (Stroebe and Schut, 1999)
**Continuing bonds research** (Klass, Silverman and Nickman, 1996)
reflections: What loss have you grieved, and what did grieving require? What helped and what didn't?
Who decides what counts as excessive grief? Where might the principle wound?
How does grief relate to love? Can you grieve fully and still call it proportion?

e.t: Do not fear what you cannot control
e.x:
Fear is the judgement that something bad is coming and that you will not be able to handle it. The first judgement may be true; the second is always false, because your capacity for virtue is always intact. Practise facing what you fear with the knowledge that your character cannot be taken.

(Disc. I.1, I.14, II.1; Ench. 1, 53; Med. IV.49, VII.16; Seneca, Letters 13, 24, 107.)

**Plain words** Fear is judging that something bad is coming and you won't cope. The first part may be true, but the second is always false: your capacity for virtue stays intact. Face what you fear knowing your character can't be taken.

*For example:* Dreading a difficult conversation, you remember that whatever happens you can still be honest and kind.
e.c: Layer V - Emotions, Passions, and the Inner Citadel
p: **Graded exposure therapy** (Foa and McLean, 2016)
**Self-efficacy** (Bandura, 1977)
f: **Courage as the mean in fear** (Aristotle, NE III.6-9)
**The obstacle is the way** (Marcus Aurelius, Meditations V.20)
reflections: What are you afraid of? Separate the bad thing from your prediction that you can't handle it.
Is it really true that you can always cope? What are the limits of this thought?
How does fear distort your choices, and what might you do if you trusted your character more?

e.t: Build the inner citadel
e.x:
Marcus uses the image of the inner citadel: a fortress within that cannot be taken by external force. Your judgements, your values, your character: these are the citadel. Everything else is the territory outside the walls. Build the citadel strong, and let the territory be what it will.

(Med. III.5, IV.3, V.29, VII.48, VIII.48; Disc. I.1, I.18.)

**Plain words** Marcus imagines an inner citadel no outside force can storm: your judgements, values and character. Everything else is territory outside the walls. Build the citadel strong, and let the rest be what it will.

*For example:* Losing your job shakes you, but your sense of who you are holds because it never lived there.
e.c: Layer V - Emotions, Passions, and the Inner Citadel
p: **Psychological flexibility as the master skill** (Kashdan and Rottenberg, 2010)
**Self-as-context** (Hayes et al., 2011)
f: **The observing self** (James, The Principles of Psychology)
reflections: What is inside your citadel, and what have you put outside that you shouldn't?
Can a citadel become a place to hide? How would you tell strength from retreat?
What attacks on your inner peace have you survived, and what protected you?

e.t: Practise self-examination daily
e.x:
Marcus's Meditations is a self-examination journal. Each entry is a practice of reviewing his thoughts, impulses, and actions. Adopt this practice: at the end of each day, review what you did, what you thought, and where you drifted. The review is not self-punishment but calibration.

(Med. I.1, II.1, III.1, V.1; Seneca, Letters 83; Disc. III.10, III.23.)

**Plain words** Marcus's Meditations is a self-examination notebook: reviewing thoughts, impulses and actions. Do the same at day's end: what did I do, what did I think, where did I drift? It's not punishment, it's calibration.

*For example:* Five minutes before bed with a notebook: what went well, what I'd redo.
e.c: Layer V - Emotions, Passions, and the Inner Citadel
p: **Reflective practice and self-monitoring** (Schön, 1983)
**Gratitude and review practices** (Emmons and McCullough, 2003)
reflections: What would you find if you reviewed today honestly? What would you do differently?
Why do daily reviews so often turn into self-criticism? How do you keep it calibrating?
Is writing it down different from thinking it? What has writing taught you?

e.t: Be gentle with yourself in the review
e.x:
Marcus tells himself not to be angry with the person who fails to live up to their principles. That person is himself. The self-examination is honest but not harsh. You are training, not judging. Return to the practice without guilt.

(Med. II.1, V.9, VI.6, VI.21, X.1, XI.9, XI.18; Disc. III.25.)

**Plain words** Marcus tells himself not to be angry with the person who falls short of their principles, who is himself. The review is honest but not harsh. You're training, not judging. Return to the practice without guilt.

*For example:* You miss a week of practice and begin again on Monday, with no speech about it.
e.c: Layer V - Emotions, Passions, and the Inner Citadel
p: **Self-compassion research** (Neff, 2003; MacBeth and Gumley, 2012)
**Self-forgiveness** (Hall and Fincham, 2005)
reflections: How do you speak to yourself after a lapse? Compare it to how you'd speak to a friend.
Is gentleness with yourself compatible with high standards? Describe a case where it was.
What would returning without guilt require you to believe?

e.t: Cultivate tranquillity (ataraxia)
e.x:
Tranquillity is not numbness. It is the state of a mind that is not disturbed by passions, that faces fortune and misfortune with equanimity, that acts from a settled centre. Cultivate it through the practices: the dichotomy of control, the discipline of desire, the examination of impressions. Tranquillity is the by-product, not the goal.

(Seneca, De Tranquillitate Animi; Med. IV.3, IV.24, VI.16, IX.31; Disc. I.4, II.1, III.3.)

**Plain words** Tranquillity isn't numbness. It's a mind not tossed about by passions, meeting fortune and misfortune evenly, acting from a settled centre. It's the by-product of the practices, not a goal to grasp.

*For example:* A nurse who stays steady in an emergency isn't cold. She's calm enough to help.
e.c: Layer V - Emotions, Passions, and the Inner Citadel
p: **Equanimity as contemplative outcome** ([Desbordes et al., 2014)
**Nonattachment** ([Sahdra et al. review](https://non-attachment.com/...)
f: **The good life as process** (Rogers, On Becoming a Person)
reflections: When have you been steady in a storm? What made it possible?
Why might chasing tranquillity make it recede? What does that suggest about its nature?
Is tranquillity always appropriate? Imagine a situation where it would be wrong.

e.t: Distinguish between healthy and unhealthy emotions
e.x:
The Stoics distinguish passions (pathē) from eupatheiai (healthy emotions). Joy (chara) is the healthy counterpart to pleasure; wish (boulesis) is the healthy counterpart to desire; caution (eulabeia) is the healthy counterpart to fear. The goal is not to eliminate emotion but to transform it from passion to eupatheia.

(Seneca, De Ira I.7; Disc. III.2; Med. VI.16; Stobaeus, Eclogae II.7.)

**Plain words** Stoics distinguish passions from healthy emotions. Joy is the healthy form of pleasure, wish of desire, caution of fear. The aim isn't to eliminate emotion but to turn passion into its healthy counterpart.

*For example:* Replacing "I must get that job" with "I'd like it and will do what I can."
e.c: Layer V - Emotions, Passions, and the Inner Citadel
p: **Emotion regulation research** (Gross, 2015)
**Positive emotions research** (Fredrickson, 2001)
f: **Right desire flowing from right understanding** (Spinoza, Ethics IV)
reflections: Pick a passion you know well. What is its healthy counterpart, and what would it feel like?
Is it possible to feel joy without risk of the passion that follows? Where do they separate?
Is the Stoic list of healthy emotions complete? Which valuable emotions seem missing?

e.t: Do not let pleasure enslave you
e.x:
Pleasure is not evil, but the pursuit of pleasure can enslave. The person who cannot be without a particular pleasure is not free. The Stoic enjoys pleasures without depending on them. Practise going without: fast from a pleasure to test your freedom from it.

(Disc. II.9, II.18, II.23; Ench. 15; Med. III.6, VI.13, VII.33; Seneca, Letters 59, 67.)

**Plain words** Pleasure isn't evil, but chasing it can enslave you. Someone who can't do without a particular pleasure isn't free. Enjoy pleasures without depending on them. Test it by fasting from one.

*For example:* A week without your daily coffee reveals whether you have it or it has you.
e.c: Layer V - Emotions, Passions, and the Inner Citadel
p: **Hedonic adaptation** (Lyubomirsky, 2011)
**Self-regulation and delay of gratification** (Mischel et al., 1989)
reflections: Which pleasure would you find hardest to give up for a month? What does that say?
Is voluntary deprivation useful, or is it a performance of discipline? How would you choose a fast?
What does freedom from a pleasure feel like when you reach it?

e.t: Do not let grief become your identity
e.x:
Grief is natural. But when grief becomes your identity, it has become a passion. The Stoic feels grief, allows it, and then returns to life. Seneca's consolation letters model this movement: feel, acknowledge, and then re-engage.

(Seneca, Letters 63, 99, 107; Med. IV.1, IV.41; Disc. I.11, III.24.)

**Plain words** Grief is natural. But when it becomes your identity, it's turned into a passion. The Stoic feels it, allows it, and returns to life. Seneca's letters model the movement: feel, acknowledge, re-engage.

*For example:* A widow who never stops being "the one who lost her husband" has lost something else too.
e.c: Layer V - Emotions, Passions, and the Inner Citadel
p: **Grief and meaning-making research** (Stroebe and Schut, 1999)
**Complicated grief research** (Shear et al., 2011)
reflections: Has any hurt become an identity for you or someone you know? What does it provide?
Is there a cost to returning to life too soon? How would you know when it is time?
How might loving someone mean carrying their absence for good? Does the Stoic view allow it?

e.t: Recognise that emotions are judgments
e.x:
The Stoic theory of emotions holds that passions are judgments: anger is the judgment that you have been wronged and revenge is appropriate; fear is the judgment that danger is imminent and overwhelming; desire is the judgment that something is good and necessary. Examine the judgment behind the emotion.

(Seneca, De Ira I.3, II.1; Disc. I.25, III.2; Med. VII.16, VII.35; Stobaeus, Eclogae II.7.)

**Plain words** In the Stoic view, passions are judgements. Anger is judging that you've been wronged and revenge is fitting. Fear is judging danger is imminent and overwhelming. Desire is judging something is good and necessary. Examine the judgement behind the feeling.

*For example:* Feeling jealous means you've judged that someone is taking what's yours. Ask whether it was ever yours.
e.c: Layer V - Emotions, Passions, and the Inner Citadel
p: **Cognitive appraisal theory of emotion** (Lazarus, 1991)
**Appraisal theory research** (Scherer, Schorr and Johnstone, 2001)
f: **Where phronesis and emotions connect** (Aristotle, NE VI)
reflections: Take your strongest emotion today and write the judgement inside it as a sentence.
If emotions are judgements, why can they persist when you know the judgement is false? What else holds them?
How does this compare with what you know of the neuroscience of emotion?

e.t: Practise emotional detachment from outcomes
e.x:
The Stoic does not detach from action but from the outcome of action. Act well, and let the result be what it will. Your responsibility is for the action, not for the result. This is not passivity; it is freedom from the anxiety of outcomes.

(Disc. I.1, I.12, I.25; Ench. 1; Med. II.9, IV.3, VII.8; Seneca, Letters 107, 123.)

**Plain words** The Stoic detaches from outcomes, not from action. Act well and let the result be what it will. You're responsible for the action, not the result. That isn't passivity, it's freedom from outcome anxiety.

*For example:* Preparing carefully for a pitch, then letting go of whether they say yes.
e.c: Layer V - Emotions, Passions, and the Inner Citadel
p: **Process goals versus outcome goals** (Vallerand, 2010)
**Acceptance and commitment** (Hayes et al., 2011)
reflections: Which outcome are you most gripped by? What would acting well and letting go look like?
Does detachment from outcome weaken motivation? What has your experience shown?
When outcomes affect other people, such as patients or children, is it right to be less attached?

e.t: Love the people you live with
e.x:
Marcus tells himself that humans are made for cooperation. To oppose them is to oppose nature. To be angry at them is to be angry at your own body. Practise love for the people in your daily life, even the difficult ones.

(Med. II.1, II.13, VII.13, VII.22, IX.1, IX.4, IX.11; Disc. III.24.)

**Plain words** Marcus says humans are made to cooperate. Opposing them goes against nature. Being angry with them is like being angry with your own body. Practise loving the people you live with, even the hard ones.

*For example:* Your roommate leaves dishes. You wash them once, then talk about it, without a speech.
e.c: Layer VI - Social, Cosmopolitan, and Duty
p: **Compassion research** (Goetz et al., 2010)
**Loving-kindness meditation** (Fredrickson et al., 2008)
f: **Ubuntu: I am because we are** (African relational philosophy)
**I-Thou as primary relation** (Buber, I and Thou)
reflections: Who in your daily life do you struggle to love? What would one act of love look like?
Is love for people who harm you possible, or does it need limits?
What does it mean to treat other humans as parts of your own body? Is it metaphor or something deeper?

e.t: Forgive those who wrong you
e.x:
The Stoic recognises that no one does wrong on purpose. Wrongdoing is the product of ignorance about what is truly good. When someone wrongs you, see the ignorance behind the act. Do not excuse the wrong, but do not personalise it either.

(Med. II.1, II.13, IV.3, VII.22, VII.63, IX.4, IX.11, XI.18; Disc. I.18.)

**Plain words** No one does wrong on purpose, says the Stoic. Wrongdoing comes from ignorance about what's truly good. When someone wrongs you, see the ignorance behind it. Don't excuse the wrong, but don't take it personally.

*For example:* A friend lets you down, and you ask what they believe is important that led to it.
e.c: Layer VI - Social, Cosmopolitan, and Duty
p: **Forgiveness research** (Worthington et al., 2007)
**The empty boat reflection** (Zhuangzi tradition)
f: **The face as ethical summons** (Levinas, Totality and Infinity)
**Compassion as co-suffering** (Scheler, The Nature of Sympathy)
reflections: Whom have you not forgiven? What would seeing their ignorance, without excusing it, change?
Do some people knowingly do wrong? How does the Stoic view cope?
What is the difference between understanding, excusing and forgiving?

e.t: Do not gossip
e.x:
Marcus tells himself to stop talking about what others are doing and to focus on his own work. Gossip is a distraction from self-improvement and a form of social comparison that breeds envy or contempt. Practise silence about others.

(Med. I.9, II.6, IV.18, V.9, VI.6; Seneca, Letters 94, 123.)

**Plain words** Marcus tells himself to stop talking about what others are doing and mind his own work. Gossip distracts from self-improvement and breeds envy or contempt through comparison. Practise silence about others.

*For example:* At lunch, you decline to discuss a colleague's divorce.
e.c: Layer VI - Social, Cosmopolitan, and Duty
p: **Social comparison research** (Festinger, 1954)
**Attention residue** (Leroy, 2009)
f: **Feed the belly, not the eye** (Laozi, Daodejing 12)
reflections: What do you gossip about, and what do you get out of it?
Is all talk about absent people gossip? Where is the line between concern and gossip?
How does gossip help or harm communities?

e.t: Speak truthfully and simply
e.x:
The Stoic speaks plainly. No pretension, no cleverness for its own sake. Say what you mean. Mean what you say. The simplest speech is often the most effective and the least likely to cause misunderstanding.

(Med. III.5, IV.16, V.9, VI.8, XI.15; Disc. III.21; Ench. 24, 33, 35, 42, 45, 46.)

**Plain words** The Stoic speaks plainly: no pretension, no cleverness for its own sake. Say what you mean and mean what you say. Simple speech is often the most effective and least likely to be misunderstood.

*For example:* Replacing "I was wondering if perhaps we might possibly..." with "Can we move the meeting?"
e.c: Layer VI - Social, Cosmopolitan, and Duty
p: **Authenticity research** (Kernis and Goldman, 2006)
**Congruence** (Rogers, On Becoming a Person)
reflections: Where do you hide behind fancy words or hedges? What are you protecting?
Is plainness always kind? When does bluntness harm?
What would your speech sound like if you said only what you meant?

e.t: Practise hospitality and kindness to strangers
e.x:
The Stoic is a citizen of the world. Every human is a fellow citizen. Treat strangers as you would treat neighbours. Kindness costs little and returns much.

(Med. IV.29, VI.14, VIII.5; Disc. III.24; Seneca, Letters 3, 9, 95; Musonius Rufus, Lectures.)

**Plain words** A Stoic is a citizen of the world, so every human is a fellow citizen. Treat strangers as neighbours. Kindness costs little and returns much.

*For example:* Giving directions to a lost tourist, walking her to the corner.
e.c: Layer VI - Social, Cosmopolitan, and Duty
p: **Prosocial spending and acts of kindness** (Dunn, Aknin and Norton, 2008)
**Intergroup contact hypothesis** (Allport, 1954; Pettigrew and Tropp, 2006)
reflections: How do you treat strangers on an average day? What would you change?
Is hospitality to strangers a virtue we can afford in a world of risk? How would you weigh it?
What does it mean to be a fellow citizen of someone you will never meet?

e.t: Do not let others' opinions govern you
e.x:
The Stoic does not seek praise or fear blame. What others think of you is outside your control and therefore indifferent. Let your own judgement of your virtue be your standard.

(Med. I.6, II.6, III.4, IV.3, IV.18, V.3, VI.16, VII.31, VIII.45, IX.30; Disc. I.1, I.12, I.20, I.25; Ench. 1, 42, 47; Seneca, Letters 20, 29, 41, 44, 73, 75, 79, 91, 94, 103, 123.)

**Plain words** The Stoic doesn't seek praise or fear blame. What others think is outside your control, so indifferent. Let your own judgement of your virtue be the standard.

*For example:* Doing the right thing at work when nobody is watching and nobody will thank you.
e.c: Layer VI - Social, Cosmopolitan, and Duty
p: **Extrinsic versus intrinsic motivation** (Kasser and Ryan, 1993)
**Self-concordance theory** (Sheldon and Elliot, 1999)
f: **The having versus being mode** (Fromm, To Have or To Be?)
reflections: Whose opinion has the strongest hold on you? Why does it matter so much?
Is it healthy to disregard others' opinions entirely? When are they a useful mirror?
How do you judge your own virtue honestly, without flattery or harshness?

e.t: Associate with people who make you better
e.x:
Seneca advises choosing friends who elevate you, not those who drag you down. The company you keep shapes your character. Be deliberate about your associations.

(Seneca, Letters 7, 9, 15, 35, 41, 44, 63, 109; Med. I.7, I.15, I.17, I.15, IV.38, V.10, VI.8, IX.11; Disc. III.16, III.24; Ench. 4, 33, 46.)

**Plain words** Seneca advises choosing friends who lift you, not drag you down. Your company shapes your character, so choose it deliberately.

*For example:* Spending less time with the friend who always complains, and more with the one who gets you thinking.
e.c: Layer VI - Social, Cosmopolitan, and Duty
p: **Social contagion and network effects on well-being** (Christakis and Fowler, 2009)
**Peer influence on behaviour** (Bandura, 1977)
reflections: Who in your life makes you better? Who doesn't? What would you do about it?
Is it fair to rank friends by their effect on you? How would you weigh loyalty against growth?
Whom do you lift? How would your friends describe that?

e.t: Practise tolerance without indifference
e.x:
The Stoic tolerates what cannot be changed but does not become indifferent to what should be changed. Tolerance of persons is not tolerance of injustice. Distinguish between accepting what is outside your control and working to change what is within it.

(Med. II.1, II.13, VII.22, IX.4, IX.11; Disc. I.12, I.18; Seneca, Letters 95, 107.)

**Plain words** The Stoic tolerates what can't be changed but isn't indifferent to what should be. Tolerating people isn't tolerating injustice. Distinguish accepting what's outside your control from working to change what's within it.

*For example:* Accepting that your father won't change, while still campaigning to improve the care home.
e.c: Layer VI - Social, Cosmopolitan, and Duty
p: **Acceptance and commitment**, accepting what cannot be changed while committing to what can (Hayes et al., 2011)
**Procedural justice and social change** (Tyler, 2006)
f: **The via media** (Bernstein, Beyond Objectivism and Relativism)
reflections: What are you tolerating that you should change? What are you trying to change that you should accept?
How do you tell the two apart in real time?
When does tolerance become complicity?

e.t: Practise empathy for wrongdoers
e.x:
The Stoic does not excuse wrongdoing but tries to understand it. The wrongdoer acts from ignorance of what is truly good. Understanding this does not remove responsibility but it reduces anger.

(Med. II.1, II.13, IV.3, VII.22, IX.4, IX.11, XI.18; Disc. I.18, III.3.)

**Plain words** Understanding why someone did wrong isn't the same as excusing it. The Stoic looks for the ignorance behind the act: what did this person think was good? Responsibility stays, but anger loses some of its fuel when you see the mistaken picture driving them.

*For example:* A driver tailgates you at speed. You think "late for something that matters to him," and your grip on the wheel eases, though you still don't like it.
e.c: Layer VI - Social, Cosmopolitan, and Duty
p: **Perspective-getting** (Epley et al., 2007)
**Compassion research** (Goetz et al., 2010)
f: **The face as ethical summons** (Levinas, Totality and Infinity)
reflections: Think of someone whose wrongdoing you struggle to understand. What might they believe is good that leads them there?
Where does empathy for a wrongdoer begin to feel like betrayal of the person they harmed? How would you hold both?
How might a justice system change if it combined accountability with this kind of understanding? Write about one concrete practice.

e.t: Do not be envious of others' success
e.x:
Envy is the judgment that another's success diminishes you. This is false. Another's success does not reduce your capacity for virtue. Practise rejoicing in others' good fortune.

(Med. VI.13, VI.16, IX.34; Seneca, Letters 109; Disc. I.9, I.20.)

**Plain words** Envy rests on the belief that someone else's success takes something from you. It doesn't. Their win leaves your capacity for virtue exactly as it was. Practise being glad when others do well, and watch how much lighter the day gets.

*For example:* A friend publishes the book you've been postponing, and you buy two copies, one to give away.
e.c: Layer VI - Social, Cosmopolitan, and Duty
p: **Social comparison** (Festinger, 1954)
**Sympathetic joy (mudita)** (Condon and Makransky, 2020)
f: **Amour-propre as comparative vanity** (Rousseau, Discourse on the Origin of Inequality)
reflections: Whose success have you privately resented, and what exactly did you think it took from you?
Some competition really is zero-sum, like one promotion for two people. How does the Stoic claim hold up there?
What would your friendships look like if gladness at one another's success were the default?

e.t: Do not compare yourself to others
e.x:
The only meaningful comparison is with yourself: are you better today than you were yesterday? Comparing yourself to others is a distraction from your own work and a source of either envy or pride.

(Med. I.9, II.6, III.4, IV.3, IV.18, V.3, VI.16, VII.31, VIII.45, IX.30; Disc. I.12, I.20, I.25.)

**Plain words** Compare yourself only with yesterday's you. Measuring against others pulls you away from your own work and breeds envy or pride. Ask whether you did better today than before, in the things that are yours to improve.

*For example:* A runner stops watching others' times and checks only whether she's more consistent than last month.
e.c: Layer VI - Social, Cosmopolitan, and Duty
p: **Social comparison processes** (Festinger, 1954)
**Relative deprivation** (Runciman, 1966)
f: **The having versus being mode** (Fromm, To Have or To Be?)
reflections: Who do you compare yourself with most, and what story do you tell afterwards? What is the comparison for?
Is all social comparison harmful? When is it useful information, for example in learning from a better practitioner?
What would "better than yesterday" mean in the part of your life that matters most to you?

e.t: Practise gratitude
e.x:
The Stoic practises gratitude for what they have. Marcus lists the things he is grateful for: his grandfather, his father, his mother, his teachers, his friends. The practice of gratitude shifts attention from what is lacking to what is present.

(Med. I.1, I.3, I.5, I.11, I.15, I.16, I.17; Seneca, Letters 9, 31; Disc. I.6, I.9, I.14, III.24.)

**Plain words** Marcus opens the Meditations by thanking his grandfather, father, mother, teachers and friends, one by one. Gratitude moves attention from what's missing to what's here. It works because it's specific, not because it's a mood.

*For example:* Writing three names on a card each Sunday, with one concrete thing each person did for you that week.
e.c: Layer VI - Social, Cosmopolitan, and Duty
p: **Gratitude and well-being** (Emmons and McCullough, 2003)
**Gratitude expression research** (Wood, Froh and Geraghty, 2010)
reflections: List ten people who made you who you are, with one specific debt to each. Which names surprised you?
Can gratitude be forced? What distinguishes a real practice from a performance?
What do you do with gratitude for people you can no longer thank?

e.t: Practise kindness
e.x:
The Stoic is kind. Not because kindness is required by a rule, but because kindness is the natural expression of a mind that understands its connection to the whole. Be kind to strangers, to family, to enemies. Kindness is not weakness; it is strength.

(Med. I.1, I.6, II.1, VI.14, VII.13, VII.22, IX.4, IX.11, IX.11; Disc. III.3, III.24; Seneca, Letters 9, 48, 95; Musonius Rufus, Lectures.)

**Plain words** A Stoic is kind, not because a rule says so but because kindness comes naturally to a mind that sees its connection to everyone else. It reaches strangers, family and enemies. Kindness isn't weakness. It takes strength to be kind when you're tired or provoked.

*For example:* Holding the door and meeting the eyes of a cashier whose day has clearly been terrible.
e.c: Layer VI - Social, Cosmopolitan, and Duty
p: **Prosocial behaviour and well-being** (Dunn, Aknin and Norton, 2008)
**Kindness interventions** (Lyubomirsky, Sheldon and Schkade, 2005)
reflections: When was kindness hardest for you? What made you do it, or not?
Is kindness different from niceness? What distinguishes them?
How does kindness toward an enemy change you, regardless of what it changes in them?

e.t: Be honest with yourself
e.x:
The Stoic is honest about their own faults. Marcus writes about his own tendencies: to be angry, to be lazy, to be impressed by the wrong things. The honesty is not self-criticism but accurate self-knowledge. Know your weaknesses so you can work on them.

(Med. I.1, I.6, I.9, II.1, III.1, V.1, VI.6, IX.2, X.1, XI.1, XI.18, XII.1.)

**Plain words** Marcus names his own faults in his notebook: his temper, his laziness, his admiration for the wrong things. The honesty isn't self-criticism. It's accurate self-knowledge. Know your weak spots so you can work on them.

*For example:* Admitting to yourself that you avoid hard conversations by staying busy, and planning one for Thursday.
e.c: Layer VI - Social, Cosmopolitan, and Duty
p: **Self-knowledge and its limits** (Vazire, 2010)
**Self-monitoring research** (Snyder, 1974)
reflections: What weakness do you know about but avoid looking at squarely? What would it cost to look?
How do you gather honest information about yourself when your own view is biased? Who tells you?
What is the difference between honest self-knowledge and shame? Write about how each feels.

e.t: Do not waste time on trivialities
e.x:
Marcus tells himself to stop being distracted by what others are doing and to focus on his own work. Seneca warns against wasting time on gossip, entertainment, and idle conversation. The Stoic is intentional about how they spend their time.

(Med. I.9, II.6, III.4, IV.18, V.9; Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 1, 2, 7; Disc. I.1, I.4, III.3.)

**Plain words** Don't spend your time on trivia. Marcus tells himself to stop watching what others are up to and attend to his own work, and Seneca warns against gossip, entertainment and idle talk. Be deliberate about where your hours go.

*For example:* Noticing you've spent forty minutes on a stranger's holiday photos and closing the app.
e.c: Layer VI - Social, Cosmopolitan, and Duty
p: **Time affluence** (Kasser and Sheldon, 2009)
**Attention management** (Leroy, 2009)
f: **Spend attention like money** (James, The Principles of Psychology)
**Life is short and do not waste it** (Seneca, On the Shortness of Life)
reflections: Where did your time actually go last week? Compare it to what you say matters most.
Is leisure trivial? Where do you draw the line between rest and waste?
What does your attention say about your values when you track it for a day?

e.t: Be a good neighbour
e.x:
The Stoic is a good neighbour: considerate, helpful, not intrusive. Marcus tells himself to be a good citizen, which begins with being a good neighbour. Do not underestimate the importance of small acts of neighbourliness.

(Med. I.6, I.9, II.1, IV.3, V.1, VI.7, IX.6, XI.5; Disc. III.7, III.24; Seneca, Letters 5, 9, 20.)

**Plain words** A good neighbour is considerate, helpful and not intrusive. Marcus's idea of citizenship begins at the front door. Don't underrate small acts: a nod, a spare key, carrying the bins in.

*For example:* Taking in a neighbour's parcel and leaving a note, without being asked.
e.c: Layer VI - Social, Cosmopolitan, and Duty
p: **Social connectedness and flourishing** (Holt-Lunstad, Smith and Layton, 2010)
**Prosocial behaviour** (Dunn, Aknin and Norton, 2008)
f: **Democracy as associated living** (Dewey, Democracy and Education)
reflections: Do you know your neighbours' names? What stands in the way of the small acts?
How do you balance helpfulness with respect for privacy?
What would a street look like if everyone practised this? What would be at risk, and what gained?

e.t: Remember that you will die
e.x:
Memento mori is the practice of holding death in mind. Not to induce fear but to clarify priorities. If you knew you would die tomorrow, what would you do today? The question is not hypothetical; you will die, and the timing is unknown. Let the awareness of death sharpen the value of life.

(Med. II.11, II.14, III.1, III.17, IV.17, IV.19, IV.48, VII.2, VII.29, VII.46, X.15, XI.1, XII.23, XII.35; Seneca, Letters 1, 4, 26, 49, 82, 91, 99, 101, 104, 122; Disc. I.14, III.24; Ench. 21.)

**Plain words** Memento mori: hold death in mind, not to scare yourself but to clarify what matters. If you'd die tomorrow, what would you do today? It isn't hypothetical. You will die, and you don't know when. Let that give your life its edge.

*For example:* Before agreeing to a meeting that bores you, you ask whether this is how you'd spend a day you'd never get back.
e.c: Layer VII - Time, Death, and Adversity
p: **Death reflection**, increases gratitude and decreases materialism (Cozzolino, 2006)
**Terror management theory** (Greenberg et al., 1986)
f: **Memento mori** (Seneca, On the Shortness of Life)
reflections: What would you change this week if you took your death seriously? Name one thing you've postponed.
Does thinking of death make you more present or more anxious? What works for you?
Why do many cultures avoid talking about death? What does that avoidance cost?

e.t: See that life is short and do not waste it
e.x:
Seneca's On the Shortness of Life argues that life is long enough for those who use it well. The problem is not that life is short but that we waste it on trivia. Audit your time. Where does it go? Is it going where you would choose?

(Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 1, 2, 7, 10, 14, 15, 20; Med. II.4, IV.17, VII.29, XI.1; Disc. I.1, I.4, III.3.)

**Plain words** Seneca says life is long enough if you use it well. The trouble isn't brevity but waste. Audit your time. Where does it go, and is that where you'd send it?

*For example:* Tracking a week in half-hour blocks and discovering that three hours a day vanish into scrolling.
e.c: Layer VII - Time, Death, and Adversity
p: **Time affluence** (Kasser and Sheldon, 2009)
**The progress principle** (Amabile and Kramer, 2011)
f: **The specious present** (James, The Principles of Psychology)
**Spend attention like money** (James, The Principles of Psychology)
reflections: Audit last week. What are the three biggest absorbers of your time? Would you choose them?
Many people cannot control their time because of work or caring duties. How should the principle be read for them?
What is the one thing you would do with a free hour if you trusted it was yours?

e.t: Practise negative visualisation
e.x:
Imagine losing what you have: your health, your loved ones, your possessions, your life. Not to induce anxiety but to prepare the mind and to appreciate what is present. The Stoic who has rehearsed loss is less devastated when it comes.

(Seneca, Letters 18, 24, 91, 107, 122; Med. III.1, III.6, VI.34; Disc. I.14, III.26.)

**Plain words** Imagine losing what you have: health, loved ones, things, your life. The point isn't anxiety. It's preparing the mind and noticing what's here. The Stoic who has rehearsed loss is less flattened when it comes.

*For example:* Picturing your partner gone for a minute while they're in the next room, then going in and just listening to them.
e.c: Layer VII - Time, Death, and Adversity
p: **Mental contrasting (WOOP)** (Oettingen, 2014)
**Stress inoculation training** (Meichenbaum, 1985)
reflections: What do you take most for granted? What would imagining its loss reveal?
When has imagining loss deepened appreciation, and when has it only made you anxious?
How does negative visualisation compare with gratitude practices? Which suits you, and why?

e.t: Treat adversity as training
e.x:
What stands in the way becomes the way. Adversity is not an obstacle to flourishing but the material of it. The person who has never faced difficulty has never tested their virtue. When hardship comes, ask: what virtue does this situation call for?

(Med. IV.1, IV.50, V.8, V.10, V.18, V.20, VI.48, VII.8, VII.19, VII.20, VII.43, VII.55, VIII.35, VIII.41, X.33; Disc. I.6, I.24, III.20; Ench. 1, 16, 19, 29, 53; Seneca, On Providence.)

**Plain words** What stands in the way becomes the way. Adversity isn't a blocker of the good life. It's raw material. Someone who has never been tested doesn't know their own virtue. When hardship arrives, ask which virtue it's calling for.

*For example:* A failed launch becomes the occasion to practise honesty with your team and customers.
e.c: Layer VII - Time, Death, and Adversity
p: **Stress-as-challenge mindset** (Crum et al., 2013)
**Post-traumatic growth research** (Tedeschi and Calhoun, 2004)
f: **The obstacle is the way** (Marcus Aurelius, Meditations V.20)
**Let obstruction do its work** (Dewey, Experience and Nature)
reflections: What obstacle in your life now might be the way? What virtue is it calling for?
Is it true that hardship builds character, or does it sometimes just wear people down? What makes the difference?
Who benefits when we tell sufferers their pain is training? How could this idea be abused?

e.t: Do not complain
e.x:
Complaining is the judgement that something should not be as it is. The Stoic accepts what is and works with it. Complaining wastes energy that could go to action or acceptance. Practise the discipline of non-complaint: when you catch yourself complaining, stop and ask what you can do.

(Med. IV.49, V.16, VI.16, VIII.4, VIII.9, XI.18; Seneca, Letters 13, 24, 67, 78, 107; Disc. I.6, I.14, I.18, III.20.)

**Plain words** Complaining is judging that things shouldn't be as they are. The Stoic accepts what's there and works with it. Complaint burns energy better spent on acting or accepting. When you catch it, stop and ask what you can do.

*For example:* Stuck in a slow queue, you use the time to reply to messages instead of sighing.
e.c: Layer VII - Time, Death, and Adversity
p: **Cognitive reappraisal** (Gross, 2015)
**Acceptance-based coping** (Hayes et al., 2011)
f: **Accept what happens as the will of providence** (Marcus Aurelius, Meditations IV.10)
reflections: What do you complain about most? What would acting or accepting look like instead?
Complaining can also be a way of bonding or sharing pain. When is it healthy?
Is there a complaint that should be voiced, such as against injustice? How do you tell?

e.t: Accept pain as part of nature
e.x:
Pain is not inherently bad. It is part of the natural order. The Stoic does not seek pain but does not flee it. When pain comes, accept it as you would accept the weather: something outside your control that you can endure with dignity.

(Med. IV.10, V.8, VI.10, VII.33, VII.64, IX.41, X.33; Seneca, Letters 24, 67, 78, 107; Disc. I.1, I.6, I.14.)

**Plain words** Pain isn't bad in itself. It's part of nature. The Stoic doesn't seek it and doesn't run from it. When pain comes, take it like weather: outside your control and bearable with dignity.

*For example:* Sitting through a dental procedure with slow breathing rather than tensing against it.
e.c: Layer VII - Time, Death, and Adversity
p: **Acceptance-based behaviour therapy for chronic pain** (McCracken, 1998; Vowles et al., 2014)
**Radical acceptance** (Linehan, 1993)
f: **The mean in pleasure and pain** (Aristotle, NE II.6)
reflections: What is your usual response to pain, physical or emotional? What would accepting it as weather look like?
Where does acceptance of pain become neglect of treatment? How do you balance them?
What do you make of those whose pain isn't bearable? What should we say, and not say, to them?

e.t: See that everything passes
e.x:
Whatever you are experiencing, it will change. The pleasant will pass; the painful will pass. The Stoic holds both lightly. Do not cling to the pleasant; do not flee the painful. Both are visitors.

(Med. II.11, II.14, III.1, III.10, IV.1, IV.35, V.23, VI.15, VII.10, VII.34, IX.21, IX.28, IX.29, IX.33, X.7, X.11, XI.1, XI.21; Seneca, Letters 24, 71, 91, 99, 107.)

**Plain words** Whatever you're feeling will change. The pleasant will pass and so will the painful. Hold both lightly. Don't cling to the nice and don't flee the nasty. Both are visitors.

*For example:* In the middle of a bad week you remind yourself that you've had bad weeks before and they ended.
e.c: Layer VII - Time, Death, and Adversity
p: **Hedonic adaptation** (Lyubomirsky, 2011)
**Impermanence as therapeutic insight** (Buddhist psychology)
reflections: What are you clinging to that is already passing? What are you fleeing that you could let visit?
Does "this too shall pass" console or dismiss? When has it done each?
How does knowing that everything passes change how you treat joy?

e.t: Remember that the whole is more important than the part
e.x:
What is good for the whole may not be pleasant for the part. The Stoic accepts their role in the larger order, even when it is difficult. This is not self-sacrifice but self-understanding: you are a part, not the whole.

(Med. II.3, IV.10, V.8, V.30, VI.42, VII.9, VII.19, VII.47, VIII.7, VIII.34, VIII.50, VIII.52, X.1, X.6, X.33, XI.1, XI.18, XII.36; Disc. I.12, I.14, I.25, III.10, III.24; Seneca, Letters 71, 95, 107; Ench. 31, 53.)

**Plain words** What's good for the whole isn't always pleasant for the part. The Stoic accepts their role in a larger order, even when it's hard. That isn't self-sacrifice. It's self-understanding: you're a part, not the whole.

*For example:* Staying late to help the team finish, even though it costs your evening, because the whole needs it.
e.c: Layer VII - Time, Death, and Adversity
p: **Self-transcendent experiences** (Yaden et al., 2017)
**Mattering and purpose** (George and Park, 2016)
f: **Participate in the world's becoming** (Whitehead, Process and Reality)
reflections: When has the good of a group cost you something? How did you decide it was worth it?
How do you stop "the good of the whole" from being used to exploit individuals?
What is your part in the larger whole you belong to? Does knowing it help?

e.t: Recognise that fame after death is meaningless
e.x:
Marcus tells himself that the fame of the dead is as worthless as the fame of the living. The person who seeks posthumous fame seeks the approval of people who do not exist yet and who will themselves die. Seek virtue, not reputation.

(Med. I.19, II.6, III.4, IV.3, IV.19, V.33, VI.16, VII.6, IX.30, X.8, XI.1, XI.27, XII.21, XII.27.)

**Plain words** Marcus reminds himself that posthumous fame is as worthless as living fame. Seeking it means seeking the approval of people who don't exist yet and who will die too. Aim at virtue, not reputation.

*For example:* Declining to polish a legacy project and spending the time with your grandchildren.
e.c: Layer VII - Time, Death, and Adversity
p: **Extrinsic motivation and well-being** (Kasser and Ryan, 1993)
**Self-determination theory** (Deci and Ryan, 2000)
f: **Contempt for fame** (Seneca, Letters from a Stoic)
**The having versus being mode** (Fromm, To Have or To Be?)
reflections: What are you doing partly for how you'll be remembered? What would you do if no one would remember?
Is wanting to be remembered a human need? Where does it become vanity?
Whose memory of you matters, and why?

e.t: Remember the brevity of life and reputation
e.x:
Marcus tells himself that the greatest emperors are already forgotten. The longest fame is short. What you do for fame is wasted. What you do for virtue lasts as long as your character lasts.

(Med. I.19, III.4, IV.3, IV.19, IV.33, IV.35, VI.24, VII.6, IX.30, XI.1, XI.27, XII.21, XII.27, XII.32.)

**Plain words** The greatest emperors are already forgotten, says Marcus. Even the longest fame is short. What you do for fame is wasted, and what you do for virtue lasts as long as your character does.

*For example:* Walking past a statue nobody can name, and deciding what you'll actually put effort into.
e.c: Layer VII - Time, Death, and Adversity
p: **Hedonic adaptation** (Lyubomirsky, 2011)
**Mortality salience** (Greenberg et al., 1986)
f: **Memento mori** (Seneca, On the Shortness of Life)
reflections: What is one thing you've done for recognition that now seems empty? What would the virtue version have been?
If character is what lasts, what is lasting about yours? What do others receive from it?
What do we owe to the forgotten whose work made our lives possible?

e.t: Recognise that change is the nature of the universe
e.x:
The universe is change. Your life is an opinion. Death is a natural process. The Stoic does not resist change but accepts it as the fundamental character of reality.

(Med. I.14, II.3, II.17, IV.1, IV.3, IV.36, IV.43, VI.15, VII.10, VII.19, VII.25, VII.34, VII.49, IX.28, IX.29, IX.35, X.1, X.7, XI.1, XI.21, XII.1, XII.20, XII.21, XII.32, XII.36.)

**Plain words** The universe is change. Your life is a view you take of it. Death is a natural process. The Stoic doesn't resist change but accepts it as the basic character of reality.

*For example:* Moving house after thirty years and treating it as one more turn of the wheel.
e.c: Layer VII - Time, Death, and Adversity
p: **Acceptance and commitment** (Hayes et al., 2011)
**Psychological flexibility** (Kashdan and Rottenberg, 2010)
reflections: What change are you resisting right now? What does the resistance cost?
How do you hold loved things in a world where everything changes? Is there something worth keeping constant?
Is acceptance of change always wise, or are there changes we should refuse? Give an example.

e.t: See the smallness of human affairs
e.x:
From the perspective of the cosmos, human affairs are tiny. The great events of your day are invisible from the stars. The Stoic practises the view from above to restore proportion. Your problems are real but they are small.

(Med. II.12, III.11, IV.1, IV.3, IV.32, V.24, VI.36, VII.48, IX.30, XII.24, XII.32; Disc. I.14, III.24; Seneca, Letters 91.)

**Plain words** From the cosmos, human affairs are tiny. Your day's great events can't be seen from the stars. The Stoic uses the view from above to restore proportion. Your problems are real, but they're small.

*For example:* Looking up at the night sky after a bad day at work and feeling the day shrink a little.
e.c: Layer VII - Time, Death, and Adversity
p: **Self-distancing** (Kross and Ayduk, 2017)
**Awe and the small-self** (Yaden et al., 2017)
