e.c: Section III - Māori Relational Philosophy (Tikanga and Whakataukī) (15 Principles)
p: **Authenticity** (Kernis and Goldman, 2006)
f: **Authenticity** (Heidegger, Being and Time; Sartre, Existentialism Is a Humanism)

e.t: Practise aroha
e.x:
Love with compassion and generosity. Aroha is not merely romantic love; it is a deep, compassionate love that motivates action on behalf of others. It is the affective dimension of tikanga, the emotional ground of right relationship.

(Māori tikanga; Mead, 2003, Tikanga Māori; Durie, 1994, Whaiora.)

**Plain words** Aroha is love with legs: compassion and generosity that motivate action on behalf of others — the emotional ground of right relationship. It's not the romantic kind only, and it's never just a feeling; it's a felt commitment that reaches outward.

*For example:* When the flood hits the marae, the aunties are already cooking — nobody organised them, nobody asked; aroha is what the kitchen runs on.
e.c: Section III - Māori Relational Philosophy (Tikanga and Whakataukī) (15 Principles)
p: **Compassionate love** (Underwood, 2008)
f: **Compassion** (Schopenhauer, On the Basis of Morality; Nussbaum, Upheavals of Thought)

e.t: Practise Te Whare Tapa Whā
e.x:
Attend to all four dimensions of your wellbeing: te taha wairua (spiritual), te taha hinengaro (mental and emotional), te taha tinana (physical), and te taha whānau (family and social). Neglect of any one dimension undermines the whole. Practise balance across all four.

(Māori health model; Durie, 1985, "A Māori Perspective of Health," Social Science and Medicine, 20(5), 483-486; Durie, 1994, Whaiora.)

**Plain words** Te Whare Tapa Whā: wellbeing is a house with four walls — spiritual, mental/emotional, physical, and family/social. If one wall crumbles, the whole house leans, no matter how strong the others. Check all four on purpose.

*For example:* The person who fixes "burnout" with gym and diet for months — then adds one weekly dinner with the cousins and finds the wall that was actually missing was the fourth one.
e.c: Section III - Māori Relational Philosophy (Tikanga and Whakataukī) (15 Principles)
p: **Holistic well-being** (Ryff, 1989)
**Biopsychosocial model** (Engel, 1977)

e.t: Practise whakawhanaungatanga
e.x:
Actively build relationships across difference. Whakawhanaungatanga is the process of establishing relationship where none existed before, of finding connection across cultural, social, or personal difference. It is the active, intentional version of whanaungatanga.

(Māori tikanga; Mead, 2003, Tikanga Māori; Durie, 1994, Whaiora.)

**Plain words** Whakawhanaungatanga is relationship-building as an active craft: establishing connection where none existed, across cultural, social, or personal difference. Not waiting for common ground — digging for it.

*For example:* The nurse who learns three words of greeting in each language of her ward's patients — small effort, and every patient's whole posture changes in the first thirty seconds.
e.c: Section III - Māori Relational Philosophy (Tikanga and Whakataukī) (15 Principles)
p: **Intergroup contact** (Pettigrew, 1998)

e.t: Practise hau
e.x:
Recognise the vital essence of life that animates all living things. Hau is the breath of life, the wind, the spirit that moves through all of creation. In tikanga, hau must be respected and protected. Do not take the hau of others; do not let your own hau be depleted.

(Māori tikanga; Mead, 2003, Tikanga Māori; Durie, 1994, Whaiora.)

**Plain words** Hau is the breath of life moving through all living things — and it must be respected and protected, in others and in yourself. Don't take what drains someone's hau; don't let your own run empty. Vitality is a shared substance, not private property.

*For example:* Someone who notices certain friendships leave them fuller and certain "harmless" obligations leave them hollowed — and starts protecting their own breath like it belongs to the people who need them.
e.c: Section III - Māori Relational Philosophy (Tikanga and Whakataukī) (15 Principles)
p: **Vitality** (Ryan and Frederick, 1997)

e.t: Practise whānau ora
e.x:
Prioritise the wellbeing of your whole family, not just individuals within it. Whānau ora is a holistic approach to family health that recognises the family as a living system. When one member suffers, the whole family is affected. When the family is well, each member flourishes.

(Māori health framework; Durie, 1994, Whaiora; Taskforce on Whānau-Centred Initiatives, 2010.)

**Plain words** Whānau ora: the family is the patient. Wellbeing isn't an individual scorecard — when one member suffers, the whole system feels it, and the treatment has to reach the system. Ask "how is the family?" not only "how are you?"

*For example:* The clinic that stops treating the asthmatic child and starts treating the house — the mould, the landlord, the stress — and the child's chart improves faster than any inhaler alone.
e.c: Section III - Māori Relational Philosophy (Tikanga and Whakataukī) (15 Principles)
p: **Family systems therapy** (Minuchin, 1974; Bowen, 1978)

e.t: Honour the vā
e.x:
Attend to the relational space between yourself and others. In Pacific (Samoan, Tongan, Fijian) philosophy, the vā is the space between people that must be carefully maintained. It is not empty; it is the living ground of relationship. Tend the vā by being present, respectful, and attentive in your interactions.

(Samoan philosophy; Tuhiwai Smith, 1999, Decolonizing Methodologies; Wendt, 1996, "Tatauing the Post-Colonial Body," Span, 42-43, 15-29.)

**Plain words** The space between you and another person isn't empty — it's the vā, the living ground of relationship, and it needs maintenance like anything alive. Be present, respectful, attentive: the between-ness is a thing you tend, not just a gap you cross.

*For example:* Two friends who never let a misunderstanding sit overnight — not because they're conflict-averse, but because they can feel the space itself going stale.
e.c: Section IV - Pacific Relational Philosophy (Vā and Relational Space) (10 Principles)
p: **Relational space and interpersonal connection** (Gergen, 2009)

e.t: Practise teu le vā
e.x:
Beautify and care for the relational space. Teu le vā is the active practice of maintaining, nurturing, and beautifying the space between people. It includes being courteous, thoughtful, and intentional in how you relate to others.

(Samoan philosophy; Tuhiwai Smith, 1999, Decolonizing Methodologies; Wendt, 1996.)

**Plain words** Teu le vā: actively beautify the relational space. Courtesy, thoughtfulness, the deliberate small gesture — the space between people is kept the way a garden is kept, by tending. Neglect is also a choice, just a worse one.

*For example:* The colleague who always leaves the shared kitchen better than they found it, remembers birthdays, sends the thank-you text — not sainthood, just someone who gardens the between.
e.c: Section IV - Pacific Relational Philosophy (Vā and Relational Space) (10 Principles)
p: **Relational maintenance** (Stafford and Canary, 1991)
f: **Care of the between** (Buber, I and Thou; Levinas, Totality and Infinity)

e.t: Practise fa'asamoa
e.x:
Live in accordance with the Samoan way. Fa'asamoa is not merely a set of customs but a way of being in the world that centres relationship, respect, and reciprocity. Where you are in a Samoan context, honour the fa'asamoa. More broadly, honour the cultural way of being of the communities you belong to or interact with.

(Samoan philosophy; Tuhiwai Smith, 1999, Decolonizing Methodologies.)

**Plain words** Live by the way of your community — fa'asamoa, the way of relationship, respect, and reciprocity — and more broadly, honour the way of whichever community you're standing in. A way of being isn't a costume; it's a coherence you either practise or perform.

*For example:* Someone far from home who keeps the protocol at family gatherings — the seating, the order of speaking, the offerings — and finds it's not constraint but the thing that makes the gathering feel like home anywhere.
e.c: Section IV - Pacific Relational Philosophy (Vā and Relational Space) (10 Principles)
p: **Cultural identity and well-being** (Phinney, 1992)
f: **Cultural embeddedness** (MacIntyre, After Virtue; Sandel, Liberalism and the Limits of Justice)

e.t: Practise tautua
e.x:
Serve your family and community. In Samoan culture, tautua (service) is not optional but a fundamental obligation. Service to family, church, and community is the path to social standing and personal fulfilment. Find ways to serve that are meaningful to you and beneficial to those you serve.

(Samoan philosophy; Tuhiwai Smith, 1999, Decolonizing Methodologies.)

**Plain words** Serve: family, community, church, the people around you — not as optional charity but as the actual path of a life. Tautua isn't a line on a CV; it's how standing and fulfilment are built in the first place. Find the service that fits your hands.

*For example:* The young man who coaches the village team, helps with the funerals, drives the aunties — and at thirty is the person the whole community quietly treats as a pillar.
e.c: Section IV - Pacific Relational Philosophy (Vā and Relational Space) (10 Principles)
p: **Prosocial behaviour and well-being** (Dunn, Aknin, and Norton, 2014, "Prosocial Spending...)

e.t: Practise respect for matai
e.x:
Honour the chiefs and elders who hold responsibility for the wellbeing of the community. In Samoan culture, the matai system is a structure of governance and care. Respect the wisdom and responsibility of those who lead. More broadly, respect those in your community who carry responsibility for the collective.

(Samoan philosophy; Tuhiwai Smith, 1999, Decolonizing Methodologies.)

**Plain words** Honour those who carry responsibility for the collective — the matai, the elders, the ones whose job is the wellbeing of the group. Respect isn't worship of rank; it's recognising that someone is holding weight you're not holding.

*For example:* The meeting where the newest member speaks last, listens to the chiefs first — and learns more in one hour about how this community decides things than in a year of documents.
e.c: Section IV - Pacific Relational Philosophy (Vā and Relational Space) (10 Principles)
p: **Respect for authority and social order** (Hofstede, 2001)

e.t: Practise talanoa
e.x:
Engage in open, inclusive dialogue. Talanoa is a Pacific method of dialogue and storytelling that values open, honest, and inclusive conversation. It is not debate or negotiation but the sharing of stories and perspectives in a way that builds relationship and understanding. Practise talanoa in your own conversations.

(Pacific philosophy; Vaioleti, 2006, "Talanoa Research Methodology," Waikato Journal of Education, 12, 21-34.)

**Plain words** Talanoa: dialogue as storytelling, not combat. Open, honest, inclusive — people share their actual perspectives and experiences, and relationship gets built in the telling. It's not a negotiation with a winner; it's a fire everyone sits around.

*For example:* The team that replaces its blame-laden post-mortems with "tell the story of what you saw" — and the room that was ready for a fight starts, unexpectedly, learning.
e.c: Section IV - Pacific Relational Philosophy (Vā and Relational Space) (10 Principles)
p: **Narrative sharing and relational bonding** (McAdams, 2008)
f: **Dialogue** (Buber, I and Thou; Gadamer, Truth and Method)

e.t: Practise va tapuia
e.x:
Recognise the sacred dimension of the relational space. Va tapuia is the understanding that the space between people is sacred, that it carries a spiritual weight that must be honoured. Do not treat your relationships as merely instrumental or transactional. Recognise their sacred dimension.

(Samoan philosophy; Tuhiwai Smith, 1999, Decolonizing Methodologies; Wendt, 1996.)

**Plain words** The space between people is sacred — va tapuia — it carries a spiritual weight, and treating relationships as transactions is the violation. Honour the dimension: some things are owed to the space itself, not to any outcome.

*For example:* The business partners who refuse to squeeze the last dollar out of a deal because "that's not how we want the space between us to look in ten years" — and are still partners in ten years.
e.c: Section IV - Pacific Relational Philosophy (Vā and Relational Space) (10 Principles)
p: **Awe and the sacred in relationships** (Keltner and Haidt, 2003)
f: **The sacred** (Otto, The Idea of the Holy)

e.t: Practise ofo
e.x:
Feel compassion for those who suffer. Ofo is the Samoan concept of compassion that arises when you witness the suffering of others. Do not suppress this feeling; let it motivate you to act.

(Samoan philosophy; Tuhiwai Smith, 1999, Decolonizing Methodologies.)

**Plain words** Ofo: the pang you feel at another's suffering. Don't suppress it or argue with it — it's the signal, and its job is to move you. Feeling it is the start of acting on it.

*For example:* Someone who sees the flood footage and doesn't scroll past — the pang itself decides the evening, and the donation and the drives follow.
e.c: Section IV - Pacific Relational Philosophy (Vā and Relational Space) (10 Principles)
p: **Empathic concern** (Batson, 2011)

e.t: Practise alofa
e.x:
Love with generosity and care. Alofa is the Samoan concept of love that encompasses affection, compassion, and generosity. It is not merely a feeling but a practice of caring for others through concrete action.

(Samoan philosophy; Tuhiwai Smith, 1999, Decolonizing Methodologies.)

**Plain words** Alofa: love as affection, compassion, and generosity in one — a practice expressed through concrete care, not a feeling waiting to strike. You love by showing up with something useful.

*For example:* The auntie whose love looks like the freezer always stocked for whoever turns up, the ride to the airport at 5 a.m., the exact-right amount in the card — nobody doubts they're loved; they can eat the evidence.
e.c: Section IV - Pacific Relational Philosophy (Vā and Relational Space) (10 Principles)
p: **Compassionate love** (Underwood, 2008)
f: **Love** (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII-VIX; Nussbaum, Upheavals of Thought)

e.t: Practise connection across the ocean
e.x:
In Pacific philosophy, the ocean is not a barrier that separates but a highway that connects. Maintain connection with your diaspora, with your ancestral homelands, and with the wider Pacific community. Distance does not dissolve relationship.

(Pacific philosophy; Hau'ofa, 1994, "Our Sea of Islands," The Contemporary Pacific, 6(1), 148-161.)

**Plain words** The ocean is a highway, not a wall: distance doesn't end relationship, and the diaspora is still one circle. Keep the connections across the water — the homeland, the relatives, the wider community. The sea connects what the map divides.

*For example:* The family that sends the boxes, funds the village roof, video-calls the Sunday to'ona'i from three time zones away — and their kids grow up knowing exactly where "home" is, though they've never lived there.
e.c: Section IV - Pacific Relational Philosophy (Vā and Relational Space) (10 Principles)
p: **Social connection across distance** (Wellman, 2001)

e.t: Practise ren (humanity/benevolence)
e.x:
Cultivate the virtue of humanity, the disposition to love and care for others. Ren is the supreme Confucian virtue, the ground of all other virtues. Practise it by wishing for the flourishing of others and working to bring it about.

(Confucius, The Analects 12.22; Mencius, The Mencius 2A6; The Doctrine of the Mean, ch. 20.)

**Plain words** Ren is humanity: the disposition to genuinely wish for others' flourishing and then work for it. It's not niceness — it's the root virtue everything else grows from. Practise it by wanting good things for people, out loud, with your hands.

*For example:* The colleague who hears about a rival's promotion and notices the pang — then deliberately congratulates them properly, and means it. The sprout gets watered either way; only one watering is ren.
e.c: Section V - Confucian Relational Ethics (15 Principles)
p: **Compassion and altruism** (Goetz et al., 2010)
**Benevolence and well-being** (Diener and Seligman, 2002)
f: **Love of humanity** (Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals)

e.t: Practise yi (righteousness/justice)
e.x:
Do what is right in every situation. Yi is the virtue of moral rightness, the disposition to do what justice requires. It is not rule-following but the practical wisdom to see what is right and do it.

(Confucius, The Analects 4.10, 4.16; Mencius, The Mencius 2A2, 6A10.)

**Plain words** Yi is doing what's right when the situation itself has to show you what that means — not rule-following but right-seeing. What does justice require here? The disposition is trained one such decision at a time.

*For example:* The referee who calls the penalty against the home crowd — the rules made it easy; yi is what makes them do it when nobody would ever know if they didn't.
e.c: Section V - Confucian Relational Ethics (15 Principles)
p: **Moral identity** (Blasi, 1984)
**Justice sensitivity** (Schmitt et al., 2005)

e.t: Practise li (ritual propriety)
e.x:
Engage in ritual and ceremony as a means of cultivating virtue and social harmony. Li is not mere etiquette; it is the embodied practice of respect, reverence, and order. Through ritual, you train your emotions, align your behaviour with moral ideals, and participate in the communal life.

(Confucius, The Analects 12.1, 12.15; Xunzi, Xunzi 19.)

**Plain words** Li is ritual propriety: the embodied practice of respect — ceremony, forms, the way things are done. Not empty etiquette: through ritual you train the emotions and take part in a shared order. The form is the workout.

*For example:* The family that keeps the birthday dinner ritual — same table, same toast, same awful song — and finds the ritual carries a depth of feeling that "quality time" never seems to deliver.
e.c: Section V - Confucian Relational Ethics (15 Principles)
p: **Ritual and well-being** (Hobson et al., 2018)

e.t: Practise zhi (wisdom)
e.x:
Cultivate the practical wisdom to distinguish right from wrong, beneficial from harmful, true from false. Zhi is not merely intellectual knowledge but moral discernment. It is the wisdom to see the right course of action and the courage to pursue it.

(Confucius, The Analects 6.22, 15.3; Mencius, The Mencius 2A6.)

**Plain words** Zhi is moral discernment: seeing right from wrong, true from false, and then having the spine to pursue it. Not intellectual horsepower — the eye that spots the right course plus the legs to walk it.

*For example:* The engineer who can't un-see the corner being cut on safety — everyone sees it, she's the one whose knowledge turns into a raised hand at the meeting.
e.c: Section V - Confucian Relational Ethics (15 Principles)
p: **Wisdom** (Baltes and Staudinger, 2000; Grossmann et al., 2010)

e.t: Practise xin (trustworthiness/integrity)
e.x:
Be reliable in your word and faithful in your commitments. Xin is the virtue of being trustworthy, of making your words and actions align. Without xin, no social relationship can endure.

(Confucius, The Analects 1.3, 1.4, 1.8; Mencius, The Mencius 4A12.)

**Plain words** Xin is trustworthiness: words and actions aligned, commitments kept. Without it, no relationship — business, friendship, or family — can survive. Be someone whose word is boringly reliable.

*For example:* The tradesman who says "Tuesday, 9 a.m." and is there Tuesday, 9 a.m., for eleven years — and charges accordingly, because that reputation is the business.
e.c: Section V - Confucian Relational Ethics (15 Principles)
p: **Trust and relationship satisfaction** (Rempel et al., 2001)

e.t: Practise zhengming (rectification of names)
e.x:
Use language accurately and call things by their proper names. When names are not correct, language does not correspond to reality; when language does not correspond to reality, action goes wrong. In your own life, be precise in your speech, honest in your self-descriptions, and clear about what you mean.

(Confucius, The Analects 13.3.)

**Plain words** Zhengming, rectification of names: call things what they actually are. When names slip, language stops matching reality, and action goes wrong. In your own life: precise speech, honest self-descriptions, no euphemisms doing your dirty work.

*For example:* The manager who stops calling layoffs "right-sizing" and starts calling them layoffs — and finds the team can finally plan around the truth instead of the fog.
e.c: Section V - Confucian Relational Ethics (15 Principles)
p: **Linguistic precision and cognitive clarity** (Langer, 1989)

e.t: Practise the five relationships
e.x:
Honour the five fundamental relationships: parent-child, ruler-subject, husband-wife, elder-younger sibling, and friend-friend. Each relationship carries specific obligations. In each, there is a role to fulfil with virtue.

(Confucius, The Analects 12.11; Mencius, The Mencius 3A4; The Doctrine of the Mean, ch. 20.)

**Plain words** Five relationships — parent-child, ruler-ruled, spouses, siblings, friends — each with its own obligations and its own virtues. Not all bonds are the same, and pretending they are is a category error. Learn what each of yours asks of you.

*For example:* Someone who shows up very differently for their friend's crisis than their parent's — not coldness, just the correct recognition that "being there" means different acts in different bonds.
e.c: Section V - Confucian Relational Ethics (15 Principles)
p: **Relational roles and well-being** (Berscheid, 1994)
f: **Role ethics** (Confucius, The Analects; MacIntyre, After Virtue)

e.t: Practise filial piety (xiao)
e.x:
Honour your parents and ancestors. Filial piety is not mere obedience; it is the recognition of the debt you owe to those who gave you life, nurtured you, and made you who you are. Honour them through care, respect, and the continuation of their values.

(Confucius, The Analects 1.2, 1.11, 2.5, 2.7, 2.8; Mencius, The Mencius 4A18, 4A19.)

**Plain words** Xiao is filial piety: honouring parents and ancestors — not blind obedience, but recognising the debt to the ones who gave, nurtured, and made you. Care, respect, and carrying forward what was worth carrying.

*For example:* The son who drives his mother to every appointment and listens to the same stories — not because he always agrees with her, but because he knows exactly what he's repaying.
e.c: Section V - Confucian Relational Ethics (15 Principles)
p: **Family bonds and well-being** (Berscheid, 1994; Mikulincer et al., 2005)
f: **Gratitude** (Seneca, On Benefits; Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII.14)

e.t: Practise the Mencian sprouts
e.x:
Nurture the four moral sentiments that are natural to human beings: the feeling of compassion (the sprout of ren), the feeling of shame and dislike (the sprout of yi), the feeling of deference and compliance (the sprout of li), and the feeling of right and wrong (the sprout of zhi). These are seeds; they must be cultivated to grow into full virtues.

(Mencius, The Mencius 2A6, 6A6, 6A10.)

**Plain words** Mencius says you were issued four moral sprouts at birth: compassion (grows into ren), shame-and-dislike (yi), deference (li), right-and-wrong (zhi). Seeds, not finished trees — the whole work is cultivation. Water them or they stay sprouts.

*For example:* Everyone at the scene of the accident feels the flinch toward the injured — that flinch is the sprout. The person who kneels down and helps is just the sprout, watered.
e.c: Section V - Confucian Relational Ethics (15 Principles)
p: **Moral foundations theory** (Haidt, 2012)
**Moral emotions** (Tangney et al., 2007)
f: **Natural virtue** (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VI.13; Mencius, The Mencius)
**Moral sentiments** (Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature)

e.t: Practise self-cultivation (xiushen)
e.x:
Make the cultivation of your own moral character your primary project. All social and political improvement begins with self-cultivation. As The Great Learning states: from the extension of knowledge, the will becomes sincere; from the sincerity of the will, the mind becomes rectified; from the rectified mind, the person is cultivated; from the cultivated person, the family is regulated; from the regulated family, the state is governed; from the governed state, the world is at peace.

(The Great Learning; Confucius, The Analects 1.4, 12.1; The Doctrine of the Mean, ch. 1.)

**Plain words** Xiushen: make your own character the primary project. The Great Learning's cascade — sincere will, rectified mind, cultivated self, regulated family, governed state — starts at step one, and step one is you. Every improvement you want out there begins as work in here.

*For example:* The coach who spends the off-season on their own temper — and finds the team's discipline improves without a single new rule being issued.
e.c: Section V - Confucian Relational Ethics (15 Principles)
p: **Self-determined personality growth** (Deci and Ryan, 2000)
**Personality change through volitional goal pursuit** (Hudson and Fraley, 2015)
f: **Care of the self** (Foucault, The History of Sexuality)

e.t: Practise the Doctrine of the Mean (zhongyong)
e.x:
Seek the golden mean in all things. Zhongyong is the practice of finding the central, balanced way between extremes. It is not compromise or moderation for its own sake but the practical wisdom to find the right measure in each situation.

(The Doctrine of the Mean; Confucius, The Analects 11.16.)

**Plain words** Zhongyong, the mean: not lukewarm compromise but finding the exact right measure in each situation — between excess and deficiency, per the moment, not per a formula. The mean for courage isn't the average of rashness and cowardice; it's whatever this situation actually requires.

*For example:* The parent who doesn't ban the teenager's phone and doesn't surrender to it either — but finds the actual right measure for this kid, this year, this problem.
e.c: Section V - Confucian Relational Ethics (15 Principles)
p: **The middle way and well-being** (Goldilocks principle in personality, Denissen et a...)

e.t: Practise harmony (he)
e.x:
Seek harmony in your relationships and in your community. Harmony is not sameness; it is the creative integration of difference. The Confucian concept of he contrasts with tong (mere agreement). True harmony requires diverse voices.

(Confucius, The Analects 12.23, 13.23, 13.27; The Analects 1.12.)

**Plain words** He is harmony as the creative integration of difference — explicitly not tong, mere sameness. True harmony needs diverse voices; a room of agreement is a quieter, poorer thing. Build the ensemble, not the choir of one note.

*For example:* The project team deliberately staffed with people who'll fight — and led so the fights compose. The result is better than any same-minded team produces.
e.c: Section V - Confucian Relational Ethics (15 Principles)
p: **Diversity and group performance** (Page, 2007)
f: **Harmony in difference** (Confucius, The Analects; Heraclitus, fragments)

e.t: Practise the rectification of the mind (zhengxin)
e.x:
When you are angry, fearful, anxious, or desiring, your judgment is distorted. Rectify your mind by attending to your emotions, calming them, and restoring clarity. A mind that is not rectified cannot see things as they are.

(The Great Learning; The Doctrine of the Mean, ch. 1.)

**Plain words** Zhengxin, rectification of the mind: anger, fear, anxiety, and craving distort judgment — you literally cannot see straight through them. So the practice is to attend to the emotion first, calm it, restore clarity, and only then decide. A distorted mind sees a distorted world.

*For example:* Someone who waits 24 hours to send the reply written at midnight in full fury — and in the morning sends a different, better one that actually gets a result.
e.c: Section V - Confucian Relational Ethics (15 Principles)
p: **Emotion regulation and cognitive clarity** (Gross, 2015)
**Mindfulness** (Kabat-Zinn, 1990)
f: **Rectification of the mind** (Confucius, The Great Learning)

e.t: Practise reciprocity (shu)
e.x:
Do not impose on others what you yourself do not desire. This is the Confucian golden rule, stated in The Analects 15.24. It is both a negative prohibition (do not do to others what you do not want done to yourself) and a positive injunction (help others achieve what you would want to achieve).

(Confucius, The Analects 12.2, 15.24; The Doctrine of the Mean, ch. 13.)

**Plain words** Shu, reciprocity: don't impose on others what you yourself don't want. The negative form is a brake; the positive form — help others toward what you'd want — is an engine. Both directions run off one question: how would this land if it landed on me?

*For example:* The person who stops forwarding the cruel joke because they know exactly how it feels to be its subject — and starts forwarding the opportunity because they know how that lands too.
e.c: Section V - Confucian Relational Ethics (15 Principles)
p: **Perspective-taking** (Galinsky et al., 2008)
**Empathic concern** (Batson, 2011)
f: **The categorical imperative** (Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals)

e.t: Practise the extension of knowledge (zhizhi)
e.x:
Extend your knowledge through the investigation of things. Knowledge is not merely book-learning but the practical understanding that comes from engaging with the world. Extend your knowledge by observing, reflecting, and testing your understanding against reality.

(The Great Learning; Confucius, The Analects 15.3.)

**Plain words** Zhizhi, extension of knowledge: learn by engaging the world — observe, reflect, test against reality. Not book-learning alone, and not vibes: understanding that survives contact with things as they are.

*For example:* The gardener who reads everything, then actually runs the small experiment — two beds, one method each — and lets the harvest, not the forum, settle the argument.
e.c: Section V - Confucian Relational Ethics (15 Principles)
p: **Experiential learning** (Kolb, 1984)
f: **Empiricism** (Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding; Aristotle, Posterior Analytics)

e.t: Practise care as a moral orientation
e.x:
Approach moral situations with a care orientation, not only a justice orientation. Care ethics, developed by Carol Gilligan and Nel Noddings, holds that moral life is fundamentally relational and that the primary moral question is not "what is just?" but "how should I respond to this person in need?"

(Gilligan, 1982, In a Different Voice; Noddings, 1984, Caring: A Feminine Approach to Ethics and Moral Education; Noddings, 2002, Starting at Home: Caring and Social Policy.)

**Plain words** Care ethics flips the primary moral question from "what is just?" to "how should I respond to this person in need?" Moral life is relational first. Not abandoning justice — adding the question the rulebook can't ask.

*For example:* Two kids break the same rule. The rulebook says identical punishment; the carer asks what each kid was actually dealing with — and justice is served by both, differently.
e.c: Section VI - Ethics of Care (15 Principles)
p: **Caregiving and well-being** (Brown et al., 2003)
**Prosocial motivation** (Grant, 2008)
f: **The ethics of care** (Held, The Ethics of Care)

e.t: Practise receptive caring
e.x:
Be receptive to the reality of the other person. Receptivity is the first phase of caring: it is the openness to being moved by the other's reality, to seeing the world from their perspective. Without receptivity, care becomes imposition.

(Noddings, 1984, Caring, ch. 3; Noddings, 2002, Starting at Home.)

**Plain words** Receptive caring: first, be actually moved by the other person's reality — see the world from where they stand. Without that first step, care becomes imposition: help shaped by your needs, not theirs. Openness before action.

*For example:* The friend who doesn't rush in with advice, but first asks what it's actually like — and only then discovers what would genuinely help, which was never what they'd assumed.
e.c: Section VI - Ethics of Care (15 Principles)
p: **Empathic accuracy** (Ickes, 1993)
f: **Openness to the other** (Levinas, Totality and Infinity)

e.t: Practise motivational displacement
e.x:
Let your response to the other's need move you to action. Motivational displacement is the second phase of caring: it is the impulse to respond, to help, to act on behalf of the other. Receptivity without displacement is mere sentiment.

(Noddings, 1984, Caring, ch. 3.)

**Plain words** Motivational displacement: let the other's need take over the controls for a moment — your energy reorganised around responding to them. Receptivity without this is just sentiment: you were moved, and did nothing. The displacement is where caring gets legs.

*For example:* Someone cancels their productive Saturday to drive a friend to the appointment — the day's plans didn't survive contact with the friend's need, and that's what caring looks like.
e.c: Section VI - Ethics of Care (15 Principles)
p: **Empathy-altruism hypothesis** (Batson, 2011)

e.t: Practise care as a practice, not a feeling
e.x:
Care is not a feeling but a practice. It involves attentiveness, responsibility, competence, and responsiveness. Practise these four elements in every caring relationship.

(Tronto, 1993, Moral Boundaries: A Political Argument for an Ethics of Care, pp. 127-130; Tronto, 2013, Caring Democracy.)

**Plain words** Care isn't a feeling — it's a practice with four working parts: attentiveness, responsibility, competence, responsiveness. Run all four or it's not care, whatever the warmth level. The feeling is optional; the elements aren't.

*For example:* The person who loves their ageing parent dearly but keeps missing the meds — warm feelings, three missing elements. The sibling who sets up the pill organiser has all four.
e.c: Section VI - Ethics of Care (15 Principles)
p: **Compassion training** (Goetz et al., 2010)

e.t: Practise attentiveness
e.x:
Be attentive to the needs of those who depend on your care. Attentiveness is the first element of care as identified by Joan Tronto. It is the disposition to notice what others need, even when they do not or cannot articulate it.

(Tronto, 1993, Moral Boundaries, pp. 127-130.)

**Plain words** Attentiveness: notice what others need, even when they can't or won't say it. The first element of care, and the one that fails silently — you can't respond to what never got noticed. Needs mostly arrive in code.

*For example:* The teacher who notices the kid whose uniform stopped fitting and quietly connects the family with the uniform bank — nobody asked, which is the point.
e.c: Section VI - Ethics of Care (15 Principles)
p: **Mindful attention** (Kabat-Zinn, 1990)
**Social attention** (Frischen et al., 2007)

e.t: Practise responsibility
e.x:
Take responsibility for responding to the needs you perceive. Responsibility is the second element of care. It is not merely seeing a need but taking ownership of the response.

(Tronto, 1993, Moral Boundaries, pp. 127-130.)

**Plain words** Responsibility: seeing a need isn't enough — take ownership of the response. The second element of care, and the difference between "somebody should do something" and "I'll be there at three."

*For example:* In every apartment block, someone notices the elderly neighbour's curtains stay drawn. Responsibility is the one who knocks instead of mentioning it at the next body-corp meeting.
e.c: Section VI - Ethics of Care (15 Principles)
p: **Responsibility and agency** (Bandura, 2001)
f: **Responsibility** (Levinas, Totality and Infinity; Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III.1)

e.t: Practise competence
e.x:
Ensure that your care is competent. Competence is the third element of care. It is not enough to mean well; you must also do well. Develop the skills, knowledge, and resources to provide effective care.

(Tronto, 1993, Moral Boundaries, pp. 127-130.)

**Plain words** Competence: meaning well is not doing well — the third element of care demands actual skill, knowledge, and resources. Bad care with a warm heart is still bad care. Get good at what you're doing for people.

*For example:* The devoted son who manages his mother's medications on vibes — and the pharmacist daughter-in-law who reviews the list, finds two dangerous interactions, and says the loving thing: "let me be competent at this."
e.c: Section VI - Ethics of Care (15 Principles)
p: **Competence and self-efficacy** (Bandura, 1977)

e.t: Practise responsiveness
e.x:
Be responsive to the other's perception of your care. Responsiveness is the fourth element of care. It is the willingness to be answerable to the other, to check whether your care is received as care, and to adjust accordingly.

(Tronto, 1993, Moral Boundaries, pp. 127-130.)

**Plain words** Responsiveness: be answerable to how your care actually lands. Check with the person: is this received as care? Then adjust. The fourth element — the one that keeps care from becoming its own vanity project.

*For example:* The helper who keeps bringing freezer meals and finally asks "is this actually useful?" — and learns what's needed is the Tuesday drive, which they'd never have guessed.
e.c: Section VI - Ethics of Care (15 Principles)
p: **Responsive parenting** (Bernstein et al., 2014)

e.t: Practise care for the dependent
e.x:
Recognise that dependency is not a deviation from the human norm but a fundamental feature of human life. Every human being is dependent at the beginning and end of life, and at many points in between. Do not stigmatise dependency; structure your life and your community to meet it.

(Kittay, 1999, Love's Labor: Essays on Women, Equality, and Dependency; Tronto, 2013, Caring Democracy.)

**Plain words** Dependency isn't a deviation from the human norm — it IS the norm: everyone starts and ends life dependent, with stretches in between. So don't stigmatise it, and don't build a life or community that pretends otherwise. Structure for meeting it.

*For example:* The workplace that designs the return-to-work plan for the parent and the post-surgery case with the same seriousness as the budget — because "independence" is a phase, not an identity.
e.c: Section VI - Ethics of Care (15 Principles)
p: **Attachment and dependency** (Mikulincer et al., 2005)
f: **Vulnerability** (Fineman, "The Vulnerable Subject," Yale Journal of Law and Feminism)

e.t: Practise care as political
e.x:
Recognise that care is not merely a private matter but a political one. The distribution of care labour, the recognition of caregivers, and the support of dependency are political questions that affect the whole society. Advocate for care to be valued, supported, and distributed fairly.

(Held, 2006, The Ethics of Care; Tronto, 2013, Caring Democracy; Noddings, 2002, Starting at Home.)

**Plain words** Care is political: who does it, who's valued for it, who's left holding it alone — those are societal decisions, not private weather. So advocate: care labour should be seen, supported, and shared fairly. The personal is structural.

*For example:* The team where "someone" always books the cake and remembers the birthdays — until that someone makes it a rotating role, and the whole team discovers how much invisible work was running under the floor.
e.c: Section VI - Ethics of Care (15 Principles)
p: **Social determinants of health** (Marmot, 2005)
f: **Justice and care** (Held, The Ethics of Care)

e.t: Practise care for the self
e.x:
Do not neglect your own care in the process of caring for others. Self-care is not selfish; it is a prerequisite for sustainable caring. You cannot pour from an empty cup.

(Noddings, 2002, Starting at Home; Tronto, 2013, Caring Democracy.)

**Plain words** Care for yourself isn't selfish — it's the prerequisite for sustainable caring. You can't pour from an empty cup, and pretending otherwise just moves the emptiness onto the people depending on you. Self-care is part of the care.

*For example:* The carer who finally takes the offered respite weekend — and returns patient enough to keep going for another year, which is exactly what the person they love needs.
e.c: Section VI - Ethics of Care (15 Principles)
p: **Self-compassion** (Neff, 2003)
**Self-care and burnout prevention** (Maslach and Leiter, 2016)
f: **Care of the self** (Foucault, The History of Sexuality; Seneca, On the Shortness of Life)

e.t: Practise relational autonomy
e.x:
Recognise that your autonomy is not achieved through isolation but through relationship. Relational autonomy is the capacity for self-determination that is developed and exercised within relationships of care and support. Seek relationships that enhance, not diminish, your autonomy.

(Nedelsky, 1989, "Reconceiving Autonomy," Yale Journal of Law and Feminism, 1(1), 7-36; Mackenzie and Oshana, 2007, "Relational Autonomy," in Autonomy, Self, and Social Identity.)

**Plain words** Relational autonomy: self-determination isn't built in isolation, it's built in relationships of support — the lone-wolf version is a myth that keeps people weak. So seek relationships that enlarge your autonomy, and notice which quietly shrink it.

*For example:* The partner who encourages the night class, covers dinner on study nights, and asks real questions about the essays — the degree says "independent achievement," but the autonomy was built by two.
e.c: Section VI - Ethics of Care (15 Principles)
p: **Relatedness and autonomy** (Deci and Ryan, 2000)
**Interdependent self-construal** (Markus and Kitayama, 1991)
f: **Relational autonomy** (Nedelsky, "Reconceiving Autonomy"; Mackenzie and Oshana, "Relational Autonomy")
**Autonomy in relationship** (Held, The Ethics of Care)

e.t: Practise care as a moral emotion
e.x:
Allow yourself to feel the moral emotions that care requires: compassion, sympathy, concern, and sometimes grief. These emotions are not weaknesses; they are the affective ground of moral responsiveness. Do not suppress them; let them guide your action.

(Held, 2006, The Ethics of Care; Noddings, 1984, Caring.)

**Plain words** Let yourself feel the moral emotions — compassion, sympathy, concern, sometimes grief. They're not noise or weakness; they're the affective ground of responding well. Suppressed, they leak; honoured, they steer.

*For example:* The manager who lets themselves actually feel the weight of a redundancy round — and because of that, does it humanely instead of by spreadsheet.
e.c: Section VI - Ethics of Care (15 Principles)
p: **Moral emotions** (Tangney et al., 2007)
f: **Moral sentiments** (Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature; Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments)

e.t: Practise care across distance
e.x:
Extend your care beyond your immediate circle. The ethics of care does not deny the special obligations of close relationship, but it does insist that care must extend to strangers, to distant others, and to the natural world.

(Held, 2006, The Ethics of Care; Tronto, 2013, Caring Democracy.)

**Plain words** Extend care past your immediate circle: strangers, distant others, the natural world. Care ethics doesn't deny special bonds — it just refuses to let them be the border of the moral map. Far-away people are people too.

*For example:* Someone whose care has always stopped at the family gate — and takes the shift cooking at the shelter once a month, discovering the distance was mostly a habit of attention.
e.c: Section VI - Ethics of Care (15 Principles)
p: **Compassion for distant others** (Batson, 2011; Singer, 2015)
f: **Cosmopolitan care** (Nussbaum, Frontiers of Justice; Held, The Ethics of Care)

e.t: Practise care for the natural world
e.x:
Extend your care to the non-human world. The ethics of care is not anthropocentric; it recognises that we are in relationship with animals, ecosystems, and the natural world. Care for them as you would care for any being in your moral circle.

(Held, 2006, The Ethics of Care; Puig de la Bellacasa, 2017, Matters of Care: Speculative Ethics in More Than Human Worlds.)

**Plain words** Extend care to the non-human world: animals, ecosystems, rivers — relationship, not resource. The moral circle isn't a human-only club. Care for them as beings you're in relationship with, because you are.

*For example:* The household that stopped thinking of the garden as décor and started thinking of it as habitat — native plants, water for the birds, the frogs back by the third summer.
e.c: Section VI - Ethics of Care (15 Principles)
p: **Nature connectedness and well-being** (Mayer and Frantz, 2004)
f: **Care for the non-human** (Puig de la Bellacasa, Matters of Care)

e.t: Practise I-Thou
e.x:
Relate to the other person not as an object (an It) but as a subject (a Thou). The I-Thou relation is the primary mode of authentic encounter, in which the other is encountered in their full, irreducible personhood. Do not reduce the other to a category, a role, or a function. Encounter them as a whole person.

(Buber, 1923/1970, I and Thou; Buber, 1965, The Knowledge of Man.)

**Plain words** Buber's distinction: you can meet a person as an It — a category, a role, a function — or as a Thou, a whole irreducible person. Most of daily life runs on It, which is fine for the bus timetable. But when it's a friend, a child, a client — the encounter itself is the thing. Don't reduce them.

*For example:* The barista is "coffee transaction" forty times a day — and once a week someone greets them as a Thou, asks about the violin they mentioned, and it changes both days.
e.c: Section VII - Dialogical Philosophy (Buber, Levinas, Marcel) (20 Principles)
p: **Contact and humanistic psychology** (Rogers, 1961)
**Relational self** (Gergen, 2009)
f: **The face of the Other** (Levinas, Totality and Infinity)

e.t: Practise the primacy of relation
e.x:
Recognise that relation is not something added to individual existence but is prior to it. You do not first exist as an isolated individual and then enter into relation; you exist in relation from the start. The Between is not a space between two pre-existing subjects but the ontological ground from which subjects emerge.

(Buber, 1923/1970, I and Thou; Buber, 1965, The Knowledge of Man, "The Word That Is Spoken.")

**Plain words** You don't exist first and then connect — you exist in relation from the very start. The "between" isn't the gap between two finished people; it's the ground the people themselves grow out of. Which means: relation is maintenance, not accessory.

*For example:* The twins' shared language, the old couple's shorthand, the team's unspoken rhythm — none of it lives in either person; it lives in the between, and it needs both of them showing up to survive.
e.c: Section VII - Dialogical Philosophy (Buber, Levinas, Marcel) (20 Principles)
p: **Relational self** (Gergen, 2009; Sedikides et al., 2011)
f: **Relational ontology** (Marcel, Being and Having; Levinas, Totality and Infinity)

e.t: Practise the face of the Other
e.x:
Encounter the Other's face as the primary moral summons. The face is not a physical feature but the manifestation of the Other's humanity that commands: "Thou shalt not kill." Before you reason about justice, before you calculate consequences, the face of the Other demands your response.

(Levinas, 1961/1969, Totality and Infinity; Levinas, 1969, "Substitution," in Otherwise Than Being.)

**Plain words** Before any reasoning about justice, the other person's face arrives as a command: this one matters, do not harm. That's Levinas — the moral summons is prior to the argument. You can reason after; the face gets first refusal.

*For example:* Someone walks past a hundred statistics about the crisis, unmoved — then one face on one screen, and suddenly they're organising the collection drive. The face is where ethics actually starts.
e.c: Section VII - Dialogical Philosophy (Buber, Levinas, Marcel) (20 Principles)
p: **Facial recognition and moral response** (Haxby et al., 2000)

e.t: Practise infinite responsibility
e.x:
Recognise that your responsibility for the Other is infinite and prior to your freedom. You do not choose to be responsible; you discover that you already are. This does not mean you can meet every need, but it means that the demand of the Other is never exhausted by what you have done.

(Levinas, 1961/1969, Totality and Infinity; Levinas, 1969, Otherwise Than Being.)

**Plain words** Your responsibility for others isn't a contract you signed — you discover you were already in it. And it's never fully discharged: whatever you've done, the demand isn't exhausted. Not a guilt trip; a description of what a human being is.

*For example:* The neighbour who noticed the hoarder's house years ago and "helped once" — and understands, reading the news later, that the once was never going to be enough, and that noticing again is still on them.
e.c: Section VII - Dialogical Philosophy (Buber, Levinas, Marcel) (20 Principles)
p: **Moral obligation and empathy** (Batson, 2011)

e.t: Practise availability (disponibilité)
e.x:
Make yourself available to the other person and to the mystery of being. Availability is Gabriel Marcel's concept of the disposition to be present, open, and receptive to the other. It is the opposite of being "unavailable" — absorbed, distracted, enclosed in oneself. Practise availability by being truly present when someone speaks to you.

(Marcel, 1951a, Being and Having; Marcel, 1967, The Philosophy of Existentialism.)

**Plain words** Disponibilité: availability — the disposition to be actually present and open, versus the absorbed, distracted, enclosed-in-oneself default. When someone speaks to you, be there for it. The opposite of availability isn't rudeness; it's absence wearing your face.

*For example:* The parent who puts the phone face-down in another room during the bedtime story — and the kid notices, and the story lands completely differently than the version told over a screen.
e.c: Section VII - Dialogical Philosophy (Buber, Levinas, Marcel) (20 Principles)
p: **Mindful presence** (Kabat-Zinn, 1990)
**Therapeutic presence** (Geller and Greenberg, 2012)

e.t: Practise fidelity
e.x:
Be faithful to your commitments, to your relationships, and to your deepest self. Fidelity is Marcel's concept of the commitment that endures through time and through the temptation to abandon it. It is not mere persistence but the creative renewal of commitment.

(Marcel, 1951a, Being and Having; Marcel, 1951b, The Mystery of Being.)

**Plain words** Fidelity isn't just persisting — it's the creative renewal of commitment, again and again, through the temptation to drop it. The vow keeps the vow current; otherwise you're just a museum of an old decision. Renew it or it's not fidelity anymore, just habit.

*For example:* The couple at year twenty who still book the anniversary trip, still ask the new questions — still married to the person each has become, not the person they were.
e.c: Section VII - Dialogical Philosophy (Buber, Levinas, Marcel) (20 Principles)
p: **Commitment and relationship stability** (Rusbult et al., 2001)
f: **Commitment** (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics VIII; Buber, I and Thou)

e.t: Practise hope
e.x:
Maintain hope as a disposition, not merely as an expectation of specific outcomes. Hope, for Marcel, is the orientation toward a future that is not guaranteed but is possible. It is not optimism (the belief that things will turn out well) but the refusal to despair in the face of uncertainty.

(Marcel, 1951b, The Mystery of Being; Marcel, 1967, The Philosophy of Existentialism, "On the Ontological Mystery.")

**Plain words** Hope isn't optimism — it doesn't predict things will go well. It's the refusal to despair while staying honest about the odds: oriented toward a future that's possible, not guaranteed. A disposition, not a forecast.

*For example:* The patient who reads the five-year survival stats — takes the hit, doesn't look away — and then books the holiday anyway. That's hope: informed, unflinching, still walking.
e.c: Section VII - Dialogical Philosophy (Buber, Levinas, Marcel) (20 Principles)
p: **Hope theory** (Snyder, 2002)
**Optimism** (Seligman, 1991)

e.t: Practise the distinction between problem and mystery
e.x:
Recognise that some questions are problems (solvable by technique) and others are mysteries (which cannot be solved but only entered). The meaning of life, the nature of love, the experience of suffering — these are mysteries, not problems. Do not approach them with the attitude of a technician. Enter them with the attitude of a participant.

(Marcel, 1951b, The Mystery of Being; Marcel, 1967, The Philosophy of Existentialism, "On the Ontological Mystery.")

**Plain words** Marcel's distinction: problems get solved by technique; mysteries get entered. The meaning of life, love, suffering — you can't fix these, only live inside them. Approaching a mystery with a technician's attitude is the error; participation is the mode.

*For example:* Someone who tries to optimise their grief into "closure" with worksheets and timelines — and finally sits shiva with the family, entering it, and the mystery does what no worksheet could.
e.c: Section VII - Dialogical Philosophy (Buber, Levinas, Marcel) (20 Principles)
p: **Meaning-making** (McAdams, 2008)
**Existential meaning** (Steger, 2009)
f: **Problem vs. mystery** (Marcel, The Mystery of Being)

e.t: Practise incarnation
e.x:
Recognise that you are not a disembodied mind but an embodied being, situated in a body, in a world, in relationships. Incarnation is Marcel's term for the fact of being a body, not merely having a body. Do not treat your body as an instrument of your mind. Live as an embodied being.

(Marcel, 1951a, Being and Having; Marcel, 1951b, The Mystery of Being.)

**Plain words** You are not a mind carrying a body around — you're a body, situated in a world, in relationships. Incarnation: living as embodied, not piloting. Treat the body as the self, not the vehicle.

*For example:* Someone who "thinks through" every decision in their head for years — then takes up dancing and discovers the body had opinions the whole time, and better ones.
e.c: Section VII - Dialogical Philosophy (Buber, Levinas, Marcel) (20 Principles)
p: **Embodied cognition** (Wilson, 2002)

e.t: Practise participation
e.x:
Do not stand apart from life as a spectator. Participate in the life you are living. Participation is Marcel's concept of the engaged, embodied, relational mode of being that contrasts with mere observation. Do not merely think about life; live it.

(Marcel, 1951b, The Mystery of Being; Marcel, 1967, The Philosophy of Existentialism.)

**Plain words** Don't be a spectator of your own life. Participation: the engaged, embodied, relational mode — versus observation from the bleachers. Thinking about life is not living it; the difference shows up in the muscles.

*For example:* The person who watches the community garden from their window for two years, analysing its politics — then takes a plot, and learns in one season what the analysis never touched.
e.c: Section VII - Dialogical Philosophy (Buber, Levinas, Marcel) (20 Principles)
p: **Engagement and flow** (Csikszentmihalyi, 1990)
**Behavioural activation** (Dimidjian et al., 2011)

e.t: Practise the word that is spoken
e.x:
Recognise that genuine communication is not the transmission of information but the creation of a shared reality. The word that is spoken between persons creates the Between, the shared space of meaning. Do not use words as tools or weapons. Let your speech create relation.

(Buber, 1965, The Knowledge of Man, "The Word That Is Spoken"; Buber, 1923/1970, I and Thou.)

**Plain words** Real communication isn't information transfer — it creates a shared reality between people. Words used as tools or weapons build nothing; words spoken to create relation build the between. Let your speech be constructive in the literal sense.

*For example:* Two ex-partners who could exchange all the "correct" texts in the world — and what actually changes things is the one conversation where each says the true thing and hears the other.
e.c: Section VII - Dialogical Philosophy (Buber, Levinas, Marcel) (20 Principles)
p: **Shared reality theory** (Hardin and Higgins, 1996)

e.t: Practise listening as a moral act
e.x:
Listen to the other person not as a means to your own ends but as an end in itself. Listening is the primary act of I-Thou relation. When you truly listen, you create the space for the other to become who they are.

(Buber, 1965, The Knowledge of Man; Rogers, 1961, On Becoming a Person.)

**Plain words** Listening is a moral act, not a data-collection method. When you truly listen — not to reply, not to fix — you create the space the other person needs to become themselves. It's the primary act of taking someone seriously.

*For example:* The friend who said "I'm not going to say anything for a while, just tell me all of it" — and forty minutes later the speaker finds, in their own words, the answer they'd been asking everyone else for.
e.c: Section VII - Dialogical Philosophy (Buber, Levinas, Marcel) (20 Principles)
p: **Active listening** (Rogers, 1961)
**Therapeutic empathy** (Elliott et al., 2011)
f: **Listening** (Buber, I and Thou; Levinas, Totality and Infinity)

e.t: Practise the primacy of ethics over ontology
e.x:
Recognise that the ethical relation precedes the ontological. Before you ask "what is being?" you must ask "what do I owe the Other?" Ethics is first philosophy, not a regional application of ontology.

(Levinas, 1961/1969, Totality and Infinity; Levinas, 1969, Otherwise Than Being.)

**Plain words** Before "what is being?" comes "what do I owe this person?" — ethics is first philosophy, not an optional chapter after the metaphysics. In practice: when in doubt about the abstractions, start from the face in front of you.

*For example:* The committee that spends months drafting principles of "stakeholder engagement" — while the cleaner's chair in their own building sits empty of any say at all. Start where the demand already is.
e.c: Section VII - Dialogical Philosophy (Buber, Levinas, Marcel) (20 Principles)
p: **Moral foundations** (Haidt, 2012)
f: **Ethics as first philosophy** (Levinas, Totality and Infinity)
**The primacy of the ethical** (Levinas, Otherwise Than Being)

e.t: Practise substitution
e.x:
Recognise that in the deepest ethical relation, you are responsible for the Other as if you were responsible for their very being. Substitution is Levinas's most radical concept: the idea that the self is constituted by its responsibility for the Other, that I am "hostage" to the Other before I am free. Do not flee from this responsibility; let it ground your selfhood.

(Levinas, 1969, Otherwise Than Being; Levinas, 1961/1969, Totality and Infinity.)

**Plain words** Levinas's most radical move: the self is constituted by responsibility for the other — you're "hostage" before you're free. You don't opt into it; it's the origin of you. Don't flee it — let it ground you.

*For example:* The eldest child who resents being "the responsible one" for years — and one day stops fighting it and realises the responsibility was never a role assigned; it's who they actually are.
e.c: Section VII - Dialogical Philosophy (Buber, Levinas, Marcel) (20 Principles)
p: **Altruism** (Batson, 2011)

e.t: Practise the trace of the Other
e.x:
Recognise that every person you encounter carries the trace of an absence, a dimension that exceeds your comprehension. The Other is never fully present, never fully knowable. Do not reduce them to what you can see. Honour what exceeds your grasp.

(Levinas, 1969, Otherwise Than Being; Levinas, 1961/1969, Totality and Infinity.)

**Plain words** Everyone carries more than you can see or know — a dimension that exceeds your grasp. Don't reduce people to what's visible: their file, their role, their worst moment. Honour what exceeds the data.

*For example:* The new colleague arrives as "the replacement hire" — until you learn she's also a carer, a widow, a marathoner; the trace is the reminder that the file was never the person.
e.c: Section VII - Dialogical Philosophy (Buber, Levinas, Marcel) (20 Principles)
p: **Theory of mind and its limits** (Apperly, 2011)

e.t: Practise the third
e.x:
Recognise that the ethical relation is not only between two (I and Thou) but also involves the third — all the other persons who also demand justice. Justice is the movement from the face-to-face encounter to the question of how to distribute responsibility among all who make claims on you.

(Levinas, 1969, Otherwise Than Being; Levinas, 1961/1969, Totality and Infinity.)

**Plain words** It's not just you and the other — there's always a third: everyone else who also makes claims on you. Justice is the move from the face-to-face encounter to the question of how responsibility gets distributed among all who call on you. Love your neighbour; adjudicate among neighbours.

*For example:* The manager who'd give anything for the struggling team member — but has eleven others with claims too — and has to turn care into a fair system, which is what the third demands.
e.c: Section VII - Dialogical Philosophy (Buber, Levinas, Marcel) (20 Principles)
p: **Justice reasoning** (Kohlberg, 1981)
**Moral dilemmas** (Haidt, 2012)
f: **Justice** (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics V; Rawls, A Theory of Justice)

e.t: Practise the ethical demand
e.x:
Recognise that the ethical demand is unconditional and absolute. It does not depend on reciprocity, on the Other's merit, or on the consequences of your action. The demand of the Other is immediate and non-negotiable.

(Levinas, 1961/1969, Totality and Infinity; Løgstrup, 1997, The Ethical Demand.)

**Plain words** The ethical demand is unconditional: it doesn't wait for reciprocity, merit, or good consequences. The other's need arrives as a claim before you've had a chance to negotiate terms. Not a bill — a fact about being human.

*For example:* The stranger whose car is in the ditch at midnight — no time to check whether they "deserve" help; the demand is immediate, and the stopped cars know it.
e.c: Section VII - Dialogical Philosophy (Buber, Levinas, Marcel) (20 Principles)
p: **Moral obligation** (Batson, 2011)
f: **The categorical imperative** (Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals)

e.t: Practise the I-It relation without abandoning it
e.x:
Do not seek to live entirely in I-Thou. The I-It relation is necessary for science, technology, and practical life. The problem is not I-It but the domination of I-It, the reduction of all relation to instrumentality. Use I-It for what it is good for, but do not let it consume the space of I-Thou.

(Buber, 1923/1970, I and Thou; Buber, 1965, The Knowledge of Man.)

**Plain words** Don't try to live entirely in I-Thou — you'd starve. The I-It relation (everything instrumental, functional, technical) is necessary for science and ordinary life. The disease is its domination: when no relation is left that isn't instrumental. Use the tool for tool-things; don't let it eat the meeting.

*For example:* A doctor runs perfectly instrumentally — tests, protocols, throughput — and still, for thirty seconds, looks up and asks the human question. The I-It does the medicine; the I-Thou does the healing.
e.c: Section VII - Dialogical Philosophy (Buber, Levinas, Marcel) (20 Principles)
p: **Instrumental vs. communal relationships** (Clark and Mills, 1993)
f: **Instrumental reason** (Horkheimer and Adorno, Dialectic of Enlightenment)

e.t: Practise the between as ontological
e.x:
Recognise that the Between — the space of relation between persons — is not a psychological construct but an ontological reality. It is the primary dimension of human existence. Do not locate meaning inside the individual subject; locate it in the Between, in the shared space of genuine encounter.

(Buber, 1965, The Knowledge of Man; Buber, 1923/1970, I and Thou; Marcel, 1951a, Being and Having.)

**Plain words** The Between — the space of relation between persons — isn't a psychological construct; it's the primary dimension of human existence. So don't locate meaning inside individual heads. Meaning lives in the shared space; tend it there.

*For example:* A friendship's "thing" — the running joke, the saved seat, the phrase only they use — no one owns it, both are made by it, and it's the most real thing either has.
e.c: Section VII - Dialogical Philosophy (Buber, Levinas, Marcel) (20 Principles)
p: **Relational self** (Gergen, 2009)
f: **Relational ontology** (Marcel, Being and Having; Levinas, Totality and Infinity)

e.t: Practise greeting as ethical act
e.x:
When you greet another person, do not merely perform a social ritual. A greeting is an ethical act: it acknowledges the existence, dignity, and worth of the other. It says, in effect, "I see you. You exist. You matter." Practise greetings as if they mean something, because they do.

(Levinas, 1961/1969, Totality and Infinity; Buber, 1923/1970, I and Thou; Ubuntu philosophy.)

**Plain words** A greeting is an ethical act, not noise before the content: it says "I see you, you exist, you matter." Practise greetings as if they mean something — because they're the smallest unit of recognition humans have.

*For example:* The security guard nobody greets all day — and the one person who says good morning, every morning, and what that thirty-second exchange does to both of their days.
e.c: Section VII - Dialogical Philosophy (Buber, Levinas, Marcel) (20 Principles)
p: **Social validation** (Pratt, 2002)
**Acknowledgment and well-being** (Verduyn et al., 2019)

e.t: Practise relational autonomy
e.x:
Recognise that your capacity for self-governance is constituted through your relationships with others. Autonomy is not independence from others but the capacity to reflect on, endorse, and live in accordance with your values within a web of relationships. Seek relationships that support your autonomy, and be a person who supports the autonomy of others.

(Nedelsky, 1989, "Reconceiving Autonomy," Yale Journal of Law and Feminism, 1(1), 7-36; Mackenzie and Oshana, 2007, "Relational Autonomy," in Autonomy, Self, and Social Identity.)

**Plain words** Autonomy isn't independence from people — it's the capacity to reflect on, endorse, and live by your own values inside your web of relationships. So build relationships that support your self-governance, and be that support for others. The lone wolf is just a wolf.

*For example:* The young adult whose family means well and swallows every decision — and the mentor who asks "and what do you want?" — one relationship shrinks autonomy, one builds it.
e.c: Section VIII - Relational Autonomy and Communitarianism (15 Principles)
p: **Self-determination theory: autonomy and relatedness** (Deci and Ryan, 2000)
**Interdependent self-construal** (Markus and Kitayama, 1991)
f: **Relational autonomy** (Nedelsky, "Reconceiving Autonomy"; Mackenzie and Oshana, "Relational Autonomy")
**Autonomy** (Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals)

e.t: Practise constitutive relationality
e.x:
Recognise that your identity is constituted by your relationships, not merely influenced by them. The communities you belong to, the traditions you inherit, the relationships you maintain — these are not external to your selfhood but constitutive of it. You cannot be fully yourself without your relational context.

(Sandel, 1982, Liberalism and the Limits of Justice; MacIntyre, 1981, After Virtue; Taylor, 1989, Sources of the Self.)

**Plain words** Your relationships don't just influence your identity — they constitute it. The communities, traditions, and bonds you maintain are not outside your selfhood; they're its material. You can't be fully yourself in a relational vacuum.

*For example:* Someone who emigrates and "starts fresh" — and discovers they're still made of the language, the table manners, the humour they thought they'd left; the self came along because it was never separable.
e.c: Section VIII - Relational Autonomy and Communitarianism (15 Principles)
p: **Social identity theory** (Tajfel and Turner, 1986)
f: **Constitutive relationality** (Sandel, Liberalism and the Limits of Justice)
**Narrative identity** (MacIntyre, After Virtue; Taylor, Sources of the Self)

e.t: Practise communitarian critique
e.x:
Recognise the limits of individualism. The liberal tradition, for all its strengths, tends to abstract persons from their social, cultural, and relational contexts. Do not accept the myth of the unencumbered self. Recognise that your values, your identity, and your moral commitments are shaped by the communities you belong to.

(Sandel, 1982, Liberalism and the Limits of Justice; MacIntyre, 1981, After Virtue; Bell, 1993, Communitarianism and Its Critics.)

**Plain words** The myth of the unencumbered self — a person with no history, community, or obligations, freely choosing everything — is exactly that, a myth. Your values and identity come shaped from communities. Recognise the limits of that individualism; you're not less free for being rooted.

*For example:* The person who insists "I'm completely self-made" — and whose work ethic, humor, and idea of success trace, item by item, to their grandmother's kitchen.
e.c: Section VIII - Relational Autonomy and Communitarianism (15 Principles)
p: **Cultural psychology** (Shweder, 1991; Markus and Kitayama, 1991)
f: **Communitarianism** (Sandel, Liberalism and the Limits of Justice; MacIntyre, After Virtue)
**Critique of the unencumbered self** (Sandel, Democracy's Discontent)

e.t: Practise recognition
e.x:
Seek recognition for yourself and extend recognition to others. Recognition is the condition of full selfhood: you cannot be fully yourself unless your identity is acknowledged by others. But recognition is not merely given; it is struggled for. Practise recognition by affirming the identity, dignity, and worth of every person.

(Honneth, 1995, The Struggle for Recognition; Taylor, 1992, Multiculturalism and the Politics of Recognition.)

**Plain words** You can't be fully yourself unless your identity is acknowledged by others — recognition is a condition of full selfhood, and it's struggled for, not handed out. So extend it deliberately: affirm others' identity, dignity, worth. Both directions matter.

*For example:* The colleague who's called "Michael" for three years though it's Mikhael — and what it does, the day someone asks how to say it properly and then says it properly.
e.c: Section VIII - Relational Autonomy and Communitarianism (15 Principles)
p: **Self-esteem and social validation** (Leary, 1999)
f: **Recognition** (Honneth, The Struggle for Recognition; Hegel, Phenomenology of Spirit)

e.t: Practise narrative identity
e.x:
Understand your life as a narrative, a story that you are both living and telling. Your identity is not a fixed substance but a developing story, shaped by the communities, traditions, and relationships that give it meaning. Reflect on the narrative arc of your life: where has it been, where is it going, what is its theme?

(MacIntyre, 1981, After Virtue; Taylor, 1989, Sources of the Self; Ricoeur, 1992, Oneself as Another.)

**Plain words** Your life is a narrative you're both living and telling — identity isn't a fixed substance but a developing story. So tend the story: where has it been, where is it going, what's its theme? You're the author as well as the character.

*For example:* Someone in a slump who re-reads their own life as story — and notices the pattern that the slumps always preceded the pivots; the narrative shifts from "things keep going wrong" to "I keep growing through."
e.c: Section VIII - Relational Autonomy and Communitarianism (15 Principles)
p: **Narrative identity** (McAdams, 2008)
**Life story model** (McAdams, 1993)
f: **Narrative identity** (MacIntyre, After Virtue; Ricoeur, Oneself as Another)
**The self as story** (Taylor, Sources of the Self)

e.t: Practise situated freedom
e.x:
Recognise that your freedom is always situated within a historical, social, and relational context. You are not free to be anything; you are free to choose how to respond to the situation in which you find yourself. Do not fantasise about unencumbered freedom. Exercise the freedom you have, where you are, with the resources available to you.

(Sartre, 1943/2003, Being and Nothingness; Heidegger, 1927/2008, Being and Time; Merleau-Ponty, 1945/2012, Phenomenology of Perception.)

**Plain words** Freedom is always situated: you're not free to be anything, you're free to choose your response to the situation you're actually in. Drop the fantasy of unencumbered freedom; exercise the real freedom where you stand, with what you have.

*For example:* The caregiver who can't change the diagnosis, the job, the family — but spends the year perfecting what's genuinely theirs: the tone of every one of their own responses.
e.c: Section VIII - Relational Autonomy and Communitarianism (15 Principles)
p: **Locus of control** (Rotter, 1966)
f: **Situated freedom** (Sartre, Being and Nothingness; Merleau-Ponty, Phenomenology of Perception)

e.t: Practise the common good
e.x:
Seek the common good, not merely your private good or the aggregate of private goods. The common good is the set of conditions that enable all members of a community to flourish. It is not achieved by maximising individual utility but by creating the social, political, and cultural conditions for shared flourishing.

(Aristotle, Politics III; MacIntyre, 1981, After Virtue; Sandel, 2009, Justice: What's the Right Thing to Do?)

**Plain words** The common good isn't your private good, and it isn't private goods added up — it's the set of conditions that let everyone in the community flourish. Create those conditions: social, political, cultural. A rising tide is not the same thing as a healthy sea.

*For example:* The neighbourhood that could each buy generators — or together fix the drainage that floods every one of them; the aggregate purchase loses to the common good.
e.c: Section VIII - Relational Autonomy and Communitarianism (15 Principles)
p: **Prosocial motivation and collective well-being** (Grant, 2008)

e.t: Practise deliberative community
e.x:
Participate in collective deliberation about the common good. Do not leave public life to politicians and experts. Engage in the deliberative practices of your community: town meetings, community organisations, public forums. Your voice matters.

(Habermas, 1996, Between Facts and Norms; Sandel, 2009, Justice; Bohman, 1996, Public Deliberation.)

**Plain words** Don't leave public life to the professionals. Join the deliberation: town meetings, community organisations, forums — the places where the common good gets worked out. Your voice is a load-bearing part of it.

*For example:* The school parents' night where the same four voices always decide — until the quiet parent who "doesn't do politics" speaks once about the bus route, and changes the year for forty kids.
e.c: Section VIII - Relational Autonomy and Communitarianism (15 Principles)
p: **Civic participation and well-being** (Flavin and Keane, 2012)
f: **Deliberative democracy** (Habermas, Between Facts and Norms; Bohman, Public Deliberation)

e.t: Practise social justice
e.x:
Work for a society in which every person has access to the conditions of flourishing: education, healthcare, meaningful work, political participation, and cultural recognition. Do not confine your moral concern to your own circle. Recognise that structural injustice — poverty, discrimination, exclusion — is a moral problem that demands your response.

(Rawls, 1971, A Theory of Justice; Nussbaum, 2000, Women and Human Development; Sen, 1999, Development as Freedom.)

**Plain words** Work for a society where everyone actually has the conditions of flourishing — education, healthcare, meaningful work, a say — and take structural injustice (poverty, discrimination, exclusion) as a moral problem that lands on you, not just "the system." Your circle isn't the border of moral concern.

*For example:* Someone whose charity ends at their postcode — and joins the wider campaign for the housing policy, discovering the food bank needs both the donated cans and the changed law.
e.c: Section VIII - Relational Autonomy and Communitarianism (15 Principles)
p: **Relative deprivation and health** (Marmot, 2005)
**Social justice and well-being** (Wilkinson and Pickett, 2009)
f: **Justice as fairness** (Rawls, A Theory of Justice)
**Capabilities approach** (Nussbaum, Women and Human Development; Sen, Development as Freedom)

e.t: Practise capabilities
e.x:
Work to ensure that every person has the capabilities — the real freedoms, not just formal rights — to live a life they have reason to value. The capabilities approach asks not "how satisfied are people?" but "what can people actually do and be?" Advocate for the conditions that expand human capabilities.

(Sen, 1999, Development as Freedom; Nussbaum, 2000, Women and Human Development; Nussbaum, 2011, Creating Capabilities.)

**Plain words** The capabilities approach asks the better question: not "how satisfied are people?" but "what can people actually do and be?" Formal rights on paper mean nothing without the real freedom to live a life you have reason to value. Advocate for the conditions that expand that.

*For example:* Two countries both guarantee education — in one, the girl walks eight unsafe kilometres to the nearest school; in the other, she doesn't. Same right, wildly different capability. Work on the difference.
e.c: Section VIII - Relational Autonomy and Communitarianism (15 Principles)
p: **Self-determination theory** (Deci and Ryan, 2000)
f: **Capabilities approach** (Sen, Development as Freedom; Nussbaum, Creating Capabilities)
**Positive freedom** (Berlin, "Two Concepts of Liberty," in Four Essays on Liberty)

e.t: Practise the recognition of difference
e.x:
Recognise that persons and communities are different, and that justice requires attending to those differences, not pretending they do not exist. Multicultural recognition is not merely tolerance; it is the affirmative acknowledgment of the value of different cultural identities.

(Taylor, 1992, Multiculturalism and the Politics of Recognition; Kymlicka, 1995, Multicultural Citizenship; Honneth, 1995, The Struggle for Recognition.)

**Plain words** Justice isn't pretending differences don't exist — it's attending to them. Multicultural recognition is affirmative acknowledgment that different cultural identities carry value, not mere tolerance with a smile. See the difference; honour it.

*For example:* The workplace holiday calendar that stops being a single tradition decorated with tokens — and actually reflects the whole room's festivals, which costs little and tells everyone they're part of the "we."
e.c: Section VIII - Relational Autonomy and Communitarianism (15 Principles)
p: **Cultural identity and well-being** (Phinney, 1992)
f: **The politics of recognition** (Taylor, Multiculturalism; Kymlicka, Multicultural Citizenship)

e.t: Practise intergenerational justice
e.x:
Consider the impact of your actions on future generations. You inherit a world you did not create and will leave a world you will not inhabit. Act as a trustee for those who come after you. Do not consume what belongs to them.

(Jonas, 1979, The Imperative of Responsibility; Rawls, 1971, A Theory of Justice, §44.)

**Plain words** You inherit a world you didn't make and leave one you won't live in — so act as trustee, not owner. Consider the impact on the people who come after: don't consume what belongs to them.
