The definition is functional: the posture exists to hold a body comfortably still for a long time so attention can work. Practically, when a position needs constant maintenance, it is not your posture yet.

(YS 2.46.)

**Plain words** The posture is defined by exactly two qualities: steady and comfortable. Not depth, not shape, not photogenic difficulty. The posture exists to hold a body comfortably still for a long time so attention can work. When assessing a posture, ask only those two questions.

*For example:* The person who quit yoga because they "couldn't do the poses" — and the teacher's question: can you sit, steady and comfortable, for ten minutes? Then you can do the only pose the tradition actually requires.
e.c: LAYER IV - THE BODY, BREATH, AND SENSES
p: **Mindful movement and yoga trials for mood and anxiety**, with the honest caveat that package trials do not isolate the posture limb (Moosburner, Cramer, et al., 2024, yoga for depressive disorder)
f: **The body as the first instrument** (Taittiriya Upanishad 2.1-2.5, the sheaths)

e.t: Relax effort into support
e.x:
The method of the posture is given in the next sutra: relax the effort, and let attention rest on something boundless (the tradition reads "ananta" as the serpent-support of the cosmos, the infinite, or a steady support without end). The bounded formulation: after finding the position, spend as much effort relaxing into it as you spent getting there. Practically, once in position, exhale and deliberately release the jaw, shoulders, and hands.

(YS 2.47-2.48.)

**Plain words** The method of the posture, in the next sutra: relax the effort, and let attention rest on something boundless — the infinite, or simply a steady support without end. After finding the position, release the effort into support. The pose is held by letting go, not by gripping.

*For example:* In the held stretch or the held seat, someone finds the exact moment to stop trying — and the posture, suddenly supported rather than performed, becomes sustainable. Effort got you there; release keeps you there.
e.c: LAYER IV - THE BODY, BREATH, AND SENSES
p: **Progressive muscle relaxation and applied relaxation**, the evidence-based tension-release protocol (Jacobson, 1938; Öst, 1988)

e.t: Move the body as contemplative practice
e.x:
The Gita instructs the practitioner to hold the body, head, and neck erect and to gaze unwaveringly at the tip of the nose; the point is not the nose, it is the unified posture of attention. The bounded principle: physical practice counts as practice when attention rides the movement. Practically, walk or stretch with full attention to sensation for ten minutes, and count it as meditation, because the tradition does.

(BG 6.13-6.14.)

**Plain words** The Gita's erect body, steady gaze — the point isn't the nose, it's the unified posture of attention. The bounded principle: physical practice counts as practice when attention rides in the movement. The body is a contemplative instrument when the mind is in it.

*For example:* Two people on the same walk: one rehearsing arguments, one feeling the footfall and the air — same mile, same pace; only one of them took the tradition's advice and moved the body as practice.
e.c: LAYER IV - THE BODY, BREATH, AND SENSES
p: **Mindful walking and mindful movement trials**, moderate evidence for depression and anxiety
f: **Walking meditation** (Thich Nhat Hanh tradition, modern Buddhist; cross-volume echo)

e.t: Regulate the breath deliberately
e.x:
Pranayama is the regulation of the breath after posture is established: making the long and subtle deliberate. The tradition ties it to a specific effect, the thinning of the veil over the mind's clarity. The modern finding is more modest and still real: slow breathing reliably shifts autonomic tone. Practically, practice a fixed ratio of slow breathing at a set time daily, not only in crisis.

(YS 2.49-2.53.)

**Plain words** Breath regulation after posture: making the long and subtle deliberate. The tradition ties it to a thinning of the veil over clarity; modern finding, more modest and still real: slow breathing reliably steadies the nervous system. Regulate the breath on purpose.

*For example:* Before the difficult conversation, someone takes five slow breaths, long exhales — not as ritual, as engineering. The tradition named the effect; the physiology agrees; the conversation goes differently.
e.c: LAYER IV - THE BODY, BREATH, AND SENSES
p: **Slow breathing and parasympathetic engagement**, a systematic review of psycho-physiological correlates (Zaccaro et al., 2018)
f: **Breath as the bridle of the mind** (Vivekananda, Raja Yoga, modern)

e.t: Use the breath to steady attention
e.x:
Among the classical supports for steadiness is the breath itself: the sutra names exhalation and the pause of breath as a direct means of mental stability. This is the tradition's own answer to the restless sit: give the mind the breath, which is always available and always moving. Practically, when scattered, extend the exhalation and count breaths before returning to the chosen object.

(YS 1.34.)

**Plain words** Among the classical supports for steadiness is the breath itself — the sutra names exhalation and the pause of breath as direct means of mental stability. The tradition's own answer to the restless sit: give the mind the breath. Always available, always with you.

*For example:* The anxious flyer who can't meditate the turbulence away — but can lengthen the exhale, count the pause, and let the breath do what the reassurances couldn't.
e.c: LAYER IV - THE BODY, BREATH, AND SENSES
p: **Expiratory emphasis and vagal tone**, the extended-outbreath technique in anxiety management

e.t: Use vivid sensory attention as a support
e.x:
Another classical steadying support: attention fixed on a sensory object, the sutra's "higher sense-experience." The principle is personalization by strength: a mind that cannot yet settle on abstraction settles on the feel of the breath at the nostril or the weight of the body on the seat. Practically, choose the sense channel that holds you most easily, and enter through it.

(YS 1.35.)

**Plain words** Another steadying support: vivid sensory attention — the feel of the breath at the nostril, the weight of the body in the seat. A mind that can't yet settle on abstraction settles on the sensory. Personalize by strength, not by what sounds advanced.

*For example:* The person who failed at mantra practice for a year — and discovers the feel of warm water on the hands at the sink holds their attention perfectly. The support was never the problem; the assignment was.
e.c: LAYER IV - THE BODY, BREATH, AND SENSES
p: **Sensory grounding techniques**, in anxiety management, and attention's binding to concrete stimuli

e.t: Cultivate an inner luminous anchor
e.x:
The tradition offers as steadying support the experience of inner light, a sorrowless luminosity; the bounded formulation is imagery-based: a point of light or bright stillness imagined within, held as an object of attention. Imagery is a genuine attentional channel, and the tradition exploits it deliberately. Practically, when external objects feel stale, hold a simple image of light and rest attention there.

(YS 1.36; BG 6.19's lamp in a windless place as image-family.)

**Plain words** The tradition offers the experience of inner light — a sorrowless luminosity — as a steadying support. The bounded formulation: imagery-based, a point of light or bright stillness imagined within, held as an object of attention. Imagery is a genuine attentional channel.

*For example:* Someone who can't visualize anything elaborate — can hold one simple image: a small steady light behind the closed eyes. Ten minutes with that image does more for their day than ten minutes of trying to think about virtue.
e.c: LAYER IV - THE BODY, BREATH, AND SENSES
p: **Imagery and mental rehearsal**, the attentional and emotional effects of guided imagery (Holmes & Mathews, 2010)

e.t: Contemplate a settled model
e.x:
The tradition names, as another support, the contemplation of a mind free of craving: resting attention on someone who exemplifies the settledness you are training. The support works by modeling, and the tradition is explicit that it is a support, not the destination. Practically, choose one exemplar, living or historical, and use the question "what would stillness look like here?" as an anchor in difficult moments.

(YS 1.37.)

**Plain words** Another support: the contemplation of a mind free of craving — resting attention on someone who exemplifies the settledness you're training. It works by modeling, and the tradition is explicit that it's a support, not the destination. Use the model; don't worship it.

*For example:* The junior surgeon who calms by recalling the senior surgeon's hands in the crisis — not magic, just the nervous system borrowing a template of steadiness until it grows its own.
e.c: LAYER IV - THE BODY, BREATH, AND SENSES
p: **Modeling and self-efficacy from exemplars** (Bandura, 1997)
f: **See the worthy, think of equaling them** (Confucius, Analects 4.17)

e.t: Learn from dream and sleep
e.x:
The support named next: knowledge derived from dream and from dreamless sleep, the tradition's acknowledgment that the mind continues processing below awareness and that its products carry information. The bounded formulation is modest: treat dreams and first-waking material as data about what the mind is working on, without building a doctrine on them. Practically, note recurring dream themes once a month as a self-study exercise.

(YS 1.38.)

**Plain words** The support named next: knowledge from dream and dreamless sleep — the mind keeps processing below awareness, and its products carry information. The bounded formulation is modest: treat dreams and first-waking material as data, not as scripture or noise.

*For example:* Someone keeps waking with the same uneasy image all week — doesn't consult an oracle, just writes it down and notices it arrived exactly during the week they were avoiding the conversation. Data.
e.c: LAYER IV - THE BODY, BREATH, AND SENSES
p: **Sleep-dependent emotional processing**, the finding that REM sleep modulates emotional memory (Walker, 2017)
f: **Dreams as the mind's other work** (Freud, The Interpretation of Dreams, as modern echo)

e.t: Choose your own contemplative object
e.x:
The list of supports ends with the open clause: "or whatever" holds the mind steady. The tradition's final word on objects is that the object serves the steadiness, not the reverse, and any object that steadies is legitimate. Practically, take the tradition's permission seriously: if peeling potatoes steadies your mind more than your mantra, practice the peeling.

(YS 1.39.)

**Plain words** The list of supports ends with the open clause: "or whatever" holds the mind steady. The object serves the steadiness, not the reverse — any object that steadies is legitimate. Take the tradition's permission seriously.

*For example:* The woman whose meditation object is her grandmother's teacup — not in any sutra, and it holds her attention like nothing else. The tradition's final word on the matter is the open clause: "or whatever."
e.c: LAYER IV - THE BODY, BREATH, AND SENSES
p: **Intervention-personalization effects**, matched practices outperform assigned ones
f: **The finger pointing at the moon** (Buddhist tradition, the Zen saying)

e.t: Withdraw the senses on schedule
e.x:
Pratyahara is defined as the senses' imitation of the mind: when the mind withdraws, the senses withdraw with it, rather than the mind following the senses out. The practice is a withdrawal of investment, on schedule, before exhaustion enforces it. Practically, schedule one sense-fast per day: twenty minutes with no input, eyes closed or on a blank wall, phone out of reach.

(YS 2.54-2.55.)

**Plain words** Sense withdrawal is defined as the senses' imitation of the mind: when the mind withdraws, the senses follow — not the other way around. The practice is a withdrawal of investment, on schedule, before exhaustion enforces it. Pull out at closing time, not at collapse.

*For example:* Someone whose evenings end with the phone dropping from a numb hand at 1:40 a.m. — versus the one who schedules the withdrawal at 10, lights low, screens parked, while the mind still has a vote.
e.c: LAYER IV - THE BODY, BREATH, AND SENSES
p: **Stimulus control and attention restoration**, the restoration of directed attention through reduced input (Kaplan, 1995)
f: **Guarding the senses** (Buddhist indriya-samvara; Laozi's twelve, Daodejing 12)

e.t: Retract like the tortoise when needed
e.x:
The Gita's image: the disciplined one draws in the senses from the objects of sense, as the tortoise draws its limbs into its shell. The image teaches that retraction is a skill of timing, not a permanent stance; the tortoise extends its limbs again when it is safe. Practically, know your withdrawal signal (rising irritation, compulsive checking) and practice the retraction before the state solidifies.

(BG 2.58.)

**Plain words** The Gita's tortoise: the disciplined one draws in the senses as the tortoise draws its limbs into its shell. The image teaches timing, not a permanent stance — the tortoise extends its limbs again when it's safe. Retract when needed; re-extend when it's time.

*For example:* Someone learns to turtle up during the toxic family weekend — fewer inputs, earlier nights, guarded exposure — and comes back out fully at work on Monday. The shell is a tool with a schedule, not a home.
e.c: LAYER IV - THE BODY, BREATH, AND SENSES
p: **Time-out and strategic disengagement**, the emotion-regulation research showing that well-timed withdrawal prevents escalation

e.t: Interrupt the chain from stimulus to ruin
e.x:
The Gita gives the tradition's clearest causal chain: dwelling on an object breeds attachment; attachment breeds craving; craving breeds anger; anger breeds delusion; delusion destroys memory; lost memory destroys wisdom; and lost wisdom destroys the person. The practice is interception at the earliest link, and the chain is taught so you can find your link. Practically, identify your usual entry link (most people enter at dwelling), and post your watch there.

(BG 2.62-2.63.)

**Plain words** The Gita's clearest causal chain: dwelling breeds attachment; attachment breeds craving; craving breeds anger; anger breeds delusion; delusion destroys memory; lost memory destroys wisdom; lost wisdom destroys the person. The practice point: the chain is interruptible at every link — earliest is cheapest.

*For example:* Someone catches the chain at "dwelling" — the third hour of refreshing the rival's profile — and steps out for a walk. The same chain, interrupted at link one, never produces the anger it would have produced by link four.
e.c: LAYER IV - THE BODY, BREATH, AND SENSES
p: **Elaboration and rumination as amplifier of craving**, the mechanism by which mental dwelling strengthens desire (Kavanagh, Andrade & May, 2005, the elaborated intrusion theory)

e.t: Let the taste itself fade
e.x:
The Gita observes two stages: for the abstinent one, objects turn away, but the taste (rasa) remains; only for the settled seer does even the taste cease. The principle is honest about extinction's timeline: the appetite may outlast the behavior, and neither its timing nor its eventual disappearance is guaranteed. Practically, do not measure progress by the first weeks, when taste still speaks; measure it at the point where the thought no longer recruits you.

(BG 2.59.)

**Plain words** Two stages, honestly named: for the abstinent one, objects turn away but the taste remains; only for the settled seer does even the taste cease. The appetite may outlast the behavior — neither its timing nor its eventual evaporation is under your control. Don't panic at the lingering.

*For example:* Someone quits the cigarettes, and eight months in still wants one at parties — the tradition's counsel: the object left; the taste is still in transit. It's not failure; it's the second stage, and it too passes.
e.c: LAYER IV - THE BODY, BREATH, AND SENSES
p: **Cue reactivity and extinction timelines**, the persistence of conditioned appetite after behavior change (Bouton, 2004)
f: **Trishna, craving as the refueler of appetite** (Buddhist tradition, the Second Noble Truth, Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)

e.t: Practice moderation in everything
e.x:
The Gita's rule is famously concrete: yoga is not for the one who eats too much or too little, sleeps too much or too little; for the one who is moderate in food and recreation, moderate in effort, moderate in sleep and waking, discipline destroys sorrow. The tradition treats moderation not as timidity but as the engineering requirement of a trainable nervous system. Practically, check the four moderations (food, sleep, effort, recreation) monthly, because they drift.

(BG 6.16-6.17.)

**Plain words** The Gita's rule, famously concrete: yoga is not for the one who eats too much or too little, sleeps too much or too little. Moderate in food, recreation, effort, sleep and waking — discipline destroys sorrow. Moderation as engineering, not as blandness.

*For example:* The ascetic month of 5 a.m. cold workouts and skipped meals that ends in a week of takeout and 10 a.m. alarms — versus the boring, moderate schedule that's still running, quietly, in month nine.
e.c: LAYER IV - THE BODY, BREATH, AND SENSES
p: **Lifestyle pillars of mental health**, the trial evidence for behavioral activation's lifestyle components (Ilardi's TLC)

e.t: Know the obstacles by name
e.x:
The tradition lists nine: illness, mental inertia, doubt, heedlessness, laziness, craving, false perception, failure to gain ground, and instability in attainment. The list is diagnostic gold, because each obstacle has a different remedy, and misdiagnosis wastes months: doubt is not laziness, and instability is not failure of ground. Practically, when practice stalls, name the obstacle before adjusting anything.

(YS 1.30.)

**Plain words** The nine obstacles, by name: illness, mental inertia, doubt, heedlessness, laziness, craving, false perception, failure to gain ground, instability in attainment. Each has a different remedy, and misdiagnosis wastes months — doubt is not laziness. Learn the list; use it.

*For example:* Someone treats their practice stall as laziness and applies discipline — more effort, more hours — and gets worse. The actual obstacle was doubt, which needs evidence, not effort. The list would have caught it in a minute.
e.c: LAYER V - STEADINESS: OBSTACLES AND SUPPORTS
p: **Differential diagnosis in behavior change**, matching barriers to interventions

e.t: Read the symptoms that ride with obstacles
e.x:
The obstacles announce themselves somatically: mental distress, despair, tremor in the body, and irregular breathing. The tradition's insight is that the body carries the score before the mind admits it. Practically, treat a tight chest and short breath in the first minutes of a sitting as information about the day, not as failure of the sitting.

(YS 1.31.)

**Plain words** The obstacles announce themselves somatically: mental distress, despair, tremor in the body, irregular breathing. The body carries the score before the mind admits it. Treat a tight chest and short breath in the first hour of practice as a flag, not a coincidence.

*For example:* The meditator who keeps waking at 4 a.m. with shallow breath — the mind says "nothing's wrong," and the body has been filing the report for weeks. The tradition reads symptoms first; the mind's press office comes second.
e.c: LAYER V - STEADINESS: OBSTACLES AND SUPPORTS
p: **Interoception as early-warning system**, the finding that bodily awareness precedes and supports emotional regulation (Khalsa et al., 2018)
f: **The body keeps the score** (van der Kolk, The Body Keeps the Score)

e.t: Take obstacles as information, not verdicts
e.x:
Synthesizing the previous two principles: an obstacle is the practice talking back to you, showing where the design needs work, not a referendum on your worth. The tradition's structure assumes obstacles are normal and builds a whole layer of supports for them. Practically, log obstacles as data (time, trigger, type) and review monthly; patterns in the log are the practice curriculum.

(YS 1.30-1.32, the design of the passage.)

**Plain words** Synthesis of the two: an obstacle is the practice talking back to you — showing where the design needs work, not a referendum on your worth. The tradition assumes obstacles are normal and builds a whole layer of supports for them. Take them as information.

*For example:* Someone hits the plateau and concludes "I'm just not a meditator" — versus the one who takes the plateau as data, adjusts the dose, the time, the object, and continues. Same plateau; one treats it as weather station, the other as a court verdict.
e.c: LAYER V - STEADINESS: OBSTACLES AND SUPPORTS
p: **Self-monitoring as intervention**, the reliable effect of tracking on behavior
f: **The obstacle is the way** (Marcus Aurelius, Meditations V.20)

e.t: Practice removes obstacles; it does not manufacture states
e.x:
The tradition's mechanism claim about practice: an instrumental cause does not produce the transformation, it removes obstacles to what nature is already doing — like the farmer who does not grow the crop but clears the channel so water reaches it. The same chapter adds that the pattern ends when what maintains it (its conditions and supports) ends. This book's adaptation of the mechanism into a design rule: when a state (calm, clarity, warmth) fails to appear, stop trying to produce it and look for the obstacle — fatigue, hunger, conflict, an unprocessed emotion, a body that has not moved — and clear that; the list is a synthesis, not the source's.

(YS 4.3 with the farmer image; YS 4.11 on removing what maintains.)

**Plain words** The mechanism claim: practice does not produce the transformation — it removes obstacles to what nature is already doing. Like the farmer who doesn't grow the crop but clears the channel so water reaches it. You're not manufacturing states; you're clearing channels.

*For example:* The person who tries to force themselves to sleep — versus the one who removes the obstacles: the late caffeine, the hot room, the screen. The sleep was always coming; the channel was blocked.
e.c: LAYER V - STEADINESS: OBSTACLES AND SUPPORTS
p: **Problem-solving therapy**, the method of defining a problem as the barrier between a current state and a goal state, then removing the barrier rather than forcing the outcome (D'Zurilla and Nezu, Problem-Solving Therapy, Springer Publishing)
f: **Art completes what nature begins** (Aristotle, Generation of Animals I.1)

e.t: Hold one practice to steady the mind
e.x:
The immediate remedy given for the obstacles is singular: the mind is steadied by one principle, one practice, held. The instruction targets the collector's vice, the habit of abandoning a practice at the first plateau for a new one. Practically, choose one steadying practice for a season and let everything else orbit it.

(YS 1.32.)

**Plain words** The immediate remedy for the obstacles is singular: the mind is steadied by one principle, one practice, held. The instruction targets the collector's vice — abandoning a practice at the first plateau for a new one. Choose one steadying practice and hold it.

*For example:* Someone with a shelf of meditation apps, each used for three weeks — versus the one who's done the same unglamorous ten minutes for four years. Only one of them has a practice; the other has a collection.
e.c: LAYER V - STEADINESS: OBSTACLES AND SUPPORTS
p: **Consistency over variety in habit formation**, the central role of repetition context (Lally et al., 2010)
f: **One thing necessary** (Gospel of Luke 10.42, as cultural parallel)

e.t: Begin with faith, energy, and memory
e.x:
The path's early supports are named as a sequence: faith (shraddha) that the practice is worth doing, which generates energy (virya), which stabilizes memory (smriti), which ripens into settledness and insight. The sequence is a motivation design: faith is not required as belief, only as working trust sufficient to fuel effort. Practically, when energy is missing, do not will harder; revisit the trust (talk to someone for whom the practice works).

(YS 1.20.)

**Plain words** The early supports, as a sequence: faith that the practice is worth doing, which generates energy, which stabilizes memory, which ripens into settledness and insight. Faith isn't required as belief in results — just enough trust to generate the next day's energy. Start the sequence anywhere it's honest.

*For example:* The beginner who can't honestly claim faith — but can claim curiosity, which funds one week of practice, which produces one small result, which produces actual faith. The sequence builds itself; you just have to start it somewhere.
e.c: LAYER V - STEADINESS: OBSTACLES AND SUPPORTS
p: **Expectancy effects and hope theory**, agency and pathways as the components of motivated persistence (Snyder, 2002)

e.t: Cultivate the fourfold stance toward people
e.x:
The tradition's most practical social psychology: steadiness of mind is cultivated by friendliness toward the happy, compassion toward the unhappy, delight toward the virtuous, and even-minded disregard (upeksha) toward the non-virtuous, the sutra's own category traditionally rendered "the wicked"; this compendium reads that category as the hostile and corrosive rather than as a license for contempt. Disregard here means even-minded non-engagement, not tolerating harm; where a relationship is abusive or dangerous, the practice is safety and boundaries, and the stance work comes later. Each stance is a prescription against the envy, contempt, and moral entanglement that churn the mind. Practically, when a person disturbs you, first identify which of the four conditions they are in, and apply the matching stance.

(YS 1.33.)

**Plain words** The fourfold stance toward people, the tradition's most practical social psychology: friendliness toward the happy, compassion toward the unhappy, delight toward the virtuous, and even-minded disregard toward the non-virtuous. Four states, four kinds of person. The envy-killer and the smug-killer in one sutra.

*For example:* Someone notices their reaction to a friend's good news is envy, not friendliness — and deliberately practices the delight instead, for their own mind's sake. The friend gets the joy twice; the envy starves.
e.c: LAYER V - STEADINESS: OBSTACLES AND SUPPORTS
p: **Compassion and loving-kindness training**, effects on positive affect and social connectedness (Fredrickson et al., 2008); **envy research** as the mechanism countered (R. H. Smith, 2000, Handbook of Social Comparison)
f: **Love as stance before feeling** (Kierkegaard, Works of Love)

e.t: Prepare the practice environment
e.x:
The Gita is exact about the setup: a firm seat, neither too high nor too low, in a clean place, with the senses and mind gathered, and the body held as one piece. The instructions look liturgical but read as environmental design for attention. Practically, designate and prepare one physical spot, and let its constancy do part of the work.

(BG 6.11-6.13; YS 2.46.)

**Plain words** The Gita's setup is exact: a firm seat, neither too high nor too low, in a clean place, senses and mind gathered, body held as one piece. It reads liturgical but functions as environmental design for attention. Prepare the practice environment on purpose.

*For example:* The person who "just can't get into it" at home — designates the corner, the cushion, the same hour, the clean surface — and discovers the mind starts dropping into practice on approach, like a dog at the park.
e.c: LAYER V - STEADINESS: OBSTACLES AND SUPPORTS
p: **Context-dependent habit and cue stability**, the finding that stable contexts automate behavior (Wood & Neal, 2007)
f: **Order in the outer as aid to the inner** (Confucian rectification)

e.t: Schedule solitude deliberately
e.x:
The Gita's virtue list includes resorting to solitary places and an ease with being alone; the tradition treats solitude as a training environment for the mind, not as misanthropy. Practically, schedule solitude as an appointment with the same status as a meeting, and protect the first fifteen minutes after rejoining people, when the practice is most erodable.

(BG 13.10-11; BG 6.10.)

**Plain words** The Gita's virtue list includes resorting to solitary places and an ease with being alone — solitude as training environment for the mind, not misanthropy. Schedule it as an appointment with the same status as a meeting, and protect it.

*For example:* The parent who hasn't been alone in a room since 2019 — books the monthly solo walk, guards it like a dentist appointment, and comes back a slightly larger person every time.
e.c: LAYER V - STEADINESS: OBSTACLES AND SUPPORTS
p: **Solitude as restoration and self-reflection**, research on positive solitude experiences (Nguyen et al., 2018)
f: **The uses of solitude** (Thoreau, Walden; cross-volume echo of the Transcendentalists)

e.t: Expect relapse and plan the return
e.x:
The tradition's fine print: in the gaps of practice, other afflictions may arise through the deep habits. Relapse is built into the model, which changes what it means when it happens: not new failure, known terrain. Practically, write a relapse plan while steady (minimum viable practice, first three steps of return), because the relapsing mind cannot be trusted to design one.

(YS 4.27-4.28.)

**Plain words** The tradition's fine print: in the gaps of practice, other afflictions may arise through the deep habits. Relapse is built into the model — which changes what it means when it happens: not new failure, known terrain. Write the relapse plan while steady.

*For example:* Someone writes their own relapse card while calm: "minimum version: 4 minutes, morning, no exceptions" — and when the bad month comes, the card keeps the practice from dying completely. The gap is bridged; nothing is rebuilt from zero.
e.c: LAYER V - STEADINESS: OBSTACLES AND SUPPORTS
p: **Relapse prevention protocols**, anticipating and planning for lapses (Marlatt & Gordon, 1985)
f: **The righteous falls seven times and rises** (Proverbs 24.16, Hebrew Bible)

e.t: Make your own self your ally
e.x:
The Gita's opening instruction to the meditator, given before any posture or technique: raise yourself by yourself, and do not trample yourself down; the self is your friend when you have mastered it, and your enemy when you have not. The classical teaching concerns self-mastery: the relationship with yourself is itself part of the work. The self-compassion application below is a modern adaptation of the teaching to the problem of relapse, not the Gita's own frame. Practically, audit the tone of your inner voice after each practice and each failure; a relapse handled as an ally's counsel returns you to the seat, while one handled as an enemy's verdict keeps you off it.

(BG 6.5-6.6.)

**Plain words** The Gita's opening instruction to the meditator: raise yourself by yourself, and don't trample yourself down — the self is your friend when you've mastered it, your enemy when you haven't. The classical teaching concerns self-mastery; the modern translation adds: stop being your own worst colleague.

*For example:* The inner voice that reviews your day like a hostile manager — versus the one that reviews like a decent coach. Same material; one voice produces paralysis, the other produces the next attempt.
e.c: LAYER V - STEADINESS: OBSTACLES AND SUPPORTS
p: **Self-compassion interventions**, meta-analytic evidence of reductions in depression, anxiety, and stress (Ferrari et al., 2019; the discipline-support reading is an extrapolation, not what the meta-analysis measured)
f: **The soul's parts as allies or factions** (Plato, Republic IV)

e.t: Ground practice in the three conditions
e.x:
The tradition's definition of when a practice becomes established: attended to for a long time, without interruption, and with a devoted heart. Each condition is a design requirement: long time (effects are cumulative), without interruption (consistency), with devotion (quality of attention during practice). Practically, audit your practice against all three, because most failures are failures of one condition, not of the practice itself.

(YS 1.14.)

**Plain words** When does a practice become established? Three conditions: attended to for a long time, without interruption, and with a devoted heart. Long time (cumulative effects), without interruption (consistency), with devotion (quality of attention). All three are design requirements — miss one and the practice stays thin.

*For example:* The gym-goer with the long time and the devotion but the interruptions — every restart costs a month of the cumulative effect. The one who does less, but never stops, ends up unrecognizable.
e.c: LAYER V - STEADINESS: OBSTACLES AND SUPPORTS
p: **Habit formation timelines and consistency effects** (Lally et al., 2010)
f: **Long obedience in the same direction** (Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil 188)

e.t: Balance solitude and company
e.x:
The tradition asks for both: solitude as practice environment, and companionship, teaching, and the fourfold stance as practice content. Neither is safe alone; unmixed solitude drifts into avoidance, unmixed company into diffusion. Practically, treat the ratio as a dial to adjust monthly, not a fixed rule.

(BG 13.10-11 with 12.13-14; YS 1.33.)

**Plain words** The tradition asks for both: solitude as practice environment, and companionship, teaching, and the fourfold stance as practice content. Neither is safe alone — unmixed solitude drifts into avoidance, unmixed company into diffusion. Treat the ratio as a dial, not a doctrine.

*For example:* The hermit year that was actually avoidance wearing robes — and the social year that was diffusion wearing a calendar. The correction was the same both times: turn the dial one notch, not to the end.
e.c: LAYER V - STEADINESS: OBSTACLES AND SUPPORTS
p: **Social support and solitude both as needs**, the dual findings on connection and restoration (Holt-Lunstad, 2010; Nguyen et al., 2018)
f: **In the world, not of it** (Gospel of John 17.14-15)

e.t: Walk the eight limbs as a curriculum
e.x:
The limbs are given as a sequence: restraint, observance, posture, breath regulation, sense withdrawal, concentration, absorption, and integration. The sequence is a dependency map: each limb creates the conditions for the next, and when a later limb fails, the fault is usually in an earlier one. Practically, treat the sequence as a diagnostic grid rather than a ladder to climb once.

(YS 2.28-2.29; YS 2.54-3.3.)

**Plain words** The eight limbs as a sequence: restraint, observance, posture, breath, withdrawal, concentration, absorption, integration. It's a dependency map — each limb creates the conditions for the next. When a later limb fails, the fault is usually upstream. Walk the curriculum in order.

*For example:* Someone struggling with concentration (limb six) for years — and the audit shows the failure upstream: no ethics (limb one) in a conduct war, no steady seat (limb three), no withdrawal (limb five). The concentration was never the problem; it was the symptom.
e.c: LAYER VI - THE ATTENTION CURRICULUM
p: **Sequenced skill acquisition and prerequisite structure**, learning-science findings on curriculum design (Bjork)
f: **The eightfold path as sequence** (Buddhist tradition, structural parallel)

e.t: Bind attention to one place
e.x:
Concentration (dharana) is defined as the binding of attention to a single place or object. The definition is deliberately narrow: not thinking about the object, not visualizing it, but returning attention to it. Practically, one object, one place of attention on it, and the practice is the return.

(YS 3.1.)

**Plain words** Concentration is defined narrowly: the binding of attention to a single place or object. Not thinking about it, not visualizing it — returning attention to it. One object, one place on it, and the practice is the returning.

*For example:* The person who thinks concentration means thinking hard about the breath — versus the one who just returns, again, to the feel of it, forty times, each return a rep. Only one of them is doing the sutra.
e.c: LAYER VI - THE ATTENTION CURRICULUM
p: **Focused-attention meditation and attentional networks**, effects on alerting and orienting (Lutz et al., 2008)

e.t: Let absorption come from continuity
e.x:
Meditation proper (dhyana) is defined as the continuous flow of cognition toward the object: the state where attention stops returning and begins resting. It is not a different skill from concentration; it is concentration after enough returns. Practically, do not chase absorption; count returns, and let the continuity accumulate on its own schedule.

(YS 3.2.)

**Plain words** Meditation proper is the continuous flow of cognition toward the object — attention stops returning and begins resting. Not a different skill from concentration; it's concentration after enough returns. Don't chase absorption; fund the returns.

*For example:* Every sit that "failed to be deep" but logged two hundred returns — that's the account the absorption is drawn on. The one who sits waiting to feel absorbed gets nothing; the one who returns gets everything.
e.c: LAYER VI - THE ATTENTION CURRICULUM
p: **Flow as absorption in activity**, the phenomenology of merged attention (Csikszentmihalyi, 1990)
f: **Wu wei as the ripening of practice** (Zhuangzi, the skill stories)

e.t: Let the object fill the field
e.x:
Absorption (samadhi) is defined by what happens to the object: it shines alone, as if emptied of the observer's own form. The tradition's point is that the observer's self-sense thins as attention fills, which is why the state feels like disappearance and is sought for the wrong reasons. Practically, treat each absorption as a state that passes, not as an arrival; the tradition measures progress by stability, not by states.

(YS 3.3.)

**Plain words** Absorption is defined by what happens to the object: it shines alone, as if emptied of the observer's own form. The observer's self-sense thins as attention fills — which is why the state feels like disappearance, and why it's so often sought for the wrong reasons.

*For example:* The musician who plays the passage and later can't recount "themselves" during it — only the music. The self-sense didn't die; it thinned while attention filled. That's the shape of it.
e.c: LAYER VI - THE ATTENTION CURRICULUM
p: **Nondual awareness research**, early studies on self-other boundaries in absorptive states (Josipovic, 2013; small literature, honestly labeled)
f: **The arrow and the target** (Mundaka Upanishad 2.2.3, becoming one with what is aimed at)

e.t: Combine the three into one skill
e.x:
The three are given a single name when practiced together: samyama, the integrated application of binding, resting, and absorption to any chosen object. The principle is transfer: attention trained as a unit can be pointed at anything, which is what makes the curriculum practical rather than ritual. Practically, treat the three as one skill practiced on different objects, not three separate achievements.

(YS 3.4.)

**Plain words** The three — binding, resting, absorption — get a single name when practiced together: samyama, integrated and pointed at any chosen object. The principle is transfer: attention trained as a unit can be aimed at anything. That's what makes the curriculum practical.

*For example:* Someone trains the attention unit on the breath for two years — then points the same trained unit at their business problem, their child's behaviour, their own anger, and finds the tool works on every material.
e.c: LAYER VI - THE ATTENTION CURRICULUM
p: **Transfer of training**, the conditions under which trained capacities generalize (Barnett & Ceci, 2002)
f: **Ordinary mind is the Way** (Zen tradition, the Zhaozhou record)

e.t: Climb the subtlety ladder
e.x:
Absorption is graded: with reasoning (vitarka), beyond reasoning (vichara), with joy (ananda), and with self-sense alone (asmita). The ladder teaches that objects differ in subtlety, and that the practice naturally refines from coarse to fine. Practically, when a coarse object (breath, sensation) becomes easy, do not celebrate; refine.

(YS 1.17.)

**Plain words** Absorption is graded: with reasoning, beyond reasoning, with joy, with self-sense alone — a ladder of subtlety. Objects differ in fineness, and the practice naturally refines from coarse to fine. When a coarse object stops yielding, move one rung subtler.

*For example:* Someone works the breath (coarse) until it's fully familiar, then notices the practice wants the subtler object — the feeling of the noticing itself. The ladder was always meant to be climbed, not camped on.
e.c: LAYER VI - THE ATTENTION CURRICULUM
p: **Progressive refinement in perceptual learning**, the improvement of discrimination with practice
f: **From the gross to the subtle** (the Upanishadic method, Taittiriya's sheaths)

e.t: Distinguish settling with and without seed
e.x:
The sutra distinguishes a settling trained on an object (seeded) from another state that follows the practiced cessation of thought and still carries the residue of latent impressions (YS 1.18); the fully seedless absorption (nirbija, YS 1.50-1.51) is the later stage in which even the impression of truth-bearing insight is stilled. The distinction matters practically: cessation-based stillness is trained, and the seedless state is described as what the training finally leaves behind. Practically, end each sitting with one minute of no chosen object, as an adaptation for learning the difference the tradition takes years to draw.

(YS 1.17-1.18 with YS 1.50-1.51.)

**Plain words** The sutra distinguishes a settling trained on an object (seeded) from a state that follows practiced cessation and still carries residue; the fully seedless absorption is a later stage. Practically: don't confuse the pleasant stillness that comes early with the trained states that come later — label them and keep going.

*For example:* The meditator who hits a lovely blank quiet in month two and spends three years trying to recreate it — versus the one who labels it "seeded settling, early," and continues the curriculum. One has a souvenir; the other has a path.
e.c: LAYER VI - THE ATTENTION CURRICULUM
p: **Open-monitoring versus focused-attention practice**, the distinction between directive and non-directive forms (Lutz et al., 2008)

e.t: Use AUM as a portable anchor
e.x:
The tradition names the syllable AUM as a chosen object of repetition, with the stated effect of removing obstacles and turning attention inward. The bounded formulation: mantra and sound as attentional anchors, portable, usable in noise, and rhythmically self-regulating. Practically, adopt one sound and use it in transit, in waiting rooms, and in the moments before difficult conversations.

(YS 1.27-1.29; Mandukya Upanishad, the syllable analyzed.)

**Plain words** The tradition names AUM as a chosen object of repetition, with the stated effect of removing obstacles and turning attention inward. The bounded formulation: mantra and sound as attentional anchors — portable, usable in noise, rhythmically self-regulating. A pocket-steadier.

*For example:* On the loud bus, in the MRI machine, in the back of the courtroom — where the breath is too subtle to hold, the sound is not. The anchor that works everywhere is the one worth having.
e.c: LAYER VI - THE ATTENTION CURRICULUM
p: **Mantra repetition and stress reduction**, the mantram-repetition trials' findings on stress and health outcomes (Bormann et al., 2006)
f: **Nembutsu recitation** (Shinran, sayings recorded in the Tannisho)

e.t: Test what arises for truth
e.x:
The insight that matures from absorption is called truth-bearing (ritambhara), and the tradition adds a caution: the insight feels certain, and certainty is not accuracy. The Gita's parallel is the intellect that crosses delusion. Practically, treat every insight from practice as a hypothesis: write it, test it against life and other people, and let evidence settle it.

(YS 1.47-1.48; BG 2.52-2.53.)

**Plain words** The insight that matures from absorption is called truth-bearing — and the tradition adds a caution: it feels certain, and certainty is not accuracy. Treat every insight from practice as a hypothesis with excellent references, and test it against the world before acting on it.

*For example:* The meditator who returns from retreat with the absolute conviction they should quit their job and move to the coast — and gives the insight two weeks of ordinary-world testing before signing anything. Half of the revelations don't survive the testing. The good half does.
e.c: LAYER VI - THE ATTENTION CURRICULUM
p: **Illusory truth and confidence-accuracy dissociation**, the finding that felt certainty tracks fluency, not truth (Fazio et al., 2015)
f: **The pragmatic maxim** (Peirce, How to Make Our Ideas Clear)
**Discernment of spirits** (Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises)

e.t: Hold powers and peak experiences lightly
e.x:
The tradition is blunt about attainments: the extraordinary capacities (siddhis) that arise with deep practice are obstacles to integration, though the world counts them as powers. The principle generalizes to every peak experience: states that flatter the self re-inflate the self the practice was thinning. Practically, when something impressive happens in practice, tell one grounded person and move on.

(YS 3.37; YS 4.1.)

**Plain words** The tradition is blunt about attainments: the extraordinary capacities that arise with deep practice are obstacles to integration, though the world counts them as powers. The principle generalizes to every peak experience: states that flatter the self re-inflate it.

*For example:* The retreat participant who comes back with the aura-readings and the cosmic dreams — collecting them like trophies — and the quiet one who noticed the same things and let them pass. The tradition says which one was practicing.
e.c: LAYER VI - THE ATTENTION CURRICULUM
p: **Spiritual bypassing and ego inflation**, the clinical literature on contemplative practice's failure modes (Masters, 2010; conceptual, honestly labeled)

e.t: Apply contemplation to master any subject
e.x:
The tradition's own application layer: samyama directed at a subject yields knowledge of it, and the sutras run through a catalogue (the body, the sequences of change, the mind itself). The bounded formulation is the learning principle: sustained, absorbed, multi-pass attention to a subject produces knowledge that scattered study cannot. Practically, apply the three-part attention skill to one domain of life per quarter.

(YS 3.16-3.29, the applications.)

**Plain words** The tradition's own application layer: sustained, absorbed, multi-pass attention directed at a subject yields knowledge of it — the sutras run through a whole catalogue. The bounded formulation is the learning principle: mastery is samyama pointed at a field.

*For example:* The diagnostician who has absorbed ten thousand ECGs — not memorized, absorbed, multi-pass — and now "just sees" the arrhythmia. The tradition would recognize the mechanism: contemplation applied to a subject.
e.c: LAYER VI - THE ATTENTION CURRICULUM
p: **Deliberate practice and deep processing**, the learning-science findings on absorbed, feedback-rich study (Ericsson)
f: **Knowledge by acquaintance through attention** (Simone Weil, "Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies," modern)

e.t: Let practice structure the day
e.x:
The Gita closes its meditation chapter with the image of "the yogi, whose mind is subdued, always practicing"; the tradition reads this as rhythm rather than as hours: practice as the day's frame, not its interruption. Practically, anchor the day at both edges (first and last twenty minutes), and let the middle be practice in motion.

(BG 6.10; BG 8.26-8.27 context, the paths of light and darkness as rhythm.)

**Plain words** "The yogi, whose mind is subdued, always practicing" — read as rhythm rather than hours: practice as the day's frame, not its interruption. Anchor the day at both edges: something deliberate at the start, something settling at the end.

*For example:* The person who "has no time to practice" — and builds the two edges: ten minutes before the phone, five minutes of review before sleep. The middle of the day follows the frame the edges set.
e.c: LAYER VI - THE ATTENTION CURRICULUM
p: **Morning and evening routines as habit anchors**, the consistency effects of temporal anchoring
f: **Mushin, no-mind in daily life** (Takuan Soho, The Unfettered Mind)

e.t: Expect stages, not leaps
e.x:
The tradition maps wisdom's arrival as seven grounds (the sutra) elaborated by the commentary into a sequence from the first clear recognition of what must be done to the final irreversibility. The stages are given so practitioners can locate themselves, and the tradition explicitly allows the process to be gradual or sudden by disposition. Practically, locate your current stage honestly, and expect the transitions to arrive as consolidations rather than as fireworks.

(YS 2.27, with Vyasa's elaboration in the Yoga-bhashya.)

**Plain words** Wisdom's arrival is mapped as stages — from the first clear recognition of what must be done to final irreversibility — so practitioners can locate themselves. The tradition explicitly places people mid-path. Expect stages, not leaps; find your rung honestly.

*For example:* Someone reads the stage map and finds themselves at "recognition, unstable" — instead of despairing at the distance to the top, they take the next rung's assignment. Maps exist to be located on.
e.c: LAYER VI - THE ATTENTION CURRICULUM
p: **Stage models of change**, the trans-theoretical model's utility for self-location (Prochaska & DiClemente, 1983)
f: **The ladder of love** (Plato, Symposium; Diotima's stages)

e.t: Hear the teaching first
e.x:
The classical method begins with shravana, listening: receiving the teaching from a source that has walked it, before the mind's commentary begins. The modern translation is learning from models: wisdom is caught through exposure before it is tested. Practically, when entering a new domain, listen twice as long as you speak.

(Shankara, Upadesasahasri, the teacher-student opening; BG 4.34.)

**Plain words** The classical method begins with shravana, listening: receiving the teaching from a source that has walked it, before the mind's commentary begins. The modern translation is learning from models — wisdom caught through exposure before it's tested.

*For example:* The newcomer to any craft who spends the first months mostly watching the masters work — absorbing before arguing — versus the one who arrives with opinions. The listening phase is not passivity; it's the method's first step.
e.c: LAYER VII - DISCRIMINATION AND SELF-INQUIRY
p: **Modeling and observational learning**, the primacy of exemplars in skill acquisition (Bandura, 1997)
f: **The disciple's ear** (Confucius, Analects; "Is it not a pleasure to learn and practice?")
**Quick to hear, slow to speak** (Epistle of James 1.19)

e.t: Examine what you hear
e.x:
The second step, manana, is deliberation: testing the teaching against reason and experience, taking it apart to see whether it holds. The tradition treats listening without examination as the cause of borrowed certainty, and examination without listening as the cause of reinvention. Practically, for each important idea you receive, write one paragraph testing it against your own evidence.

(Shankara, Upadesasahasri; Vivekachudamani, attributed.)

**Plain words** The second step, manana, is deliberation: testing the teaching against reason and experience, taking it apart to see if it holds. Listening without examination breeds borrowed certainty; examination without listening breeds reinvention. Do both, in order.

*For example:* The student who hears the teaching and immediately demands "but how do we know?" — right instinct, wrong order. First receive it whole; then take it apart. The tradition's sequence is shravana, then manana, not both at once.
e.c: LAYER VII - DISCRIMINATION AND SELF-INQUIRY
p: **Comprehension-strategy instruction**, the learning-science finding that deep processing improves when learners are taught to interrogate the material directly (Pressley et al., 1992)
f: **Learning without thought is labor lost** (Confucius, Analects 2.15)
**The midwife of ideas** (Socrates, in Plato's Theaetetus)

e.t: Assimilate until it changes perception
e.x:
The third step, nididhyasana, is not thinking but dwelling: returning attention to the understood truth until it becomes how the mind sees, the way an absorbed language stops being translated. The tradition places all the weight here, because understanding without assimilation evaporates under pressure. Practically, choose one truth per month and revisit it daily until it colors perception unprompted.

(Shankara, Upadesasahasri; YS 1.14's three conditions apply here.)

**Plain words** The third step, nididhyasana, is not thinking but dwelling: returning attention to the understood truth until it becomes how the mind sees — the way an absorbed language stops being translated. All the weight is here; understanding without assimilation changes nothing.

*For example:* Someone "understands perfectly well" that the anxiety is a false alarm — and the understanding changes nothing, because it's still being translated. The one who dwells on it daily until it's just how they see it — that one stops flinching.
e.c: LAYER VII - DISCRIMINATION AND SELF-INQUIRY
p: **Consolidation through spaced repetition and application**, the finding that revisiting strengthens and reorganizes (Bjork)
f: **Truth realized, not merely held** (Vivekananda, Jnana Yoga, modern)

e.t: Run "not this, not this" as a procedure
e.x:
The Upanishadic method for approaching what cannot be objectified: negate each thing it is not, exhaustively and in order, without asserting what remains. The procedure is a discipline of elimination applied to your own identifications: I am not this role, not this emotion, not this body, not this history. The instruction ends where assertion would begin. Practically, run the negation as a weekly exercise, and stop at the silence rather than the conclusion.

(Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.3.6, neti neti; 4.2.3-4.4.23 context.)

**Plain words** The Upanishadic method for what can't be objectified: "not this, not this" — negate each thing it is not, exhaustively, in order, without asserting what remains. Run it on your own identifications: I am not this role, not this emotion, not this history. See what's left standing.

*For example:* Someone strips the identity piece by piece — not the job, not the divorce, not the diagnosis, not the opinions — and finds the inquiry itself steadier than any of the things it removed. The procedure works as a procedure.
e.c: LAYER VII - DISCRIMINATION AND SELF-INQUIRY
p: **Cognitive defusion and delabeling**, the de-identification from thought content (Hayes et al., 2011; Bernstein et al., 2015)
f: **The negative way** (Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed I.58)

e.t: Separate the seer from the seen daily
e.x:
The Drig-Drisya-Viveka procedure, attributed to Shankara's circle: take any experience and sort it into the seen (qualities, changes, objects) and the seeing (the fact of awareness of them), repeatedly, until the sorting is reflexive. The book's standing caveat applies: this is offered as procedure, with the ontology open. Practically, one sort per day, at a moment of strong feeling: what in this is the seen, what is the seeing?

(Drig-Drisya-Viveka, attributed; YS 2.18-2.20 as the Yogic parallel.)

**Plain words** The seer-seen sorting procedure: take any experience and sort it into the seen (qualities, changes, objects) and the seeing (the fact of awareness of them) — repeatedly, until the sorting is reflexive. A daily discipline, not a doctrine to believe.

*For example:* In the middle of a mood, someone runs the sort: the mood is seen, the seeing of it is not the mood — and the mood, now seen rather than been, loses about a third of its vote. Same mood; different seat.
e.c: LAYER VII - DISCRIMINATION AND SELF-INQUIRY
p: **Self-distancing and third-person self-talk**, the reliable effects on emotion and reasoning (Kross, 2014; Grossmann & Kross, 2014)

e.t: Test experience layer by layer
e.x:
The Taittiriya maps the person as sheaths: body, energy, mind, understanding, and bliss; each is to be examined and, in the method, seen as an object of awareness rather than as the self. The bounded formulation: experience comes in layers, and each layer can be the object of attention rather than the identity. Practically, when overwhelmed, locate the layer (is this body, energy, emotion, thought?) and attend to it as object rather than as self.

(Taittiriya Upanishad 2.1-2.5, the pancha kosha.)

**Plain words** The Taittiriya maps the person as sheaths: body, energy, mind, understanding, bliss — each layer examined as an object of awareness rather than as the self. Experience comes in layers, and each layer can be the object while something witnesses it. Test them, layer by layer.

*For example:* Someone assumes the fatigue is "them" — then tests it as a layer: is the fatigue the seer or the seen? Seen, it turns out. The layer-map is doing its work when the fatigue becomes weather instead of identity.
e.c: LAYER VII - DISCRIMINATION AND SELF-INQUIRY
p: **Interoceptive and somatic awareness as layered processing**, the evidence that body-focused attention changes emotional experience (Khalsa et al., 2018)

e.t: Ask who is aware
e.x:
The self-inquiry (atma-vichara) of the Advaita line: turning attention from the object toward the one aware of it, not to find a thing but to exhaust the search's assumptions. The book states the standing dispute plainly: Advaita's atman and Buddhism's anatman disagree about what the inquiry finally shows, and the practice teaches the inquiry, not the verdict. Practically, ask "who is aware of this?" and treat the question, not the answer, as the practice.

(Ramana Maharshi, modern articulation of the Advaita line; the Upanishadic "who" questions, Kena 1.1-2.4.)

**Plain words** Atma-vichara, self-inquiry: turn attention from the object toward the one aware of it — not to find a thing, but to exhaust the search's assumptions. The standing dispute (Advaita's atman, Buddhism's anatman) is honestly flagged: the procedure works either way; the metaphysics is disputed.

*For example:* Someone asks "who is aware of this worry?" and looks back for the looker — finds no object there, but the worry has lost its grip in the meantime. The inquiry's value, most days, is in the asking.
e.c: LAYER VII - DISCRIMINATION AND SELF-INQUIRY
p: **Default mode network and self-referential processing**, the finding that contemplative practice alters self-related network activity (Brewer et al., 2011; neural evidence, doctrinally neutral)
f: **The unanswerable koan** (Zen tradition, The Gateless Gate)

e.t: Read the great statements as prompts, not doctrines
e.x:
The four classical mahavakyas ("consciousness is the absolute" from the Aitareya; "that thou art" from the Chandogya; "I am the absolute" from the Brihadaranyaka; "this self is the absolute" from the Mandukya) are given in the tradition as liberating truths: statements whose full assimilation is held to release the hearer from misidentification, and they are not offered as debate propositions. This book's bounded adaptation: use each as a meditation prompt for a week, and notice what loosens.

(Aitareya Upanishad 3.3; Chandogya 6.8.7; Brihadaranyaka 1.4.10; Mandukya 2.)

**Plain words** The four great statements — "consciousness is the absolute," "that thou art," "I am the absolute," "this self is the absolute" — are given as prompts for inquiry, not doctrines to recite. Use them as questions to stand in, not answers to hold.

*For example:* The practitioner who repeats "that thou art" as a slogan gets nothing but smugness — versus the one who uses it as a probe: "that? this ordinary irritation is what?" — and the statement starts doing its actual work.
e.c: LAYER VII - DISCRIMINATION AND SELF-INQUIRY
p: **Self-affirmation and identity-restructuring prompts**, modest but real effects of value-identity statements (Cohen & Sherman, 2014)
f: **That thou art, read relationally** (Shankara's tradition on Chandogya 6.8.7)

e.t: Know your field and its knower
e.x:
The Gita's distinction: the body-and-mind is the field (kshetra), and the awareness of it is the field-knower (kshetrajna); the chapter then says the knower in all fields is the same in kind. The bounded formulation: in every experience there is the content and the knowing of it, and training includes telling them apart under pressure. Practically, in conflict, ask "what is the field here (facts, feelings) and what knows it?" before speaking.

(BG 13.1-3.)

**Plain words** The Gita's distinction: the body-and-mind is the field; the awareness of it is the field-knower. In every experience there's the content and the knowing of it — learn to tell them apart, because everything practical follows from the sorting.

*For example:* The athlete who learns to read the field (the body's fear) without mistaking it for the knower — "the field is reporting danger; the knowing of it is steady" — performs differently in the final minutes.
e.c: LAYER VII - DISCRIMINATION AND SELF-INQUIRY
p: **Metacognitive monitoring**, the separation of knowing from content (Flavell, 1979)

e.t: Trust verification over tradition alone
e.x:
The Kena's questions ("by what impelled does the mind fall on its object?... what is the eye of the eye?") are the tradition's own demand that the teaching be verified in experience rather than received on authority; the Gita sends the student to inquire of the wise rather than to merely obey them. Practically, keep a verification notebook: one column for received truth, one for what your own experience has actually shown. The methodological reading is a modern one; the Kena itself poses its questions in a devotional register.

(Kena Upanishad 1.4-2.4; BG 4.34.)

**Plain words** The Kena's questions — "by what impelled does the mind fall on its object? what is the eye of the eye?" — are the tradition demanding verification in experience, not reception on authority. Trust verification over tradition alone; the tradition itself insists.

*For example:* The student who takes the teaching on faith and the one who takes it to the lab of their own week — the tradition's own texts side with the second student. The questions are the curriculum.
e.c: LAYER VII - DISCRIMINATION AND SELF-INQUIRY
p: **Active learning and self-testing**, the superiority of retrieval and verification over passive receipt (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006)

e.t: Let knowledge purify action
e.x:
The Gita's claim is strong: nothing purifies like knowledge, and knowledge, once assimilated, acts on conduct the way fire acts on fuel. The practical reading runs both directions: act from what you have verified, and let your actions test your knowledge. Practically, after each significant decision, note which piece of knowledge it expressed, and audit the knowledge after the outcome.

(BG 4.33-4.38.)

**Plain words** Nothing purifies like knowledge, says the Gita — and knowledge, assimilated, acts on conduct the way fire acts on fuel. The practical reading runs both directions: act from what you've verified, and let your actions test your knowledge. After each significant act, check the knowledge it ran on.

*For example:* Someone "knows" the colleague's behaviour is insecurity-driven — then snaps at them anyway — and audits the gap: the knowledge wasn't actually running the action yet. The fire hadn't reached the fuel.
e.c: LAYER VII - DISCRIMINATION AND SELF-INQUIRY
p: **Implementation of knowledge as behavior change**, the intention-behavior gap and its bridges (Sheeran, 2002)

e.t: Keep urgency without hurry
e.x:
The Katha's summons, "Arise, awake; having reached the great, learn" (Katha 1.3.14, with the razor's-edge path image that follows), is the tradition's answer to procrastination at the level of life itself: the stakes are real, the time is finite, and practice delayed is the one reliable loss. The famous rendering "arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached" is Vivekananda's modern paraphrase of this verse, and is labeled as such here. Practically, convert urgency into scheduled practice rather than into pressure on yourself.

(Katha Upanishad 1.3.14.)

**Plain words** "Arise, awake; having reached the great, learn" — with the razor's-edge image — is the tradition's answer to procrastination at the level of life itself: the stakes are real, the time is finite, practice delayed is the one regret that compounds. Urgency without hurry.

*For example:* The person who's been "meaning to start" for a decade — reads the Katha's summons as fuel, not as panic: no sprinting, but no more pretending there's no clock either.
e.c: LAYER VII - DISCRIMINATION AND SELF-INQUIRY
p: **Deadline structure and implementation intentions**, the benefits of specified timing over vague urgency (Gollwitzer, 1999)

e.t: Keep the question alive
e.x:
The tradition's inquiry is not designed to terminate in an answer that closes it; the questions ("who is aware?", "what is this?") are described as the practice itself, kept alive rather than answered. Closing the question re-inflates the self that holds the answer. Practically, carry one open question as you would carry a koan, and resist the first answer that flatters you.

(Katha's "the sharp path"; Zen's live question.)

**Plain words** The inquiry is not designed to terminate in an answer that closes it — "who is aware?" is the practice itself, kept alive rather than answered. Closing the question re-inflates the self that holds the answer. Carry the question; let it work.

*For example:* Someone gets the "answer" in a retreat and spends two years defending it — versus the one who keeps the question running quietly in the background of every experience. The second one is still practicing; the first one is still defending.
e.c: LAYER VII - DISCRIMINATION AND SELF-INQUIRY
p: **Intolerance of uncertainty as a risk factor, tolerance as a strength**, the clinical literature (Dugas et al., 1998; uncertainty-tolerance research)
f: **Learned ignorance** (Nicholas of Cusa, De Docta Ignorantia; cross-tradition echo)

e.t: Act, release the fruits
e.x:
The Gita's central verse and the tradition's clearest articulation of process over outcome: action alone is your right, never its fruits. The instruction is not to abandon outcomes (the tradition immediately adds effort toward good outcomes) but to release the ego's lien on them, because the lien is what converts effort into anxiety. Practically, for your most important current project, define your part (inputs, quality, consistency) and the world's part (response, timing, results), and sign only your part.

(BG 2.47.)

**Plain words** The Gita's central verse: action alone is your right, never its fruits. Not abandoning outcomes — the tradition immediately adds effort toward good ones — but releasing the ego's lien on them, because the lien is the suffering. Work fully; sign nothing over to your self-worth.

*For example:* Two candidates prep identically for the exam — one's identity rides on the result, one's doesn't. Same marks possible; only one of them can survive either outcome. The lien was never on the exam; it was on the self.
e.c: LAYER VIII - ACTION IN THE WORLD
p: **Process versus outcome focus**, the performance literature showing process focus under pressure outperforms outcome focus
f: **Nishkama karma** (the Gita's own term; Vivekananda's Karma Yoga, modern)

e.t: Hold success and failure level
e.x:
Evenness (samatva) is defined as yoga itself: the mind held level in gain and loss, pleasant and painful. The tradition's reason is structural: the valuation that swings with outcomes is the swing. Practically, choose a levelness exercise for the day's swings: one sentence spoken to yourself at each peak and each valley, the same sentence.

(BG 2.48.)

**Plain words** Evenness is defined as yoga itself: the mind held level in gain and loss, pleasant and painful. The reason is structural — the valuation that swings with outcomes is the swing. Choose a levelness exercise for the day's swings: one sentence spoken at the top, one at the bottom.

*For example:* Someone writes the same three-word note on the day of the triumphant launch and the day of the layoff announcement — "this too, level" — and the note does what the note is for: reminding the swing that there's a floor and a ceiling, both held.
e.c: LAYER VIII - ACTION IN THE WORLD
p: **Equanimity as outcome measure**, defined as reduced reactivity to affective stimuli (Desbordes et al., 2014)

e.t: Redefine skill as evenness
e.x:
The Gita names yoga "skill in action" and defines it in context as the evenness just described (the parallel with choking research is a process comparison, not a validation): the skill of acting is the skill of remaining unperturbed while acting fully. This inverts the usual reading of skill as speed or brilliance. Practically, in your craft, measure sessions not by output alone but by output minus turbulence (how much inner weather accompanied the work).

(BG 2.50.)

**Plain words** The Gita names yoga "skill in action" and defines it as evenness: the skill of acting is the skill of remaining unperturbed while acting fully. This inverts the usual reading — the skill isn't the outcome, it's the levelness carried through the act.

*For example:* Watch two surgeons in the same crisis: same hands, same speed — one white-knuckled and contracted, one level and full. The tradition's definition of skill picks the second one every time, regardless of who wins the round.
e.c: LAYER VIII - ACTION IN THE WORLD
p: **Choking under pressure**, the performance research on why self-focus and outcome-focus degrade skill (Beilock, 2010)
f: **Wu wei as the mark of mastery** (Zhuangzi, Cook Ding)

e.t: Work as offering
e.x:
The Gita's yajna framework: action dedicated as offering rather than performed as acquisition, with the world sustained by the wheel of mutual giving. The bounded formulation removes the ritual: dedicate the work (to a person, a craft, a generation) before beginning it, and let the dedication steady the doing. Practically, open each workday with one sentence naming whom the work serves.

(BG 3.9-3.16.)

**Plain words** Work as offering: action dedicated rather than performed as acquisition — the ritual removed, the dedication kept. Dedicate the work (to a person, a craft, a generation) before beginning it, and let the dedication do what the self's lien used to do.

*For example:* The same shift on the ward, dedicated at the start to the patients in it — and the hours run differently from the same hours run as acquisition. Nothing external changed; the frame did.
e.c: LAYER VIII - ACTION IN THE WORLD
p: **Self-transcendent purpose at work**, the effects of prosocial purpose on persistence and performance (Yeager et al., 2014)
f: **Ora et labora** (Benedictine motto, drawn from the Rule's balance of the Divine Office and manual labor, Rule 43.3 and 48)

e.t: Act for the world's welfare
e.x:
The Gita's social mandate: as the ignorant act with attachment, the wise act for the holding together of the world (lokasangraha); the exemplar king attained perfection by action, not withdrawal. The tradition explicitly forbids using contemplative ideals to abandon necessary work. Practically, hold one role in your life as service-in-form (a committee, a shift, a mentoring hour) and keep it when contemplation tempts you to simplify everything away.

(BG 3.20, 3.25.)

**Plain words** As the ignorant act with attachment, the wise act for the holding-together of the world — lokasangraha. The tradition explicitly forbids using contemplative ideals to abandon necessary work. Withdrawal is not the advanced move; participation is.

*For example:* The person who uses "non-attachment" to justify checking out of the community's problems — versus the one whose practice shows up as the opposite: more present, more useful, better company. The tradition's exemplar king attained perfection by action, not withdrawal.
e.c: LAYER VIII - ACTION IN THE WORLD
p: **Volunteering and prosocial engagement effects on well-being and health** (Post, 2005)
f: **Citizen of the world** (Diogenes of Sinope, in Diogenes Laertius VI.63)
**Democracy as associated living** (Dewey, Democracy and Education)

e.t: Never abstain from necessary action
e.x:
The Gita's hard line: no one remains actionless even for a moment, and the attempt to abstain from action while the body and the world demand it is self-deception; abstention from necessary action is also action, worse. Practically, when in doubt about whether to act, apply the test of necessity (does the situation require this of me?) before the test of desire (do I want to?).

(BG 3.4-3.8.)

**Plain words** The hard line: no one remains actionless even for a moment — and abstention from necessary action is also action, worse. When in doubt about whether to act, apply the necessary-action test before the contemplative one.

*For example:* The "above it all" colleague who abstains from the toxic meeting as a spiritual act — and the toxicity runs the meeting unopposed. The abstention was an action, all right; the tradition just grades it lower.
e.c: LAYER VIII - ACTION IN THE WORLD
p: **Avoidance as the maintenance mechanism of anxiety and depression**, the behavioral-activation literature (Martell et al., 2010)

e.t: Give up the doer's claim
e.x:
The deeper layer of non-attachment: not only the fruits but the authorship is released; the Gita says the wise see that the strands of nature do their work while the seer watches, and the perfected one acts without the inner announcement of "I do this." The bounded formulation: attribute outcomes to the whole system (causes, collaborators, conditions) that produced them, including your own body-mind. Practically, strike "I" from one accomplishment story per week and watch what remains true.

(BG 14.19; BG 5.8-5.9.)

**Plain words** The deeper layer: not only the fruits but the authorship is released. The wise see the strands of nature do their work while the seer watches — the perfected one acts without the inner announcement of "I do this." Attention shifts from the self's claim to the work's needs.

*For example:* The jazz musician mid-solo — the training did the work, the self is not announcing anything, and the phrase arrives. Everyone who's been in that flow knows the announcement would have killed it.
e.c: LAYER VIII - ACTION IN THE WORLD
p: **Fundamental attribution error**, the robust bias toward over-crediting the self (Ross, 1977); **self-serving attribution** and its reversal in depression research
f: **The gunas act on the gunas** (BG 3.27-3.28, the tradition's own formulation)

e.t: Know the three strands
e.x:
The Gita's descriptive psychology: sattva (lucidity, binding by attachment to ease and knowledge), rajas (passion, binding by craving and restlessness), tamas (inertia, binding by negligence and sleep). Each strand binds in its own way, and the first step is seeing which is currently running you. The book's caution: this is a descriptive typology, not a validated scientific taxonomy. Practically, name the strand before choosing the response: lucidity clarifies, passion energizes, inertia requires activation before anything else.

(BG 14.5-14.9.)

**Plain words** The three strands: sattva (lucidity, binding by attachment to ease and knowledge), rajas (passion, binding by craving and restlessness), tamas (inertia, binding by negligence and sleep). Each binds in its own way — and the first step is seeing which one is currently running you.

*For example:* Someone learns the map and starts reading their states like weather reports: "this is rajas, third day running" — and the reading itself, without force, starts shifting the mix. You can't choose your weather without knowing it.
e.c: LAYER VIII - ACTION IN THE WORLD
p: **Temperament and arousal-based typologies as conceptual parallels**, behavioral activation and inhibition systems (Carver & White, 1994; a conceptual parallel, honestly labeled)
f: **Circumstances and the flow of nature** (Zhuangzi's transformation-of-things)

e.t: Eat, give, and act by effect, not by craving
e.x:
The Gita grades food, gifts, and austerity by their effects: the food that promotes life, virtue, strength, health, and ease (sattvic) versus the food that is burnt, stale, or leftover from craving; the gift given to the worthy at the right time and place versus the gift given grudgingly for display. The principle generalizes: grade inputs by their downstream effects, not by their immediate appeal. Practically, run a one-week audit of food and giving against the sattvic criteria, and let the effects choose.

(BG 17.7-10; BG 17.20-22.)

**Plain words** The Gita grades food, gifts, and austerity by their effects: the food that promotes life, strength, health, and ease versus the food that's burnt, stale, or leftover from craving; the gift given to the worthy at the right time and place versus the rest. Choose by effect, not by craving.

*For example:* Someone notices the fourth coffee of the afternoon isn't chosen by the body's needs — it's chosen by the craving, and the effect ledger says so. The grading system turns a moral lecture into a shopping guide.
e.c: LAYER VIII - ACTION IN THE WORLD
p: **Dietary patterns and mental health**, the observational and trial evidence for Mediterranean-style patterns
**Prosocial spending** (Dunn et al., 2008)

e.t: Practice austerity of body, speech, and mind
e.x:
The Gita's triple austerity: of body (reverence, cleanliness, non-harm), of speech (true, beneficial, non-agitating speech), and of mind (serenity, gentleness, silence, self-mastery). The grading by intention matters: austerity performed for display is named as demonic. Practically, adopt one austerity per month, one per domain, and keep it private per principle 40.

(BG 17.14-17.19.)

**Plain words** Triple austerity: of body (reverence, cleanliness, non-harm), of speech (true, beneficial, non-agitating), of mind (serenity, gentleness, silence, self-mastery). The grading by intention matters: austerity performed for display is named as vanity. Check the audience of your discipline.

*For example:* The person doing the 5 a.m. cold-plunge routine who makes sure everyone at work hears about it — same practice as the silent one, graded entirely differently. The intention is the third austerity.
e.c: LAYER VIII - ACTION IN THE WORLD
p: **Behavioral practice as identity change**, the finding that doing reshapes self-concept

e.t: Transcend the strands while acting
e.x:
The Gita describes the one who sits like a witness, unmoved by the strands, who regards pleasure and pain, praise and blame alike, and names such a one as fit for the absolute. The bounded formulation: use the strand-map to gain freedom of movement within it, choosing your dominant strand deliberately rather than being chosen.
