Practically, when tamas says "not now," do the two-minute entry; when rajas says "more," schedule the stop; when sattva says "rest in this," set a review.

(BG 14.22-14.26.)

**Plain words** The one who sits like a witness, unmoved by the strands — pleasure and pain, praise and blame alike — is named as fit for the absolute. The bounded formulation: use the strand-map to gain freedom of movement within it. Choose your mix like a pilot chooses altitude.

*For example:* Someone needs rajas for the launch week and sattva for the aftermath — and, knowing the map, schedules both on purpose instead of being weathered by whichever arrives. The strands become instruments; the witness is the player.
e.c: LAYER VIII - ACTION IN THE WORLD
p: **Metacognitive regulation of state**, the capacity to observe and shift one's own arousal and engagement (Flavell, 1979; state-matching interventions)
f: **Above the battle of the elements** (Emerson's "Brahma," Transcendentalist echo)

e.t: Avoid the three gates of ruin
e.x:
The Gita names the three: craving (kama), anger (krodha), and greed (lobha), the gates to self-destruction, and prescribes their rejection with the resolve "these three I renounce." The naming is precise because the three reinforce each other in a loop. Practically, learn your usual entry gate (blocked craving becoming anger, fear becoming greed) and post the watch there.

(BG 16.21-16.22.)

**Plain words** The three gates of ruin: craving, anger, and greed — named precisely because they reinforce each other in a loop. Learn your gate order (which one opens the others for you) and post a guard there.

*For example:* Someone maps their own loop: greed opens craving, craving frustrated turns to anger — and the guard goes on gate one. The loop that ran their twenties gets a gatekeeper in their forties.
e.c: LAYER VIII - ACTION IN THE WORLD
p: **Delay discounting and craving loops** (Bickel et al., 2014); **anger as blocked goal pursuit** (Berkowitz's reformulation)

e.t: Cultivate the divine dispositions
e.x:
The Gita opens its sixteenth chapter with the list of the godlike: fearlessness, purity of heart, self-restraint, steadfastness in knowledge and concentration, charity, study, austerity, honesty, non-harm, truth, absence of anger, renunciation, tranquility, aversion to fault-finding, compassion, gentleness, modesty, and patience. The list functions as a character curriculum: read weekly, it works as an examination of conscience without the guilt. Practically, take one disposition per fortnight as a theme, and log moments of opportunity.

(BG 16.1-16.3.)

**Plain words** The Gita's list of the godlike dispositions: fearlessness, purity of heart, self-restraint, steadfastness, charity, honesty, non-harm, absence of anger, tranquility — the portrait given as a curriculum, not a personality test. Take one disposition per season and practise it on purpose.

*For example:* Someone picks "absence of anger" for the season and treats every flare-up as the season's homework — not suppressing, studying. By spring, the disposition has a pulse.
e.c: LAYER VIII - ACTION IN THE WORLD
p: **Character strengths interventions**, the VIA framework's use of signature strengths (Niemiec, 2018)
f: **The catalogue of virtues** (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II)

e.t: Renounce the inner claim, not the outer duty
e.x:
The Gita distinguishes the renunciation of the fruit (which it endorses) from the renunciation of the activity (which it largely does not, where the activity is one's own duty). The practical rule: give up the lien, keep the work. Practically, in one ongoing obligation you resent, experiment with full performance with fully released claim, and observe the change in the work's quality.

(BG 18.9; BG 5.13; BG 3.19.)

**Plain words** The Gita distinguishes renouncing the fruit (endorsed) from renouncing the activity (largely not, where it's your duty). The practical rule: give up the lien, keep the work. In one ongoing obligation, release the claim and watch the work continue — often better.

*For example:* The parent who keeps every duty of the school run and drops the claim to gratitude for it — the run continues, lighter. The lien was the suffering; the lift was never the work.
e.c: LAYER VIII - ACTION IN THE WORLD
p: **Detached persistence**, commitment to process with nonattachment to single outcomes (as in acceptance and commitment therapy)
f: **In the world, not of it** (Gospel of John 17.14-15)

e.t: See action within rest and rest within action
e.x:
The Gita's paradox: the wise see inaction in action and action in inaction; the one who sits in activity (whose actions are consumed by knowledge) rests, and the one who sits still while craving is busy. The bounded formulation: rest is defined by inner weather, not by posture, and activity can be restful when unclaimed. Practically, schedule one restful action per week (an act done with full attention and no claim) and treat it as rest.

(BG 4.18; BG 4.19.)

**Plain words** The paradox: the wise see inaction in action and action in inaction — the one whose actions are consumed by knowledge rests even while working, and the one who sits still while craving is busy. Rest is defined by inner weather, not by furniture.

*For example:* Two people in the same deck chair on the same beach: one is on holiday, one is rehearsing a war. Only one of them is resting — and it's not the one who "did nothing" all week.
e.c: LAYER VIII - ACTION IN THE WORLD
p: **Effortless attention and flow's recovery profile**, the finding that absorbed activity can restore rather than deplete (Csikszentmihalyi's recovery studies)
f: **Wu wei** (Laozi, Daodejing 38 context, the direct parallel)

e.t: Unify contemplation and action
e.x:
The Gita dismisses the quarrel between the way of knowledge and the way of action as a distinction children argue over: they are one; each is the other done properly. The traditions make the same point structurally, which is why the curriculum alternates between them. Practically, treat every contemplative insight as incomplete until it has changed an action, and every action as incomplete until it has been examined.

(BG 5.4-5.5; BG 3.3.)

**Plain words** The Gita dismisses the quarrel between the way of knowledge and the way of action as a distinction children argue over: they are one — each is the other done properly. Contemplation and action, unified; the split was always the artifact.

*For example:* The team's best problem-solver turns out to be the one with the steadiest attention — and the resident meditator's practice shows up as better meetings. The two "different paths" keep arriving at the same door.
e.c: LAYER VIII - ACTION IN THE WORLD
p: **Learning loops and action research**, the cyclical model of act-examine-act (pragmatist experimental living)
f: **Theoria and praxis as one round** (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics X)

e.t: Match your stance to the other's condition
e.x:
The social application of the fourfold stance taught in principle 65: friendliness to the happy (against envy), compassion to the unhappy (against pity), delight in the virtuous (against competitive comparison), and even-minded disregard toward the hostile (against entanglement). Each stance is a discipline, and the discipline is chosen by the other's state, not by your mood. Practically, in your hardest relationship, identify their current state and practice the prescribed stance for a week before judging whether the relationship can work.

(YS 1.33, social application; BG 12.13-14.)

**Plain words** The social application of the fourfold stance: friendliness to the happy (against envy), compassion to the unhappy (against pity), delight in the virtuous (against competitive comparison), even-minded disregard toward the hostile (against engagement). Match the stance to the condition.

*For example:* At the reunion: the friend with the dream job gets warmth, the friend in the rough year gets compassion, the humble one gets delight, and the provocateur gets nothing at all. Four doors, four stances, no leakage.
e.c: LAYER IX - RELATIONAL LIFE
p: **Social support matching**, the finding that support must match the recipient's needs to be effective (Cutrona, 1990)

e.t: See the self in others and others in the self
e.x:
The Gita's relational yoga: the one who sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self, who regards the pleasure and pain of others as his own, is called the highest. The tradition's method for this is not sentiment but perspective-taking trained to the point of reflex. Practically, in one disagreement per day, spend the first minute arguing the other side to yourself before speaking.

(BG 6.29-6.32.)

**Plain words** The relational yoga: see the self in all beings and all beings in the self — the pleasure and pain of others regarded as your own. Not sentiment; perspective-taking trained to the point of reflex. The method is practice, not feeling.

*For example:* The commuter who spends the year deliberately taking the other passengers' eyes — tired nurse, scared student, proud father — and finds the crowd slowly stops being an obstacle course and starts being a room of relatives.
e.c: LAYER IX - RELATIONAL LIFE
p: **Self-other overlap and perspective-taking**, the measured inclusion of other in the self (Aron et al., 1992)
f: **Tat tvam asi, the relational reading** (Chandogya 6.8.7; the ethical interpretation)

e.t: Be the portrait
e.x:
The Gita's description of the person dear to the tradition: free from malice toward all beings, friendly, compassionate, without possessiveness and ego, patient, content, self-controlled, resolute, unmoved by the world's agitations and not a cause of the world's agitation. The portrait is given as a practice object: read it, and each day take one clause as the day's practice. Practically, post the portrait where you work, and let one clause per day be your theme.

(BG 12.13-14.)

**Plain words** Be the portrait: free from malice, friendly, compassionate, without possessiveness and ego, patient, content, self-controlled, resolute, unmoved by agitations and not a cause of them. The portrait is given as a mirror — hold it up monthly and check the likeness, feature by feature.

*For example:* Someone tapes the portrait to the inside of the journal and does the monthly check: malice — down one; possessiveness — holding; patience — regressed. The mirror does what mirrors do: makes the changes visible.
e.c: LAYER IX - RELATIONAL LIFE
p: **Ideal-self congruence and approach goals**, the motivation research on moving toward an envisioned self (Higgins, 1987)
f: **The likeness of the serene** (Cicero, De Finibus III)

e.t: Do not agitate the world
e.x:
The Gita's test of maturity runs both directions: the person who neither agitates the world nor is agitated by it. Each clause is a practice: to be a non-agitating presence (speech, timing, demands) and to become hard to agitate (equanimity under provocation). Practically, pick your most agitating environment and practice both clauses there for a month.

(BG 12.15.)

**Plain words** The test of maturity runs both directions: the person who neither agitates the world nor is agitated by it. Two practices in one — be a non-agitating presence (speech, timing, demands), and become hard to agitate (equanimity under provocation). Pick your weaker clause.

*For example:* The office's two extremes: the one whose entrances raise the room's temperature, and the one who melts at every email. The mature position is the colleague who does neither — the one everyone instinctively keeps in the loop.
e.c: LAYER IX - RELATIONAL LIFE
p: **Emotional contagion and co-regulation**, the research showing one person's state spreads through groups (Hatfield et al., 1994)

e.t: Bear the opposites
e.x:
The Gita's early training instruction: the contact of the senses (heat and cold, pleasure and pain) comes and goes; they are transient, and the wise learn to bear them. The capacity named is titiksha, tolerance, treated as trainable rather than inborn. Practically, practice small voluntary bearances (cold shower's last thirty seconds, the queue, the hunger before the meal) as reps of the general capacity.

(BG 2.14; Vivekachudamani's titiksha, attributed.)

**Plain words** Heat and cold, pleasure and pain — the contact of the senses comes and goes; they are transient, and the wise learn to bear them. Titiksha, tolerance — trainable, not inborn. Practice small voluntary bears: the cold shower, the hunger gap, the boring hour.

*For example:* Someone trains on the small bears — waits out the itch to check the phone, takes the walk in the rain — and finds the big bears (the illness, the layoff) are met with a capacity that was built at small scale.
e.c: LAYER IX - RELATIONAL LIFE
p: **Distress tolerance training**, the DBT module's evidence (Linehan, 1993)

e.t: Honor the teacher-student bond
e.x:
The tradition's transmission method is relational: knowledge passes from the settled to the unsettled through sustained proximity, and the Gita instructs the student to learn by inquiry, service, and questioning rather than by sampling. The bounded formulation: choose teachers deliberately, serve the learning (not the teacher's ego), and graduate. Practically, for your current most important learning, name your teacher (book, person, practice) and structure the service component.

(BG 4.34; Chandogya 6, Uddalaka and Shvetaketu as the model; Upadesasahasri.)

**Plain words** The transmission is relational: knowledge passes from the settled to the unsettled through sustained proximity — by inquiry, service, and questioning rather than sampling. Choose teachers for proximity over prestige, and stay long enough for the settling to transmit.

*For example:* The student who collects certificates from famous names versus the one who spent three years assisting a local master — the tradition's odds favor the second; the settling transmits through proximity, not through syllabi.
e.c: LAYER IX - RELATIONAL LIFE
p: **Mentoring effects**, the developmental literature on sustained guidance (Rhodes, 2002, Stand by Me)

e.t: Meet people where they are
e.x:
The Gita's instruction to the wise: do not disturb the minds of those attached to action and its rewards; let them work and rejoice while you act with discipline. The principle is pedagogical humility: teaching beyond readiness hardens rather than opens. Practically, with one person you want to fix, stop advancing the argument for a week, model instead, and let the model do the slow work.

(BG 3.26.)

**Plain words** Do not disturb the minds of those attached to action and its rewards — let them work and rejoice while you act with discipline. Pedagogical humility: teaching beyond readiness hardens rather than opens. With one person in your life, practise saying less.

*For example:* The convert who lectures their whole family at every dinner — versus the one who just lives differently and answers questions when asked. The tradition's rule: the second one is the teacher; the first is just another agitation.
e.c: LAYER IX - RELATIONAL LIFE
p: **Readiness-matched intervention**, the stage-of-change finding that unmatched advice entrenches (Prochaska & DiClemente, 1983)

e.t: Let relationship sharpen self-knowledge
e.x:
The Gita's diagnostic: relationships are where practice is proven, because the other person's pleasure and pain mirroring yours is the test of whether your equanimity is real or performed. The tradition treats difficulty in relationships as curriculum, not as interruption. Practically, in your most difficult relationship, treat each flare-up as a scheduled experiment: what did this show about my practice?

(BG 6.32, the parallel of others' states as one's own.)

**Plain words** Relationships are where practice is proven — the other person's pleasure and pain mirroring yours is the test of whether your equanimity is real or performed. Treat difficulty in relationships as curriculum, not interruption.

*For example:* The meditator who is serene everywhere except within fifteen minutes of their mother — and finally takes the hint: the mother is the exam the retreat was studying for.
e.c: LAYER IX - RELATIONAL LIFE
p: **Relationships as the arena of self-expansion and conflict growth** (Aron)

e.t: Keep company that supports the practice
e.x:
The Gita's counsel on association appears both positively (the wise are met through inquiry) and negatively (the virtue list includes disengagement from fault-finding company), and the Upanishadic method itself assumes a protected learning environment. The bounded formulation: curate your closest five the way you curate your inputs. Practically, name your five most-contacted people, and ask which direction each pulls the practice.

(BG 13.11 context, the company of the settled; Chandogya 6 context, the protected teaching.)

**Plain words** Keep company that supports the practice: the wise met through inquiry, and disengagement from fault-finding company — the tradition is explicit in both directions. The bounded formulation: audit your five closest voices; are they practice or friction?

*For example:* Someone notices the group chat has become a two-hour nightly complaint ritual — and redirects a third of that energy to the friend who's actually building something. The audit doesn't require drama; it requires re-weighting.
e.c: LAYER IX - RELATIONAL LIFE
p: **Social contagion of health behaviors**, the longitudinal findings on networks shaping behavior (Christakis & Fowler, 2007)
f: **The friend as a second self** (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX)

e.t: Practice the virtue list as a relational curriculum
e.x:
The Gita's thirteenth chapter virtue list (humility, unpretentiousness, non-injury, patience, uprightness, service to teacher and elders, purity, steadfastness, self-control, dispassion, absence of egoism, non-attachment to home and family, even-mindedness in desired and undesired, devotion, solitude, distaste for the crowd, steadfastness in self-knowledge) is explicitly social: most clauses name how to be among people. Practically, take one clause per week as a relationship practice, and review Sundays.

(BG 13.7-13.11.)

**Plain words** The Gita's virtue list — humility, unpretentiousness, non-injury, patience, uprightness, service, purity, steadfastness, self-control, dispassion, absence of egoism, even-mindedness — is a relational curriculum: every virtue is tested on someone. Practise the list with people, not in the abstract.

*For example:* Someone "practises patience" alone until it's real — then the toddler throws the bowl, and the list's true testing environment arrives. The virtues were always social; the solitude was just training camp.
e.c: LAYER IX - RELATIONAL LIFE
p: **Weekly-review implementation intentions**, the evidence for scheduled reflection

e.t: Combine the paths by disposition
e.x:
Vivekananda's modern synthesis, offered here as adaptation: four yogas (knowledge, devotion, action, and meditation) as four doors into one room, each person entering by the door their temperament opens. The classical sources support the plurality (the Gita teaches paths by inclination), while the synthesis is nineteenth-century. Practically, name your lead path, name your support path, and sequence them: lead in the morning, support in the evening.

(Vivekananda, Raja Yoga and Karma Yoga, 1896, modern; BG 3.3, paths by disposition.)

**Plain words** Vivekananda's synthesis: four yogas — knowledge, devotion, action, meditation — as four doors into one room, each person entering by the door their temperament opens. Don't force your door on others, and don't apologise for yours. Combine the paths by disposition.

*For example:* The same wisdom reached by the scholar's door (knowledge), the carer's door (action), the mystic's door (devotion) — the room is one; the arguing starts only when everyone insists their door is the building.
e.c: LAYER X - INTEGRATION AND MATURATION
p: **Person-activity fit**, the matching of intervention to disposition
f: **Truth is one, the sages name it many** (Rig Veda 1.164.46)

e.t: Use the limbs as a diagnostic grid
e.x:
The troubleshooting practice that pairs with principle 72's curriculum: when the advanced stalls, walk the grid downward. Meditation failing: check sense withdrawal (inputs). Withdrawal failing: check breath and body (regulation). Regulation failing: check observances (contentment, study, moderation). Conduct failing: check restraints (harm, truth, taking, energy, grasping). An editorial rule of thumb, not an established empirical finding: many stalls appear to resolve at the level of ethics or body rather than technique. Practically, keep the grid as a monthly audit, cross-referencing principle 72's curriculum.

(YS 2.28-2.29, the sequence as diagnostic.)

**Plain words** The troubleshooting grid, paired with the curriculum: when the advanced stalls, walk the grid downward. Meditation failing: check the inputs (withdrawal). Withdrawal failing: check breath and body. Regulation failing: check conduct. The fault is almost always downstream of what you're practising.

*For example:* Someone fights their "concentration problem" for a year — then audits upward and finds the actual fault: 5 a.m. doom-scrolling. The grid reads bottom-up: no withdrawal, no regulation, no meditation. Fix the base.
e.c: LAYER X - INTEGRATION AND MATURATION
p: **Functional analysis of behavior**, the ABC diagnostic of antecedents and consequences
f: **The whole prior to the parts** (Aristotle, Parts of Animals I)

e.t: Sequence by need, not prestige
e.x:
The curriculum's trap: practicing what flatters (advanced concentration) while neglecting what is needed (sleep, ethics, moderation). The tradition's own sequence is need-ordered, and this principle protects it. Practically, once per season, rank your actual needs against your actual practice, and move practice time toward the top of the needs list.

(YS 2.28-2.29; BG 6.16-6.17.)

**Plain words** The curriculum's trap: practising what flatters (advanced concentration) while neglecting what's needed (sleep, ethics, moderation). The tradition's own sequence is need-ordered. Once per season, rank your actual needs against your actual practice — and obey the ranking.

*For example:* The meditator with the sophisticated practice and the four-hour sleep debt — the season's honest ranking says: bed. The advanced technique can wait; it was built on the foundations being skipped.
e.c: LAYER X - INTEGRATION AND MATURATION
p: **Needs-based intervention sequencing**,

e.t: Take no experience as final
e.x:
The neti neti procedure applied to attainments: every state, however luminous, is a state, and the tradition's counsel is to use it and pass through. The Buddhist raft parable makes the same point: the teaching that carries you across is the first thing to release on arrival. Practically, when a breakthrough arrives, write it down, thank it, and schedule the return to basics within the week.

(Brihadaranyaka 2.3.6 applied; Buddhist tradition, Alagaddupama Sutta, MN 22.)

**Plain words** Neti neti applied to attainments: every state, however luminous, is a state — use it and pass through. The Buddhist raft parable says the same: the teaching that carries you across is the first thing to release on arrival. Take no experience as final.

*For example:* The retreat's transcendent week — treated as a room passed through, not a home. The practitioner who moves on carries the benefit; the one who camps there carries the memory.
e.c: LAYER X - INTEGRATION AND MATURATION
p: **Hedonic adaptation applied to positive states**, the decay of even peak experiences (Frederick & Loewenstein, 1999)

e.t: Expect freedom to show up in conduct
e.x:
The tradition's mature position, most developed in the later Vedanta line: liberation while living (jivanmukti), visible not in withdrawal or in claims but in conduct: reduced reactivity, harmless speech, levelness under gain and loss, service without lien. The test offered is behavioral, which makes it checkable. Practically, audit your freedom claims against the last month's conduct, and let conduct be the measure.

(The jivanmukti doctrine, Vidyaranya and the Yoga Vasistha line, labeled as the later tradition's development.)

**Plain words** Liberation while living — visible not in withdrawal or claims but in conduct: reduced reactivity, harmless speech, levelness under gain and loss, service without lien. The test of any realization is the Tuesday after. Expect freedom to show up in conduct.

*For example:* The teacher who claims the big realization — and the one whose realization shows up as the way they handle the cancelled flight. The tradition's scoreboard only prints conduct.
e.c: LAYER X - INTEGRATION AND MATURATION
p: **Behavioral integrity as the measure of change**, the principle that outcomes are assessed in behavior

e.t: Serve with what you realize
e.x:
The integration of knowledge and love: realization that does not issue in service is, by the tradition's own test, incomplete, because the realization is precisely that the boundary between self and other was a mis-taking. The bounded formulation closes the loop with action: the fruit of inquiry is a changed way of being among people. Practically, attach each year's practice to one person or project served.

(BG 3.20 with 6.29-6.32; Vivekananda's Karma Yoga, modern.)

**Plain words** Realization that does not issue in service is, by the tradition's own test, incomplete — because the realization was precisely that the boundary between self and other was a mis-taking. Serve with what you realize; the loop closes in action.

*For example:* The practitioner whose insight deepens and whose calendar quietly fills with other people's needs — not as duty, as consequence. The realization and the service turn out to be the same event.
e.c: LAYER X - INTEGRATION AND MATURATION
p: **Purpose-linked practice**, the effects of self-transcendent goals on well-being

e.t: Rebuild from the basics when the advanced stalls
e.x:
The tradition's own practice instruction, and the companion to principle 125's diagnostic grid: when integration fails, return to the restraints and observances; when the cathedral cracks, inspect the foundation. The return is not regression but the tradition's designed maintenance cycle. Practically, schedule an annual "foundations month": restraints, observances, posture, breath, moderation audit.

(YS 2.28-2.32 revisited; BG 6.16-6.17.)

**Plain words** When integration fails, return to the restraints and observances — when the cathedral cracks, inspect the foundation. The return is not regression; it's the tradition's own practice instruction. Rebuild from the basics when the advanced stalls.

*For example:* The advanced student whose year falls apart — sleep, diet, speech — and whose teacher's prescription is the beginner's course: yamas and niyamas, five daily. The tradition never treated the basics as the thing you graduate from.
e.c: LAYER X - INTEGRATION AND MATURATION
p: **Booster sessions and maintenance scheduling**, the relapse-prevention design (Marlatt & Gordon, 1985)

e.t: Practice the same principle at every scale
e.x:
The tradition's fractal design: the training of attention on the breath and the training of a life are the same operation at different scales: bind, steady, release the claim. The Gita says the same of seeing the self in all beings. Practically, take one day per month as a scaled practice: run the day as one sitting, with the same beginning, the same return-when-wandering, and the same dedication at the end.

(YS 3.4 applied; BG 6.29-6.32 applied.)

**Plain words** The fractal design: training attention on the breath and training a life are the same operation at different scales — bind, steady, release the claim. Take one day per month and run the operation at life-scale deliberately.

*For example:* Someone realises their whole year is a sit: bind attention to the chosen work, steady through the distractions, release the claim on the results — the breath practice and the annual plan turn out to be one instruction at two zoom levels.
e.c: LAYER X - INTEGRATION AND MATURATION
p: **Transfer and consolidation across contexts**, the generalization literature (Barnett & Ceci, 2002)
f: **As above, so below** (Hermes Trismegistus, Emerald Tablet)

e.t: End in rest, not striving
e.x:
The final principle returns to the first: the goal is described as a resting, the seer at home in its own nature, the lake settled, the lamp in a windless place not flickering. The tradition's last word on striving is that striving is a means, and the sign of maturity is that striving can be set down. Practically, end each practice not with a push but with one full minute of deliberate non-doing, and let the practice's last taste be rest.

(YS 1.3; YS 4.34; BG 6.19.)

**Plain words** The final principle returns to the first: the goal is described as a resting — the seer at home in its own nature, the lake settled, the lamp in a windless place not flickering. Striving is a means, and the sign of maturity is that striving gets quieter. End in rest, not striving.

*For example:* The long-practised person at the end of the path doesn't look accomplished — they look at home. The striving that got them there is the first thing that settled.
e.c: LAYER X - INTEGRATION AND MATURATION
p: **Rest and recovery as active components of practice**, the restoration literature

e.t: Understand rather than condemn
e.x:
Spinoza states his method in the preface to Part III: he will consider human actions and appetites exactly as if they were lines, planes, and bodies. The maxim that summarizes the method is given in the Political Treatise: not to mock, not to lament, not to detest, but to understand. This is the master attitude of the whole Ethics. Anger, addiction, envy, and grief are treated as natural events with causes, like weather, and the first move is always the same: understand the mechanism before judging the person, including yourself. Practically, when a strong reaction arises, in yourself or another, postpone the verdict and look for the cause first.

(Ethics III, Preface; Political Treatise I.4, the maxim's formulation.)

**Plain words** Spinoza's maxim: not to mock, not to lament, not to detest, but to understand. Anger, addiction, envy, grief — treat them as natural events with causes, like weather. The first move is always the same: postpone the verdict, look for the mechanism.

*For example:* The colleague's meltdown stops being "what's wrong with him" and becomes "what's the mechanism?" — the sleep debt, the custody fight, the threatened role. Understanding doesn't excuse the behaviour; it replaces gossip with engineering.
e.c: LAYER I - NATURE, GOD, AND NECESSITY
p: **Emotion understanding as regulation**, the consistent finding that accurately labeling and explaining an emotional response reduces its intensity more than judging it does (Lieberman et al., 2007, affect labeling; Gross, 2015, reappraisal research)
f: **The obstacle as material** (Marcus Aurelius, Meditations V.20)
**Diagnosis before prescription** (Galen, On the Therapeutic Method)

e.t: See everything as one system
e.x:
God and Nature are one and the same thing, Spinoza says, using his famous formula deus sive natura: God, or in other words, Nature. Whatever exists is in Nature, and nothing exists outside it. The practical effect of this axiom is a change of frame: your failure, your enemy, your illness, and your mood are not foreign intrusions into reality but movements of the same single process that carries the stars. This does not mean approval; it means you stop splitting the world into the way things should be and the way things are, which is the split that generates most preventable suffering.

(Ethics I, especially P14 and P15.)

**Plain words** Deus sive natura: God, or in other words, Nature — whatever exists is in Nature, nothing outside it. The practical effect is a frame change: no outside. Your life, your body, your city, your problem — all one system, no enemies from beyond the walls.

*For example:* The person who frames their health, their mood, and their finances as separate problems with separate villains — and starts seeing the one system: the same stress is running the sleep, the spending, and the temper. One system, one fix point.
e.c: LAYER I - NATURE, GOD, AND NECESSITY
p: **Affective events as constructed within a whole person-context system**, the contemporary consensus that emotion is not an intrusion into cognition but part of one processing stream (Barrett, 2017)

e.t: Accept that nothing is contingent
e.x:
Things could not have been otherwise. Spinoza demonstrates that nothing in Nature is contingent, and that all things follow by the same necessity as the properties of a triangle follow from its nature. The principle is not fatalism, which would counsel passivity; it is the removal of the counterfactual burden, the exhausting rehearsal of how things should have gone. Practical translation: when something has happened, the question "how could this have been avoided" is useful only once, for learning; after that, you are arguing with geometry.

(Ethics I, P29 and P33, with the scholium on the will.)

**Plain words** Nothing is contingent: things could not have been otherwise — all things follow by the same necessity as a triangle's properties. Not fatalism (which would say effort is pointless): the necessity includes your effort as part of the mechanism. The past is unchangeable because it's complete.

*For example:* Someone replays the divorce for years — "if only I'd said" — and the Spinozist frame lands: given everything that each person was at that moment, it went the only way it could. The replay isn't processing; it's arguing with a finished proof.
e.c: LAYER I - NATURE, GOD, AND NECESSITY
p: **Counterfactual rumination as a risk factor for depression and complicated grief**, the finding that repetitive "if only" thinking maintains distress (Nolen-Hoeksema, 1991)

e.t: Stop reading purposes into events
e.x:
Nature has no goal set before it, Spinoza argues in the appendix to Part I. All final causes are human fictions: because people act on purposes, they assume Nature does too, and then read the weather, the illness, and the loss as messages addressed to them. The appendix is one of the most practical pages in early modern philosophy, because it removes an entire layer of interpretive suffering: the event itself is bad enough; the conviction that it was aimed at you is the addition. Practically, when something painful happens, separate the event from every story about what it means, and notice how much of the pain lives in the story.

(Ethics I, Appendix.)

**Plain words** Nature has no goal set before it — all final causes are human fictions. People act on purposes, so they assume Nature does too, and then read the weather, the illness, and the loss as messages addressed to them. Stop reading purposes into events. The storm isn't about you.

*For example:* The illness arrives and the search begins: what is this teaching me? what did I do to attract this? — and the Spinozist answer is quieting: nothing; it's a virus. Meaning you make; the event just happened. The meaning-making is yours, which is better news, not worse.
e.c: LAYER I - NATURE, GOD, AND NECESSITY
p: **Teleological bias**, the well-documented human tendency to over-attribute purpose and design to events (Kelemen, 2004, promiscuous teleology research)
f: **Wu wei and the way that does nothing yet nothing is left undone** (Laozi, Daodejing 37)
**The rain falls on the just and the unjust** (Gospel of Matthew 5.45, as cultural parallel)

e.t: Treat yourself as part of nature
e.x:
The preface to Part III says it directly: people are not outside nature, and human affect is not a defect in the universe but a natural fact like hot and cold. You are a mode of Nature, not its judge. The practical consequence for self-relations is large: self-hatred treats your jealousy or fear as a personal scandal, which both intensifies it and hides its cause; treating it as nature treats it as a mechanism you can study and steer.

(Ethics III, Preface; I, P15.)

**Plain words** People are not outside nature, and human affect is not a defect in the universe but a natural fact like hot and cold. You are a mode of Nature, not its judge. For self-relations this is huge: your anxiety and your appetite are weather, not sins.

*For example:* The person who hates themselves for being "so emotional" — and finally treats the emotion like temperature: a fact of the system, to be managed, not a moral failing to be confessed. The thermostat was never a sinner.
e.c: LAYER I - NATURE, GOD, AND NECESSITY
p: **Self-compassion as healthier than self-judgment**, meta-analytic evidence across depression, anxiety, and stress outcomes (Ferrari et al., 2019)
f: **Original nature, nothing to add** (Huineng, Platform Sutra)

e.t: Treat mind and body as one thing
e.x:
Mind and body are one and the same individual, conceived now under the attribute of thought, now under the attribute of extension. This is the famous mind-body identity stated in Part III's second scholium, and it makes Spinoza the patron of every modern embodied approach to emotion. There is no purely mental problem that does not have a bodily face, and no bodily state that leaves thinking untouched. Practically, when the mind is stuck, work the body, and when the body is depleted, do not expect clean thinking; the dualist split is itself a diagnostic error.

(Ethics III, P2 scholium; II, P7 scholium.)

**Plain words** Mind and body are one and the same individual, conceived now as thought, now as extension — the famous identity. Spinoza is the patron of every "it's all connected" insight: the pit in the stomach IS the worry, not the logo of it.

*For example:* The person who insists their burnout is "just stress, nothing physical" — and the body's file arrives: the sleep, the gut, the jaw. One individual, two reports. The reports always match; that's the identity.
e.c: LAYER I - NATURE, GOD, AND NECESSITY
p: **Interoception as the substrate of emotional regulation**, the evidence that bodily awareness supports affective control (Khalsa et al., 2018)
f: **The body as the first instrument** (Taittiriya Upanishad 2.1-2.5)

e.t: Keep thought and world in parallel
e.x:
The order and connection of ideas is the same as the order and connection of things. Whatever happens in your mind is not a private film over the world but the world itself, considered as thought. The principle grounds Spinoza's realism and his therapy at once: because your ideas are events in the same order as everything else, examining them is not narcissism but navigation.

(Ethics II, P7 and its scholium.)

**Plain words** The order and connection of ideas is the same as the order and connection of things. Your mind isn't a private film over the world — it's the world considered as thought. Realism grounded: think clearly and you track the actual; think badly and you're still tracking something — badly.

*For example:* Two managers describe the same failing team — one's account matches the metrics, the other's matches their mood. The ideas and the things run on the same tracks; the second manager's train just isn't on them.
e.c: LAYER I - NATURE, GOD, AND NECESSITY
p: **Predictive processing**, the current framework in which mind and world are modeled as one loop of prediction and correction (Clark, 2013, "Whatever next?")
f: **As above, so below** (Hermes Trismegistus, Emerald Tablet)
**The mirror of nature** (Dewey, Experience and Nature)

e.t: Treat good and evil as relations, not properties
e.x:
Spinoza refuses to place good and evil in things themselves: by good he will mean what is useful to our power of living, and by evil what hinders it, and the same thing can be good to one person, bad to another, and indifferent to a third. This is not relativism, because the standard is fixed (power of living) even though the applications vary. Practically, when you call something bad, complete the sentence: bad for what, for whom, over what timescale. Most moral vertigo dissolves when the missing end of the sentence is supplied.

(Ethics IV, Preface.)

**Plain words** Good and evil aren't in things: by good Spinoza means what's useful to your power of living, by evil what hinders it — and the same thing can be good for one, bad for another, indifferent to a third. Relations, not properties. Stop arguing about the thing; ask for whom.

*For example:* The 5 a.m. routine that transforms one person and hospitalises another — the routine was never the good; the fit was. The endless "what's the best diet/method/schedule" arguments dissolve once the question becomes "best for which machine?"
e.c: LAYER I - NATURE, GOD, AND NECESSITY
p: **Workability as a criterion**, the ACT proposal that inner events be assessed by whether they function toward valued living rather than by their literal content (Hayes et al., 2011)
f: **The mean relative to us** (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II)

e.t: Measure perfection as power, not as judgment
e.x:
Perfection, for Spinoza, is degree of reality and power of acting; imperfection is not sin but diminished capacity. A person in despair is not wicked, they are weak in power, which relocates the entire moral question from blame to engineering: what would increase this person's power of acting? Practically, audit your assessments of people, including yourself, and translate each judgment into a power question: what does this state of mind make this person able or unable to do?

(Ethics II, Definition 6; IV, Preface.)

**Plain words** Perfection is degree of reality and power of acting; imperfection is not sin but diminished capacity. A person in despair is not wicked — they're weak in power. This relocates the whole moral question from blame to engineering. You don't judge the dim lamp; you fix the current.

*For example:* The "toxic" family member whose cruelty looks, in the Spinozist lens, like a small engine making loud noises — diminished capacity, not demonic intent. The response changes from outrage to the practical: what would actually increase this person's power? Usually: not another fight.
e.c: LAYER I - NATURE, GOD, AND NECESSITY
p: **The quiet ego**, a growth-oriented, less-defensive identity structure associated with well-being (Wayment and Bauer, 2017)
f: **Virtue as power, vice as weakness** (Plato, Protagoras)

e.t: Know yourself as striving
e.x:
Each thing, as far as it can by its own power, strives to persevere in its being. This is the conatus, and it is not one drive among others; it is the essence of the thing, the actual essence from which desire, joy, sadness, love, and hate are built. To see yourself as striving is more accurate than to see yourself as a rational agent who sometimes has urges: you are striving first, and reason is one of its instruments. Practically, when behavior confuses you, do not ask "what is wrong with this person," ask "what is this striving to preserve, and is it working?"

(Ethics III, P6, P7, and P12 with scholium.)

**Plain words** The conatus: each thing, as far as it can by its own power, strives to persevere in its being — and this striving is your essence, the thing desire, joy, sadness, love, and hate are built from. Know yourself as striving. The self isn't a static thing; it's a verb with a direction.

*For example:* Every appetite in the life — the snack, the status post, the third coffee — reads, under the conatus lens, as the same single striving wearing different costumes. The diet that fights the costumes loses; the life that addresses the striving wins.
e.c: LAYER I - NATURE, GOD, AND NECESSITY
p: **Intrinsic motivation and organismic growth tendencies**, self-determination theory's parallel claim that human beings have inherent tendencies toward development (Deci and Ryan, 2000)
f: **Will to power as self-overcoming** (Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil 13)
**Eros as the drive of life toward more life** (Plato, Symposium)

e.t: Read joy and sadness as power signals
e.x:
Joy is the passage from a lesser to a greater perfection, sadness the passage from a greater to a lesser. This is Spinoza's geometry of mood: affects are not colors painted on experience but velocity vectors, readings of whether your power of acting is rising or falling. The diagnostic use is immediate. Joy that leaves you weaker in the aftermath was mislabeled by someone; sadness that quietly strengthens you may be growth. Practically, judge each affect by its residue over days, not by its first taste.

(Ethics III, P11 scholium; P6; definitions of Joy and Sadness, Part III end.)

**Plain words** Joy is the passage from lesser to greater perfection; sadness the passage from greater to lesser. Affects are velocity vectors, not colours — readings of whether your power of acting is rising or falling. Track the vector, not just the mood.

*For example:* Someone rates their days by how they felt — and starts rating them by direction: is my capacity rising or falling this week? The flat-but-improving week turns out to be the good one; the pleasant-but-collapsing week was the trap.
e.c: LAYER II - CONATUS: THE STRIVING ENGINE
p: **Affect-as-information**, the finding that feeling states are read by the mind as data about the situation (Schwarz and Clore, 1983)
f: **Hedonic tone as the mind's thermometer** (Buddhist vedana, the feeling-tone analysis; Samyutta Nikaya 36.19)
**The pendulum of desire** (Schopenhauer, The World as Will and Representation)

e.t: Name your desire precisely
e.x:
Desire is appetite together with the consciousness of appetite; it is conatus aware of itself. Because desire is the essence, an imprecise desire produces an imprecise life. Spinoza's practice, used across the whole Ethics, is to translate vague appetites into specific ones: not "I want to be happy" but "I want this person's regard, this security, this freedom." Naming does not grant the desire; it makes it workable.

(Ethics III, P9 scholium; Desire, definition 1 of the affects.)

**Plain words** Desire is appetite plus consciousness of appetite — conatus aware of itself. And an imprecise desire produces an imprecise life. Spinoza's practice: translate vague appetites into named ones. "I want more" is not a desire; it's a fog.

*For example:* Someone "wants a change" for two years — and finally translates: not a change; specifically, fewer meetings, more craft, one honest colleague. The vague version was unfundable; the named version was achievable in a month.
e.c: LAYER II - CONATUS: THE STRIVING ENGINE
p: **Goal specificity effects**, the reliable finding that concrete goals outperform abstract intentions (Gollwitzer, 1999, implementation intentions)
f: **Trishna as the structure of wanting** (Buddhist Second Noble Truth)

e.t: Understand love and hate as attached affects
e.x:
Love is joy accompanied by the idea of an external cause; hate is sadness with the idea of an external cause. This is deliberately deflationary: love is not a cosmic mystery but a joy that has been attributed to a person or thing, which is why objects of love and objects of resentment have such a grip. The grip is the attribution, and attributions can be examined. Practically, when an attachment is destroying you, do not attack the love; examine the attribution that this person is the sole cause of your power.

(Ethics III, P13 and P14, definitions of Love and Hate.)

**Plain words** Love is joy accompanied by the idea of an external cause; hate is sadness with the idea of an external cause. Deliberately deflationary: love is a joy attributed to a person or thing — which explains both the idealisation and the blame that follow.

*For example:* The new relationship where every good mood gets credited to the partner — love's bookkeeping — and the first bad month gets debited to them too. The Spinozist note isn't cynical; it's just accurate accounting: the joy was yours; the attribution was yours too.
e.c: LAYER II - CONATUS: THE STRIVING ENGINE
p: **Attachment theory**, the account of love bonds as systems of felt security and its regulation (Bowlby, Attachment and Loss)
f: **Eros as lack reaching toward wholeness** (Plato, Symposium, Diotima's ladder)
**Metta as unconditional friendliness** (Buddhist tradition, Metta Sutta)

e.t: Expect to imagine others as like yourself
e.x:
From the similarity of natures, Spinoza derives that we imagine others to be affected as we are: we picture their inner states by copying our own onto them. This is projection stated as physics, three centuries before the term. Its practical warning is double: your map of other people is mostly autobiography, and their map of you is mostly their autobiography. Practically, before acting on a strong reading of someone's motives, ask which of your own states you are copying onto them.

(Ethics III, P27.)

**Plain words** From the similarity of natures, we imagine others to be affected as we are — projection stated as physics, three centuries before the term. Expect the projection in yourself and in others: your picture of their inner state is a copy of your own, pasted on.

*For example:* The manager assumes everyone wants the promotion — because they do — and the quiet ones keep leaving. Their inner states were never surveyed; they were copied. The retention problem was a projection problem.
e.c: LAYER II - CONATUS: THE STRIVING ENGINE
p: **Egocentric projection in social inference**, the anchoring of other-mind estimates on one's own states (classic projection research, Holmes, 1968; modern anchoring accounts)
f: **Fellow feeling** (Hume, Treatise of Human Nature, Book III)
**Sympathy** (Adam Smith, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, opening)

e.t: Guard against affect contagion
e.x:
Affects spread by imitation: if we imagine a person affected with some affect, we come to be affected alike, which is why crowds can turn in a moment, why fear is more contagious than reason, and why one despondent member of a household can set its tone for a season. Spinoza treats this as mechanism, not as legend. Practically, treat the emotional weather of your closest people as an environmental factor you are exposed to, and adjust your exposure the way you would adjust exposure to weather.

(Ethics III, P27 with scholium and corollaries; IV, P33 on pity's spread.)

**Plain words** Affects spread by imitation: imagine a person affected with some affect and you come to be affected alike — crowds turn in a moment, fear is more contagious than reason, one despondent member can set a household's tone. Guard against contagion: know your exposure, choose your rooms.

*For example:* The group chat after the layoffs — panic propagating through five phones in an afternoon — and the one member who noticed the contagion and muted it for 24 hours. Not denial; quarantine. The fear was real; the spreading was optional.
e.c: LAYER II - CONATUS: THE STRIVING ENGINE
p: **Emotional contagion** (Hatfield, Cacioppo and Rapson, 1994); **social network contagion of behavior and mood** (Christakis and Fowler, 2007)
f: **The crowd is untruth** (Kierkegaard, The Crowd Is Untruth)
**Beware the moods of the many** (Laozi, Daodejing 20)

e.t: Watch the desires you copy
e.x:
Emulation, in the affect definitions, is desire for a thing that arises because we imagine other people desire the same thing. Spinoza's insight is that much of wanting is borrowed: the crowd's appetite for an object is part of the object's perceived value, which is why fashions, bubbles, and envy share a single root. Practically, before pursuing something, strip out the others-want-it component and check what remains; if nothing remains, you have located a copied desire.

(Ethics III, definition of Emulation.)

**Plain words** Emulation: desire for a thing that arises because we imagine others desire it. Much of wanting is borrowed — the crowd's appetite for an object is part of the object's perceived value. Watch the desires you copy; audit them for authorship.

*For example:* The wishlist assembled entirely from what others are seen wanting — the bag, the car, the coast — and the audit question that empties half of it: did I want this before I saw them with it? No author, no purchase.
e.c: LAYER II - CONATUS: THE STRIVING ENGINE
p: **Social proof and preference contagion**, the findings that perceived others' preferences shape valuation (Cialdini, 2001, as synthesis; Berger's contagion research as framework)
f: **We imitate what we admire in others** (La Rochefoucauld, Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims)

e.t: Treat hope and fear as one system
e.x:
Hope and fear are defined as a joy or sadness born of the image of a future thing whose outcome is uncertain; they are inseparable, since hope cannot be without fear nor fear without hope. The pair is the mind's response to uncertainty, and Spinoza's analysis is unsentimental: as uncertainty goes, the pair goes, and the person who lives by them lives on a see-saw. The remedy is not to cultivate more hope but to reduce the uncertainty that feeds both.

(Ethics III, definitions of Hope and Fear; IV, P47 and P48.)

**Plain words** Hope and fear are one system: joy or sadness born of the image of an uncertain future thing. Hope cannot be without fear, nor fear without hope — the pair is the mind's response to uncertainty. Treat them as one weather system, not two problems.

*For example:* The person oscillating all week between "it's going to be fine" and "it's going to be a disaster" — the same mechanism, alternating poles — and the Spinozist move that actually helps: shrinking the uncertainty with information, which quiets both poles at once.
e.c: LAYER II - CONATUS: THE STRIVING ENGINE
p: **Intolerance of uncertainty as a maintaining factor in anxiety**, with tolerance training as the clinical target (Dugas et al., 1998; uncertainty-tolerance research)
f: **Hope and fear as passions of the ignorant** (Epictetus, Discourses, on the passions)

e.t: Calibrate confidence against evidence
e.x:
The definitions pair hope with doubt and confidence with despair: each confident state rides on an uncertain outcome, and each collapses into its negative when the outcome shifts. Spinoza's point is not that confidence is bad but that it is a loan against an unknown; the overconfident and the despairing are the same person at different moments of the same bet. Practically, state your confidence as a probability with a reason, so that events can update it instead of destroying it.

(Ethics III, definitions of Confidence and Despair.)

**Plain words** Hope pairs with doubt, confidence with despair — each confident state rides an uncertain outcome and collapses into its negative when the outcome shifts. Confidence isn't bad; it's a claim about the world. Calibrate it against evidence, or the collapse is scheduled.

*For example:* The founder's "we're definitely raising this round" — 90% confidence on 40% evidence — and the despair that arrives on schedule with the rejection. The calibration wasn't pessimism; it would have been preparation.
e.c: LAYER II - CONATUS: THE STRIVING ENGINE
p: **Overconfidence and calibration**, the judgment literature's dissociation of confidence from accuracy (Moore and Healy, 2008, the two forms of overconfidence)
f: **Withhold assent from the insufficient** (Epictetus, Discourses, on assent)

e.t: Diagnose ambition and the hunger for esteem
e.x:
Ambition is an immoderate desire for the esteem of others, and Spinoza tracks it with clinical precision: it waxes with every sign of favor, wanes with every slight, and makes its owner hostage to the opinions of strangers. The principle is not that esteem is worthless; it is that esteem placed at the center of identity produces a life run by remote control. Practically, notice where your plans change shape when you imagine an audience, and run one important project entirely without one.

(Ethics III, P39 with scholium; definition of Ambition.)

**Plain words** Ambition: an immoderate desire for the esteem of others — it waxes with every favour, wanes with every slight, and makes its owner hostage to the opinions of strangers. Diagnose it clinically, in yourself first. The hunger is real; the food is unstable.

*For example:* The executive who checks the likes at traffic lights, whose week is set by one comment thread — Spinoza's three-century-old description, running in their pocket. The diagnosis isn't shame; it's the first line of the treatment: whose opinions are holding the keys?
e.c: LAYER II - CONATUS: THE STRIVING ENGINE
p: **Contingent self-worth**, the finding that self-esteem staked on others' approval is unstable and costly (Crocker, 2002, contingencies of self-worth research)
f: **Escape from freedom and the approval trap** (Fromm, Escape from Freedom)
**The vainglorious man** (Moliere, The Misanthrope, as literary parallel)

e.t: Convert pity into compassion and equity
e.x:
Pity is sorrow at another's harm, and Spinoza's verdict is severe but double-edged: pity is more often harmful than useful, because it adds one sad person to the world instead of helping, yet he concedes that for those not yet guided by reason, it is better than indifference. The rational person does good not from pity but from equity, from the settled determination to act justly. The practical distinction survives translation: feeling someone's pain and being moved by it are different skills, and only the second feeds anyone.

(Ethics III, P22 and P27 scholium; IV, P50.)

**Plain words** Pity is sorrow at another's harm — and Spinoza's verdict is severe: pity adds one sad person to the world instead of helping. Yet he concedes it's a stage worth having if reason hasn't arrived. The conversion: from feeling sad about them to doing something useful for them — compassion and equity.

*For example:* The friend who responds to the job loss with tears and head-shaking — pity, adding sadness to sadness — versus the one who edits the résumé and makes three calls. Same information; only one of them helped.
e.c: LAYER II - CONATUS: THE STRIVING ENGINE
p: **Empathic distress versus compassion**, the imaging finding that suffering-with and caring-for are distinct states, with different burnout profiles (Klimecki et al., 2013)
f: **Pity as inequality's emotion** (Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil, on Mitleid)

e.t: Take envy seriously as hatred
e.x:
Envy is hatred insofar as it disposes a person to be pained by another's good fortune and to rejoice in another's ill fortune. Spinoza's contribution is to strip the romanticism from it: envy is not a shade of longing but straight hatred with a specific trigger, and it is fed by comparison. Practically, when someone else's success disturbs you, treat that as diagnostic data about where you have placed your worth, and audit the comparison rather than feeding the story.

(Ethics III, the definition of Envy; P24 and its scholium.)

**Plain words** Envy is hatred: being pained by another's good fortune, rejoicing in their ill fortune. Spinoza strips the romance — envy is not a shade of longing but straight hatred with a specific target. Taking it seriously is the beginning of treating it.

*For example:* The "benign envy" that's rebranded every year as motivation — and the test that catches it: did their failure just taste a little good? That taste is the diagnosis. The tradition treats it as hatred, which is why the affirmations never worked.
e.c: LAYER II - CONATUS: THE STRIVING ENGINE
p: **Envy as upward-comparison distress**, the social-comparison account of when others' goods hurt (R. H. Smith, 2000, Handbook of Social Comparison)
f: **Irshya as the poison of comparison** (Buddhist afflictions list)

e.t: Practice gratitude as repayment of love
e.x:
Gratitude, in Spinoza's table, is the desire to do good to one who has done us good from love. It is an active affect, a form of strength, not a social nicety, and it is trained by noticing what has actually been given. Spinoza's reason is structural: the grateful person lives inside a web of acknowledged favors, which is both an accurate picture of reality (no one is self-made) and a position of power.

(Ethics III, the definitions of Gratitude and Anger; the gratitude-vengeance pair.)

**Plain words** Gratitude is the desire to do good to one who has done us good from love — an active affect, a form of strength, not a nicety. Trained by noticing what has actually been given. The repayment of love keeps love in circulation.

*For example:* The person who keeps an actual ledger of what's been done for them — the mentor's hours, the friend's quiet rescue — and repays in kind, forward. The gratitude isn't polite; it's the mechanism by which the good stuff compounds.
e.c: LAYER II - CONATUS: THE STRIVING ENGINE
p: **Gratitude interventions**, modest but reliable effects on well-being (Wood et al., 2010)
f: **Gratitude as a virtue of the great** (Seneca, De Beneficiis)

e.t: Separate self-esteem from vanity and self-abasement
e.x:
Self-esteem is joy born of one's own power of acting; its two counterfeits are pride, thinking more of oneself than is true, and humility, thinking less. Both are errors of measurement, and both are passive: the vain and the self-abasing are equally run by imagined audiences. Genuine self-esteem, by contrast, is the felt sense of capacity, and it is built only by acting and observing the results. Practically, build one real competence per season and let the esteem follow the evidence.

(Ethics III, P26, P28, P29; definitions of Pride and Humility.)

**Plain words** Self-esteem is joy born of one's own power of acting. Its counterfeits: pride (thinking more of oneself than is true) and humility (thinking less) — both errors of measurement, both passive. The vain and the self-abasing are equally run from outside; only the measured self is free.

*For example:* The braggart and the self-deprecator turn out to be the same machine — both rating themselves by imagined audiences — while the third colleague just states what they can and can't do. Only one of the three is talking about a self they actually measured.
e.c: LAYER II - CONATUS: THE STRIVING ENGINE
p: **Contingent versus true self-esteem**, and competence-based self-efficacy (Crocker, 2002; Bandura, 1997)
f: **Pride as ignorance, humility as its mirror error** (Buddhist mana, the affliction of comparing)
**The middle between arrogance and self-contempt** (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV, on megalopsychia)

e.t: Expect fluctuation, and read it as structure
e.x:
Spinoza names a specific misfortune of the passionate life: animi fluctuatio, the fluctuation of the soul, being drawn now by this affect, now by its opposite, like a boat on choppy water. Ambition pulls one way, fear another, love another. The condition is not a character flaw but the predictable result of multiple partial causes without a coordinating one. Practically, when you notice inner weather swinging, do not treat each swing as the truth; treat the swing itself as the datum, and look for the competing strivings underneath.

(Ethics III, P17 scholium, the fluctuatio analysis.)

**Plain words** Animi fluctuatio: the fluctuation of the soul — drawn now by this affect, now by its opposite, like a boat on choppy water. Ambition pulls one way, fear another, love a third. Expect the fluctuation and read it as structure: multiple forces, unresolved, all pulling.

*For example:* The person who wants the promotion AND dreads it, wants the relationship AND wants out — not confusion, chop. The Spinozist move isn't to pick a side but to map the forces: name each pull, and the water starts to show which one is deepest.
e.c: LAYER II - CONATUS: THE STRIVING ENGINE
p: **Rumination and goal conflict as amplifiers of mood swing**, the finding that unresolved strivings maintain oscillation (Emmons and King, 1988; Nolen-Hoeksema, 1991)
f: **The double-minded man, unstable in all his ways** (Epistle of James 1.8)
**The mind as tortoise or as wind** (BG 6.34)

e.t: Treat greed, luxury, and drunkenness as species of madness
e.x:
In the scholium to IV P44, Spinoza says that greed, ambition, and lust for luxury are species of madness: fixed, self-reinforcing appetites that have outgrown their function and now consume the person. The analysis is important because it is mechanical, not moralistic; the miser is not evil, he is captured, and the capture is visible in his narrowing. Practically, watch for the appetite that has stopped responding to satisfaction: that is the signature of the transition from appetite to possession.

(Ethics IV, P44 scholium; Letter 19 and the drunkard of Letter 58, treated below.)

**Plain words** Greed, ambition, and lust for luxury are species of madness: fixed, self-reinforcing appetites that have outgrown their function and now consume the person. The analysis is clinical, not moral — addiction three centuries before the term, in a scholium.

*For example:* The shopping behaviour that started as comfort and became the comfort — the mechanism serving itself. Spinoza's frame removes the moral theatre and replaces it with the clinical question: what is this appetite now for? Its original job ended years ago.
e.c: LAYER II - CONATUS: THE STRIVING ENGINE
p: **Delay discounting and the narrowing of reward systems**, the behavioral-economics account of compulsive pursuit (Bickel et al., 2014)
f: **The Rich Fool** (Gospel of Luke 12.16-21, as cultural parallel)
**The jar of the Danaids** (Greek myth, as literary parallel)

e.t: Study the drunkard, and keep your seat
e.x:
In the letter to G. H. Schuller, Spinoza gives his compact statement of the human predicament: people are conscious of their desires and ignorant of the causes that determine them; the drunkard, in the scholium's example, believes his speech is free while the wine is doing the talking. Knowledge of what is good, at the moment of appetite, is a weak force by itself. The practical use is the moral of the remedies, stated in advance: do not rely on insight alone at the moment of temptation; rely on arrangement, on the environment and the stronger affect prepared in advance.

(Correspondence, Letter 58 to Schuller; Ethics III, P2 scholium, the drunkard passage.)

**Plain words** The Schuller letter: people are conscious of their desires and ignorant of the causes that determine them. The drunkard believes his speech is free and graceful — everyone at the table has other data. Study the drunkard, and keep your seat: consciousness is not self-knowledge.

*For example:* The person absolutely certain they're arguing from principle — and everyone in the room can see the hunger or the fatigue driving it. The drunkard's speech always sounds fine from inside the drunkard. That's the whole point of getting data from outside.
e.c: LAYER II - CONATUS: THE STRIVING ENGINE
p: **The intention-behavior gap**, the robust finding that insight and intention are weak predictors of in-the-moment behavior (Sheeran, 2002; Gollwitzer, 1999, on planning as the bridge)
f: **The spirit is willing, the flesh is weak** (Gospel of Matthew 26.41)
**Knowing and doing as one** (Wang Yangming, Chuanxilu)

e.t: Drop the illusion of free will
e.x:
Men believe themselves free, Spinoza writes, because they are conscious of their volitions and ignorant of the causes that determine them. The belief in a free, uncaused will is not a harmless vanity; it is the foundation of the revenge system, of the belief that people deserve suffering for what they did. Spinoza's determinism is the deepest compassion machine in his system: understanding causation replaces the entire apparatus of blame with the entire apparatus of remedy. Practically, keep both halves: responsibility as a working concept for conduct, causation as the true account for understanding.

(Ethics II, P35 scholium; III, P2 scholium.)

**Plain words** Men believe themselves free because they're conscious of their volitions and ignorant of the causes that determine them. The free-will belief isn't harmless: it's the foundation of the revenge system — punishing people as if they were uncaused causes. Drop the illusion; keep the responsibility.

*For example:* The parent who rages at the "choice" of the addicted child as if it were made freely in a vacuum — and the treatment centre's framing: determined appetite, treatable causes. The rage was always a metaphysical error wearing a moral costume.
e.c: LAYER II - CONATUS: THE STRIVING ENGINE
p: **Unconscious determination of choice**, the experimental literature on post-hoc rationalization of action (Wegner, 2002, The Illusion of Conscious Will; Bargh's automaticity research)
f: **No doer behind the deed** (Buddhist anatman analysis)
**The eternal recurrence as a determinism test** (Nietzsche, The Gay Science 341)

e.t: See decisions as victories of the strongest appetite
e.x:
Spinoza's analysis of deliberation: when a person says they decided, what happened is that one appetite outmuscled the others, and the mind then narrates the outcome as a free choice. This does not abolish planning; it relocates it. If decisions are won by the strongest appetite, then the work is done before the decision point, in training which appetites are strong. Practically, when you must decide in a weakened state, postpone the decision to a rested one; the strongest appetite changes with rest.

(Ethics III, P2 scholium; II, P48-49.)

**Plain words** Deliberation, Spinoza-style: when you say "I decided," what happened is one appetite outmuscled the others, and the mind narrates the outcome as free choice. This doesn't abolish planning — it relocates the work: arrange the appetites, and the "decision" follows.

*For example:* The person who "decides" to start exercising on Monday — while the appetites (comfort, shame-avoidance, habit) vote otherwise — and the Spinozist move: don't argue with the vote, change the electorate. Gym bag by the door. Early night. The "decision" then makes itself.
e.c: LAYER II - CONATUS: THE STRIVING ENGINE
p: **Ego depletion and state-dependent choice**, with the honest caveat that the resource model is contested while the state-dependence of choice is not (Hagger et al., 2016, the registered replication debate, cited as contested)
f: **The will is not a separate faculty** (Hume, Treatise, on the will as direct impression)
**Right effort before the choice** (Buddhist eightfold path, right effort)

e.t: Understand bondage as being determined from outside
e.x:
A person is in bondage when they are determined by external causes rather than by their own nature: tossed by forces they did not arrange, pleased and pained by objects they did not choose. Spinoza's image is brutal and exact: the ignorant person is not only driven by external causes, like a wave of the sea, never conscious of themselves, of God, or of things, and scarcely aware of their own pleasures. The principle names the enemy precisely, which is half of defeating it: freedom is not the absence of causes but the internalization of them.

(Ethics IV, Preface; IV, P47 scholium; V, P42 scholium, the wave's restatement.)

**Plain words** Bondage: being determined by external causes rather than your own nature — tossed by forces you didn't arrange, pleased and pained by objects you didn't choose. The image is brutal and exact. Freedom, by contrast, is being determined by what you are.

*For example:* The person whose mood is set by the market, the reviews, the weather, the algorithm — pleased and pained by objects they never chose. The first question of the unbound life isn't "what do I want?" but "who's been choosing my inputs?"
e.c: LAYER III - BONDAGE: THE MECHANICS OF PASSION
p: **External locus of control and learned helplessness**, the classic findings linking perceived external determination to depression (Seligman, 1975, Helplessness; Rotter, 1966)
f: **The sleepwalker** (Zhuangzi, Inner Chapters, the butterfly as emblem)

e.t: Learn how hatred self-perpetuates
e.x:
Hatred is increased by returned hatred, and destroyed by love, so that hatred is returned for hatred, and the cycle Spinoza describes is the exact blueprint of every feud: each injury justifies the counter-injury, which becomes the next injury's justification. His prescription is counterintuitive and structural: meet hatred with kindness, not as a moral ornament but as the only intervention that removes the fuel. Practically, in one running conflict, run the experiment Spinoza prescribes: answer coldness with one act of genuine benefit, and watch the system rather than the moment.

(Ethics III, P43; the note to IV, P73: hatred overcome with love.)

**Plain words** Hatred is increased by returned hatred and destroyed by love: the cycle is the blueprint of every feud — each injury justifies the counter-injury, which becomes the next injury's justification. Spinoza states the engineering plainly: you cannot hate your way out of a hatred cycle. Someone has to stop returning it.

*For example:* The family feud in its fortieth year — every funeral re-litigating 1984 — and the one member who stops returning the hatred, not from weakness but from having read the schematic. The cycle doesn't end with the last hater; it ends with the first non-returner.
e.c: LAYER III - BONDAGE: THE MECHANICS OF PASSION
p: **Forgiveness interventions and reciprocity dynamics**, the evidence that unilateral prosocial moves reliably shift hostile spirals (Worthington, 2001, Five Steps to Forgiveness; Dunbar's gossip-cooperation findings as background)
f: **Repay injury with uprightness, kindness with kindness** (Confucius, Analects 14.34, where Confucius corrects the very proposal to repay injury with kindness)

e.t: Read anger as blocked striving with a wounded self-regard
e.x:
In the affect definitions, anger is the desire to repay one who has injured us or someone we love, and its closest allies are emulation and wounded esteem. Anger is not primary energy; it is a secondary emotion over a frustrated conatus with an audience of the self. Spinoza's counsel is not suppression (the remedies explain why that fails) but decomposition: name the blocked striving under the anger, and the anger loses its single-mindedness.

(Ethics III, definitions of Anger and Revenge; P39 scholium on esteem.)

**Plain words** Anger is the desire to repay one who has injured us — a secondary emotion over a frustrated striving, with wounded self-regard as its closest ally. Not primary energy: it's the symptom. Read the anger as blocked striving, and the treatment aims upstream.

*For example:* The employee's fury at the colleague's promotion — surface: repayment-desire; underneath: their own striving, blocked and unacknowledged. The anger dissolves not when it's punished but when the striving gets a channel.
e.c: LAYER III - BONDAGE: THE MECHANICS OF PASSION
p: **Frustration-aggression and blocked-goal accounts of anger**, the reformulated model in which anger tracks goal obstruction (Berkowitz's reformulation; Novaco's anger treatment research)

e.t: Treat indignation carefully
e.x:
Indignation is hatred toward one who has done evil to another. Spinoza is careful with it because it feels like virtue: the moral circuits of the person run on it. But as hatred, it is bondage with a clear conscience, and it can be enjoyed indefinitely. The test Spinoza supplies is the test of the active affects: does the indignation increase your power of acting, or does it merely feed on itself while the situation continues? Practically, convert indignation into its useful component, which is the decision to act, and set the rest down.

(Ethics III, definition of Indignation; the pity-anger family.)

**Plain words** Indignation is hatred toward one who has done evil to another — and Spinoza is careful with it because it feels like virtue. The moral circuits run on it. But as hatred, it's bondage with a clear conscience, and it can be enjoyed indefinitely. Treat indignation carefully: verify, then act — don't marinate.

*For example:* The person who "stands for justice" in the comment thread every evening — the indignation masquerading as ethics — versus the one who verifies, files the complaint, donates, and closes the laptop. Both indignant; only one of them free.
e.c: LAYER III - BONDAGE: THE MECHANICS OF PASSION
p: **Moral outrage and its self-rewarding loop**, research on outrage as reinforcing and divisive (Crockett's moral outrage studies, 2013-2017, cited as emerging)
f: **Righteous anger as the subtlest passion** (Evagrius Ponticus, Praktikos, on anger)
**The fury of the virtuous** (Nietzsche, Genealogy of Morals, Essay 1, the critique of ressentiment)

e.t: Let repentance go
e.x:
Spinoza's most modern page: repentance is not a virtue but a doubling of the problem. The repentant person is sorry, and then sorry for having been sorry, and the pain is consumed twice while nothing changes in the machinery. The free person, he says, avoids repentance not by never erring but by integrating the error once, as information, and moving on. Practically, when you catch the loop of self-recrimination, ask what single lesson the event contains, extract it in one sentence, and stop paying interest on the same mistake.

(Ethics IV, P54; the analysis of repentance as doubled sorrow.)

**Plain words** Repentance, Spinoza's most modern page: not a virtue but a doubling of the problem — sorry, and then sorry for being sorry, the pain consumed twice while nothing changes in the machinery. The free person avoids repentance — not by being shameless, but by correcting and moving.

*For example:* The person who spent the year after the failed business apologising to everyone — and the Spinozist correction: the machinery needs one thing (the post-mortem, the repayment plan) and got another (twice-consumed pain). The apology tour was the second consumption.
e.c: LAYER III - BONDAGE: THE MECHANICS OF PASSION
p: **Shame versus guilt**, the robust distinction that shame (global self-condemnation) predicts avoidance and relapse while guilt (specific behavior) predicts repair (Tangney and Dearing, 2002)
f: **Amor fati as the end of repentance** (Nietzsche, Ecce Homo)
**Let the dead bury the dead** (Gospel of Luke 9.60)

e.t: Distinguish shame from guilt's signal
e.x:
Shame is sorrow accompanied by the idea of another's contempt; it is a social affect, an audience emotion, and its object is the whole self rather than the act. Spinoza's framework makes the practical distinction automatic: shame that reformulates as specific, actionable guilt is useful, because it names a repairable act; shame that remains global is just suffering with spectators. Practically, when shame arrives, translate it once into the specific act and the specific repair, and set the global verdict down.

(Ethics III, definition of Shame.)

**Plain words** Shame is sorrow accompanied by the idea of another's contempt — a social affect, an audience emotion, and its object is the whole self rather than the act. The practical distinction: shame that reinforces the act's correction can be useful; shame that just wounds the self is the trap.

*For example:* The kid caught lying feels the flash — audience emotion, whole-self — and the parent's task is the Spinozist split: the act needs correcting, the self doesn't need destroying. "The lie was wrong" versus "you're a liar." One of those sentences does the work.
e.c: LAYER III - BONDAGE: THE MECHANICS OF PASSION
p: **Shame versus guilt**, the robust distinction in which guilt predicts repair and shame predicts avoidance and relapse (Tangney and Dearing, 2002)
f: **The self is not the deed** (Buddhist analysis of identification)

e.t: Do not build on humility
e.x:
