**Body-based practices as adjuncts**, breathing, exercise, and relaxation are complements, not substitutes, for treatment (Schuch et al., 2018; Hofmann et al., 2010)
f: **The raft, not the destination** (Buddhism, Alagaddupama Sutta)
r: If you have a clinical condition, seek professional treatment. Use body-based practices as complements (supports), not substitutes. Do not self-treat severe conditions with lifestyle alone.

e.t: Learn to assess and monitor biophysiological health: regular check-ups
e.x:
Biophysiological health can be monitored: sleep, energy, HRV, medical markers (thyroid, iron, vitamin D). Regular assessment provides early detection and feedback.

**Plain words** Keep up routine check-ups, and mention mood and energy when you go — mental health problems sometimes have physical contributors, and a clinician is the right person to decide what to test.

*For example:* The therapist who asks "when was your last blood test?" — a question that sometimes finds a physical cause hiding behind a mood. The lab is part of the mental health team.
e.c: LAYER VII — SPECIFIC BIOPHYSIOLOGICAL CHALLENGES & BOUNDARY CONDITIONS
p: **Physiological monitoring**, tracking sleep, energy, and HRV provides feedback (Thayer et al., 2012; Laborde et al., 2017)
**Medical check-ups**, regular medical evaluation detects treatable conditions (Stover & Stover, 2011)
r: Monitor biophysiological health: track sleep and energy, keep up routine medical check-ups, and mention mood and energy when you go — let the clinician decide what to test.

e.t: Build biophysiological maintenance: ongoing care and adaptation
e.x:
Biophysiological health is not a one-time achievement; it requires ongoing maintenance, adaptation to changing circumstances (ageing, illness, life changes), and retention of what works.

**Plain words** The body is a lifelong maintenance project, not a one-time fix — ageing, illness, and life changes keep rewriting the manual. What worked at thirty needs adjusting at fifty. The maintenance IS the achievement; there's no "done."

*For example:* The runner who becomes a swimmer who becomes a walker — same body, three eras, each with its own servicing schedule. The adaptation is the health; the routine is just the current version of it.
e.c: LAYER VII — SPECIFIC BIOPHYSIOLOGICAL CHALLENGES & BOUNDARY CONDITIONS
p: **Biophysiological maintenance**, sleep, exercise, nutrition, and stress management require ongoing practice (McEwen, 2007; Sapolsky, 2004)
**Adaptation across the lifespan**, physiological needs change with age and circumstance (Lövdén et al., 2010; Stern, 2002)
f: **The examined life as ongoing practice** (Socrates, Apology 38a)
r: Build biophysiological maintenance: regular sleep, exercise, nutrition, stress management, and medical check-ups. Adapt as circumstances change. Retain what works; adjust what does not.

e.t: Flourish socially
e.x:
Adaptive flourishing is not an individual achievement. The EEMM's sociocultural level is not an optional layer on top of the individual; it is constitutive. The person is, in Aristotle's phrase, a political animal (Aristotle, NE I.7, 1097b11; Political 1253a2–18). Flourishing — in ancient Greek eudaimonia, in modern subjective and psychological well-being — is achieved within a life-world of relationships, institutions, and cultural meanings. Everything else in the sociocultural domain builds on the recognition that adaptation happens in context.

**Plain words** Nobody flourishes alone — the hermit's hut is built by a village. Your relationships, institutions, and culture aren't decoration on your flourishing; they're the material it's made of. Feed the social fabric and it feeds you back.

*For example:* The person who "doesn't need anyone" and has their worst year exactly when the friendships were let lapse — the body kept score of the isolation even when the philosophy said otherwise.
e.c: LAYER I — FIRST PRINCIPLES: THE SOCIAL NATURE OF THE PERSON
p: Social relationships are among the strongest correlates of well-being, health, and mortality (Holt-Lunstad et al., 2010, 2017; House et al., 1988). The effect is not a mere association: loneliness predicts cardiovascular, metabolic, and immune outcomes through identifiable mechanisms (Holt-Lunstad et al., 2017; Hawkley and Cacioppo, 2010; Cacioppo et al., 2011). Sociality is a primary evolutionary adaptation of the human species (Caporael, 1997; Brewer and Caporael, 2006; Tomasello, 2014).
f: Aristotle — Thinker: Aristotle — Reference: Nicomachean Ethics, I.7, 1097b11. Ubuntu — "A person is a person through other persons" — Thinker: Tutu — Reference: Tutu (1999). Mauss — gift exchange as the social form of flourishing — Thinker: Mauss — Reference: Mauss (1954).
**Other:**, This Book's principle 1 is the sociocultural counterpart. **EEMM link:** This is the sociocultural level's foundational principle — the context in which all six dimensions are enacted.
r: See principle 23 for the practical steps.

e.t: Treat the person as embedded in nested systems
e.x:
Treat the person as embedded in a set of nested systems — microsystems (family, peers), mesosystems (school, workplace), exosystems (community institutions), and macrosystems (culture, policy, economy) — in Urie Bronfenbrenner's ecological model. A change in one system propagates to the others; adaptation at the individual level is inseparable from adaptation at the family, community, and institutional levels.

**Plain words** You live inside nested circles — family, workplace, community, culture, economy — and a shift in any one ripples through all the others. You can't always control the circles, but you can know which one a problem actually lives in. Diagnose the ring before treating yourself.

*For example:* The kid who "can't focus at school" whose real problem is a housing ring, not a brain ring — the fix was the apartment, not the tutoring. Wrong ring, wrong fix.
e.c: LAYER I — FIRST PRINCIPLES: THE SOCIAL NATURE OF THE PERSON
p: Bronfenbrenner (1979, 2005); the process-person-context-time (PPCT) model (Bronfenbrenner and Morris, 2006); developmental evidence that outcomes emerge from person-environment interactions over time (Lerner, 2006; Sameroff, 2010); social-epidemiological evidence on neighborhood effects on health (Diez Roux and Mair, 2010).
f: Bronfenbrenner — Thinker: Bronfenbrenner — Reference: Bronfenbrenner (1979). See also Whitehead — organic society — Thinker: Whitehead — Reference: Whitehead (1933), Part IV, Ch. II.

**Other:**, The "ecological" framing of flourishing recurs in modern public-health and community psychology (Bronfenbrenner, 2005; Biglan et al., 2012). **EEMM link:** The nested-systems principle maps directly onto the EEMM's nested levels (biophysiological within sociocultural).
r: See principle 56 for institutional design. In clinical practice, see principle 72 on systems-based intervention.

e.t: Use the self-culture link, not a fixed self
e.x:
Treat the self not as a fixed essence but as a cultural form. Hazel Markus and Shinobu Kitayama (1991) distinguished the independent self, dominant in European-American contexts, from the interdependent self, dominant in East Asian, Latin American, African, and many Indigenous contexts. Neither is the self per se; each is a cultural achievement, and each carries its own forms of flourishing and suffering. Treat your own self-construal as a variable, not a constant.

**Plain words** The self is a cultural shape, not a fixed crystal — some cultures build independent selves, others interdependent ones. Yours isn't the default; it's one of the builds. Knowing this makes your own reactions negotiable instead of obvious.

*For example:* The meeting where one person says "I just think..." and another says "We've been thinking..." — both are just selves, built by different cultures. Neither is lying about what a self is.
e.c: LAYER I — FIRST PRINCIPLES: THE SOCIAL NATURE OF THE PERSON
p: Markus and Kitayama (1991); Heine et al. (1999); Kitayama et al. (2007); Boucher (2011); Grossmann et al. (2012) on dialectical vs. analytic reasoning; Kağitçibaşi (2005) on the autonomous-related self.
f: Stuart Hall — cultural identity as ongoing construction — Thinker: Stuart Hall — Reference: Hall (1990). Du Bois — double consciousness — Thinker: Du Bois — Reference: Du Bois (1903).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** The self-dimension of the EEMM is enacted at the sociocultural level here — the self is a cultural construction, not a given.
r: In reflection, ask which aspects of your "personality" are cultural rather than essential. In intercultural contact, resist the assumption that your self-form is the default.

e.t: Treat culture as both a resource and a constraint
e.x:
Culture is not a neutral backdrop. It supplies meaning, identity, belonging, and practices that make flourishing possible — and it imposes norms, expectations, and exclusions that make flourishing harder for those who do not fit. The adaptive stance is not to romanticize or demonize culture but to see it as both: a toolkit of meaning and a field of constraint. This dual view parallels the biophysiological reading of stress as a signal, not only a threat.

**Plain words** Culture is both a gift and a tax — it hands you meaning, belonging, and practices, and it charges you norms, expectations, and exclusions. Neither romanticising nor trashing it; the move is knowing which parts serve you and which parts are billing you.

*For example:* The tradition that gave you your whole social world and also gave you the belief that rest is laziness — you can keep the table and question the guilt. That's the skill.
e.c: LAYER I — FIRST PRINCIPLES: THE SOCIAL NATURE OF THE PERSON
p: Schwartz (1990, 1994) on cultural value dimensions (autonomy, embeddedness, hierarchy, mastery, harmony); Triandis (1989) on individualism-collectivism; Hofstede (1980) on cultural distance; the dual role of culture in health outcomes (Kirmayer, 2012).
f: Gadamer — the fusion of horizons — Thinker: Gadamer — Reference: Gadamer (1960), Part II. Herder — cultural pluralism — Thinker: Herder — Reference: Herder (1774).

**Other:**, The dual view is the standard stance of critical cross-cultural psychology (Kirmayer, 2012). **EEMM link:** Culture is the context that selects among behavioral variants in the EEMM's variation-selection-retention cycle.
r: In cultural self-examination, identify which norms serve your flourishing and which constrain it (see principle 15). In intercultural work, treat cultural mismatch as a signal, not a personal failure.

e.t: Use cultural fluency as a skill, not a trait
e.x:
Treat cultural fluency — the ability to read, navigate, and switch among cultural codes — as a learnable skill, not a fixed endowment. This is particularly important for migrants, bicultural people, and anyone operating across cultural boundaries.

**Plain words** Cultural fluency is a skill, not a blood type — reading, navigating, switching between cultural codes. Migrants and bicultural people do it daily; anyone can learn. It's not betrayal of your culture; it's multilingualism with behaviour.

*For example:* The employee who code-switches between the direct style of the head office and the indirect style of the family business — not two-faced, just bilingual. Fluent in both rooms.
e.c: LAYER I — FIRST PRINCIPLES: THE SOCIAL NATURE OF THE PERSON
p: Bicultural identity integration (Benet-Martínez and Haritatos, 2005; Huynh et al., 2011); cultural frame-switching (Hong et al., 2000); cultural intelligence (Earley and Ang, 2003); the role of cultural fluency in migrant adaptation (Ward et al., 2001).
f: Confucius — the junzi as culturally fluent — Thinker: Confucius — Reference: Analects. Mauss — techniques of the body across cultures — Thinker: Mauss — Reference: Mauss (1934).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Cultural fluency is the attentional and cognitive skill of reading the sociocultural context.
r: See principle 73 for acculturation strategies and principle 74 for biculturalism.

e.t: Treat the social environment as a designable context
e.x:
Treat not just the immediate social environment but the broader sociocultural context — neighborhoods, institutions, policies, norms — as designable. This is the founding principle of social prevention: environments that nurture flourishing can be built, and environments that generate suffering can be modified. Adaptive flourishing is not only a personal practice but a collective project.

**Plain words** The social environment isn't weather — it's architecture. Neighbourhoods, institutions, policies, norms: designed things, which means they can be redesigned. Environments that make people sick were built; environments that make people well can be.

*For example:* The intersection redesigned so nobody jaywalks anymore — nobody got more disciplined. The environment changed and the behaviour followed. Same physics works for schools and offices.
e.c: LAYER I — FIRST PRINCIPLES: THE SOCIAL NATURE OF THE PERSON
p: Biglan et al. (2012) on nurturing environments; Institute of Medicine (2009) on preventing mental, emotional, and behavioral disorders; Wahlbeck et al. (2015) on population-level prevention; WHO (2022) World Mental Health Report; community-intervention evidence (Wandersman and Florin, 2003).
f: Dewey — democracy as a way of life — Thinker: Dewey — Reference: Dewey (1916). Whitehead — the social function of education — Thinker: Whitehead — Reference: Whitehead (1929).

**Other:**, The design principle is the bridge between these principles and public-health prevention science (Biglan et al., 2012). **EEMM link:** The EEMM's context dimension is not a fixed backdrop but a designable parameter.
r: See principle 56 (institutional design) and principle 75 (systems-level intervention).

e.t: Treat social change as a normal condition, not a crisis
e.x:
Treat rapid social change — migration, technological change, economic disruption, cultural pluralization — as a normal condition of modern life, not an aberration to be resisted. The adaptive stance is not to idealize a static past but to build the capacity to flourish amid change.

**Plain words** Social change is a constant, not an emergency — migration, technology, upheaval are the normal weather of modern life. Longing for a static past is nostalgia, not strategy. The skill is adaptation capacity, not time-freezing.

*For example:* The industry that "waited for things to go back to normal" — normal had left, permanently, and was never coming back. The ones who adapted had the same information. Different relationship to change.
e.c: LAYER I — FIRST PRINCIPLES: THE SOCIAL NATURE OF THE PERSON
p: The literature on acculturation and migration (Berry, 1997; Sam and Berry, 2010); on rapid social change and mental health (Kirmayer and Minas, 2009); on the "cultural mismatch" between WEIRD samples and the rest of the world (Henrich et al., 2010; Medin et al., 2017); on generational value change (Inglehart and Welzel, 2005).
f: Whitehead — the social function of education in a changing world — Thinker: Whitehead — Reference: Whitehead (1929). Dewey — reconstruction in philosophy — Thinker: Dewey — Reference: Dewey (1920).

**Other:**, The "change as normal" stance is the sociocultural version of the principle (treat motivation as evolving). **EEMM link:** The EEMM's context dimension includes temporal change, not just spatial context.
r: See principle 73 for acculturation strategies and principle 76 for digital and technological change.

e.t: Treat the sociocultural level as nested within the biophysiological
e.x:
Treat the sociocultural level as the context in which the biophysiological level operates. The biophysiological level (sleep, nutrition, stress, exercise, interoception) is enacted in a social world — a family that eats together or alone, a workplace that permits or forbids sleep, a neighborhood that is safe or dangerous for exercise. The two levels are nested, and interventions at one level propagate to the other.

**Plain words** Your biology runs on social rails — sleep, food, stress, movement all happen in a social world. The family that eats together or alone, the job that permits rest or doesn't: your body's habits have social landlords. Fix the lease where you can.

*For example:* The insomniac who fixes their sleep by fixing their evening — the household quiet hours were the treatment. The melatonin was fighting the architecture.
e.c: LAYER I — FIRST PRINCIPLES: THE SOCIAL NATURE OF THE PERSON
p: The social gradient of health (Marmot, 2004; Marmot and Wilkinson, 2006) — health outcomes track social position; the social patterning of stress physiology (McEwen, 1998); the embodiment of social experience (Krieger, 2005); the social determinants of mental health (WHO, 2010).
f: Whitehead — the organism-environment unity — Thinker: Whitehead — Reference: Whitehead (1933), Part IV, Ch. I.
**Other:**, The nesting is the EEMM's own structure (Hayes). **EEMM link:** The two levels of the EEMM are biophysiological and sociocultural; the nesting runs both ways.
r: In public-health practice, see principle 75 (systems-level intervention). In individual practice, treat your social environment as part of your body's environment.

e.t: Treat the sociocultural level as measurable
e.x:
Treat the sociocultural level as measurable, in the same way the biophysiological level is. Cultures, communities, and institutions can be characterized — by value surveys (Schwartz, 1994; Hofstede, 1980; Inglehart-Welzel, 2005), by cultural-consonance measures (Dressler and Bindon, 2000), by social-network analysis (Wasserman and Faust, 1994), by well-being measures (OECD, 2013; Diener, 2000; Clark et al., 2018), and by epidemiological surveillance of social determinants (Marmot and Wilkinson, 2006). Measurement makes design possible; design makes improvement possible.

**Plain words** Culture can be measured — values surveys, cultural-consonance studies, community indicators. "You can't quantify culture" is folklore; the tools exist and are used. What gets measured gets designed. Measure your communities before you redesign them.

*For example:* The community programme that assumed what the neighbourhood needed versus the one that surveyed it first — the survey version found out the priority was the bus route, not the workshops. Data beat the guess.
e.c: LAYER I — FIRST PRINCIPLES: THE SOCIAL NATURE OF THE PERSON
p: OECD (2013) Guidelines on Measuring Subjective Well-being; Diener (2000) on subjective well-being; Clark et al. (2018) on the economics of well-being; Foundations (2017) and Holmes (2022) on the International Wellbeing Group's framework; national well-being accounts (Veenhoven, 2010).
f: Aristotle — phronesis as the practical wisdom of policy — Thinker: Aristotle — Reference: Nicomachean Ethics, VI.

**Other:**, The measurement principle is the sociocultural counterpart of the biophysiological one. **EEMM link:** Measurement enables the EEMM's variation-selection-retention cycle at the sociocultural level.
r: In policy practice, use well-being measures alongside economic measures (see principle 65). In community practice, use social-network and cultural-consonance measures to characterize the local context.

e.t: Treat the sociocultural level as interventionable
e.x:
Treat the sociocultural level as interventionable, in the same sense. Community interventions (Wandersman and Florin, 2003), policy interventions (Biglan et al., 2012), cultural interventions (Gone, 2011; Mutamba et al., 2021), and institutional design (Ostrom, 1990) are all established forms of sociocultural intervention. The adaptive stance is not fatalism about social conditions but active engagement with them.

**Plain words** Communities and cultures can be intervened on — programmes, policies, institutional design. Not just individuals on couches; whole populations move. Prevention at the level of the village beats treatment at the level of the person.

*For example:* The clean-water effect in mental health: the community that added street lighting and youth programmes saw depression rates move — nobody's individual therapy did that. The intervention was upstream.
e.c: LAYER I — FIRST PRINCIPLES: THE SOCIAL NATURE OF THE PERSON
p: The evidence base for community-level intervention (Wandersman and Florin, 2003); for policy-level prevention (Biglan et al., 2012); for cultural adaptation of interventions (Castro et al., 2010; Gone, 2011); for institutional design (Ostrom, 1990).
f: Dewey — democracy as experimental — Thinker: Dewey — Reference: Dewey (1916).

**Other:**, The intervention principle is the sociocultural counterpart of the biophysiological one. **EEMM link:** Interventions at the sociocultural level are the EEMM's context-selection mechanisms.
r: See principle 75 for systems-level intervention and principle 56 for institutional design.

e.t: Treat the sociocultural level as plural
e.x:
Treat the sociocultural level as plural. There is no single cultural form of flourishing; there are many. The pluralism of flourishing (emotional, psychological, social) extends to the cultural level: Latin American relational forms (Vergara, 2023), East Asian interdependent forms (Kitayama et al., 2007), African communal forms (Ubuntu; Tutu, 1999), Indigenous holistic forms (Durie, 1985, 1998; Fernando, 2014), and European-American individualistic forms (Markus and Kitayama, 1991) are all legitimate cultural achievements. The adaptive stance is to respect the plurality without collapsing into relativism.

**Plain words** There is no single correct human flourishing — Latin American relational versions, East Asian versions, East African versions, each complete and valid. Plural, not ranked. Your version is a dialect, not the language.

*For example:* The Australian definition of a good life and the Japanese one disagreeing about individuality — and both producing centenarians who smile. The outcomes converge; the paths differ.
e.c: LAYER I — FIRST PRINCIPLES: THE SOCIAL NATURE OF THE PERSON
p: The cultural-constructions literature (Uchida et al., 2004; Diener and Suh, 2000; Kitayama and Markus, 2000); the critique of WEIRD centrism (Henrich et al., 2010; Medin et al., 2017; Gurwitz et al., 2023); the global-majority well-being frameworks (Durie, 1985, 1998; Fernando, 2014; Mutamba et al., 2021).
f: Herder — cultural pluralism — Thinker: Herder — Reference: Herder (1774). Stuart Hall — identity as cultural construction — Thinker: Stuart Hall — Reference: Hall (1990).

**Other:**, The pluralist stance is the cultural version of the foundational pluralism principle. **EEMM link:** The EEMM's sociocultural level is itself plural — there are many sociocultural contexts, not one.
r: In cross-cultural practice, treat each cultural form of flourishing as valid within its own terms (see principle 78). In intercultural dialogue, use the pluralist stance.

e.t: Use cultural values as a lens, not a cage
e.x:
Treat cultural values — Schwartz's autonomy, embeddedness, hierarchy, mastery, and harmony; Hofstede's individualism, power distance, uncertainty avoidance, masculinity, and long-term orientation; Inglehart and Welzel's survival vs. self-expression values — as a lens through which to understand your own and others' behavior, not a cage that determines it. Values are statistical tendencies, not individual destinies.

**Plain words** Cultural values are a lens, not a cage — they're real and they shape what you see, but you can take the lens off and examine it. Schwartz, Hofstede: the frameworks are maps, and maps are for reading, not living on.

*For example:* "In our family we don't discuss money" — a value-lens that feels like physics until you look at it. It's a lens. Lenses can be cleaned, upgraded, occasionally replaced.
e.c: LAYER II — CULTURE AS CONTEXT: VALUES, MEANING, AND THE SOCIAL CONSTRUCTION OF FLOURISHING
p: Schwartz (1990, 1994); Hofstede (1980); Inglehart and Welzel (2005); Triandis (1989); the individualism-collectivism literature and its critiques (Oyserman et al., 2002; Boucher, 2011).
f: Schwartz — cultural values as theory — Thinker: Schwartz — Reference: Schwartz (1994). Herder — cultural pluralism — Thinker: Herder — Reference: Herder (1774).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Cultural values are the sociocultural context's selection criteria — they determine which behavioral variants are retained.
r: In reflection, identify your own value profile (see principle 15). In intercultural work, use values as a first approximation, then check against individual behavior.

e.t: Treat cultural meaning as constructed, not given
e.x:
Treat cultural meaning — what counts as a good life, a good death, a good family, a good career — as socially constructed, not given. The meaning of "happiness" itself varies across cultures: in North American contexts, happiness is defined in terms of personal achievement and high-arousal positive affect; in East Asian contexts, in terms of interpersonal connectedness and a balance between positive and negative affect (Uchida et al., 2004). The adaptive stance is to see your own cultural meanings as one construction among many.

**Plain words** What counts as a good life, death, family, or career is constructed — built by people, inherited by you. "Happiness" itself means different things in different cultures. The constructions are real in their effects and negotiable in their hold.

*For example:* The definition of success absorbed at fifteen from a culture that measures it in square metres — at forty, you get to notice it was a definition, not a fact. Definitions can be rewritten.
e.c: LAYER II — CULTURE AS CONTEXT: VALUES, MEANING, AND THE SOCIAL CONSTRUCTION OF FLOURISHING
p: Uchida et al. (2004) on cultural constructions of happiness; Diener and Suh (2000) on culture and subjective well-being; Kitayama and Markus (2000) on culture and self; the cross-cultural well-being literature (Veenhoven, 2010; Andonian, 2017; Graham, 2017; Vergara, 2023).
f: Gadamer — the fusion of horizons — Thinker: Gadamer — Reference: Gadamer (1960), Part II. Berger and Luckmann — the social construction of reality — Thinker: Berger and Luckmann — Reference: Berger and Luckmann (1966).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Cultural meaning is the sociocultural context's interpretive framework — it shapes what counts as adaptive.
r: In reflection, examine which of your "life goals" are cultural constructions. In intercultural contact, treat the other's construction of the good life as valid within its own terms.

e.t: Use cultural identity as a resource, not a constraint
e.x:
Treat cultural identity — your identification with a cultural group, tradition, or community — as a resource, not a constraint. Cultural identity supplies belonging, meaning, continuity, and a repertoire of practices; it constrains when it becomes rigid, exclusionary, or imposed. The adaptive stance is to own your cultural identities without being owned by them.

**Plain words** Cultural identity is a resource — belonging, meaning, a repertoire of practices — until it hardens into a wall. Keep it as a garden, not a bunker. Feed from it without being fenced by it.

*For example:* The tradition that gives you the recipes, the songs, and the strong spine — and the moment you realise it also said who you couldn't marry. Keep the songs; renegotiate the fence.
e.c: LAYER II — CULTURE AS CONTEXT: VALUES, MEANING, AND THE SOCIAL CONSTRUCTION OF FLOURISHING
p: Phinney (1990) on ethnic identity; Phinney and Ong (2007) on the multigroup ethnic identity measure; Sellers et al. (1998) on racial identity; Cross (1991) on nigrescence; Stuart Hall (1990) on cultural identity as construction; Schwartz et al. (2010) on identity in cultural context.
f: Stuart Hall — cultural identity as construction — Thinker: Stuart Hall — Reference: Hall (1990). Ricoeur — narrative identity — Thinker: Ricoeur — Reference: Ricoeur (1985), Vol. 3.
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Cultural identity is the self-dimension of the EEMM at the sociocultural level.
r: See principle 74 for biculturalism and principle 73 for acculturation. In identity work, treat your cultural identity as a living tradition, not a fixed inheritance.

e.t: Use cultural self-examination as a practice
e.x:
Use cultural self-examination — the deliberate examination of your own cultural assumptions, norms, and biases — as a regular practice. This is the sociocultural version of metacognition and self-compassion. The aim is not self-flagellation but clarity: to see the water you swim in.

**Plain words** Examine your own culture regularly — your assumptions, norms, biases — the way you'd examine your own thinking. Not self-flagellation; just noticing that your "normal" is local. Every fish needs one lesson about water.

*For example:* "Obviously the couple pays for the wedding" — said as physics, is in fact one culture's arrangement. The examination doesn't require changing it; it requires knowing it's a choice.
e.c: LAYER II — CULTURE AS CONTEXT: VALUES, MEANING, AND THE SOCIAL CONSTRUCTION OF FLOURISHING
p: Cultural self-awareness as a component of cultural intelligence (Earley and Ang, 2003); cultural humility (Tervalon and Murray-García, 1998; Hook et al., 2013); the critique of implicit-bias training's mixed evidence (Greenwald et al., 2009; Forscher et al., 2019).
f: Socrates — the unexamined life — Thinker: Socrates — Reference: Plato, Apology, 38a. Confucius — the junzi's self-examination — Thinker: Confucius — Reference: Analects.
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Cultural self-examination is the metacognitive dimension of the EEMM at the sociocultural level.
r: Regularly ask: which of my assumptions are cultural? In intercultural contact, practice perspective-taking (see principle 33). In reflective practice, use the cultural form of the "examined life".

e.t: Use cultural relativism methodologically, not morally
e.x:
Use cultural relativism methodologically — as a research stance that treats each culture on its own terms — not morally, as a stance that treats all practices as equally good. The methodological stance is essential for understanding; the moral stance is a mistake. Female genital mutilation, honor killings, and caste discrimination are cultural practices, and they cause suffering; the adaptive stance is to understand them culturally and to oppose them morally.

**Plain words** Use cultural relativism as a method, not a morality — understand each culture on its own terms, without pretending all practices are equally good. Understanding is a scholarly stance; endorsement is a separate decision. You can comprehend without approving.

*For example:* The anthropologist who can explain a practice rigorously and still criticise it — the explanation is the method, the judgement is the ethics. Both are needed; confusing them ruins each.
e.c: LAYER II — CULTURE AS CONTEXT: VALUES, MEANING, AND THE SOCIAL CONSTRUCTION OF FLOURISHING
p: The distinction between cultural relativism as method and as moral stance (Rosaldo, 1989; Clifford, 1988); the human-rights critique of relativism (Donnelly, 1989); the capability approach as a universalist framework sensitive to cultural difference (Sen, 1999; Nussbaum, 2000).
f: Sen — capability as universal — Thinker: Sen — Reference: Sen (1999). Nussbaum — the capability approach — Thinker: Nussbaum — Reference: Nussbaum (2000).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** The EEMM's pluralism (principle 11) is methodological, not moral — adaptive flourishing has universal criteria even amid cultural plurality.
r: In intercultural work, use methodological relativism to understand before you judge (see principle 33). In moral reasoning, retain universal commitments to human dignity and capability (Nussbaum, 2000).

e.t: Treat cultural evolution as real
e.x:
Treat cultural evolution — the change of cultural traits (norms, practices, beliefs, technologies) over time through variation, selection, and transmission — as real and ongoing. Cultures are not static essences; they are populations of practices that change through the EEMM's own variation-selection-retention cycle. The adaptive stance is to participate consciously in cultural evolution rather than to be passively carried by it.

**Plain words** Cultures evolve — norms, practices, beliefs change over generations through variation and selection. No culture is a static essence; they're all works in progress, including yours. Tradition is a moving stream, not a museum.

*For example:* "We've always done it this way" — the "always" is doing enormous work. The tradition is two generations old and was itself an innovation. Streams look still from far away.
e.c: LAYER II — CULTURE AS CONTEXT: VALUES, MEANING, AND THE SOCIAL CONSTRUCTION OF FLOURISHING
p: Cultural evolution theory (Boyd and Richerson, 1985; Richerson and Boyd, 2005; Mesoudi, 2011); gene-culture coevolution (Laland et al., 2010); cultural niche construction (Kendal et al., 2011); the empirical study of value change (Inglehart and Welzel, 2005).
f: Dewey — reconstruction in philosophy — Thinker: Dewey — Reference: Dewey (1920). Whitehead — the social function of education — Thinker: Whitehead — Reference: Whitehead (1929).
**Other:**, The cultural-evolution stance is the sociocultural version of the EEMM's own core mechanism. **EEMM link:** Cultural evolution is the EEMM operating at the sociocultural level.
r: In cultural participation, treat your practices as contributions to cultural evolution. In policy, treat cultural change as designable (see principle 56).

e.t: Treat language as a cultural practice, not just a medium
e.x:
Treat language not just as a neutral medium of communication but as a cultural practice that shapes thought, identity, and social relations. The strong Sapir-Whorf hypothesis is false; the weak version — that language influences habitual thought and attention — has empirical support (Boroditsky, 2011; Lupyan et al., 2020). The adaptive stance is to attend to the language you use, the concepts it makes available, and the identities it constructs.

**Plain words** Language isn't a neutral pipe — it shapes thought, identity, and relations. The strong version is false; the weak version is true and matters. Your vocabulary is quietly steering what you notice.

*For example:* The language with seven words for snow and the one with one — both populations see the same field, but one of them sees distinctions the other literally has no hooks for. Vocabulary is attention.
e.c: LAYER II — CULTURE AS CONTEXT: VALUES, MEANING, AND THE SOCIAL CONSTRUCTION OF FLOURISHING
p: Linguistic relativity (Boroditsky, 2011; Lupyan et al., 2020); language and identity (Norton, 2000); code-switching as cultural practice (Gumperz, 1982); bilingualism and cognition (Bialystok, 2017).
f: Wittgenstein — language games — Thinker: Wittgenstein — Reference: Wittgenstein (1953). Herder — language as the spirit of a people — Thinker: Herder — Reference: Herder (1772).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Language is the cognitive and self-dimension of the EEMM at the sociocultural level.
r: In communication, attend to the conceptual repertoire your language provides. In intercultural contact, respect code-switching as a legitimate practice, not a deficiency.

e.t: Treat religion and spirituality as legitimate resources
e.x:
Treat religion and spirituality as legitimate resources for adaptive flourishing, not as irrational leftovers to be dismissed. The evidence is substantial: religious involvement is associated with lower mortality (Chida et al., 2008), better mental health (VanderWeele, 2017, 2025), and stronger social connection (VanderWeele et al., 2016). The mechanisms are social (community), psychological (meaning, coping), and behavioral (norms against smoking, excessive drinking). The adaptive stance is neither credulity nor dismissal but informed engagement.

**Plain words** Religion and spirituality are legitimate resources — associated with lower mortality, better mental health, real community. Not irrational leftovers; functional technology. You don't have to believe to respect the machinery, or to borrow what works.

*For example:* The atheist who joins the community choir at the church — the benefits arrive without the doctrine. The ritual, the belonging, the weekly rhythm: hardware you can use regardless of your software.
e.c: LAYER II — CULTURE AS CONTEXT: VALUES, MEANING, AND THE SOCIAL CONSTRUCTION OF FLOURISHING
p: Chida et al. (2008) meta-analysis on religious involvement and mortality; VanderWeele et al. (2016) on religious service attendance and mortality; VanderWeele (2017, 2025) on religion and health; Hill and Pargament (2003) on religion as a coping resource; Koenig et al. (2012) handbook of religion and health.
f: James — the varieties of religious experience — Thinker: James — Reference: James (1902). Eliade — the sacred and the profane — Thinker: Eliade — Reference: Eliade (1957).
**Other:**, The religion-as-resource stance is consistent with the pluralism of flourishing. **EEMM link:** Religion is a major sociocultural context — it supplies community, meaning, and practice.
r: For religious and spiritual practitioners, use community, ritual, and meaning as supports (see principle 26). For non-religious people, treat secular analogues (community, ritual, meaning) as legitimate substitutes.

e.t: Treat secular meaning as legitimate
e.x:
Treat secular meaning — meaning found in family, work, art, nature, community, and projects, without religious framing — as fully legitimate. The adaptive stance is not to require religion for meaning; it is to respect both religious and secular forms. This is the meaning-level version of the principle (emotional pluralism).

**Plain words** Secular meaning is fully legitimate — meaning found in family, work, art, nature, and projects, no religion required. Neither needs to diminish the other. The stance is respect for both routes up the mountain.

*For example:* The believer and the non-believer both moved to tears by the same forest — one calls it cathedral, one calls it complex systems. Both are having the meaning. Both are right.
e.c: LAYER II — CULTURE AS CONTEXT: VALUES, MEANING, AND THE SOCIAL CONSTRUCTION OF FLOURISHING
p: The meaning-in-life literature (Steger, 2012; Martela and Steger, 2016); secular sources of meaning (Frankl, 1946/1959; Csikszentmihalyi, 1990); the empirical study of eudaimonic well-being (Ryff and Singer, 2008; Keyes, 2002).
f: Frankl — meaning without religion — Thinker: Frankl — Reference: Frankl (1946/1959). Sartre — existential meaning as a project — Thinker: Sartre — Reference: Sartre (1943).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Meaning is the motivational and self-dimension of the EEMM at the sociocultural level.
r: In meaning work, identify your own sources of meaning without assuming a religious form. In community work, respect both religious and secular participants.

e.t: Treat cultural traditions as living, not static
e.x:
Treat cultural traditions — religious, philosophical, artistic, culinary, familial — as living practices that change, not static essences to be preserved unchanged. The adaptive stance is to participate in tradition as a living conversation, not to embalm it. This is Gadamer's point: tradition is not the dead weight of the past but the ongoing fusion of horizons.

**Plain words** Traditions are living conversations, not embalmed corpses — they change, absorb, drop things, and pick things up. Participate in the conversation; don't freeze it. The tradition that can't change is already dead.

*For example:* The holiday dinner that's unrecognisable to great-grandmother — different foods, different faces, same function. The tradition didn't die; it evolved. That's what living things do.
e.c: LAYER II — CULTURE AS CONTEXT: VALUES, MEANING, AND THE SOCIAL CONSTRUCTION OF FLOURISHING
p: The cultural-evolution literature (Boyd and Richerson, 1985; Richerson and Boyd, 2005); the study of tradition and innovation (Kashima, 2000); the psychology of ritual and its functions (Hobson et al., 2018).
f: Gadamer — the fusion of horizons — Thinker: Gadamer — Reference: Gadamer (1960), Part II. Whitehead — the social function of education — Thinker: Whitehead — Reference: Whitehead (1929).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Tradition is the retention mechanism of the EEMM at the sociocultural level.
r: In cultural participation, contribute to the living tradition rather than merely replicating it (see principle 17). In intergenerational transmission, treat tradition as a conversation between generations.

e.t: Use cultural humility as a practice
e.x:
Use cultural humility — the practice of approaching other cultures with openness, curiosity, and a willingness to examine one's own assumptions — as a deliberate practice. Cultural humility differs from cultural competence: competence implies mastery of the other; humility implies lifelong learning and self-examination (Tervalon and Murray-García, 1998).

**Plain words** Cultural humility beats cultural competence — not "I've mastered your culture" but "I'm ready to learn, and to check my own assumptions." Competence claims arrival; humility assumes travel. The stance is beginner's mind with a passport.

*For example:* The clinician who asks "what does your family do when someone's sick?" instead of assuming — that's humility. The one who read a chapter and "knows how Chinese families work" — that's competence overreaching.
e.c: LAYER II — CULTURE AS CONTEXT: VALUES, MEANING, AND THE SOCIAL CONSTRUCTION OF FLOURISHING
p: Tervalon and Murray-García (1998) on cultural humility; Hook et al. (2013) on cultural humility in therapy; Foronda et al. (2016) on cultural humility in nursing; the cultural-formulation approach in psychiatry (Lewis-Fernández and Aggarwal, 2015).
f: Socrates — Socratic ignorance — Thinker: Socrates — Reference: Plato, Apology, 21d. Confucius — humility as virtue — Thinker: Confucius — Reference: Analects.
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Cultural humility is the attentional and self-dimension of the EEMM at the sociocultural level.
r: In intercultural contact, practice "not knowing" as a stance (see principle 33). In professional practice, use the cultural-formulation interview to understand the client's cultural context.

e.t: Cultivate social connection as a primary good
e.x:
Cultivate social connection as a primary good, not as an optional extra. The evidence is among the strongest in the sociocultural literature: social relationships predict health, well-being, and mortality as strongly as smoking, obesity, and physical inactivity (Holt-Lunstad et al., 2010, 2017). The adaptive stance is to treat connection as a design parameter of life, not a residual.

**Plain words** Connection is a primary good, not a luxury — relationships predict health and mortality as strongly as smoking and obesity. That's not a metaphor; it's an effect size. Treat your social life like a vital sign, because it is one.

*For example:* The GP who asks about friendships like they ask about smoking — because the answer predicts the decade. The patient who laughed at the question is now walking with a neighbour.
e.c: LAYER III — SOCIAL CONNECTION AND BELONGING
p: Holt-Lunstad et al. (2010, 2017) on social relationships and mortality; House et al. (1988) on social relationships and health; Uchino (2006) on social support and physiology; Hawkley and Cacioppo (2010) on loneliness; the "loneliness epidemic" literature (Holt-Lunstad, 2017).
f: Aristotle — friendship as a constituent of eudaimonia — Thinker: Aristotle — Reference: Nicomachean Ethics, VIII–IX. Ubuntu — personhood through relationship — Thinker: Tutu — Reference: Tutu (1999).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Social connection is the sociocultural context's most direct influence on the biophysiological level.
r: Schedule time with people as you schedule sleep and exercise. Prioritize one or two close relationships over many weak ones (see principle 25). In periods of transition, treat connection as the first thing to rebuild.

e.t: Treat loneliness as a signal, not a stigma
e.x:
Treat loneliness as a signal, not a stigma. Loneliness is not a character defect; it is an evolved signal, like hunger or pain, that prompts reconnection (Cacioppo et al., 2011). The signal can misfire — leading to withdrawal, hypervigilance, and self-fulfilling isolation — but the adaptive stance is to treat it as information, not identity.

**Plain words** Loneliness is a signal, like hunger — an evolved alarm that says "reconnect," not a character verdict. The alarm can misfire, driving withdrawal that deepens the isolation. Hear it as information, not as truth about your worth.

*For example:* The lonely person who cancels plans because "nobody really wants me there" — that's the alarm misfiring, cutting the very wire it's meant to ring. The signal says go; the shame says hide. Believe the signal.
e.c: LAYER III — SOCIAL CONNECTION AND BELONGING
p: The evolutionary account of loneliness (Cacioppo et al., 2011; Cacioppo and Cacioppo, 2018); the loneliness-mortality link (Holt-Lunstad et al., 2010; Elovainio et al., 2017); the cognitive-bias model of loneliness (Cacioppo and Hawkley, 2009); interventions for loneliness (Masi et al., 2011).
f: Aristotle — friendship and the good life — Thinker: Aristotle — Reference: Nicomachean Ethics, VIII. Frankl — meaning in connection — Thinker: Frankl — Reference: Frankl (1946/1959).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Loneliness is the affect-dimension of the EEMM responding to the sociocultural context.
r: When lonely, treat the signal as a prompt to reach out, not to withdraw (see principle 23). Use the cognitive reappraisal of loneliness as a signal, not a judgment. In chronic loneliness, seek professional support.

e.t: Prioritize the quality of relationships over the quantity
e.x:
Prioritize the quality of relationships over the quantity. A small number of close, reciprocal, supportive relationships predicts well-being and health better than a large number of weak ties (Pinquart and Sörensen, 2000; Hawkley and Cacioppo, 2010). The adaptive stance is to invest in depth rather than breadth.

**Plain words** Quality beats quantity in relationships — three real ones outweigh three hundred contacts. Depth is the nutrient; breadth is just plumbing. Invest where there's reciprocity.

*For example:* The wedding with 200 guests and the hospitalisation with three visitors — the true portfolio shows up in a crisis. The contacts were never the same thing as the friends.
e.c: LAYER III — SOCIAL CONNECTION AND BELONGING
p: Pinquart and Sörensen (2000) on social support and well-being; Hawkley and Cacioppo (2010) on loneliness; relationship-quality and health outcomes (Uchino, 2006); the Dunbar number and network structure (Dunbar, 2016); weak ties and information flow (Granovetter, 1973).
f: Aristotle — the three kinds of friendship — Thinker: Aristotle — Reference: Nicomachean Ethics, VIII.3–8. Montaigne — friendship as the highest human bond — Thinker: Montaigne — Reference: Montaigne, Essays, "Of Friendship."
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Relationship quality is the sociocultural context's most direct influence on the affect-dimension of the EEMM.
r: Identify your closest relationships and invest in them (see principle 23). Maintain weak ties for information and opportunity, but do not mistake them for intimacy.

e.t: Use community as a resource
e.x:
Use community — the networks of people, institutions, and practices that surround you — as a resource for adaptive flourishing. Community supplies support, meaning, identity, and practical help; it also makes demands. The adaptive stance is to give and receive within community, not to consume it.

**Plain words** Community is a resource that also bills you — support, meaning, identity, practical help, in exchange for demands. The healthy stance is both giving and receiving. The taker and the martyr both break the same machine.

*For example:* The neighbour who borrows your drill and brings soup when you're sick — the exchange is the community. The one who never asks for anything is as outside it as the one who never gives.
e.c: LAYER III — SOCIAL CONNECTION AND BELONGING
p: Sense of community (McMillan and Chavis, 1986); community psychology (Wandersman and Florin, 2003); social capital and health (Kawachi and Berkman, 2000); religious community and health (VanderWeele et al., 2016); community-intervention evidence (Biglan et al., 2012).
f: Aristotle — the polis as the context of eudaimonia — Thinker: Aristotle — Reference: Nicomachean Ethics, I.7. Ubuntu — community as personhood — Thinker: Tutu — Reference: Tutu (1999).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Community is the sociocultural context's institutional form.
r: Join communities that align with your values (see principle 27). Contribute to community as well as drawing from it. In religious or spiritual communities, use the community as a support (see principle 19).

e.t: Choose communities that align with your values
e.x:
Choose communities that align with your values, not just any community. Communities are not neutral; they shape your norms, your aspirations, and your behavior. The adaptive stance is to select and shape your communities deliberately, as you select your environment.

**Plain words** Communities aren't neutral — they set your norms, aspirations, and defaults. Choose them like you'd choose a co-author of your life, because that's what they are. Drift is a choice too.

*For example:* The gym friend group, the startup crowd, the church committee — each quietly rewires what "normal" means within a year. Nobody announces it. The community edits you.
e.c: LAYER III — SOCIAL CONNECTION AND BELONGING
p: Social-network effects on behavior (Christakis and Fowler, 2007, 2008); social contagion of emotion (Kramer et al., 2014; Coviello et al., 2014); group norms and behavior (Tajfel and Turner, 1979); reference groups and aspiration (Merton, 1968).
f: Aristotle — the role of the polis in character formation — Thinker: Aristotle — Reference: Nicomachean Ethics, II.1. Confucius — choosing one's community — Thinker: Confucius — Reference: Analects.
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Community selection is the EEMM's context-selection at the sociocultural level.
r: Audit your communities for value alignment (see principle 26). Where misaligned, either work to change the community or leave it. In community selection, treat the community's norms as you would treat your own habits.

e.t: Use social support as a two-way practice
e.x:
Use social support as a two-way practice — both receiving and giving. Receiving support buffers stress (Cohen and Wills, 1985); giving support predicts well-being and mortality independently (Brown et al., 2003; Poulin et al., 2013). The adaptive stance is reciprocity, not dependence or martyrdom.

**Plain words** Support is a two-way circuit — receiving buffers stress, giving predicts health. Both directions need traffic. The one-way helper is hiding; the one-way receiver is draining.

*For example:* The friend who lets you bring the soup when she's ill — the letting is the gift. Refusing help isn't independence; it's robbing someone of the chance to matter.
e.c: LAYER III — SOCIAL CONNECTION AND BELONGING
p: Cohen and Wills (1985) on stress-buffering; Brown et al. (2003) on giving and mortality; Poulin et al. (2013) on helping and well-being; the support-matching literature (Cutrona and Russell, 1990).
f: Aristotle — friendship as mutual benefit and virtue — Thinker: Aristotle — Reference: Nicomachean Ethics, VIII. Levinas — the ethical priority of the other — Thinker: Levinas — Reference: Levinas (1961).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Social support is the sociocultural context's most direct influence on the stress physiology of the biophysiological level.
r: When in need, ask for help directly. When able, give help without expectation of return. Balance the two over time, not at every moment.

e.t: Treat belonging as a need, not a preference
e.x:
Treat belonging — the felt sense of being accepted, included, and valued by a group — as a need, not a preference. Belonging predicts well-being, health, and behavior; its absence predicts alienation, disengagement, and extremism (Baumeister and Leary, 1995; Walton and Cohen, 2007; Lambert et al., 2013).

**Plain words** Belonging is a need, not a preference — the felt sense of being accepted and valued. Its absence predicts alienation, disengagement, and extremism. People join terrible groups when good ones are closed. Belonging is a nutrient with a dark side when it's missing.

*For example:* The teenager who finds "family" in the worst available crowd — the need was legitimate, the supply was toxic. The need doesn't ask permission; it finds a vendor.
e.c: LAYER III — SOCIAL CONNECTION AND BELONGING
p: Baumeister and Leary (1995) on the need to belong; Walton and Cohen (2007) on belonging uncertainty; Lambert et al. (2013) on belonging and meaning; belonging and health (Holt-Lunstad et al., 2017); the belonging-intervention literature (Walton and Cohen, 2011).
f: Aristotle — the political animal — Thinker: Aristotle — Reference: Nicomachean Ethics, I.7. Ubuntu — personhood through community — Thinker: Tutu — Reference: Tutu (1999).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Belonging is the affect-dimension of the EEMM responding to the sociocultural context.
r: In education and work, create conditions of belonging (see principle 56). In personal life, treat belonging as a design parameter (see principle 23).

e.t: Use weak ties as a bridge
e.x:
Use weak ties — acquaintances, colleagues, neighbors, casual contacts — as a bridge to information, opportunity, and novelty. Mark Granovetter (1973) showed that job opportunities come disproportionately through weak ties, not strong ones. The adaptive stance is to maintain a portfolio of weak ties alongside your close relationships.

**Plain words** Weak ties — acquaintances, neighbours, the person at the coffee shop — carry disproportionate opportunity. Jobs, information, novelty flow through them precisely because they're not your inner circle. Tend the periphery.

*For example:* The job that came through the guy you chat with at the gym — never through your five closest friends, who all know what you know. The periphery sees what the core can't.
e.c: LAYER III — SOCIAL CONNECTION AND BELONGING
p: Granovetter (1973) on the strength of weak ties; social-network structure and information flow (Burt, 1992); weak ties and well-being (Sandstrom and Dunn, 2014); the Dunbar number and network layers (Dunbar, 2016).
f: Aristotle — utility friendship — Thinker: Aristotle — Reference: Nicomachean Ethics, VIII.3–5. Simmel — the metropolis and mental life — Thinker: Simmel — Reference: Simmel (1903).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Weak ties are the sociocultural context's information network.
r: Maintain casual contacts through regular, low-cost interactions (greetings, brief conversations). Use weak ties for information and opportunity; use strong ties for support and intimacy.

e.t: Treat social comparison as a double-edged sword
e.x:
Treat social comparison — the tendency to evaluate oneself against others — as a double-edged sword. Upward comparison can inspire; it can also deflate. Downward comparison can comfort; it can also breed complacency or schadenfreude. Social media has industrialized comparison (see principle 76). The adaptive stance is deliberate comparison management.

**Plain words** Comparison is a double-edged tool — upward can inspire or deflate; downward can comfort or corrode. Social media has industrialised the comparison engine and set it to "upward, curated." Know the tool; handle with intention.

*For example:* Scrolling a feed of promotions and beaches — the comparison is with a highlight reel edited by professionals. You're comparing your whole life to a trailer. That's not information; that's a beating.
e.c: LAYER III — SOCIAL CONNECTION AND BELONGING
p: Festinger (1954) on social comparison; Collins (1996) on upward comparison; Buunk et al. (1990) on comparison and affect; social media and comparison (Vogel et al., 2014; Verduyn et al., 2017); envy and well-being (Smith et al., 1999).
f: Stoics — the dichotomy of control — Thinker: Epictetus — Reference: Enchiridion, 1. Montaigne — the personal measure — Thinker: Montaigne — Reference: Montaigne, Essays.
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Social comparison is the self-dimension of the EEMM responding to the sociocultural context.
r: In comparison, ask: is this inspiring or deflating? If deflating, either reframe or limit the comparison (see principle 76). In social media use, curate feeds to reduce upward comparison.

e.t: Treat social influence as inevitable and manageable
e.x:
Treat social influence — conformity, norm-following, obedience, imitation — as inevitable and manageable. Solomon Asch's conformity experiments and Stanley Milgram's obedience experiments showed how powerful social influence is; the adaptive stance is not to deny influence but to manage it deliberately (see principle 27).

**Plain words** Social influence is inevitable — conformity, norm-following, obedience run deep. The experiments are famous for a reason: the pull is strong. The stance isn't immunity; it's knowing when the current is steering.

*For example:* The meeting where everyone agrees and you agree too — then in the corridor, everyone privately disagrees with everyone. The current did that. Learn to notice the water you're swimming in.
e.c: LAYER III — SOCIAL CONNECTION AND BELONGING
p: Asch (1951, 1956) on conformity; Milgram (1963, 1974) on obedience; Cialdini (2001) on influence; normative vs. informational influence (Deutsch and Gerard, 1955); descriptive vs. injunctive norms (Cialdini et al., 1990).
f: Stoics — inner freedom — Thinker: Epictetus — Reference: Enchiridion. Mill — individuality — Thinker: Mill — Reference: Mill (1859).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Social influence is the sociocultural context's most direct influence on the overt-behavior dimension of the EEMM.
r: In group settings, notice the pull to conform. Use norms deliberately: surround yourself with people whose norms you want (see principle 27). In institutional design, use default options and social norms to shape behavior (see principle 56).

e.t: Treat perspective-taking as a skill
e.x:
Treat perspective-taking — the deliberate attempt to see the world from another's point of view — as a learnable skill. Perspective-taking improves empathy, reduces prejudice, and improves negotiation (Galinsky et al., 2008; Todd et al., 2011; Ku et al., 2015). It is not a panacea: it can backfire when the other's perspective is hostile or when it leads to projection. The adaptive stance is deliberate, disciplined perspective-taking.

**Plain words** Perspective-taking is a learnable skill, not a personality gift — the deliberate act of seeing from another's position. It improves empathy, negotiation, and reduces prejudice. Like any skill: reps, feedback, gradual gains.

*For example:* The negotiation that unlocks when one side finally says "what does a good outcome look like for you?" — one question, and the whole geometry changes. That's the skill, applied once.
e.c: LAYER III — SOCIAL CONNECTION AND BELONGING
p: Galinsky et al. (2008) on perspective-taking and prejudice; Todd et al. (2011) on perspective-taking and empathy; Ku et al. (2015) on perspective-taking and negotiation; the limits of perspective-taking (Epley et al., 2004; Ames, 2004); cultural perspective-taking (Mor et al., 2013).
f: Buber — I-Thou — Thinker: Buber — Reference: Buber (1923). Confucius — shu (reciprocity) — Thinker: Confucius — Reference: Analects.
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Perspective-taking is the cognitive and self-dimension of the EEMM at the sociocultural level.
r: In intercultural contact, ask "how would this look from their position?" rather than "how would I feel in their position?" (see principle 22). In conflict, use perspective-taking to understand before responding (see principle 45).

e.t: Treat knowledge as social
e.x:
Treat knowledge as social. Human knowledge is not the achievement of isolated minds; it is a collective achievement, distributed across communities of inquiry, institutions, and practices. This is the sociocultural version of the principle (treat cognition as embodied and embedded). The adaptive stance is to participate in knowledge communities deliberately.

**Plain words** Knowledge is social — not isolated minds achieving truths, but communities of inquiry, institutions, and practices. Even your own "private" thoughts are built from inherited language and concepts. Your mind has co-authors.

*For example:* The brilliant insight you had in the shower — assembled from a teacher's phrase, a book's argument, a friend's joke. Original, yes. Solo, never.
e.c: LAYER IV — SOCIAL EPISTEMOLOGY AND COLLECTIVE INTELLIGENCE
p: Social epistemology (Goldman, 1999; Kitcher, 1990); distributed cognition (Hutchins, 1995); collaborative memory (Rajaram and Pereira-Pasarin, 2010); the science of science (Ziman, 1968); transactive memory (Wegner, 1987).
f: Peirce — the community of inquiry — Thinker: Peirce — Reference: Peirce (1877). Dewey — democracy as inquiry — Thinker: Dewey — Reference: Dewey (1916).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Knowledge is the cognitive dimension of the EEMM at the sociocultural level.
r: In knowledge work, use collaboration deliberately (see principle 35). In personal knowledge management, treat your notes and references as a social system, not a private one.

e.t: Use collective intelligence deliberately
e.x:
Use collective intelligence — the ability of groups to solve problems that individuals cannot — deliberately. Groups can outperform their best members (Surowiecki, 2005); they can also fall prey to groupthink, polarization, and information cascades (Sunstein and Hastie, 2015). The adaptive stance is to design group processes that capture the benefit and avoid the failure modes.

**Plain words** Groups can be smarter than their smartest member — or dumber than their dumbest. The difference is design: independence of views, diversity, aggregation. Collective intelligence isn't a vibe; it's an engineering problem.

*For example:* The estimation meeting where everyone guesses privately first, then shares — versus the one where the loudest speaks first and anchors the room. Same people, wildly different output. That's the design.
e.c: LAYER IV — SOCIAL EPISTEMOLOGY AND COLLECTIVE INTELLIGENCE
p: The wisdom of crowds (Surowiecki, 2005); groupthink (Janis, 1972); group polarization (Moscovici and Zavalloni, 1969; Isenberg, 1986); the hidden-profiles problem (Stasser and Titus, 1985); Delphi and prediction markets (Surowiecki, 2005).
f: Peirce — the community of inquiry — Thinker: Peirce — Reference: Peirce (1877). Mill — the marketplace of ideas — Thinker: Mill — Reference: Mill (1859).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Collective intelligence is the cognitive dimension of the EEMM at the sociocultural level.
r: In group decision-making, use structured processes: independent judgment before discussion (to avoid anchoring), devil's advocacy (to avoid groupthink), and diverse membership (to capture hidden profiles). See principle 36 for the failure modes.

e.t: Guard against epistemic failure modes
e.x:
Guard against the characteristic failure modes of collective knowledge — groupthink (Janis, 1972), polarization (Sunstein, 2002), echo chambers and epistemic bubbles (Nguyen, 2020), misinformation and conspiracy (Lewandowsky et al., 2012; van der Linden, 2022), and epistemic injustice (Fricker, 2007). The adaptive stance is to treat these as design problems, not moral failings.

**Plain words** Collective knowledge has failure modes — groupthink, polarisation, echo chambers, cascades. Know the failure modes like you know your own cognitive biases: not to eliminate them, but to install the alarms. Groups need checklists too.

*For example:* The unanimous decision that nobody privately agreed with — each person assuming the others believed it. Classic groupthink. The fix is embarrassingly simple: anonymous first votes.
e.c: LAYER IV — SOCIAL EPISTEMOLOGY AND COLLECTIVE INTELLIGENCE
p: Janis (1972) on groupthink; Sunstein (2002) on the law of group polarization; Nguyen (2020) on echo chambers; Lewandowsky et al. (2012) on misinformation; van der Linden (2022) on inoculation against misinformation; Fricker (2007) on epistemic injustice.
f: Mill — the marketplace of ideas — Thinker: Mill — Reference: Mill (1859). Peirce — the fixation of belief — Thinker: Peirce — Reference: Peirce (1877).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Epistemic failure modes are the cognitive dimension of the EEMM failing at the sociocultural level.
r: In information consumption, diversify sources deliberately. In group settings, invite dissent (see principle 35). In misinformation management, use prebunking rather than debunking (van der Linden, 2022).

e.t: Use epistemic diversity as a resource
e.x:
Use epistemic diversity — the inclusion of different perspectives, backgrounds, and cognitive styles in knowledge communities — as a resource. Diverse groups outperform homogeneous groups on complex problems (Hong and Page, 2004; Page, 2007); the mechanism is that diversity brings different heuristics, information, and perspectives to bear.

**Plain words** Epistemic diversity is a resource — different perspectives and cognitive styles make groups better on complex problems. Homogeneous groups are faster and wronger. Comfort is the price of the better answer.

*For example:* The team of five identical thinkers that solves the problem in ten minutes — and the mixed team that argues for an hour and finds the flaw the fast team shipped. The discomfort was the work.
e.c: LAYER IV — SOCIAL EPISTEMOLOGY AND COLLECTIVE INTELLIGENCE
p: Hong and Page (2004) on diversity and problem-solving; Page (2007) on the difference; Phillips et al. (2004) on diverse groups and decision-making; the value of cognitive diversity (Reynolds and Lewis, 2017).
f: Peirce — the community of inquiry — Thinker: Peirce — Reference: Peirce (1877). Arendt — the space of appearance — Thinker: Arendt — Reference: Arendt (1958).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Epistemic diversity is the cognitive dimension of the EEMM thriving at the sociocultural level.
r: In team composition, prioritize epistemic diversity (different expertise, backgrounds, cognitive styles) alongside demographic diversity. In knowledge work, actively seek out perspectives that differ from your own (see principle 36).

e.t: Treat trust as social capital
e.x:
Treat trust — the general confidence that others will behave cooperatively and that institutions will function — as social capital. High-trust societies have better health, higher well-being, and stronger economies (Putnam, 2000; Wilkinson and Pickett, 2009). The adaptive stance is to build trust through cooperative behavior, not to deplete it through defection.

**Plain words** Trust is infrastructure — the confidence that others will cooperate and institutions will function. High-trust communities are healthier, wealthier, and easier to live in. And trust is built in small, boring, repeated keepings-of-word.

*For example:* The neighbour who returns the borrowed ladder on time, every time — that's the whole economy of trust, compounding quietly. The community's health is built from a hundred returned ladders.
e.c: LAYER IV — SOCIAL EPISTEMOLOGY AND COLLECTIVE INTELLIGENCE
p: Putnam (2000) on social capital; trust and health (Kawachi et al., 1999); generalized trust and cooperation (Ostrom and Ahn, 2009); the trust game literature (Berg et al., 1995).
f: Levinas — the ethical relation — Thinker: Levinas — Reference: Levinas (1961). Habermas — communicative rationality — Thinker: Habermas — Reference: Habermas (1981).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Trust is the sociocultural context's cooperation infrastructure.
r: In social interactions, default to trust with verification, not to distrust. In institutions, build trust through transparency, accountability, and reciprocity (see principle 56).

e.t: Treat cooperation as an evolutionary strategy
e.x:
Treat cooperation — working together for mutual benefit — as an evolutionary strategy, not a naive ideal. Humans are neither purely selfish nor purely altruistic; we are conditional cooperators who reciprocate, punish defectors, and build institutions to sustain cooperation (Axelrod, 1984; Ostrom, 1990; Nowak, 2006). The adaptive stance is to cooperate conditionally and to design institutions that make cooperation stable.

**Plain words** Cooperation is an evolutionary strategy, not naivety — humans are conditional cooperators who reciprocate and punish defectors. Neither saints nor sharks; accountants. Build systems where cooperation pays and defection costs.

*For example:* The colleague who helps until they're helped-once too often, then stops — that's not bitterness, that's the accounting. Conditional cooperation is the species' firmware.
e.c: LAYER IV — SOCIAL EPISTEMOLOGY AND COLLECTIVE INTELLIGENCE
p: Axelrod (1984) on the evolution of cooperation; Ostrom (1990) on governing the commons; Nowak (2006) on the five rules of cooperation; strong reciprocity (Fehr and Gächter, 2002); the interdependence-theory account of cooperation (Van Lange et al., 2014).
f: Aristotle — the political animal — Thinker: Aristotle — Reference: Nicomachean Ethics, I.7. Ubuntu — personhood through community — Thinker: Tutu — Reference: Tutu (1999).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Cooperation is the sociocultural context's evolutionary mechanism.
r: In social dilemmas, cooperate first, reciprocate, and punish defection when necessary (see principle 38). In institutional design, create conditions for stable cooperation (see principle 56).

e.t: Treat institutions as knowledge infrastructures
e.x:
Treat institutions — universities, scientific societies, journals, regulatory bodies, media organizations — as knowledge infrastructures that make collective intelligence possible. Institutions are not neutral; they shape what counts as knowledge, who is heard, and what is funded. The adaptive stance is to participate in and improve knowledge institutions, not to abandon them.

**Plain words** Institutions are knowledge infrastructure — universities, journals, media, regulators: the plumbing of collective intelligence. They're not neutral; they shape what counts as knowledge and who gets heard. Maintain the plumbing; it beats the alternative.

*For example:* The peer review that feels like bureaucracy until the retracted paper that slipped through it — the plumbing is annoying, and the alternative is worse. Institutions are slow so that truth can be fast.
e.c: LAYER IV — SOCIAL EPISTEMOLOGY AND COLLECTIVE INTELLIGENCE
p: The science of science (Ziman, 1968); peer review and its failure modes (Smith, 2006); replication and reform (Nosek et al., 2015; Open Science Collaboration, 2015); institutional economics (North, 1990).
f: Peirce — the community of inquiry — Thinker: Peirce — Reference: Peirce (1877). Dewey — democracy as experimental — Thinker: Dewey — Reference: Dewey (1916).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Institutions are the sociocultural context's knowledge-retention mechanism.
r: In knowledge work, participate in institutional reform (open science, replication, pre-registration). In information consumption, evaluate the institution behind a claim, not just the claim itself.

e.t: Treat expertise as real but fallible
e.x:
Treat expertise — the specialized knowledge of trained practitioners — as real but fallible. Expertise is not a fraud; experts reliably outperform novices in their domains (Ericsson et al., 1993; Kahneman and Klein, 2009). But experts also fail, are overconfident, and are subject to institutional pressures. The adaptive stance is calibrated trust: trust expertise, verify claims, and maintain epistemic humility.

**Plain words** Experts are real and fallible — they outperform novices in their domain, and they're overconfident at its edges. The stance is neither worship nor contempt: respect the expertise, check the confidence. Trust the plumber's diagnosis of the pipes; verify the plumber's predictions about the market.

*For example:* The epidemiologist's disease model is worth respecting; the same epidemiologist's stock tips are worth nothing. Domain expertise has a fence around it. The skill is knowing where the fence is.
e.c: LAYER IV — SOCIAL EPISTEMOLOGY AND COLLECTIVE INTELLIGENCE
p: Ericsson et al. (1993) on deliberate practice; Kahneman and Klein (2009) on expert intuition; Tetlock (2005) on expert political judgment; Goldstein and Gigerenzer (2002) on fast-and-frugal heuristics.
f: Peirce — the community of inquiry — Thinker: Peirce — Reference: Peirce (1877). Socrates — Socratic ignorance — Thinker: Socrates — Reference: Plato, Apology, 21d.
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Expertise is the cognitive dimension of the EEMM institutionalized at the sociocultural level.
r: In seeking advice, consult experts in their domain of expertise, not outside it. In evaluating expert claims, ask for evidence, base rates, and confidence intervals. In your own expertise, maintain calibration.

e.t: Treat epistemic injustice as a real harm
e.x:
Treat epistemic injustice — the unfair treatment of people as knowers — as a real harm. Miranda Fricker (2007) distinguished testimonial injustice (a speaker's credibility unfairly deflated) and hermeneutical injustice (a gap in collective interpretive resources that prevents someone from understanding their own experience). Both are sociocultural causes of suffering; both are designable problems.

**Plain words** People can be wronged as knowers — their credibility unfairly discounted, or the concepts to describe their experience simply not existing yet. That's a real harm, not a technicality. When someone's testimony keeps getting discounted, notice the pattern, not just the instance.

*For example:* The woman whose pain reports were "anxiety" for a decade before the diagnosis showed up on a scan — the harm wasn't only the missed disease; it was years of being treated as a poor witness to her own body. The knowing was real; the reception was broken.
e.c: LAYER IV — SOCIAL EPISTEMOLOGY AND COLLECTIVE INTELLIGENCE
p: Fricker (2007) on epistemic injustice; intersectionality (Crenshaw, 1989; Cole, 2009); the testimonial-injustice literature (Medina, 2013); hermeneutical injustice and mental health (Crichton et al., 2017).
f: Fricker — epistemic injustice — Thinker: Fricker — Reference: Fricker (2007). Arendt — the space of appearance — Thinker: Arendt — Reference: Arendt (1958).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Epistemic injustice is the cognitive and self-dimension of the EEMM failing at the sociocultural level.
r: In listening, give credibility to speakers from marginalized groups (see principle 22). In interpreting experience, attend to the collective concepts available (e.g., "sexual harassment" as a hermeneutical resource that did not exist before the 1970s).

e.t: Use communication norms as design parameters
e.x:
Treat communication norms — the rules of discourse in a community (who speaks, who interrupts, how disagreement is expressed, what counts as evidence) — as design parameters. Habermas's ideal speech situation (1981) and the deliberative-democracy literature (Fishkin, 2009) show that norms can be designed to improve the quality of collective judgment.

**Plain words** The rules of who speaks, who interrupts, and what counts as evidence are design choices — not laws of nature. Change the rules, change the outputs. Most meetings and families run on inherited rules nobody ever examined.

*For example:* The team where the loudest voice always wins, redesigned to round-robin turns — same people, same facts, different decisions. The norm was the hidden variable.
e.c: LAYER IV — SOCIAL EPISTEMOLOGY AND COLLECTIVE INTELLIGENCE
p: Habermas (1981) on communicative rationality; deliberative democracy (Fishkin, 2009); group discussion and judgment (Sunstein and Hastie, 2015); psychological safety and team performance (Edmondson, 1999).
f: Habermas — communicative rationality — Thinker: Habermas — Reference: Habermas (1981). Arendt — the space of appearance — Thinker: Arendt — Reference: Arendt (1958).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Communication norms are the sociocultural context's discourse infrastructure.
r: In meetings, establish norms: equal turn-taking, evidence-based disagreement, and psychological safety (Edmondson, 1999). In online discourse, design for slow thinking rather than fast reaction.

e.t: Treat the WEIRD critique as a standing corrective
e.x:
Treat the WEIRD critique — the observation that much psychological research over-relies on Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic samples (Henrich et al., 2010) — as a standing corrective. The critique does not invalidate psychology; it requires the field to test its claims across populations and to treat cultural generality as an empirical question, not an assumption.

**Plain words** Most psychology research studies WEIRD samples — Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, Democratic — and treats the findings as human nature. Sometimes they are; sometimes they're local. The critique is a standing corrective, not a wrecking ball: check the sample before you apply the finding to your life.

*For example:* The famous fairness-findings that turn out to shift with the culture they're tested in — the effect was real in Boston and different in other places. The science wasn't wrong; the generalisation was.
e.c: LAYER IV — SOCIAL EPISTEMOLOGY AND COLLECTIVE INTELLIGENCE
p: Henrich et al. (2010) on the WEIRD problem; Medin et al. (2017) on cultural variance; Gurwitz et al. (2023) on representation; the replication-and-generalization literature (Open Science Collaboration, 2015; Klein et al., 2018).
f: Herder — cultural pluralism — Thinker: Herder — Reference: Herder (1774). Stuart Hall — cultural identity as construction — Thinker: Stuart Hall — Reference: Hall (1990).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** The WEIRD critique is the EEMM's own pluralism applied to the science that supports it.
r: In applying research findings, ask: was this tested in populations like mine? In research, prioritize diverse sampling. In applying these principles, treat cultural generality as a question (see principle 11).

e.t: Use social identity as a resource and a risk
e.x:
Treat social identity — the part of the self that derives from group memberships (nationality, ethnicity, religion, profession, gender, class) — as both a resource and a risk. Social identity supplies belonging, meaning, and support (Tajfel and Turner, 1979; Haslam et al., 2009); it also supplies in-group bias, out-group derogation, and intergroup conflict (Tajfel, 1981; Sidanius and Pratto, 1999). The adaptive stance is to own your identities while managing their risks.

**Plain words** Your group memberships — nationality, profession, gender, faith — are both a resource and a risk. They supply belonging and backup; they can also supply blind spots and walls. Use the membership, watch the edges.

*For example:* The profession that gave you identity, network, and pride — and quietly taught you that other professions are lesser. Same membership, both effects. The skill is keeping the first and auditing the second.
e.c: LAYER V — SOCIAL IDENTITY, GROUPS, AND INTERGROUP RELATIONS
p: Tajfel and Turner (1979) on social identity theory; Haslam et al. (2009) on the social cure; the group-identification and health literature (Jetten et al., 2012); in-group bias and minimal groups (Tajfel et al., 1971).
