f: Stuart Hall — cultural identity as construction — Thinker: Stuart Hall — Reference: Hall (1990). Ricoeur — narrative identity — Thinker: Ricoeur — Reference: Ricoeur (1985), Vol. 3.
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Social identity is the self-dimension of the EEMM at the sociocultural level.
r: In identity work, treat group memberships as sources of support and meaning (see principle 23). In intergroup settings, monitor for in-group bias (see principle 46).

e.t: Guard against in-group bias
e.x:
Guard against in-group bias — the tendency to favor one's own group and derogate others. The minimal-group paradigm (Tajfel et al., 1971) showed that even arbitrary group assignments produce bias. The bias operates through perception (in-group homogeneity effect), evaluation (in-group favoritism), and behavior (discrimination). The adaptive stance is deliberate debiasing.

**Plain words** In-group bias fires even for arbitrary groups — random assignment is enough; the experiments prove it. The bias operates through perception, not malice: your group's flaws look situational, theirs look essential. Knowing the mechanism is most of the defence.

*For example:* "We're under pressure" versus "they're always sloppy" — the same missed deadline, two different explanations, assigned by team colours. That's the bias, running quietly. Everyone's doing it, which is why you check yourself first.
e.c: LAYER V — SOCIAL IDENTITY, GROUPS, AND INTERGROUP RELATIONS
p: Tajfel et al. (1971) on minimal groups; in-group favoritism vs. out-group derogation (Brewer, 1999); out-group homogeneity (Park and Rothbart, 1982); the contact hypothesis and prejudice reduction (Pettigrew and Tropp, 2006; Saguy et al., 2011).
f: Buber — I-Thou — Thinker: Buber — Reference: Buber (1923). Levinas — the ethical priority of the other — Thinker: Levinas — Reference: Levinas (1961).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** In-group bias is the self and cognition dimensions of the EEMM failing at the sociocultural level.
r: In judgment, check whether your evaluation would differ if the person were in-group vs. out-group. In intergroup contact, seek cooperative, equal-status contact (see principle 47).

e.t: Use intergroup contact as a prejudice-reduction tool
e.x:
Use intergroup contact — cooperative, equal-status interaction between members of different groups — as a prejudice-reduction tool. Gordon Allport's contact hypothesis (1954) has substantial meta-analytic support: contact reduces prejudice across a wide range of groups and contexts (Pettigrew and Tropp, 2006). The conditions matter: cooperation, common goals, equal status, and institutional support.

**Plain words** Contact works — cooperative, equal-status interaction across group lines measurably reduces prejudice. Not acquaintance-from-afar; actual working contact. The conditions matter: cooperation, equal footing, common goal. It's the most reliable prejudice-reduction tool we have.

*For example:* The two departments that hated each other until the joint project with shared deadlines — six months later, "those people" became "the folks in analytics, who are actually pretty good at this." Contact did what lectures couldn't.
e.c: LAYER V — SOCIAL IDENTITY, GROUPS, AND INTERGROUP RELATIONS
p: Allport (1954) on the contact hypothesis; Pettigrew and Tropp (2006) meta-analysis; Saguy et al. (2011) on contact and inequality; the extended-contact effect (Wright et al., 1997); the limits of contact (Dixon et al., 2010).
f: Buber — I-Thou — Thinker: Buber — Reference: Buber (1923). Ubuntu — personhood through community — Thinker: Tutu — Reference: Tutu (1999).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Intergroup contact is the sociocultural context's mechanism for reducing intergroup suffering.
r: In intergroup settings, create conditions of cooperative, equal-status contact. In personal life, seek genuine contact across group lines (see principle 33). Recognize that contact alone does not change structures (Dixon et al., 2010).

e.t: Treat discrimination as a health determinant
e.x:
Treat discrimination — unfair treatment based on group membership — as a health determinant. The evidence is substantial: perceived discrimination predicts poorer mental and physical health, including cardiovascular and metabolic outcomes (Pascoe and Smart Richman, 2009; Paradies et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2019; Major et al., 2018). The mechanisms include stress physiology, health behaviors, and access to care.

**Plain words** Discrimination is a health determinant — unfair treatment based on group membership shows up in cardiovascular, metabolic, and mental-health outcomes. This is physiology, not just feelings. When a group has worse health, look at the treatment before the lifestyle.

*For example:* The stress of always being the one watched in the shop, always the one asked to justify your presence — that vigilance has a medical bill attached. The health disparity starts upstream of the clinic.
e.c: LAYER V — SOCIAL IDENTITY, GROUPS, AND INTERGROUP RELATIONS
p: Pascoe and Smart Richman (2009) meta-analysis; Paradies et al. (2015) on racism and health; Williams et al. (2019) on discrimination and health; Major et al. (2018) on stigma and health; Meyer (2003) on minority stress.
f: Arendt — the space of appearance — Thinker: Arendt — Reference: Arendt (1958). Levinas — the ethical priority of the other — Thinker: Levinas — Reference: Levinas (1961).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Discrimination is the sociocultural context generating suffering through the biophysiological level.
r: In health care, screen for discrimination as part of the social history. In policy, treat discrimination reduction as health policy (see principle 75). In personal life, recognize the health impact of discrimination and seek support.

e.t: Treat intersectionality as an analytic lens
e.x:
Treat intersectionality — the analytic framework that examines how multiple group memberships (race, gender, class, sexuality, disability) interact to shape experience and outcomes — as a lens. Kimberlé Crenshaw (1989) introduced the term to capture how Black women's experience was not captured by either race or gender alone. The adaptive stance is to see the person at the intersection, not as a sum of categories.

**Plain words** People sit at intersections — race, gender, class, disability — and the combinations have their own effects, not just the sum of parts. A lens, not a hierarchy of hardships: the point is precision about how experience actually works.

*For example:* "Women face X and Black people face Y" — and the Black woman in the meeting faces neither exactly, but a third thing with its own address. The intersection is real real estate; it's where specific experiences live.
e.c: LAYER V — SOCIAL IDENTITY, GROUPS, AND INTERGROUP RELATIONS
p: Crenshaw (1989) on intersectionality; Cole (2009) on intersectionality in psychology; McCall (2005) on intersectional methodology; Bowleg (2008) on the challenges of intersectionality research; Jones (2000) on levels of racism.
f: Arendt — plurality — Thinker: Arendt — Reference: Arendt (1958). Du Bois — double consciousness — Thinker: Du Bois — Reference: Du Bois (1903).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Intersectionality is the EEMM's pluralism applied to the self at the sociocultural level.
r: In clinical and policy work, attend to the interaction of identities, not just their sum. In research, use intersectional designs (see Cole, 2009).

e.t: Treat minority stress as a mechanism
e.x:
Treat minority stress — the chronic stress experienced by members of stigmatized groups due to prejudice, discrimination, and concealment — as a mechanism of health disparities. Ilan Meyer's model (2003) distinguishes distal stressors (discrimination, violence), proximal stressors (internalized stigma, concealment, vigilance), and resilience factors (community, identity).

**Plain words** Minority stress is a mechanism — chronic extra stress from prejudice, discrimination, and concealment, with health effects that compound over years. Not weakness; weather. Living under a permanent drizzle does measurable damage, whatever the umbrella.

*For example:* The constant low-grade calculus of "is it safe to be fully myself here" — run at every new office, every new neighbourhood — that calculation is the stressor. It's exhausting in a way the majority never runs the software.
e.c: LAYER V — SOCIAL IDENTITY, GROUPS, AND INTERGROUP RELATIONS
p: Meyer (2003) on minority stress; the LGBT-health literature (Institute of Medicine, 2011); internalized stigma (Corrigan et al., 2009); concealment and health (Pachankis, 2007); the stigma-and-health framework (Major and O'Brien, 2005).
f: Levinas — the ethical priority of the other — Thinker: Levinas — Reference: Levinas (1961). Arendt — plurality — Thinker: Arendt — Reference: Arendt (1958).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Minority stress is the sociocultural context generating suffering through the stress physiology of the biophysiological level.
r: In clinical work with stigmatized clients, assess minority stress. In community work, build resilience factors (community, identity, pride). In policy, reduce distal stressors (see principle 75).

e.t: Use group identity for social cure
e.x:
Use group identity for social cure — the well-documented finding that strong, positive group identification predicts better health, well-being, and resilience (Haslam et al., 2009; Jetten et al., 2012). The mechanism is social support, meaning, and collective efficacy. The adaptive stance is to build and use group identities deliberately, alongside the debiasing of principle 46.

**Plain words** Group identity is medicine — strong, positive group identification predicts better health and resilience. The mechanism is support, meaning, and collective self-esteem. The group you belong to can literally be a health intervention. Choose good groups; join them properly.

*For example:* The footy club, the choir, the veterans' group — the members who show up weekly have measurably better decades than the isolated with identical diagnoses. The group is doing pharmacology.
e.c: LAYER V — SOCIAL IDENTITY, GROUPS, AND INTERGROUP RELATIONS
p: Haslam et al. (2009) on the social cure; Jetten et al. (2012) on group identity and health; the group-identification and depression literature (Cruwys et al., 2014); collective efficacy and health (Sampson et al., 1997).
f: Aristotle — the political animal — Thinker: Aristotle — Reference: Nicomachean Ethics, I.7. Ubuntu — personhood through community — Thinker: Tutu — Reference: Tutu (1999).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** The social cure is the sociocultural context supporting the biophysiological level through social identity.
r: In personal life, cultivate group memberships that are positive and supportive (see principle 23). In community work, build collective identity and efficacy (see principle 56).

e.t: Treat collective efficacy as a community resource
e.x:
Treat collective efficacy — a group's shared belief in its capacity to achieve goals — as a community resource. Collective efficacy predicts neighborhood safety, health, and well-being (Sampson et al., 1997). The adaptive stance is to build collective efficacy through successful collective action.

**Plain words** Collective efficacy — a group's shared belief that it can get things done — predicts safer, healthier neighbourhoods. Not optimism; track record plus trust. Communities build it the way individuals build confidence: small wins, stacked.

*For example:* The street that organised one clean-up day, then a crossing campaign, then a park revival — three years on, the whole street believes things can change, because the street keeps changing them. That's collective efficacy compounding.
e.c: LAYER V — SOCIAL IDENTITY, GROUPS, AND INTERGROUP RELATIONS
p: Sampson et al. (1997) on collective efficacy and neighborhood violence; Bandura (2000) on collective efficacy; community empowerment (Wallerstein, 2006); the community-capacity literature (Goodman et al., 1998).
f: Dewey — democracy as experimental — Thinker: Dewey — Reference: Dewey (1916). Arendt — action in plurality — Thinker: Arendt — Reference: Arendt (1958).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Collective efficacy is the sociocultural context's motivational dimension.
r: In community organizing, start with achievable wins to build efficacy (see principle 56). In personal life, join groups that have a track record of efficacy.

e.t: Treat status as a real but manageable variable
e.x:
Treat status — one's position in a social hierarchy — as a real but manageable variable. Status predicts health through the social gradient (Marmot, 2004); the Whitehall studies showed that civil servants' health tracked their rank, even among those not in poverty. The mechanisms include control, stress, and dignity. The adaptive stance is to manage status concerns rather than deny them.

**Plain words** Status is a real biological variable — health tracks rank, even among people who aren't poor. The gradient runs through autonomy, respect, and control over life. The lesson isn't to chase status; it's to build environments with less rank-related stress.

*For example:* The civil servants one grade down with worse heart health than the grade above — same income bracket, different status. The body reads the org chart. Respect and control are nutrients.
e.c: LAYER V — SOCIAL IDENTITY, GROUPS, AND INTERGROUP RELATIONS
p: Marmot (2004) on status syndrome; the Whitehall studies (Marmot et al., 1978, 1991); status and health (Sapolsky, 2005); the psychosocial-gradient literature (Wilkinson and Pickett, 2009).
f: Aristotle — magnanimity (megalopsychia) — Thinker: Aristotle — Reference: Nicomachean Ethics, IV.3. Nietzsche — the will to power as life — Thinker: Nietzsche — Reference: Nietzsche (1883–85).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Status is the motivational dimension of the EEMM at the sociocultural level.
r: In status pursuit, distinguish earned status (competence, contribution) from dominance (force, fear). In health, recognize that status loss (retirement, unemployment) is a health risk and plan for it.

e.t: Treat social class as a real variable
e.x:
Treat social class — one's position in the economic and cultural hierarchy — as a real variable, not a taboo. Class shapes health, education, opportunity, and culture (Bourdieu, 1984; Lareau, 2011). The adaptive stance is to see class clearly, without shame or contempt.

**Plain words** Class is real — it shapes health, education, opportunity, and culture. Neither taboo nor destiny. See it clearly: the habitus you inherited, the capital you have or lack. Not shame, not pride — accuracy.

*For example:* "We don't talk about money" and "the right schools" — class is a set of inherited instructions nobody hands you the manual for. Naming the class effects out loud is how they stop running your life silently.
e.c: LAYER V — SOCIAL IDENTITY, GROUPS, AND INTERGROUP RELATIONS
p: Bourdieu (1984) on cultural capital; Lareau (2011) on class and childrearing; the social-class and health literature (Adler and Stewart, 2010); class and cognition (Kraus et al., 2012); scarcity (Mullainathan and Shafir, 2013).
f: Marx — class as a social relation — Thinker: Marx — Reference: Marx (1867). Bourdieu — habitus — Thinker: Bourdieu — Reference: Bourdieu (1984).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Class is the sociocultural context's economic dimension.
r: In cross-class interactions, notice your own class assumptions (see principle 22). In policy, treat class-based health disparities as designable (see principle 75). In personal life, recognize the cognitive effects of scarcity (Mullainathan and Shafir, 2013).

e.t: Treat gender as a cultural system
e.x:
Treat gender — the social meanings and roles attached to sex — as a cultural system, not a biological destiny. Gender shapes health, behavior, and well-being through norms, expectations, and structures (Ridgeway, 2011; Connell, 2002). The adaptive stance is to see gender as a system and to navigate it deliberately.

**Plain words** Gender is a cultural system layered on biology — norms, expectations, structures. Not a biological destiny, and not imaginary either: real effects on health, behaviour, and opportunity. The system can be examined and reformed, by you, in your own house.

*For example:* "Boys don't cry" and "girls aren't good at maths" — instructions, delivered early, billed as observations. The system runs on people repeating it. Examining it at your own kitchen table is how it stops.
e.c: LAYER V — SOCIAL IDENTITY, GROUPS, AND INTERGROUP RELATIONS
p: Ridgeway (2011) on gender as a system of social relations; Connell (2002) on gender; the gender-and-health literature (Bird and Rieker, 2008); gender norms and well-being (Heilman et al., 2017); the role-congruence literature (Eagly and Karau, 2002).
f: de Beauvoir — one is not born a woman — Thinker: de Beauvoir — Reference: de Beauvoir (1949). Butler — gender performativity — Thinker: Butler — Reference: Butler (1990).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Gender is the sociocultural context's role system.
r: In gender relations, notice norms and their enforcement (see principle 32). In identity work, treat your gender identity as a legitimate form of self. In health, recognize gender differences in help-seeking and diagnosis.

e.t: Design institutions for flourishing
e.x:
Design institutions — workplaces, schools, hospitals, governments, and the built environment — for adaptive flourishing, not only for efficiency or profit. The nurturing-environments framework (Biglan et al., 2012) and the population-prevention literature (Wahlbeck et al., 2015) show that environments can be designed to reduce suffering and promote flourishing.

**Plain words** Institutions can be designed for flourishing, not just efficiency — workplaces, schools, hospitals, the built environment. The evidence exists: nurturing environments are buildable. The only question is whether flourishing is on the design brief.

*For example:* The hospital designed around patient recovery — light, quiet, gardens — versus the one designed around staff logistics. Same medicine, different outcomes. The building was practising healthcare.
e.c: LAYER VI — INSTITUTIONAL AND ECOLOGICAL DESIGN
p: Biglan et al. (2012) on nurturing environments; Institute of Medicine (2009) on prevention; Wahlbeck et al. (2015) on population-level prevention; WHO (2022) World Mental Health Report; Ostrom (1990) on institutional design; nudge and choice architecture (Thaler and Sunstein, 2008).
f: Dewey — democracy as a way of life — Thinker: Dewey — Reference: Dewey (1916). Whitehead — the social function of education — Thinker: Whitehead — Reference: Whitehead (1929).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Institutional design is the EEMM's context-selection at the sociocultural level.
r: In workplace design, build for autonomy, belonging, and purpose (see principle 57). In school design, build for belonging and growth (see principle 58). In policy, use well-being measures alongside economic ones (see principle 65).

e.t: Design workplaces for flourishing
e.x:
Design workplaces for adaptive flourishing. The evidence is substantial: autonomy-supportive management, psychological safety, work-life balance, and fair pay predict well-being, productivity, and retention (Deci and Ryan, 2000; Edmondson, 1999; Warr, 1987; Karasek, 1979). The demand-control-support model (Karasek and Theorell, 1990) shows that high demand with low control and low support is the harmful combination.

**Plain words** Workplaces can be designed for flourishing: autonomy-supportive management, psychological safety, balance, fair pay. These predict well-being and productivity — the business case and the human case point the same way. Culture isn't a poster; it's a design decision.

*For example:* The team where you can say "I don't know" without a penalty — versus the one where admitting error is career damage. One of these teams learns faster and burns out slower. The design did that.
e.c: LAYER VI — INSTITUTIONAL AND ECOLOGICAL DESIGN
p: Karasek (1979) and Karasek and Theorell (1990) on demand-control-support; Edmondson (1999) on psychological safety; Deci and Ryan (2000) on autonomy support; Warr (1987) on work and well-being; the job-demands-resources model (Demerouti et al., 2001).
f: Aristotle — work and leisure — Thinker: Aristotle — Reference: Nicomachean Ethics, X.7. Dewey — occupation as inquiry — Thinker: Dewey — Reference: Dewey (1916).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Workplace design is the sociocultural context's most direct influence on adult daily life.
r: In management, provide autonomy, clear expectations, and support. In job design, match demands to resources. In career choice, weigh autonomy and purpose alongside pay.

e.t: Design schools for flourishing
e.x:
Design schools for adaptive flourishing. The evidence: belonging interventions improve achievement (Walton and Cohen, 2011); social-emotional learning improves academic and life outcomes (Durlak et al., 2011); growth-mindset interventions improve achievement for at-risk students (Yeager et al., 2019).

**Plain words** Schools can be designed for flourishing — belonging improves achievement, social-emotional learning improves everything, growth-mindset interventions help. Education isn't just content delivery; it's environment design for developing humans.

*For example:* The school that spent the first week on belonging exercises — "everyone's new here, everyone struggles" — and watched the failure rate drop. The algebra didn't change; the feeling of being alone in it did.
e.c: LAYER VI — INSTITUTIONAL AND ECOLOGICAL DESIGN
p: Walton and Cohen (2011) on belonging interventions; Durlak et al. (2011) on social-emotional learning; Yeager et al. (2019) on growth mindset; the school-climate literature (Thapa et al., 2013); the Zone of Proximal Development (Vygotsky, 1978).
f: Vygotsky — the ZPD — Thinker: Vygotsky — Reference: Vygotsky (1978). Dewey — education as growth — Thinker: Dewey — Reference: Dewey (1916).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** School design is the sociocultural context's most direct influence on child and adolescent development.
r: In teaching, build belonging and psychological safety. In curriculum, include social-emotional learning. In assessment, use mastery-oriented rather than performance-oriented feedback.

e.t: Design neighborhoods for flourishing
e.x:
Design neighborhoods — the physical and social environment of daily life — for adaptive flourishing. The evidence: walkable neighborhoods, green space, and social cohesion predict physical activity, mental health, and well-being (Diez Roux and Mair, 2010; Branas et al., 2011; Sampson et al., 1997).

**Plain words** Neighbourhoods are health infrastructure — walkability, green space, and social cohesion predict activity, mental health, and connection. Your postcode does more daily biology than your GP. Invest in the design of where you live.

*For example:* The same person, two addresses — one with a park and a corner shop, one with neither — two different activity levels, two different social lives. The address was prescribing.
e.c: LAYER VI — INSTITUTIONAL AND ECOLOGICAL DESIGN
p: Diez Roux and Mair (2010) on neighborhoods and health; Branas et al. (2011) on green space and violence; Sampson et al. (1997) on collective efficacy; the built-environment literature (Jackson, 2003); nature and well-being (Hartig et al., 2014; White et al., 2019).
f: Aristotle — the polis — Thinker: Aristotle — Reference: Nicomachean Ethics, I.7. Jacobs — the death and life of great American cities — Thinker: Jacobs — Reference: Jacobs (1961).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Neighborhood design is the sociocultural context's physical infrastructure.
r: In neighborhood choice, prioritize walkability, green space, and social cohesion. In civic engagement, support neighborhood improvement. In daily life, use green space deliberately.

e.t: Design digital environments for flourishing
e.x:
Design digital environments — social media, platforms, and the online public sphere — for adaptive flourishing. The evidence is mixed but concerning: passive social-media use predicts lower well-being (Verduyn et al., 2017; Kross et al., 2013), while active use and connection predict higher well-being (Valkenburg et al., 2022). The design of platforms — algorithmic feeds, engagement metrics, notification — shapes outcomes (see principle 76).

**Plain words** Digital environments are designed environments — feeds, autoplay, engagement metrics. Passive use harms; active connection helps. The environment is adjustable: curate it like a garden, not a weather system you merely endure.

*For example:* The same app, used to message three friends versus scrolled for two hours — two different mental-health outcomes. The tool isn't neutral; the usage pattern is the design.
e.c: LAYER VI — INSTITUTIONAL AND ECOLOGICAL DESIGN
p: Verduyn et al. (2017) on passive vs. active use; Kross et al. (2013) on Facebook and well-being; Valkenburg et al. (2022) on social media and well-being; Twenge et al. (2018) on smartphones and adolescent mental health; the digital-wellbeing literature (Vanden Abeele, 2021).
f: Arendt — the space of appearance — Thinker: Arendt — Reference: Arendt (1958). Habermas — the public sphere — Thinker: Habermas — Reference: Habermas (1962).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Digital environments are the sociocultural context's attentional infrastructure.
r: In personal use, prefer active (messaging, creating) to passive (scrolling) use. In platform design, build for connection and well-being rather than engagement alone. In parenting, treat digital environments as designable (see principle 76).

e.t: Treat economic inequality as a health determinant
e.x:
Treat economic inequality — the gap between rich and poor — as a health determinant. The Spirit Level literature (Wilkinson and Pickett, 2009) argues that more unequal societies have worse health and social outcomes; the evidence is debated but substantial (Pickett and Wilkinson, 2015; for critiques, see Snowdon, 2010).

**Plain words** Inequality is a health determinant in itself — more unequal societies have worse outcomes across the board, including for the people near the top. The gap does biology, not just economics. Care about the ratio, not just your own number.

*For example:* The wealthier-but-unequal society with worse health than its poorer-but-equal neighbour — the average income was higher; the trust and health were lower. The gap was the exposure.
e.c: LAYER VI — INSTITUTIONAL AND ECOLOGICAL DESIGN
p: Wilkinson and Pickett (2009); Pickett and Wilkinson (2015) on inequality and health; the status-anxiety mechanism (Marmot, 2004); the social-capital mechanism (Kawachi and Berkman, 2000); critiques (Snowdon, 2010).
f: Rawls — justice as fairness — Thinker: Rawls — Reference: Rawls (1971). Sen — capability and equality — Thinker: Sen — Reference: Sen (1999).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Inequality is the sociocultural context's distributional dimension.
r: In policy, treat inequality reduction as health policy (see principle 75). In personal life, recognize the stress of status comparison in unequal environments (see principle 31).

e.t: Treat social capital as a community resource
e.x:
Treat social capital — the networks, norms, and trust that enable collective action — as a community resource. Robert Putnam (2000) documented the decline of social capital in America (Bowling Alone); the health literature shows that social capital predicts health outcomes (Kawachi et al., 1999).

**Plain words** Social capital — networks, norms, trust — is a community resource that can be built and spent. It's been declining for decades. You build it with boring things: showing up, joining, reciprocating. The compound interest is real.

*For example:* The bowling league, the church committee, the parents' group — the "pointless" meetings that turn out to be the infrastructure of a functioning neighbourhood. Decline them all and find out what they were holding up.
e.c: LAYER VI — INSTITUTIONAL AND ECOLOGICAL DESIGN
p: Putnam (2000) on social capital; Kawachi et al. (1999) on social capital and health; bonding vs. bridging social capital (Putnam, 2000); the collective-efficacy literature (Sampson et al., 1997).
f: Tocqueville — associations in America — Thinker: Tocqueville — Reference: Tocqueville (1835). Dewey — democracy as association — Thinker: Dewey — Reference: Dewey (1916).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Social capital is the sociocultural context's cooperation infrastructure.
r: In community building, cultivate both bonding (within-group) and bridging (across-group) capital. In civic engagement, participate in associations (see principle 56).

e.t: Treat migration and acculturation as a designable process
e.x:
Treat migration and acculturation — the process of adapting to a new cultural context — as a designable process, not a natural disaster. John Berry's model (1997) distinguishes four strategies: integration (maintaining the heritage culture while adopting the host culture), assimilation (abandoning the heritage culture), separation (maintaining the heritage culture without adopting the host culture), and marginalization (abandoning both). Integration predicts the best outcomes; marginalization the worst.

**Plain words** Migration and acculturation are designable processes, not natural disasters — Berry's model: integrate (keep heritage, adopt the new), assimilate, separate, marginalise. Integration — both — consistently does best. You can steer this; many people don't know it's steerable.

*For example:* The family that keeps the language, the food, and the festivals while adopting the new country's civic life — kids in both worlds, fluent in both. That's integration, and it's the healthiest build on the menu.
e.c: LAYER VI — INSTITUTIONAL AND ECOLOGICAL DESIGN
p: Berry (1997, 2005) on acculturation; Sam and Berry (2010) on acculturation and well-being; Virta et al. (2004) on identity and acculturation; the immigration paradox (Marks et al., 2014); the segmented-assimilation literature (Portes and Zhou, 1993).
f: Gadamer — the fusion of horizons — Thinker: Gadamer — Reference: Gadamer (1960), Part II. Stuart Hall — cultural identity as construction — Thinker: Stuart Hall — Reference: Hall (1990).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Acculturation is the EEMM's context-change mechanism at the sociocultural level.
r: See principle 73 for the full acculturation-strategy guidance. In policy, support integration rather than assimilation or separation (see principle 75).

e.t: Treat cultural adaptation of interventions as a necessity
e.x:
Treat the cultural adaptation of interventions — modifying psychological treatments, prevention programs, and public-health interventions for specific cultural contexts — as a necessity, not an optional refinement. Evidence-based interventions developed in WEIRD contexts do not automatically transfer; adaptation improves outcomes (Castro et al., 2010; Gone, 2011; Hall et al., 2016).

**Plain words** Interventions need cultural adaptation — a programme that works in one context needs translation to work in another. Not optional refinement; core engineering. Evidence-based plus culture-adapted, or it isn't evidence-based here.

*For example:* The therapy protocol imported wholesale into a culture where talking about family shame to a stranger is itself the pathology — the technique was fine; the delivery was broken. Adapted, it works. Unadapted, it doesn't arrive.
e.c: LAYER VI — INSTITUTIONAL AND ECOLOGICAL DESIGN
p: Castro et al. (2010) on cultural adaptation; Gone (2011) on Indigenous healing; Hall et al. (2016) on cultural adaptation of cognitive-behavioral therapy; the cultural-formulation approach (Lewis-Fernández and Aggarwal, 2015); the global-mental-health literature (Patel et al., 2010).
f: Gadamer — the fusion of horizons — Thinker: Gadamer — Reference: Gadamer (1960), Part II. Herder — cultural pluralism — Thinker: Herder — Reference: Herder (1774).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Cultural adaptation is the EEMM's variation-selection-retention applied to interventions.
r: In clinical work, use the cultural-formulation interview (see principle 72). In program design, adapt rather than transplant. In global mental health, task-share and adapt (Patel et al., 2010).

e.t: Use well-being measures in policy
e.x:
Use well-being measures in policy, alongside economic measures. The OECD's 2013 Guidelines on Measuring Subjective Well-being established a standard framework; national well-being accounts now exist in the UK, New Zealand, and elsewhere. The adaptive stance is to treat well-being as a design criterion of policy, not a byproduct.

**Plain words** Well-being can be measured at the national level and used in policy — the frameworks exist, some governments use them. GDP was also once a new idea. What gets measured gets governed. Ask your policymakers what they're measuring.

*For example:* The country that asks "how is life going?" alongside "how is the economy?" in official statistics — a boring administrative change that quietly reorders what counts as success. The spreadsheet is the policy.
e.c: LAYER VI — INSTITUTIONAL AND ECOLOGICAL DESIGN
p: OECD (2013) Guidelines; Diener (2000) on subjective well-being; Clark et al. (2018) on the economics of well-being; the International Wellbeing Group's framework (Foundations, 2017; Holmes, 2022); national well-being accounting (Veenhoven, 2010; Andonian, 2017).
f: Aristotle — phronesis in politics — Thinker: Aristotle — Reference: Nicomachean Ethics, VI. Bentham and Mill — utility and policy — Thinker: Bentham, Mill — Reference: Bentham (1789); Mill (1863).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Well-being measurement is the EEMM's measurement principle (principle 9) applied at the policy level.
r: In policy evaluation, include well-being measures alongside GDP and health indicators. In advocacy, use well-being data to make the case for prevention (see principle 75).

e.t: Treat marginalization as a clinical and social issue
e.x:
Treat marginalization — the social exclusion of individuals or groups from full participation in society — as both a clinical and a social issue. Marginalization predicts poor mental and physical health (Meyer, 2003; Paradies et al., 2015); it also requires social, not only individual, intervention.

**Plain words** Marginalisation is both a clinical and a social issue — exclusion from full participation damages health, and the treatment is partly clinical, partly structural. A therapist can help you cope with the wall; only policy moves the wall.

*For example:* The client's depression is real and treatable — and partly caused by the housing policy that concentrated disadvantage on their street. Treat the person; name the cause. Both are clinical acts.
e.c: LAYER VII — SPECIFIC SOCIOCULTURAL CHALLENGES & BOUNDARY CONDITIONS
p: The marginalization literature (Berry, 1997; Sam and Berry, 2010); collective self-esteem and marginalization (Crocker et al., 1994); minority stress (Meyer, 2003); the health-effects literature (Paradies et al., 2015).
f: Levinas — the ethical priority of the other — Thinker: Levinas — Reference: Levinas (1961). Arendt — the right to have rights — Thinker: Arendt — Reference: Arendt (1951).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Marginalization is the sociocultural context generating suffering through both the biophysiological and sociocultural levels.
r: In clinical work, assess marginalization as part of the cultural formulation (see principle 72). In social work, treat marginalization as a target of intervention (see principle 75). In personal life, recognize marginalization as a health risk and seek support.

e.t: Treat intergenerational trauma as a real mechanism
e.x:
Treat intergenerational trauma — the transmission of trauma effects from one generation to the next through family, culture, and epigenetics — as a real mechanism. The evidence includes historical trauma in Indigenous communities (Whitbeck et al., 2004; Gone, 2011), Holocaust survivor families (Yehuda et al., 2015), and the epigenetics of trauma (Yehuda et al., 2016; for caution, see Heard et al., 2018).

**Plain words** Intergenerational trauma is a real mechanism — transmitted through family, culture, and even biology. What happened to grandparents shows up in grandchildren's stress systems. Not destiny; inheritance. And inheritances can be worked with.

*For example:* The family where nobody spoke of the war, and the grandchildren flinch at raised voices without knowing why — the silence was the transmission. Naming it, telling it, ritualising it: that's how the chain gets edited.
e.c: LAYER VII — SPECIFIC SOCIOCULTURAL CHALLENGES & BOUNDARY CONDITIONS
p: Whitbeck et al. (2004) on historical trauma; Gone (2011) on Indigenous healing; Yehuda et al. (2015, 2016) on intergenerational trauma and epigenetics; the critique of the epigenetic literature (Heard et al., 2018); the family-transmission literature (Solomon et al., 2014).
f: Arendt — the banality of evil — Thinker: Arendt — Reference: Arendt (1963). Ricoeur — memory, history, forgetting — Thinker: Ricoeur — Reference: Ricoeur (2000).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Intergenerational trauma is the sociocultural context generating suffering across generations.
r: In clinical work with affected communities, use trauma-informed and culturally grounded approaches (see principle 72). In community work, support collective healing (Gone, 2011).

e.t: Treat rapid social change as a stressor
e.x:
Treat rapid social change — technological, economic, and cultural change — as a stressor. The mechanisms include the disruption of social networks, the loss of cultural meaning, and the acceleration of daily life (Rosa, 2013; Rosa and Trejo-Mathys, 2013).

**Plain words** Rapid social change is a stressor in its own right — disrupted networks, lost meanings, accelerated pace. Not an excuse, an exposure. The treatment is partly community: keeping the threads while the fabric changes.

*For example:* The village-to-city generation with higher illness rates than either village or city natives — the move itself was the exposure. The ones who kept their associations and festivals did better. The threads were the treatment.
e.c: LAYER VII — SPECIFIC SOCIOCULTURAL CHALLENGES & BOUNDARY CONDITIONS
p: The social-change literature (Inglehart and Welzel, 2005); cultural mismatch and acculturative stress (Berry, 1997); acceleration (Rosa, 2013); the digital-wellbeing literature (Vanden Abeele, 2021; Valkenburg et al., 2022).
f: Whitehead — the social function of education in change — Thinker: Whitehead — Reference: Whitehead (1929). Dewey — reconstruction — Thinker: Dewey — Reference: Dewey (1920).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Rapid social change is the EEMM's context dimension changing faster than the biophysiological level can adapt.
r: In periods of change, prioritize social connection (see principle 23) and meaning. In community work, build resilience through connection and identity (see principle 51).

e.t: Treat cultural bereavement as a real loss
e.x:
Treat cultural bereavement — the grief experienced by migrants and refugees at the loss of their homeland, language, and culture — as a real loss, not a vague nostalgia. Cultural bereavement is a recognized clinical syndrome (Eisenbruch, 1991; Papadopoulos, 2007).

**Plain words** Cultural bereavement is real grief — the loss of homeland, language, and world, experienced by migrants and refugees. Not vague nostalgia; a recognised clinical loss. Grieve it properly. It deserves the same respect as any bereavement.

*For example:* The grandfather weeping at a song from the old country, dismissed as "being sentimental" — that was a funeral for a whole world. It deserves the courtesy we give every funeral.
e.c: LAYER VII — SPECIFIC SOCIOCULTURAL CHALLENGES & BOUNDARY CONDITIONS
p: Eisenbruch (1991) on cultural bereavement; Papadopoulos (2007) on refugee mental health; the migration-and-mental-health literature (Bhugra, 2004); the refugee-trauma literature (Fazel et al., 2005).
f: Ricoeur — narrative identity — Thinker: Ricoeur — Reference: Ricoeur (1985), Vol. 3. Mauss — the gift and the bond — Thinker: Mauss — Reference: Mauss (1954).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Cultural bereavement is the affect-dimension of the EEMM responding to the loss of the sociocultural context.
r: In clinical work with migrants and refugees, assess cultural bereavement (see principle 72). In personal life, treat the grief of migration as legitimate and seek support.

e.t: Treat climate change as a sociocultural stressor
e.x:
Treat climate change — and its social effects (displacement, conflict, economic disruption) — as a sociocultural stressor. The evidence includes climate anxiety (Hickman et al., 2021), displacement (McLeman and Smit, 2006), and the mental-health effects of extreme weather (Berry et al., 2010).

**Plain words** Climate change is a sociocultural stressor — displacement, conflict, anxiety — with mental-health effects already measurable. Not a future problem; a current exposure. The coping is partly collective, which is unusual: this one is processed better together.

*For example:* The young people carrying measurable eco-anxiety — the distress is not pathology; it's an accurate response to real data. What helps is action in company. The anxiety is the alarm working.
e.c: LAYER VII — SPECIFIC SOCIOCULTURAL CHALLENGES & BOUNDARY CONDITIONS
p: Hickman et al. (2021) on climate anxiety; the climate-and-mental-health literature (Berry et al., 2010; Doherty and Clayton, 2011); climate displacement (McLeman and Smit, 2006); the solastalgia concept (Albrecht et al., 2007).
f: Whitehead — the organism-environment unity — Thinker: Whitehead — Reference: Whitehead (1933), Part IV, Ch. I. Arendt — action in plurality — Thinker: Arendt — Reference: Arendt (1958).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Climate change is the EEMM's context dimension at planetary scale.
r: In climate anxiety, distinguish functional concern from paralyzing despair. In collective action, treat climate response as a project of adaptive flourishing (see principle 56).

e.t: Treat loneliness in older adults as a public-health issue
e.x:
Treat loneliness in older adults — the social disconnection of ageing — as a public-health issue. Social isolation in older adults predicts mortality, dementia, and depression (Holt-Lunstad et al., 2010, 2017; Wilson et al., 2007).

**Plain words** Loneliness in older adults is a public-health issue — isolation predicts mortality, dementia, and depression. The treatment is community infrastructure, not just individual effort. Visit your older neighbours; it's not charity, it's medicine.

*For example:* The regular visitor programme that measurably reduces hospital admissions — the visitors aren't bringing medical care, they're bringing the thing the body was missing: company. The prescription was social.
e.c: LAYER VII — SPECIFIC SOCIOCULTURAL CHALLENGES & BOUNDARY CONDITIONS
p: Holt-Lunstad et al. (2010, 2017) on social isolation and mortality; Wilson et al. (2007) on loneliness and dementia; the ageing-and-social-connection literature (Cornwell and Waite, 2009); the elder-orphan problem (Carney et al., 2016).
f: Aristotle — friendship in the later life — Thinker: Aristotle — Reference: Nicomachean Ethics, VIII–IX. Cicero — On Old Age — Thinker: Cicero — Reference: Cicero (44 BC).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Loneliness in older adults is the sociocultural context generating suffering through the biophysiological level.
r: In ageing, prioritize social connection (see principle 23). In community design, build for intergenerational contact (see principle 59). In policy, treat social isolation as a health risk (see principle 75).

e.t: Use cultural formulation in clinical practice
e.x:
Use the cultural-formulation interview (CFI) in clinical practice. The CFI, part of the DSM-5, is a structured way to elicit the client's cultural understanding of their distress, its causes, and its appropriate treatment (Lewis-Fernández and Aggarwal, 2015; Aggarwal et al., 2016). It is the clinical instrument of principles 22 and 64.

**Plain words** The cultural formulation interview — a structured way to ask what the client's culture says about their distress and its proper treatment. Ten questions, better care. Your culture's story about your illness is clinically relevant data.

*For example:* "What do your family and friends think caused this?" — the answer that reveals the whole treatment context. The spirits, the curse, the imbalance, the chemistry: all of it is clinically relevant. Ask, don't assume.
e.c: LAYER VII — SPECIFIC SOCIOCULTURAL CHALLENGES & BOUNDARY CONDITIONS
p: Lewis-Fernández and Aggarwal (2015) on the CFI; Aggarwal et al. (2016) on the CFI's use; the cultural-competence literature (Sue et al., 2009); cultural humility in therapy (Hook et al., 2013).
f: Gadamer — the fusion of horizons — Thinker: Gadamer — Reference: Gadamer (1960), Part II. Buber — I-Thou — Thinker: Buber — Reference: Buber (1923).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** The CFI is the clinical instrument of the EEMM's sociocultural level.
r: In clinical assessment, use the CFI to elicit the client's cultural model. In treatment planning, adapt interventions to the cultural context (see principle 64). In supervision, attend to cultural dynamics.

e.t: Use acculturation strategies deliberately
e.x:
Use acculturation strategies — Berry's integration, assimilation, separation, and marginalization (1997) — deliberately, especially in migration and cultural transition. Integration (maintaining heritage culture while adopting the host culture) predicts the best outcomes; marginalization (losing both) predicts the worst. The choice is not automatic; it is a decision.

**Plain words** Acculturation strategies can be chosen — integration, assimilation, separation, marginalisation. Integration (heritage plus the new) does best on the outcomes. Most people drift; you can steer. Knowing the menu is the first move.

*For example:* The migrant who deliberately keeps the mother tongue at home and the local language at work — that's not divided loyalty, it's the integration strategy, chosen. The ones who choose do better than the ones who drift.
e.c: LAYER VII — SPECIFIC SOCIOCULTURAL CHALLENGES & BOUNDARY CONDITIONS
p: Berry (1997, 2005); Sam and Berry (2010) on acculturation and well-being; Virta et al. (2004) on identity; the immigration paradox (Marks et al., 2014); the biculturalism literature (Benet-Martínez and Haritatos, 2005; Huynh et al., 2011).
f: Gadamer — the fusion of horizons — Thinker: Gadamer — Reference: Gadamer (1960), Part II. Stuart Hall — cultural identity as construction — Thinker: Stuart Hall — Reference: Hall (1990).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Acculturation strategy is the EEMM's context-selection at the individual level.
r: See principle 63 for the policy version. In personal migration, choose integration: maintain your heritage culture while learning the host culture. In second-generation identity, use bicultural identity integration (see principle 74).

e.t: Use bicultural identity integration as a strength
e.x:
Use bicultural identity integration — the capacity to hold two cultural identities without conflict, and to switch between them fluently — as a strength. Bicultural integration predicts well-being and creativity (Benet-Martínez et al., 2002; Benet-Martínez and Haritatos, 2005; Saad et al., 2013).

**Plain words** Bicultural identity integration is a strength — holding two cultural identities without conflict, switching fluently. It predicts well-being and creativity. The bilingual of selves. Not confusion; range.

*For example:* The person who is one self at the family table and another at the office, fluent in both, translating constantly — it looks like burden and measures as creativity. The switching itself is the skill.
e.c: LAYER VII — SPECIFIC SOCIOCULTURAL CHALLENGES & BOUNDARY CONDITIONS
p: Benet-Martínez et al. (2002) on bicultural identity integration; Benet-Martínez and Haritatos (2005) on BII and well-being; cultural frame-switching (Hong et al., 2000); the biculturalism-and-creativity literature (Saad et al., 2013); the bicultural stress literature (Sirin et al., 2013).
f: Stuart Hall — cultural identity as construction — Thinker: Stuart Hall — Reference: Hall (1990). Du Bois — double consciousness — Thinker: Du Bois — Reference: Du Bois (1903).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Bicultural identity integration is the self-dimension of the EEMM thriving at the sociocultural level.
r: In bicultural life, treat both identities as legitimate (see principle 11). In code-switching, treat it as fluency, not inauthenticity. In bicultural stress, seek support (see principle 72).

e.t: Use systems-level intervention for social suffering
e.x:
Use systems-level intervention — policy, community programs, and institutional change — for social suffering. Individual therapy cannot treat the social determinants of health; systems-level intervention is required (Biglan et al., 2012; Wahlbeck et al., 2015; WHO, 2022; O'Connor et al., 2022).

**Plain words** Some suffering needs systems-level treatment — policy, programmes, institutional change. Individual therapy can't treat a social determinant. The skill for helpers: treat the person and name the cause. The naming is not radical; it's clinical accuracy.

*For example:* The therapist whose client's insomnia is partly the shift-work schedule — the sleep hygiene is real and the schedule is the cause. Treating the person while advocating for the schedule is the complete treatment.
e.c: LAYER VII — SPECIFIC SOCIOCULTURAL CHALLENGES & BOUNDARY CONDITIONS
p: Biglan et al. (2012) on nurturing environments; Wahlbeck et al. (2015) on population prevention; WHO (2022) World Mental Health Report; O'Connor et al. (2022) on suicide prevention; the social-determinants literature (Marmot and Wilkinson, 2006; WHO, 2010).
f: Dewey — democracy as experimental — Thinker: Dewey — Reference: Dewey (1916). Rawls — justice as fairness — Thinker: Rawls — Reference: Rawls (1971).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Systems-level intervention is the EEMM's context-selection at the policy level.
r: In advocacy, use the evidence base for prevention (Biglan et al., 2012). In policy, treat social determinants as health policy (see principle 65). In community work, build collective efficacy (see principle 52).

e.t: Treat digital and technological change as a designable environment
e.x:
Treat digital and technological change — social media, AI, and the online public sphere — as a designable environment, not an inevitable fate. The evidence on digital well-being is mixed but actionable: passive use harms well-being, active use helps; algorithmic feeds shape attention and comparison; design choices matter (Verduyn et al., 2017; Valkenburg et al., 2022; Vanden Abeele, 2021).

**Plain words** The digital world is a designable environment, not an inevitable fate — the evidence is mixed but actionable: passive use harms, active use can help, design steers both. You're the designer of your own usage, and partly, of your community's. Treat it as architecture, not weather.

*For example:* The household that redesigned its digital defaults — devices out of bedrooms, one screen-free day — not by willpower, but by moving the furniture. The environment changed; the behaviour followed. That's design, working.
e.c: LAYER VII — SPECIFIC SOCIOCULTURAL CHALLENGES & BOUNDARY CONDITIONS
p: Verduyn et al. (2017) on passive vs. active use; Valkenburg et al. (2022) on social media and well-being; the digital-wellbeing literature (Vanden Abeele, 2021); the attention-economy critique (Wu, 2016; Zuboff, 2019); adolescent mental health and technology (Twenge et al., 2018; Orben and Przybylski, 2019).
f: Arendt — the space of appearance — Thinker: Arendt — Reference: Arendt (1958). Habermas — the public sphere — Thinker: Habermas — Reference: Habermas (1962).
**Other:**, **EEMM link:** Digital environments are the EEMM's attentional and social context at the designable level.
r: In personal use, prefer active to passive, curate feeds, and set time boundaries. In platform design, build for well-being (see principle 60). In parenting, treat digital environments as designable (see principle 58).

e.t: Reflective listening: guess the meaning
e.x: When someone tells you something, don't just repeat their words back. Make a *guess* at what they mean underneath, and say the guess as a statement. "I'm feeling kind of down today" → "Like you don't have much energy." If your guess lands, the conversation deepens; if it misses, they correct you, and the correction is itself information.
e.c: 9. Social and Relational
p: Complex reflections are a core clinical MI skill; the research base is for clinician-delivered MI, and this self-use adaptation has not been directly tested (indirect evidence).

e.t: The "Yes, but" flip
e.x: Notice when your own change-talk gets cancelled by a "but": "I really want to work out regularly, but I am so busy." Drapkin calls these "Yes, but's" — you give yourself some change talk and then snatch it back.
e.c: 5. Values and Motivation
p: Drapkin cites the MI literature that more change talk predicts more behavior change (reported by the source book); the specific "but → and" self-talk move is her lay adaptation and has not been independently tested.

e.t: Notice your reactance: the push-back hand
e.x: Try this with a friend: put your palms together and start gently pushing. Most of the time, they push back — not out of ill will, but because being pushed makes humans push back. That's reactance.
e.c: 9. Social and Relational
p: Psychological reactance (Brehm) is an established construct; the palm-pushing demo is an illustrative teaching device, not an empirical claim (conceptual parallel).

e.t: The autonomy statement
e.x: When someone is ambivalent about a change (or when you're coaching yourself), try saying the autonomy statement out loud: "It's your call. You're the one who gets to decide." Said to a friend, this removes the pressure of you being the push-back hand. Said to yourself, it removes the coercion from your own inner voice.
e.c: 5. Values and Motivation
p: Autonomy support is a core MI stance with clinical support; the specific self-use phrasing here is an adaptation (indirect evidence).

e.t: Ask, Offer, Ask
e.x: Before you tell someone what to do, ask permission: "Would it be OK if I mention a few possibilities?" If yes, give the advice briefly. Then ask again: "What do you make of that? Does any of it fit for you?"
e.c: 9. Social and Relational
p: Ask–Offer–Ask is part of clinical MI protocols; the lay version has not been directly tested (indirect evidence).

e.t: Importance and confidence rulers
e.x: Pick a change you're considering. Two questions:
e.c: 5. Values and Motivation
p: Rulers are part of clinical MI protocols; the self-use version has not been directly tested (indirect evidence).

e.t: The decisional-balance caution
e.x: "Weigh the pros and cons" sounds neutral and wise. But there's a case where it doesn't help: when you've *already* decided you want to change and you're ambivalent about following through. In that case, an equal list of reasons-for and reasons-against strengthens the ambivalence — you end up with a balanced scale and no movement.
e.c: 5. Values and Motivation
p: Miller & Rollnick cite empirical MI literature (footnote 14) that decisional balance with ambivalent clients decreases commitment; WIKI has not independently re-verified (reported by the source book).

e.t: Notice the fixing reflex
e.x: When someone tells you about a problem, notice the urge that arrives first: the urge to *fix it*. Give advice, reassure, solve, say "Have you tried…?" Miller & Rollnick call this the fixing reflex — well-meant, and a common reason conversations go in circles.
e.c: 9. Social and Relational
p: The fixing reflex is a descriptive insight about a common interpersonal pattern, not an efficacy claim (conceptual parallel).

e.t: "What happened to you?" (trauma-informed reframe)
e.x: When you're trying to understand someone's struggle (or your own), notice which question you're asking. "What's wrong with you?" looks for a defect inside the person. "What happened to you?" looks for the history that shaped them.
e.c: 9. Social and Relational
p: A framing shift, not a treatment claim (conceptual parallel).

e.t: Setback, not relapse
e.x: When you slip back into an old behavior, notice the word your mind reaches for. "Relapse" implies there are only two outcomes — perfection or failure — and that once the rule is broken, there's nothing to lose. Miller argues the term itself frames slipping as more catastrophic than it needs to be.
e.c: 7. Behavioral Activation and Habit
p: Miller (2015) is a real published argument (reported by the source book); the abstinence violation effect literature (Baumeister, Heatherton & Tice 1994; DiClemente & Crisafulli 2022) is cited by the book; the lay self-use version is an adaptation (indirect evidence).

e.t: Give complex affirmations
e.x: A simple affirmation comments on something specific someone did: "You said that well." "You saw the warning signs and took action." A complex affirmation comments on an enduring strength: "What you did took real courage." "Once you make up your mind about something, you persist until you succeed." "You're someone people can rely on."
e.c: 9. Social and Relational
p: Miller & Rollnick teach the distinction and cite supporting literature (reported by the source book).

e.t: Offer two or three options, not one
e.x: When you're helping someone choose a course of action, don't offer one option at a time. Offering a single option invites the reflexive "why that won't work" — the push-back hand. Offering two or three at once lets the person compare and choose, which is a different mental move from defending against a push.
e.c: 5. Values and Motivation
p: Part of clinical MI protocols; the lay version has not been directly tested (indirect evidence).

e.t: Cultivate your Compassionate Self
e.x: Sit upright. Take one minute of slow, comfortable breathing — sensing "slowing down the body, slowing down the mind."
e.c: 6. Emotion and Compassion
p: **Cultivate your Compassionate Self** — practice card from CFT literature

e.t: Compassion for a struggling version of yourself
e.x: After settling into your Compassionate Self (see CFT001 — take a minute of slow breathing, then imagine having the qualities of kindness, wisdom, confidence, and courage), bring to mind a specific situation where a struggling version of you is present — a moment when you were anxious, ashamed, or afraid.
e.c: 6. Emotion and Compassion
p: **Compassion for a struggling version of yourself** — practice card from CFT literature

e.t: The Two Teachers: change the tone, keep the lesson
e.x: Think of two teachers who gave you the same correction — one with contempt, one with warmth. You learned the lesson from both; only one of them made you want to keep going.
e.c: 6. Emotion and Compassion
p: **The Two Teachers: change the tone, keep the lesson** — practice card from CFT literature

e.t: Compassionate Thinking: name the part, then look from the other side
e.x: Give your inner states names — "Anxious Me," "the Critic," "the Procrastinator." Not as labels to identify *with*, but as separate voices you can *talk about* rather than *talk from*.
e.c: 6. Emotion and Compassion
p: **Compassionate Thinking: name the part, then look from the other side** — practice card from CFT literature

e.t: Perfect Nurturer: imagine an ideal compassionate figure
e.x: Sit quietly with the breathing from CFT001 (slow, comfortable rhythm). Now imagine a being — human or not — who fully understands you, accepts you as you are, and wishes the very best for you. Someone (or something) who would never judge or ridicule you.
e.c: 6. Emotion and Compassion
p: **Perfect Nurturer: imagine an ideal compassionate figure** — practice card from CFT literature

e.t: Safe Place with an affiliative welcome
e.x: Sit comfortably, eyes closed. Take a minute of slow, comfortable breathing (from CFT001). Now bring to mind a place that feels safe, calm, peaceful, and where you belong — a beach, a forest, a room, anywhere.
e.c: 6. Emotion and Compassion
p: **Safe Place with an affiliative welcome** — practice card from CFT literature

e.t: Two-Chair dialogue: compassionate self ↔ vulnerable self (solo-adapted)
e.x: Set up two chairs facing each other. One is the "vulnerable chair" — the anxious, angry, sad, or ashamed part of you. The other is the "compassionate chair" — your Compassionate Self (see CFT001).
e.c: 6. Emotion and Compassion
p: **Two-Chair dialogue: compassionate self ↔ vulnerable self (solo-adapted)** — practice card from CFT literature

e.t: Compassionate letter to yourself
e.x:
Write a letter to yourself about a difficulty you are carrying — written from the perspective of someone who understands your circumstances and wants to help: someone with kindness, patience, and courage to spare. Acknowledge what hurts. Include why your response makes sense given what you have lived through. Include, plainly, what would help.

Take days if you need them; the letter improves with a few sittings. Write about the difficulty without dramatising or minimising it.

Then keep the letter and reread it in the moments you would normally turn on yourself. Some people write several — one for the voice that says you are lazy, one for the voice that says you are alone — and keep them where the hardest moments find them.

Adapted from Kolts, *CFT Made Simple* (2016), compassionate letter-writing instructions (after Gilbert, 2009, 2010).
e.c: 6. Emotion and Compassion
p: **Compassionate letter to yourself** — practice card from CFT literature

e.t: Cognitive acceptance: watch thoughts float by
e.x: Step 1: Identify one negative or recurring thought you struggle with.
e.c: 2. Acceptance and Willingness
p: **Cognitive acceptance: watch thoughts float by** — practice card from CBT/Acceptance literature

e.t: Try not to think of elephants
e.x: For the next thirty seconds, do not think about elephants. Not even a little. Set a timer.
e.c: 2. Acceptance and Willingness
p: **Try not to think of elephants** — practice card from CBT/Acceptance literature

e.t: Carry the thought on paper
e.x: Write a negative recurring thought on a piece of paper ("I'm going to fail miserably"). Fold it up and put it in your pocket. Carry it around for the rest of the day.
e.c: 2. Acceptance and Willingness
p: **Carry the thought on paper** — practice card from CBT/Acceptance literature

e.t: Passengers on the bus (metaphor practice)
e.x: Imagine you're driving a bus. Your negative thoughts are passengers — nasty, scary-looking ones barking orders and being obnoxious. You could stop the bus and argue with them, but that defeats the whole purpose of the trip. You could follow them around making sure they don't misbehave, but then you're not driving.
e.c: 2. Acceptance and Willingness
p: **Passengers on the bus (metaphor practice)** — practice card from CBT/Acceptance literature

e.t: Look through the lens of time
e.x: Pick something currently bothering you. Write a one-sentence description of it. Then run it through temporal lenses:
e.c: 2. Acceptance and Willingness
p: **Look through the lens of time** — practice card from CBT/Acceptance literature

e.t: Coping cards
e.x:
When you have worked out a balanced response to a recurring distorted thought — in a journal, in a calm hour, with your full attention — write that response on a card small enough to carry. One thought, one card, in your own words.

Carry it in your wallet. Put copies where the trouble happens: the car, the fridge, the desk drawer. Read it when the original thought shows up hot. Stress can make a balanced response harder to recall exactly when you need it; the card keeps it available.

A card can hold a response ("one unproductive day does not make me a failure") or an action plan ("when I feel like hiding: 1. walk the block, 2. call someone, 3. ten minutes of cleaning") — or both sides, response on one side, plan on the other.

Adapted from Tolin, *Doing CBT* (1st ed., 2016), cognitive restructuring chapters, printed pp. 351–353; and Riggenbach, *The CBT Toolbox* (2nd ed., 2021), tools 5.24–5.25.
e.c: 3. Cognitive Flexibility and View-Lightness
p: **Coping cards** — practice card from CBT literature

e.t: The downward arrow
e.x:
Take a thought that hurts — say, "if I get sick in public, it will be a disaster." Instead of arguing with it, follow it down. Ask: suppose that did happen — what would be bad about that? Answer. Then ask about the answer: and if that were true, what would that mean? Keep going, assuming each answer is true for the sake of discussion, until the answers stop producing anything underneath.

The descent has two uses. Asked toward consequences ("what would happen then?"), it tests the catastrophe: the feared event, examined step by step, usually turns out to be survivable and shorter-lived than it feels. Asked toward meaning ("what would that mean about me?"), it reaches the load-bearing belief the surface thought stands on — "I'm undesirable," "I'm helpless" — which can then be examined like any other belief: evidence for, evidence against, alternatives.

Treat what you reach as a hypothesis about what the thought means to you, not as a hidden truth.

Adapted from Tolin, *Doing CBT* (1st ed., 2016): the decatastrophizing use at printed pp. 337–338, the core-belief use at printed pp. 373–374 (after Greenberger & Padesky, 2016, and Burns, 1980, as cited there).
e.c: 3. Cognitive Flexibility and View-Lightness
p: **The downward arrow** — practice card from CBT literature

e.t: The Raisin meditation
e.x: Take a few raisins (or nuts). Set aside five to ten minutes. Hold one in your palm and look at it as if you have never seen anything like it. Feel its weight. See the folds and ridges. Turn it over between your fingers and notice the texture. Hold it under your nose and notice any scent. Place it in your mouth without chewing — notice how your hand and tongue know exactly what to do. Explore it with your tongue for thirty seconds. Then take one conscious bite and notice the taste released. Chew slowly, and before swallowing, see if you can catch the first intention to swallow as it arises. Follow the sensation of swallowing. Then notice the aftertaste, and the automatic tendency to reach for another.
e.c: 1. Attention and Awareness
p: **The Raisin meditation** — practice card from MBCT literature

e.t: Bring raisin mind to one routine activity
e.x: Choose one activity you do daily without thinking — brushing your teeth, showering, drinking your morning tea, taking out the rubbish, walking between rooms. For one week, do that activity each day with full attention. You do not have to slow it down, and you do not have to enjoy it. Just be fully awake to it as you do it.
e.c: 1. Attention and Awareness
p: **Bring raisin mind to one routine activity** — practice card from MBCT literature

e.t: The Three-minute Breathing Space
e.x: A three-step mini-meditation you can run in three minutes, one minute, or ten seconds. **Step 1 — become aware:** adopt an erect, dignified posture. Ask: what thoughts are going through the mind? What feelings are here? What body sensations? Acknowledge them without trying to change them. **Step 2 — gather:** narrow attention onto the breath. Ride the in-breath, ride the out-breath. **Step 3 — expand:** widen awareness to the body as a whole — the posture, the face, the shoulders, the whole body breathing. Use it twice a day at set times, and whenever you feel under pressure.
e.c: 1. Attention and Awareness
p: **The Three-minute Breathing Space** — practice card from MBCT literature

e.t: The Habit Releaser
e.x: Once this week, deliberately break a small habit. Change chairs — notice which chair you always sit in at home, at work, in a café, and choose a different one. Take a different route to work. Sit in a different part of the room. Notice how much of your life runs on autopilot, and how much perception sharpens when the pattern is broken.
e.c: 7. Behavioral Activation and Habit
p: **The Habit Releaser** — practice card from MBCT literature

e.t: Sounds and Thoughts meditation
e.x: Sit comfortably. First, rest on the breath for a few minutes. Then open to sounds — near, far, in front, behind. Do not search for sounds; just receive them as they arise. Notice the tendency to label each sound and, below the label, return to the raw sensation of the sound itself. After four or five minutes, shift the same stance to thoughts: see thoughts as events in the mind, arising, lingering, and passing away — like clouds moving across a spacious sky. Do not try to make them come or go.
e.c: 1. Attention and Awareness
p: **Sounds and Thoughts meditation** — practice card from MBCT literature

e.t: Exploring Difficulty meditation
e.x: Sit and settle with the breath for a few minutes. Then, if a difficulty is present (or you gently bring one to mind — something mild and unresolved), allow the thought or feeling to rest on the workbench of the mind. Do not try to fix, analyze, or solve it. Instead, drop your attention into the body and find the physical sensations that come with the difficulty. Then deliberately move your focus to the part of the body where the sensations are strongest. Breathe into that region on the in-breath, and breathe out from it on the out-breath. Explore the sensations with friendly curiosity.
e.c: 2. Acceptance and Willingness
p: **Exploring Difficulty meditation** — practice card from MBCT literature

e.t: The Befriending meditation
e.x: Sit with dignity and wakefulness. Settle on the breath. Then, in stages, offer these phrases: **May I be free from suffering. May I be as happy and healthy as it is possible for me to be. May I have ease of being.** Drop each phrase like a pebble into a deep well — then listen for any reaction in thoughts, feelings, or body. If self-kindness is hard, bring to mind a person (or pet) who loved you unconditionally; once you feel their love, return to offering it to yourself. Then move to a loved one, then a neutral stranger, then — optionally — a difficult person. Each stage: repeat the phrases, pause, listen.
e.c: 6. Emotion and Compassion
p: **The Befriending meditation** — practice card from MBCT literature

e.t: Approach, don't avoid (the mouse in the maze)
e.x: When you notice yourself bracing against a task, a conversation, or a feeling, ask which direction you are facing. Are you moving *toward* something (helping the mouse find the cheese) or *away* from something (fleeing the owl)? In a real experiment, students who solved a maze by avoiding an owl did 50% worse on a later creativity test than students who solved the same maze by helping a mouse find cheese. The same act, different spirit, different aftermath: avoidance closes the mind; approach opens it.
e.c: 5. Values and Motivation
p: **Approach, don't avoid (the mouse in the maze)** — practice card from MBCT literature

e.t: Mindfulness bells
e.x: Pick two or three ordinary activities from your day and turn them into bells — pre-set reminders to stop and attend. Preparing food: notice the feel of the knife, the smell released as vegetables are chopped. Getting into the car: take three conscious breaths before turning the key. Waiting for the kettle: notice the sound of the water, the steam, your feet on the floor. The activity does not change; what changes is that it now also *calls you back*.
e.c: 1. Attention and Awareness
p: **Mindfulness bells** — practice card from MBCT literature

e.t: The kindness pool (unblock the spring)
e.x: Picture kindness as a clear pool fed by a small spring. You can ration the pool — give each person you meet a thimbleful as they pass — and watch it shrink. Or you can unblock the spring that feeds it, so the pool is continuously replenished. The practice (Befriending meditation, MB007) is the unblocking. When you notice yourself rationing kindness — holding back warmth because you are tired or drained — ask: is the pool actually low, or is the spring blocked?
e.c: 6. Emotion and Compassion
p: **The kindness pool (unblock the spring)** — practice card from MBCT literature

e.t: Word repetition
e.x:
Start with a neutral word such as "milk." Say it once, slowly, and notice what shows up with it: images, sensations, maybe a taste. Then say the word out loud, over and over, as fast as you can, for thirty seconds.

Notice what happens by the end. Most people find the images have thinned out, and what remains is the sound of the word and the movements of speaking it — a word being produced, rather than a scene being delivered.

If it was tolerable with the neutral word, try it with a word that usually hooks you — "failure," "weak," "danger." The aim is not to prove the word false or to force its charge away, only to experience it for a moment as a word.

Adapted from Stoddard & Afari, *The Big Book of ACT Metaphors* (2014), printed pp. 71–72; see also Blackledge, *Cognitive Defusion in Practice* (2017), ch. 7, which discusses the word-repetition study of Masuda, Hayes, Sackett & Twohig (2004).
e.c: 3. Cognitive Flexibility and View-Lightness
p: **Word repetition** — practice card from ACT literature

e.t: Sing the thought, or say it in a silly voice
e.x:
Choose a familiar, manageable self-critical thought — one you have already examined at least once, not a fresh wound. Say it once normally. Then sing it to a well-known tune, or say it in an exaggerated character voice: a cartoon mouse, a film superhero.

Notice whether the change in delivery changes how the sentence lands. The words are the same; the delivery is not. Some people find the thought loosens its grip when it arrives in absurd packaging; others notice mainly that they were able to step outside it long enough to play with it.

The thought does not need to become funny, harmless, or false — and if the exercise starts to feel like mocking your own real difficulty, drop it and use another defusion approach. The option exists; it is not obligatory.

Adapted from Blackledge, *Cognitive Defusion in Practice* (2017), ch. 7 (Changing Language Parameters), which includes the source's caution that these techniques land better on familiar material and can invalidating if used too early or too glibly.
e.c: 3. Cognitive Flexibility and View-Lightness
p: **Sing the thought, or say it in a silly voice** — practice card from ACT literature

e.t: Listen to the storyteller for thirty seconds
e.x:
Close your eyes and, for thirty seconds, do nothing except listen to what your mind is saying. Do not argue with it, do not follow it anywhere. Just listen, the way you would listen to a radio playing in another room.

Notice what the stream contains: predictions, judgments, memories, instructions, warnings. Then ask one question: is following the current story useful for what you need to do next? Some of what the mind produces is fact; much of it is commentary on fact. The thirty seconds is spent learning to tell the difference from the outside.

This is not a silence exercise — the mind will keep talking. The practice is the listening.

Adapted from Harris (2009, p. 119), retold in Stoddard & Afari, *The Big Book of ACT Metaphors* (2014), printed pp. 80–81.
e.c: 3. Cognitive Flexibility and View-Lightness
p: **Listen to the storyteller for thirty seconds** — practice card from ACT literature

e.t: Core and satellite values
e.x:
Take the values you have already sorted by importance. Put the three most important in a pile at the center; scatter the remaining seven around them, roughly the way electrons circle a nucleus. Read each of the three core cards a few times.

Now step back three feet from the arrangement and look at it. Say what you see: these values matter to me; they are part of who I am; they do not exhaust who I am. Step back another three feet and look again.

The step backward is the exercise. A value laid out on the floor can be seen whole — something you carry, rather than something you must obey. Notice whether any of them has quietly become a rule that leaves no room for context.

Adapted (simplified) from Blonna, *Maximize Your Coaching Effectiveness with ACT* (2015), pp. 72–74, where the ranking is done over ten life-domain envelopes or slots before the values within them are ranked; this version assumes a values list you already have.
e.c: 5. Values and Motivation
p: **Core and satellite values** — practice card from ACT literature

e.t: The values whiteboard
e.x:
When thinking about a values conflict keeps going in circles — honesty against kindness, ambition against family — write the conflict on a whiteboard or a large sheet of paper. Write what your mind says about it: the arguments, the scripts, the key words. Write the images you see when you close your eyes, and the emotions and body sensations that come with them. Fill the board.

Now put six feet between you and the board. Look at it from there and say: my mind has a lot to say about this — how interesting. From that distance, ask which parts of what you wrote are useful for choosing your next action, and write your answer on a different part of the board.

The exercise is not a verdict on the conflict. It is a way of seeing everything the conflict consists of at once, from a position where you are not inside it.

Adapted from Blonna, *Stress Less, Live More* (2010), as presented in Blonna, *Maximize Your Coaching Effectiveness with ACT* (2015), pp. 80–81.
e.c: 5. Values and Motivation
p: **The values whiteboard** — practice card from ACT literature

e.t: The matrix sort
e.x:
Draw a large plus sign on a sheet of paper. The horizontal line divides what you do in the world of the five senses (above the line) from what happens inside you — thoughts, feelings, memories (below the line). The vertical line divides moves away from discomfort (left) from moves toward what matters to you (right).

Take today and sort it. Bottom right: the name of someone or something important to you. Bottom left: one uncomfortable thought or feeling that shows up and stands in the way of acting for that person or thing. Upper left: one thing you can be seen doing when that discomfort is running the show. Upper right: one thing you can be seen doing that moves you toward what matters.

That is the whole practice, and it is repeatable daily. The sorting itself is the training: every action gets half-classified as you take it — toward or away, and done in contact with the world or in the grip of inner weather. Over time, notice which people, places, and sensations reliably hook you into the away side. Then choose one workable toward move and check what happens.

Adapted from Polk, Schoendorff, Webster & Olaz, *The Essential Guide to the ACT Matrix* (2016), chs. 1 and 3.
e.c: 11. Inquiry, Experimentation, and Process
p: **The matrix sort** — practice card from ACT literature
